name: 5-Amino-1MQ
evidenceNote: Every published result comes from mice or cultured cells. No human trial of 5-Amino-1MQ has been registered or reported, so nothing is known about its effects, safety, or dosing in people.
summary: 5-Amino-1MQ is a lab-made NNMT inhibitor that reduced fat in obese mice. It has never been tested in people and is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: 5-Amino-1MQ is a small synthetic molecule, not a peptide, that blocks an enzyme called NNMT involved in fat-cell energy use. In obese mice it cut body weight by about 5% in 11 days and shrank fat tissue without lowering food intake. Those animal studies are the whole evidence base: no human trial exists. It is not FDA-approved, it is not on either federal compounding list, and in January 2026 the FDA issued a warning letter to a compounder over products made with it. Versions sold online are untested research chemicals.

blocks.text: 5-Amino-1MQ, short for 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium, is a small synthetic molecule built on a quinoline ring. Despite being sold alongside peptides, it is not a peptide at all: it contains no amino acids. It was designed at the University of Texas Medical Branch as one of a series of compounds meant to block nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT), an enzyme found in fat tissue, liver, and muscle [1].

The research group picked NNMT because higher levels of the enzyme had been linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes. Their aim was to test whether shutting the enzyme down could reverse weight gain in animals, which would mark NNMT as a target worth developing drugs against [1]. The compound has since been used as a laboratory tool in muscle and cancer studies, all in animals or cells [2][5].

NNMT attaches a methyl group (a small carbon tag) to nicotinamide, a form of vitamin B3. In doing so it uses up two molecules cells rely on: nicotinamide, which is recycled into NAD+, a coenzyme central to energy metabolism, and SAM, the main methyl donor in the body. Blocking NNMT is therefore expected to leave more of both available inside the cell [1].

In cultured fat cells, the methylquinolinium compounds did exactly that. They lowered the enzyme's product (1-methylnicotinamide), raised NAD+ and SAM, and reduced the cells' production of new fat. The compounds crossed cell membranes well and did not inhibit related methyltransferase enzymes or the enzymes of the NAD+ recycling pathway, which suggested they were selective for NNMT [1].

The working theory is that more NAD+ and SAM shifts fat cells toward burning energy rather than storing it. That chain of events has been shown in cells and inferred in mice. It has not been measured in a human body.

No. 5-Amino-1MQ has never been submitted to the FDA as a drug and has no approved use. Because it is not part of any approved medicine, a pharmacy cannot simply compound it on request: compounders may only use bulk ingredients that appear on the FDA's lists or meet narrow exceptions.

The FDA made its position explicit in a January 20, 2026 warning letter to GenoGenix, a Florida outsourcing facility. The agency stated that 5-Amino-1MQ is not on the 503B bulks list, is not used to make any drug on the shortage list, and does not qualify for the interim policy that lets some substances under review be used. Products the firm made with it were therefore not eligible for the 503B exemptions [4].

The founding study treated male mice made obese on a high-fat diet. Nine mice received 5-Amino-1MQ by subcutaneous (under the skin) injection three times a day for 11 days, and nine received saline. The treated mice lost about 5% of their starting weight while the controls gained about 1%. Their main abdominal fat pad was roughly 35% smaller, fat cells were more than 30% smaller, and total cholesterol was about 30% lower. Food intake did not differ meaningfully between groups, and the authors saw no obvious adverse effects over the short study [1].

A 2019 study from the same group tested the compound in 24-month-old mice after a chemical injury to a leg muscle. Treated animals showed more active muscle stem cells, regenerating fibers nearly twice the cross-sectional area of controls, and roughly 70% more peak force in the injured muscle [2].

A 2022 follow-up combined the inhibitor with a switch to a low-fat diet in obese mice. That pairing brought weight and fat down to the level of lean mice faster than the diet change alone, and it produced a distinct gut bacteria profile. One author founded, and another works for, Ridgeline Therapeutics, a company developing NNMT inhibitors [3].

Aged mice with a muscle injury
Larger regenerating fibers and about 70% more force [2]
Obese mice switched to a low-fat diet
Faster return to lean weight; changed gut bacteria [3]
Slower tumor growth with an immunotherapy drug [5]

blocks.text: Researchers studying bladder cancer have also used the compound to block NNMT in tumor-supporting cells in mice, where it slowed tumor growth [5]. That work treats it as a research probe, not a candidate weight-loss drug.

What is missing matters more than what exists. There are no studies in people, no data on how the molecule is absorbed when swallowed (the mouse work used injections), and no long-term safety data in any species. NNMT also has roles outside fat tissue, and what happens when it is blocked for months is unknown.

5-Amino-1MQ is widely sold as capsules or powder labeled for research use. These products are not reviewed by any regulator, so their purity, strength, and contents are unverified. Oral capsules are a particular gap: every published animal result comes from injected doses, and there is no published study showing how much of a swallowed capsule reaches the bloodstream [1].

Claims that it builds muscle, burns fat, or slows aging in people extend mouse findings to humans without data. The FDA has treated compounded versions as ineligible for the usual compounding exemptions, which means a clinic offering it is outside the system that normally checks drug quality [4].

name: Abaloparatide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2017 for postmenopausal osteoporosis on the strength of an 18-month trial of more than 2,400 women, and in 2022 for men with osteoporosis after a 228-man bone density trial.
summary: Abaloparatide (Tymlos) is a daily injectable peptide that builds new bone. FDA-approved for osteoporosis in women after menopause and in men.
keyTakeaway: Abaloparatide is a lab-made 34-amino-acid peptide modeled on parathyroid hormone-related protein. Injected once daily under the skin, it stimulates bone-forming cells rather than only slowing bone loss. In the ACTIVE trial, new spine fractures fell from 4.2% on placebo to 0.6% over 18 months, an 86% relative reduction. The FDA approved it as Tymlos in 2017 for postmenopausal osteoporosis and added men in 2022. Total lifetime use beyond 2 years is not advised on the label, and dizziness, nausea, and a racing heart are common early on.

blocks.text: Abaloparatide is a synthetic peptide of 34 amino acids sold in the United States as Tymlos. It is an analog of the first 34 amino acids of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), a signaling molecule the body uses in bone, cartilage, and other tissues. Its sequence matches PTHrP at 76% of positions and parathyroid hormone itself at 41% [1].

Most osteoporosis drugs are antiresorptives: they slow the cells that break bone down. Abaloparatide belongs to the smaller anabolic group, which drives the cells that lay new bone down. Its closest relative is teriparatide, a fragment of parathyroid hormone that works on the same receptor [3].

Bone is constantly rebuilt: osteoclasts dissolve old bone and osteoblasts fill the space with new tissue. Abaloparatide binds the parathyroid hormone type 1 receptor (PTH1R) and activates cyclic AMP signaling inside target cells. Given once a day, that brief signal stimulates osteoblasts and builds bone on both the spongy inner surfaces and the dense outer shell [1].

Timing matters here: the label ties the bone-building effect to once-daily dosing, a brief pulse rather than steady exposure [1]. Abaloparatide is thought to sharpen that pulse further: it favors a receptor shape that produces more transient signaling than parathyroid hormone does, which researchers link to a stronger net building effect [5].

In animal studies, the gains in bone mineral density translated into measurably stronger vertebrae and long bones [1]. In people, the test that matters is fewer fractures, which is what the pivotal trial measured.
Yes. The FDA approved Tymlos as a new molecular entity in April 2017 and approved a new indication in December 2022 [2]. The current label covers two groups [1]:

items: Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high risk of fracture, meaning a past osteoporotic fracture or several risk factors, or who did not respond to or could not tolerate other treatments. In this group it lowers the risk of spine and other fractures [1].
Men with osteoporosis at high risk of fracture, to increase bone density, under the same risk definition [1].

items.text: FDA approves Tymlos for postmenopausal osteoporosis [2].
Two labeling supplements with new clinical data are approved [2].
FDA approves a new indication; the label now includes men with osteoporosis [1][2].

blocks.text: The approval rests mainly on ACTIVE, an 18-month phase 3 trial at 28 sites in 10 countries. It enrolled 2,463 postmenopausal women with low bone density and either prior fractures or very low scores. They were randomized to daily blinded injections of abaloparatide 80 mcg or placebo, or to open-label teriparatide 20 mcg [3].

rows: Non-spine fractures after 6 months of alendronate (25 months)

blocks.text: That works out to an 86% relative drop in new spine fractures and a 43% drop in other fractures. The fracture benefit held after patients switched to alendronate, an antiresorptive, for six months [1].

For men, the ATOM trial randomized 228 men aged 40 to 85 to abaloparatide or placebo for 12 months. Spine bone density rose 8.5% on the drug against 1.2% on placebo, with smaller gains at the hip [4]. That trial measured density, not fractures, which is why the male indication is worded as increasing bone density [1].
In the women's trial, side effects more common than with placebo included [1]:

In men, the most frequent reactions were redness, swelling, or pain at the injection site, along with dizziness and joint pain [1]. About 10% of women on abaloparatide stopped because of side effects, against 6% on placebo [1].

The label lists several warnings. Blood pressure can drop on standing in the hours after a dose, so the first doses are given where the person can sit or lie down. It can raise blood calcium and urine calcium. Allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with this class of drug [1].

Rats given high doses developed osteosarcoma, a bone cancer, in a dose-dependent way. Whether this happens in humans is unknown; observational studies of the drug class have not shown an increased risk. The label advises avoiding it in people already at higher risk of osteosarcoma, such as those with Paget's disease or prior skeletal radiation, and states that safety beyond 2 years has not been studied [1].

sections.heading: How does abaloparatide compare to teriparatide?

blocks.text: The two drugs are cousins: both are daily injections that act on PTH1R, and both build bone. ACTIVE included a teriparatide arm, so some direct comparison exists, although that arm was open-label and the trial was not designed to prove one better than the other [3].

rows: Binds the longer-signaling shape more strongly [5]

blocks.text: A follow-up analysis of ACTIVE estimated that fewer women needed abaloparatide than teriparatide to prevent one non-spine or major osteoporotic fracture, while the numbers for spine fractures were similar. The analysis was written by authors including company employees, and the trial was not powered for a head-to-head verdict [5].

name: Acetyl hexapeptide-8
evidenceNote: There is at least one randomized, placebo-controlled human trial showing smoother skin around the eyes after 4 weeks, but trials are small and short, and whether the peptide reaches facial muscles through skin is unresolved.
summary: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 (Argireline) is a cosmetic peptide marketed as topical Botox. Small trials show modest wrinkle smoothing; skin penetration is doubtful.
keyTakeaway: Acetyl hexapeptide-8, sold as Argireline, is a six amino acid peptide copied from the end of SNAP-25, a protein nerves use to release signals to muscles. In lab tests it partly blocks that release, the same machinery botulinum toxin targets, which is why it is marketed as a topical alternative to Botox. A randomized trial in 60 adults found less eye-area roughness after 4 weeks. But the peptide is water-loving and fairly large, so it crosses skin poorly. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an FDA-approved drug, and a safety panel cleared it only at concentrations up to 0.005%.

blocks.text: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 is a short synthetic peptide with the sequence Ac-Glu-Glu-Met-Gln-Arg-Arg-NH2, six amino acids capped at both ends [1]. It was first described in 2002 under the trade name Argireline by researchers in Alicante, Spain, who designed it to imitate the wrinkle-relaxing action of botulinum toxin without its toxicity [1].

It is now one of the most widely used peptides in anti-aging skin care, found in face creams, eye creams and serums. It is often described as a botox-like peptide, a phrase that sets expectations well above what the evidence shows [3].

Muscles contract when nerve endings release acetylcholine. That release depends on the SNARE complex, a set of proteins that lets tiny vesicles fuse with the nerve's membrane and empty their contents. SNAP-25 is one of those proteins, and botulinum toxins relax muscles by disabling this same machinery [1].

Acetyl hexapeptide-8 copies a short stretch of SNAP-25's N-terminal end. The idea is that it competes with the real protein and interferes with how the SNARE complex assembles, so less acetylcholine gets released and the muscle contracts less forcefully [1][2]. In lab tests the peptide did reduce neurotransmitter release, with a potency comparable to botulinum toxin A, but its maximum effect was far smaller [1]. In plain terms, it can nudge the process but cannot shut it down.

The bigger question is delivery. To relax a muscle, a peptide applied to the face would have to pass through the outer skin layer and reach the nerve endings beneath. A 2025 review concluded that acetyl hexapeptide-8 is hydrophilic and relatively large, so it penetrates the lipid-rich outer layer poorly, and that whether it ever reaches the neuromuscular junction remains uncertain [3]. Some of the smoothing seen in studies may come from hydration or other skin effects rather than muscle relaxation.

No. Acetyl hexapeptide-8 is a cosmetic ingredient. Under US law, cosmetic products and their ingredients do not need FDA approval before sale, color additives being the exception, and the companies that make and sell them are responsible for their safety [4].

What a product claims also matters. The FDA classifies products by intended use: something meant to beautify is a cosmetic, while something meant to affect the structure or function of the body is a drug [5]. A cream marketed to relax muscles the way an injection does would be making a claim about body function, which moves it toward drug territory.

The ingredient's safety has been reviewed by the Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety. It concluded that acetyl hexapeptide-8 is safe as currently used at concentrations up to 0.005%, and that there was not enough data to call it safe above that [6].

blocks.text: The 2013 trial is the strongest single piece of evidence. It was randomized and placebo-controlled, and it used both expert grading and silicone casts of the skin measured by machine. Its weaknesses are size, a 4-week length and allocation of three treated people for every one on placebo, leaving only about 15 in the control group [2].

The 2002 study, run by the inventors, showed the headline 30% figure but did not describe a placebo comparison in its summary [1]. The 2026 serum studies could not separate the effect of acetyl hexapeptide-8 from niacinamide, gluconolactone, kelp extract and a second peptide in the same product, and they were run by researchers at the company behind the serum [7]. The 2025 review summed up the field: results in trials are encouraging, but the mechanism on intact skin is not established and better delivery systems are needed [3].

sections.heading: Is it a substitute for Botox?

blocks.text: Not in any measured sense. Botulinum toxin is injected into the muscle, acts directly at the nerve ending, and its wrinkle effect is long lasting [1]. Acetyl hexapeptide-8 is applied to the skin surface, is poorly absorbed, and at most slows part of the release process with far less maximal effect in lab tests [1][3]. No published trial has compared the two head to head. The realistic expectation from the human data is a modest softening of fine expression lines while the product is in use.

name: Acetyl octapeptide-3
evidenceNote: No published human study has tested acetyl octapeptide-3 on its own. Its mechanism is borrowed from work on its shorter parent, argireline, and the one clinical study that included it tested a multi-ingredient microneedle patch.
summary: Acetyl octapeptide-3 (SNAP-8) is a longer version of the anti-wrinkle peptide argireline, sold in creams and serums. It has no human trial of its own.
keyTakeaway: Better known by its trade name SNAP-8, acetyl octapeptide-3 is an eight-amino-acid cosmetic peptide made by adding two amino acids to argireline. Like argireline, it is designed to mimic part of SNAP-25, a protein nerve endings need to release their signal, in the hope of relaxing the small muscle contractions behind expression lines. That idea comes from argireline research; no published trial has tested SNAP-8 alone in people. As a cosmetic ingredient it needs no FDA approval, and it does not work the way Botox injections do.

blocks.text: Acetyl octapeptide-3 is a synthetic chain of eight amino acids: glutamic acid, glutamic acid, methionine, glutamine, arginine, arginine, alanine and aspartic acid, capped with an acetyl group at one end and an amide at the other [1]. It is sold under the trade name SNAP-8 and appears on some labels as acetyl glutamyl heptapeptide-3 [1].

Its first six amino acids are the same sequence as argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-3, also called acetyl hexapeptide-8), the best-known peptide in the so-called topical Botox category [1][2]. SNAP-8 extends that sequence by two amino acids, alanine and aspartic acid. It is used almost entirely in creams, serums and patches aimed at forehead and eye lines.

For a muscle to contract, the nerve ending above it has to release a chemical messenger. That release depends on the SNARE complex, a set of proteins including SNAP-25 that docks the messenger's packet against the nerve membrane. Botulinum toxin, the active ingredient in Botox, disables this same machinery [2].

Argireline's sequence was patterned on the N-terminal end of SNAP-25, so that it could crowd the real protein out and keep the SNARE complex from assembling [3]. In lab tests it reduced messenger release with a potency similar to botulinum toxin type A but with much lower overall effect [2]. Acetyl octapeptide-3 is built on the same design idea with a longer copy of SNAP-25. No independent peer-reviewed study has measured how strongly SNAP-8 itself blocks the SNARE complex, so its mechanism is inferred from argireline.

The practical question is whether enough of an eight-amino-acid peptide gets through skin to reach nerve endings in the muscle below. That has not been shown, which is one reason newer products pair it with microneedles that physically breach the outer skin layer [4].

No. FDA does not approve cosmetics or cosmetic ingredients before sale, apart from color additives, and the companies that make and market them carry legal responsibility for their safety [5]. Acetyl octapeptide-3 reaches the market on that basis.

The wording on the label decides the legal category. FDA classes a product by its intended use: one meant to improve appearance is a cosmetic, while one meant to affect the structure or function of the body is a drug [6]. A cream that claims to make lines look smoother stays a cosmetic. A claim that it relaxes muscles or works like an injection describes a drug effect that no SNAP-8 product has been approved for.

Most evidence in this family concerns argireline. In the original 2002 report, a cream with 10% argireline reduced wrinkle depth by up to 30% after 30 days in a small group of healthy women [2]. A 2013 randomized trial in 60 Chinese adults applied argireline or placebo around the eyes twice daily for four weeks and found improvement in 48.9% of the argireline group against none on placebo [3].

For acetyl octapeptide-3 itself, the published human evidence is a 2024 study of a dissolving microneedle patch. The patch combined hyaluronic acid, acetyl octapeptide-3, a vitamin C derivative and a lipid signalling molecule, and 24 healthy adults wore it under one eye overnight with a hyaluronic acid only patch under the other, for 28 days [4]. The full patch improved eye wrinkles, skin water loss, elasticity and lift compared with the plain patch, with no adverse effects reported [4].

Up to 30% less wrinkle depth at 30 days [2]
Microneedle patch with acetyl octapeptide-3 and two other actives, 24 adults

blocks.text: Because the 2024 patch contained several active ingredients, the study cannot say how much, if anything, the octapeptide contributed. No published trial has compared SNAP-8 with argireline head to head, or SNAP-8 with placebo on its own.

sections.heading: How does acetyl octapeptide-3 compare to acetyl hexapeptide-8?

blocks.text: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 (argireline) is the six-amino-acid original; acetyl octapeptide-3 is the same chain plus two more [1]. Argireline has its own mechanism studies and several small controlled trials, including the 60-person randomized trial and a 2017 trial in 24 volunteers that combined it with another peptide [2][3][7]. SNAP-8 has neither its own mechanism paper nor its own trial.

Claims that SNAP-8 is stronger than argireline come from the ingredient's marketing, not from published comparisons. In lab measures of nerve signal blocking, argireline is far weaker than injected botulinum toxin, and nothing suggests the longer version closes that gap [2].

name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5
evidenceNote: Its proposed action rests on a single cell-culture enzyme test, and the only human data are small, uncontrolled studies of eye creams that also contain other active ingredients.
summary: A short peptide added to eye creams marketed for puffiness. Lab data are thin, human studies are small and uncontrolled, and the FDA does not approve cosmetics.
keyTakeaway: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a short, four-amino-acid peptide sold to cosmetic makers under the trade name Eyeseryl and added to eye creams aimed at puffiness and dark circles. Its proposed action is blocking angiotensin-converting enzyme in the skin, which has been shown only in a cell-culture test. The human evidence is a 20-person, uncontrolled study of an eye cream that combined it with other actives, so its own contribution cannot be separated. The FDA does not approve cosmetics or their ingredients, so there is no FDA status to check.

blocks.text: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a synthetic chain of four amino acids with an acetyl group capping one end. It is a cosmetic ingredient, supplied to manufacturers under the trade name Eyeseryl, and it appears mainly in products for the delicate skin around the eyes [1][2].

Commercial eye creams that list it usually pair it with other cosmetic peptides, such as acetyl hexapeptide-8 (Argireline) and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, and market the blend for firmer eye contours, fewer fine lines, and less visible puffiness and dark circles [2]. It is not a medicine and is not taken by injection or by mouth.

Cosmetic peptides are usually grouped into signal peptides, carrier peptides, neurotransmitter-inhibiting peptides and enzyme-inhibiting peptides [3]. Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is described as an inhibitor of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), the same enzyme targeted by a class of blood pressure drugs. The theory is that blocking ACE in the skin reduces the leakiness of tiny blood vessels, which lets fluid drain from under the eyes and lessens swelling [1].

The direct evidence for that action is limited. A 2021 laboratory study tested five cosmetic peptides on human skin cells and measured ACE activity, finding an optimal concentration of acetyl tetrapeptide-5 for that effect in culture [4]. A result in cells grown in a dish does not show that a cream applied to the skin delivers enough of the peptide to the right place to change fluid balance.

Penetration is the central question for any topical peptide. A 2026 safety review by industry scientists summarized expert panel findings on several short cosmetic peptides, concluding that little if any crosses the skin into the body [3]. Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 was not among the peptides in that panel's reviews, so the same conclusion has not been formally reached for it [3].

No. Cosmetic ingredients are outside the FDA approval system: under US law, cosmetic products and their ingredients do not go through FDA approval before they are sold; color additives are the only exception. The FDA can still act against a cosmetic once it is on the market if it is unsafe or mislabeled [5].

What a company says about a product matters. The FDA decides whether something is a cosmetic or a drug by its intended use, judged largely from its claims. A product that promises to affect the structure or function of the body, or to treat a condition, is regulated as a drug [6]. That is why eye creams with this peptide speak of reducing the look of puffiness rather than treating fluid retention.

There are no published randomized, placebo-controlled trials of acetyl tetrapeptide-5 on its own. The human data come from studies of finished products. In one open-label study, 20 women aged 45 to 60 used an eye contour cream twice a day; the cream contained acetyl tetrapeptide-5 together with acetyl hexapeptide-3, a collagen-stimulating peptide and cross-linked hyaluronic acid [1].

rows: Crow's feet roughness measured by profilometry [1]
62% reported medium to very marked improvement

blocks.text: These figures show that the women's skin and their own ratings improved while using the cream. They cannot show what acetyl tetrapeptide-5 contributed, because there was no comparison group and the cream contained several actives. Ratings people give their own skin, when they know what they are using, are also prone to optimism.

The same 2021 cell study also tested peptide combinations that included acetyl tetrapeptide-5 against oxidative damage in skin cells, and one mixture reduced markers of that damage [4]. That supports further testing, not a conclusion about how a cream performs on a face.

No specific side effects of acetyl tetrapeptide-5 have been reported in the published studies, but those studies were small and short. Expert reviews of other short cosmetic peptides have found skin and eye irritation to be none to slight and no skin allergy, with products tolerated in studies lasting one to seven months [3].

Any leave-on product near the eyes can still irritate, often because of fragrance or preservatives rather than the active ingredient. Because ACE inhibition is the claimed mechanism, it is worth noting that there is no evidence of any effect on blood pressure from a topical cosmetic, and none would be expected if, as with similar peptides, very little is absorbed [3].

name: Adamax
evidenceNote: We found no published study of Adamax itself, in people or animals. Everything said about it is borrowed from rat studies of its parent peptide, Semax, and a modified molecule cannot be assumed to behave like its parent.
summary: Adamax is a research-chemical name for a modified version of the peptide Semax. It has no published studies of its own and no approval.
keyTakeaway: Adamax is a name online research-chemical sellers use for a modified form of Semax, a seven amino acid peptide derived from a fragment of the stress hormone ACTH. Sellers describe it as Semax with an acetyl cap and an adamantane group added to help it reach the brain. We found no peer-reviewed study and no registered trial of Adamax. The rat studies cited in its marketing, showing that Semax raises the brain growth factor BDNF, were done on Semax, not Adamax. It is not FDA-approved, and its identity and purity in any vial are unverified.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Not FDA-approved; no regulatory filing of any kind

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Unknown for Adamax; its parent Semax raises BDNF and TrkB signaling in rat brain

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: None published on Adamax itself

atGlance.value: Only as a research chemical, with no identity or purity standard

blocks.text: Adamax is a product name, not a name from the scientific literature. Research-chemical sellers use it for a version of the peptide Semax that they describe as carrying two changes: an acetyl group on one end and an adamantane group, a bulky cage-shaped carbon structure, on the other. The stated aim is to protect the peptide from enzymes and help it cross into the brain.

None of that has been documented in a peer-reviewed paper we could find. A PubMed search for Adamax returns no study of this compound [4], and ClinicalTrials.gov lists no trial of it [5]. That means its exact structure, its stability, and whether it reaches the brain at all are seller claims rather than published findings.

Its parent, Semax, is better described. Semax is a seven amino acid peptide, Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro, built on the 4 to 10 fragment of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In the rat studies it was given into the nose [1][2].
No one has published how Adamax works, because no one has published a study of it. The mechanism sellers describe is borrowed from Semax.

For Semax, the evidence comes mainly from rats. Researchers found specific, reversible binding sites for labeled Semax on cell membranes from the basal forebrain, a brain region involved in attention and memory. Three hours after Semax was given into the nose, levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that supports nerve cell growth and plasticity, had risen in that region but not in the cerebellum [1]. In the hippocampus, a single dose raised BDNF protein about 1.4-fold, increased activation of its receptor TrkB about 1.6-fold, and went along with better performance on a conditioned avoidance task [2].

Adding an adamantane group changes a molecule's size, fat solubility and shape. Any of those changes can alter whether a peptide still fits its target, how long it lasts and where it goes in the body. So even if Semax's rat data are taken at face value, they do not transfer automatically to Adamax.

No. Adamax has not been approved by the FDA or any other regulator, and there is no record of an application. Its parent Semax is not FDA-approved either. Semax was nominated to the FDA as a bulk substance for compounding, and the nomination was later withdrawn, which leaves it on the FDA's list among nominated-then-withdrawn peptides rather than in an approved or evaluated category [3].

Adamax is sold online labeled for research use only. There is no pharmacopeia standard for it, so nothing guarantees that a given vial contains the described molecule, at the stated amount, without contaminants or bacterial toxins.

For Adamax itself, there is nothing to summarize. We found no published cell, animal or human study, and no registered trial [4][5]. Statements online about its potency, half-life or dose are not traceable to any published measurement.

rows: Yes, including rat studies of BDNF and TrkB [1][2]

blocks.text: The Semax studies behind Adamax's marketing were small rat experiments measuring brain chemistry hours after a dose, with one simple behavior test [1][2]. They are reasonable early science for Semax. They are not evidence that Adamax improves memory, focus or mood in people, and on our scale they put Adamax at the lowest rung: no human data and no animal data of its own.

sections.heading: Is Adamax just a stronger Semax?

blocks.text: That is how it is marketed, but the claim is untested. Modifying a peptide can make it last longer, and it can also make it bind less well, reach the wrong tissue or behave unpredictably. Without published comparisons of Adamax and Semax in the same experiment, there is no basis for calling it stronger, longer-acting or better at entering the brain [1][4]. A buyer is effectively testing an uncharacterized molecule on themselves.

name: Afamelanotide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2019 on the strength of two randomized, placebo-controlled trials in erythropoietic protoporphyria, with long-term follow-up data from clinical practice in Europe.
summary: Afamelanotide (Scenesse) is a tanning-hormone analog implanted under the skin to give people with EPP more pain-free time in light.
keyTakeaway: Afamelanotide is a lab-made, longer-lasting version of alpha-MSH, the hormone that tells skin to make dark melanin. Sold as Scenesse, a 16 mg implant placed under the skin every two months, it won FDA approval in 2019 for adults who have erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare inherited condition in which light causes painful reactions. In the US trial, median pain-free time in direct sun rose to 69 hours over six months versus 41 on placebo. It is not approved for tanning or vitiligo, and online "Melanotan" products are not the approved drug.

atGlance.value: Approved October 2019 as Scenesse, for adults with EPP

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Activates the MC1R receptor on pigment cells, raising dark eumelanin in the skin

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Adults with EPP, to lengthen the time they can spend in light without pain

blocks.text: Afamelanotide is a synthetic peptide modeled on alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), the body's signal for producing melanin. Two of its amino acids are swapped (it is written [Nle4, D-Phe7]-alpha-MSH), which makes it more stable and more active than the natural hormone [3][2].

In the US it is sold by Clinuvel as Scenesse, a dissolving rod about 1.7 cm long that holds 16 mg of drug and is placed under the skin above the hip bone [1]. It is the approved form of the molecule once known as Melanotan I, and it should not be confused with Melanotan II, a different compound.

The molecule was first made in 1980, the first alpha-MSH analog of its kind, and was soon given to human volunteers, in whom daily injections produced long-lasting skin darkening [2]. It came out of a University of Arizona program in the 1980s that hoped to create a sunless tan able to shield fair skin from cancer [4].
Its development shifted toward rare light-sensitivity disorders, and a slow-release implant replaced the daily injections [2].

items.text: Afamelanotide first synthesized as a stabilized alpha-MSH analog [2]
European Commission authorizes Scenesse for adults with EPP, under exceptional circumstances because the disease is so rare [5]
Results of two randomized EPP trials published in the New England Journal of Medicine [7]
FDA approves Scenesse with priority review and orphan drug status [6]

blocks.text: Afamelanotide binds the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) on melanocytes, the pigment cells of the skin. That signal raises production of eumelanin, the dark form of melanin, and does so without sun or UV exposure [1]. MC1R signaling also switches on antioxidant defenses, DNA repair, and anti-inflammatory activity in skin cells [2].

In EPP, a rare inherited condition, light sets off acute phototoxic reactions with severe pain [7]. Extra eumelanin in the skin is thought to raise the amount of light a person can tolerate before a reaction begins. Fair skin types and common MC1R variants did not blunt the pigment response in volunteer studies [2].

Yes. The FDA approved Scenesse on October 8, 2019. It was the first drug cleared for EPP, and the approval covers adults who have had phototoxic reactions, with the goal of more time in light without pain [6]. The European Commission had authorized it in December 2014 for preventing phototoxicity in adults with the same condition [5].

The approval is narrow. The label states that safety and effectiveness in children have not been established, and the implant must be inserted by a trained health care professional [1]. Afamelanotide is also being tested in vitiligo, but it is not approved for that use; Clinuvel's phase 3 study combining the drug with narrowband UVB light finished enrolling more than 200 patients in May 2025 [10].

Scenesse is prescribed only for adults with EPP who have had painful reactions to light. One implant is placed every two months [1]. Two randomized, double-blind trials compared it with a placebo implant [7]:

rows: Median 69.4 hours with afamelanotide vs 40.8 hours with placebo [7]
Median 6.0 hours vs 0.8 hours; fewer phototoxic reactions (77 vs 146) [7]

blocks.text: Quality of life improved in both trials [7]. A follow-up of 117 patients treated in routine care in the Netherlands, run at the request of the European Medicines Agency, found that 98% stayed on treatment for a median of two years, time outdoors rose by about 6 hours a week, and reactions that did occur were less painful [8].

In the pooled trials, the most common side effects within six months were reactions at the implant site (21% vs 10% on placebo), nausea (19% vs 14%), sore throat, cough, and tiredness [1]. Skin darkening (4%) and new or darker moles (4%) were more frequent than on placebo [1].

The label carries two warnings. Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported after approval, and treatment stops if one occurs. Because the drug can darken existing moles and freckles, a full-body skin check is advised twice a year [1]. The NIH's LiverTox database reports no link to liver injury [9].

Products labeled Melanotan are sold online for tanning, but they are not Scenesse. Dermatologists warned as early as 2013 that unregulated and counterfeit Melanotans were on sale before afamelanotide was ever approved [3]. A 2026 McGill University report noted that some vials are mislabeled and may contain neither Melanotan compound, and that most social media posts promoting them do not mention that they are unregulated [4]. Injectable powders bought this way have not been checked for identity, purity, or dose.

name: AHK-Cu
evidenceNote: The only published hair study of AHK-Cu itself used hair follicles and cells kept alive in a dish. No study has applied it to people's scalps or skin and measured the result.
summary: AHK-Cu is a copper-bound tripeptide used in hair and skin cosmetics. Its hair-growth case rests on one lab study of isolated follicles.
keyTakeaway: AHK-Cu is a three-amino-acid peptide (alanine, histidine, lysine) carrying a copper ion, a cousin of the better-known GHK-Cu. It appears in scalp serums and skin creams as a cosmetic ingredient, which the FDA does not approve before sale. Its reputation comes from a 2007 study in which tiny amounts lengthened human hair follicles kept alive in the lab and helped follicle cells multiply. No human trial has tested it, and a product that claims to regrow hair is legally a drug, not a cosmetic.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Not approved; used as a cosmetic ingredient, which needs no FDA approval

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Thought to support hair follicle cells and slow their death, based on lab work

atGlance.label: Topical form
atGlance.value: Scalp serums, hair tonics and skin creams

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: One ex vivo follicle study; no human trials

atGlance.label: Evidence strength
atGlance.value: Low research

blocks.text: AHK-Cu is a tripeptide, a chain of three amino acids, made of L-alanine, L-histidine and L-lysine, with a copper ion (Cu2+) held in the structure [1]. On ingredient lists it may appear as copper tripeptide-3. It is a close relative of GHK-Cu, which swaps the alanine for glycine and is the copper peptide most often studied for skin repair [4].

The two names are easy to confuse, but the research does not transfer from one to the other. GHK-Cu has a broad body of research across several tissues behind it [4]. AHK-Cu has a much smaller literature, almost all of it focused on hair follicles [1].

The proposed target is the dermal papilla, a cluster of specialized cells at the base of each hair follicle that signals the follicle to grow. In lab cultures, AHK-Cu made these cells multiply faster [1].

The same study looked at markers of apoptosis (programmed cell death). Treated cells had a higher ratio of the survival protein Bcl-2 to the death-promoting protein Bax, and lower levels of the cut, active forms of caspase-3 and PARP, two enzymes involved in cell death. The drop in the count of dying cells itself did not reach statistical significance [1]. The authors proposed that AHK-Cu supports growth by helping papilla cells multiply and survive.

Copper peptides as a group are thought to influence wound repair and collagen production, and GHK-Cu has been linked to new blood vessel growth and fibroblast support [4]. Whether AHK-Cu shares those actions in living skin has not been shown.

No. In skin and hair products it is used as a cosmetic ingredient, and US law does not require cosmetics or their ingredients to get FDA approval before they are sold, with color additives the only exception [3]. The company making or selling the product is legally responsible for its safety, and no specific safety tests are required by law [3].

What a product claims matters. FDA decides whether something is a cosmetic or a drug by its intended use, and it lists restoring hair growth and regenerating cells as examples of claims that make a product a drug, even if it is sold as a cosmetic [2]. A scalp serum that promises to regrow hair is therefore making a drug claim that no AHK-Cu product has been approved to make.
AHK-Cu is also sold in vials for injection or microneedling. Those products are research chemicals with no FDA approval and no human safety data for that route.

The key study, from Seoul National University, was published in 2007. Researchers took human scalp hair follicles and grew them ex vivo (alive, outside the body) and also cultured dermal papilla cells. Very low concentrations of AHK-Cu, in the range of 10 to the minus 12 to 10 to the minus 9 molar, lengthened the follicles and increased papilla cell growth [1].

rows: Does it affect hair follicles in the lab?
Yes: longer isolated follicles and more papilla cell growth in one study [1]
Shifted cell-death markers, but the fall in dying cells was not significant [1]
Does it grow hair on a person's scalp?
Never tested in a published human trial
No: different peptide, separate research base [4]

blocks.text: That is the whole AHK-Cu specific evidence base for hair. Nobody has published a trial in which people applied it to the scalp and had hair counts, density or shedding measured against a placebo. Concentrations that work on a follicle in a dish also say little about how much of a cream gets through intact skin to the follicle.

There is also no published information on how often it causes skin irritation, how it behaves with long-term use, or what happens when it is injected. People with copper metabolism disorders such as Wilson's disease are a group in whom any added copper exposure is usually approached with caution, though no study has examined AHK-Cu in them.

sections.heading: How does AHK-Cu differ from GHK-Cu?

blocks.text: Both are copper complexes of a three-amino-acid peptide ending in histidine and lysine. GHK occurs naturally in human blood and has been studied in tissue repair, including skin, lung, bone, liver and stomach lining [4]. AHK-Cu is a synthetic variant chosen for hair products and has one published follicle study [1].

Marketing often borrows GHK-Cu findings for AHK-Cu, or presents the two as interchangeable. A single amino acid change can alter how a peptide binds copper and how cells respond, so each needs its own evidence.

name: Albiglutide
evidenceNote: FDA approved it in 2014 for type 2 diabetes after the eight-trial HARMONY program. The approval still stands on paper, but the product was discontinued for commercial reasons and has not been sold since 2018.
summary: Albiglutide (Tanzeum) is a weekly GLP-1 drug for type 2 diabetes, approved in 2014 and discontinued by GSK for commercial reasons by 2018.
keyTakeaway: Albiglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist made by fusing two copies of a modified GLP-1 to human albumin, which let it be injected once a week. FDA cleared it in 2014, under the brand Tanzeum, as a diabetes treatment. In the HARMONY Outcomes trial of 9,463 people with heart disease, it cut heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death by 22% versus placebo. It lowered HbA1c less than daily liraglutide in a head-to-head trial and caused more injection-site reactions. GSK stopped selling it for commercial reasons, not safety, and it is no longer available anywhere.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Approved in 2014 (BLA 125431); marketing status discontinued

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Activates GLP-1 receptors to raise insulin when glucose is high and slow stomach emptying

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Glucose control in type 2 diabetes in adults, added to diet and exercise

atGlance.label: How it's taken
atGlance.value: Once-weekly injection under the skin from a pen that mixed powder with liquid

atGlance.label: Evidence strength
atGlance.value: FDA approved

blocks.text: Albiglutide is a recombinant fusion protein, meaning it is grown in cells from a single engineered gene rather than built by chemical synthesis. It joins two copies of a GLP-1 fragment end to end and fuses them to human albumin. In each GLP-1 copy, one amino acid (alanine at position 8) is swapped for glycine so that the enzyme DPP-4 cannot cut it [1].

GlaxoSmithKline developed it and sold it in the United States as Tanzeum and in Europe as Eperzan. It was one of the first once-weekly GLP-1 drugs and came as a pen holding a dry powder that the user mixed with liquid before each injection [1][3].

items.text: The European Union authorizes the drug as Eperzan [6].
FDA approves Tanzeum for type 2 diabetes under biologics license 125431 [2].
The HARMONY 7 head-to-head trial finds once-weekly albiglutide lowers HbA1c less than once-daily liraglutide [5].
HARMONY Outcomes is published in The Lancet, showing fewer cardiovascular events than placebo [4].
The European Commission withdraws the EU authorization at GSK's request, for commercial reasons [6].

blocks.text: Like the gut hormone it copies, albiglutide binds the GLP-1 receptor. That prompts the pancreas to release more insulin when glucose is high and slows the emptying of the stomach [3]. Because the insulin effect depends on glucose being elevated, low blood sugar was uncommon unless albiglutide was combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea [1].

Its long action comes from the albumin half of the molecule together with the DPP-4 resistant change. The label gives an elimination half-life of about five days, which made weekly dosing workable [1]. Its effect on weight was modest: across the HARMONY trials, weight change was generally no different from placebo, with a clear advantage only against glimepiride, a diabetes drug that tends to add weight [3].

Yes, but it is not on the market. FDA approved Tanzeum on April 15, 2014, and the agency's Drugs@FDA database still lists the license while marking the product as discontinued [2]. GSK stopped marketing it worldwide; in Europe, the European Commission withdrew the authorization on October 29, 2018, after GSK said it was permanently ending sales for commercial reasons [6].

Tanzeum's one indication was glucose control for adults living with type 2 diabetes, used together with diet and exercise. The label said it was not meant as a first-line choice for people not controlled on diet and exercise alone, and that it had not been studied in people with a history of pancreatitis [1]. Approval rested on eight phase 3 HARMONY trials that enrolled more than 5,000 patients [3].

rows: Type 2 diabetes on diet and exercise
HbA1c down 0.7% (30 mg) and 0.9% (50 mg) vs up 0.2% on placebo
HbA1c down 0.6% vs up 0.3% (placebo), down 0.3% (sitagliptin), down 0.4% (glimepiride)
HbA1c down 0.78% vs 0.99%; failed to show non-inferiority
9,463 patients with type 2 diabetes and heart disease

blocks.text: The final US label, dated 2017, stated that no trial had yet established conclusive evidence of reduced cardiovascular risk, so the HARMONY Outcomes benefit published in 2018 never made it onto Tanzeum's prescribing information [1][4]. In that trial, rates of pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, and medullary thyroid cancer did not differ between albiglutide and placebo [4].

In the label's pooled placebo-controlled trials, the reactions seen in at least 5% of patients and more often than with placebo were upper respiratory infection, diarrhea, nausea, injection-site reaction, cough, back pain, joint pain, sinusitis, and flu [1]. Injection-site reactions stood out: 18% on albiglutide against 8% on placebo [1]. Against liraglutide, albiglutide caused more injection-site reactions (12.9% vs 5.4%) but fewer digestive complaints (35.9% vs 49.0%) [5].

The label carried the class boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumors. Rodent cancer studies could not be run with albiglutide itself, but other GLP-1 drugs had caused these tumors in rodents, and its use was contraindicated when medullary thyroid cancer had occurred in the patient or a relative, or with MEN 2 [1]. Other warnings covered acute pancreatitis, low blood sugar with insulin or sulfonylureas, serious allergic reactions such as angioedema (deep tissue swelling), and post-marketing reports of acute kidney injury, some needing dialysis, usually after severe digestive side effects [1].

name: Amycretin
evidenceNote: Randomized, placebo-controlled phase 1 and phase 2 trials in several hundred people show large weight loss and lower blood sugar. Phase 3 trials started in 2026 and have not reported, so long-term safety and effects on health outcomes are unknown.
summary: Amycretin (now zenagamtide) is Novo Nordisk's one-molecule GLP-1 and amylin agonist for obesity and diabetes. It is in phase 3 and not approved.
keyTakeaway: Amycretin, now called zenagamtide, is a single Novo Nordisk peptide that activates both GLP-1 and amylin receptors, two hormone systems that each reduce appetite. In an early randomized trial, people on the 20 mg weekly injection lost 22.0% of body weight at 36 weeks while the placebo group gained 1.9%. A daily tablet version lowered HbA1c by up to 1.4 points in type 2 diabetes. Stomach side effects were common. It is not FDA-approved: phase 3 trials, including one against semaglutide, began in 2026 and will run for years. Nothing sold online under this name is the trial drug.

blocks.text: Amycretin is an experimental peptide drug from Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes. It now carries the international nonproprietary name zenagamtide, and newer publications and trial listings use that name [1].

Its distinguishing feature is that one molecule acts on two hormone systems. Semaglutide, the drug in Wegovy, acts on the GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor alone [8]. Amycretin pairs GLP-1 activity with amylin activity in a single peptide, so both signals arrive from one injection or one tablet [2].

It is being studied in two forms: a once-weekly subcutaneous (under the skin) injection and a once-daily tablet. Both have reached phase 3, the final stage of testing before a company can apply for approval [4].

GLP-1 is a gut hormone that helps regulate appetite and calorie intake, and its receptor sits in several brain areas that control eating [8]. Amylin is a second hormone, released by the same pancreatic cells that make insulin, in step with insulin after a meal. It slows the rate at which food leaves the stomach, suppresses glucagon (a hormone that raises blood sugar), and reduces food intake through the brain [9].

Amycretin is a unimolecular agonist, meaning a single peptide that switches on GLP-1, amylin, and calcitonin receptors at once [1]. The aim is for the two appetite signals to add together. Whether that beats existing single-target drugs is the question a head-to-head phase 3 trial against semaglutide is designed to answer [5].
No. Amycretin is an investigational drug and is not approved anywhere. It is available only to people enrolled in Novo Nordisk's clinical trials.

The first phase 3 trial, AMAZE 1, began in February 2026. It plans to enroll about 1,150 adults with obesity, randomized to one of four weekly doses or placebo alongside diet and exercise, with weight change measured at 84 weeks. Its primary completion date is listed as June 2029 [4]. Other phase 3 trials registered in 2026 include a head-to-head comparison with semaglutide [5], a study of the tablet form [6], a heart outcomes trial in people with established cardiovascular disease [7], and a type 2 diabetes trial against insulin glargine [10].

blocks.text: The injectable form was tested in a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 1b/2a study at one research center in Texas. Participants with a BMI of 27 to 39.9 received rising weekly doses for up to 36 weeks. Weight loss grew with dose and treatment length [2].

Those numbers come from small groups, and many participants dropped out, often for reasons the investigators judged unrelated to side effects [2]. Results from early trials of this size may not hold up in larger, longer phase 3 programs, so the phase 3 readouts will matter more than these.

The tablet form was first tested in a first-in-human study with treatment lasting up to 12 weeks, whose main purpose was safety. Across 144 participants, 62% reported at least one side effect, all mild or moderate, and most were gastrointestinal [3]. A larger 36-week phase 2 trial then gave daily tablets of 6, 25, or 50 mg to 186 adults with type 2 diabetes already taking metformin. HbA1c (a measure of average blood sugar over about three months) fell by 0.9, 1.3, and 1.4 percentage points from baseline, which was 0.5, 0.99, and 1.09 points more than placebo [1].

Side effects match those of other GLP-1 and amylin drugs. In the diabetes trial, gastrointestinal effects occurred in 26% to 47% of people taking amycretin depending on dose, against 23% on placebo [1]. Approved GLP-1 drugs carry label warnings for pancreatitis and gallbladder disease [8], and trials of amycretin so far are too small to show whether it shares those risks.

Some research chemical websites list powders labeled amycretin. The investigational drug is supplied only through registered studies such as AMAZE 1 [4], so anything bought online is a different, unregulated product of unknown identity and purity. Doses used in the trials cannot be assumed to apply to it.

name: Angiotensin II
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in December 2017 under priority review on the ATHOS-3 trial, a randomized, placebo-controlled study of 321 adults in shock. The trial showed a clear blood pressure effect but was not powered to prove a survival benefit.
summary: Angiotensin II (Giapreza) is a synthetic copy of a natural blood-pressure hormone, given by IV drip in intensive care to adults in septic or distributive shock.
keyTakeaway: Angiotensin II is a hormone the body makes to tighten blood vessels and hold blood pressure up. A synthetic version, sold as Giapreza, was approved by the FDA in 2017 for adults in septic or other distributive shock, where blood vessels relax so much that pressure collapses. It is used only in hospitals, as an intravenous infusion added to other vasopressors. In the ATHOS-3 trial, 69.9% of patients reached the blood pressure target at 3 hours, against 23.4% on placebo. Death rates at 28 days did not differ significantly. Blood clots are the main safety concern, so the label calls for clot prevention alongside it.

blocks.text: Angiotensin II is a naturally occurring peptide hormone that sits at the center of the renin-angiotensin system, the chain of signals that keeps blood pressure and body fluid in balance. When blood pressure drops, the kidneys release an enzyme called renin, which starts a cascade ending in angiotensin II [1].

As a medicine, angiotensin II is a synthetic version of the human hormone, made by La Jolla Pharmaceutical and sold as Giapreza [2]. It is a critical care drug: it is diluted in saline and run continuously into a vein, usually through a central line, in patients whose blood pressure stays dangerously low despite fluids and standard vasopressors [2].

The story starts in 1898, when Tigerstedt and Bergman found that kidney extracts raised blood pressure and named the active material renin. In 1934 Harry Goldblatt produced high blood pressure in dogs by narrowing a kidney artery [1].

Around 1936, two teams working independently, one at the University of Buenos Aires and one at Eli Lilly in Indianapolis, used Goldblatt's method and found a short-acting pressor substance in blood leaving the starved kidney. Both concluded that renin was an enzyme acting on a blood protein to make it. The Argentine group called the product hypertensin and the American group called it angiotonin. In 1958 Eduardo Braun-Menéndez and Irving Page agreed on a single name, angiotensin [1].
Decades later, the hormone returned as a treatment. The ATHOS-3 trial results were published in 2017 [3], and the FDA approved Giapreza that December under priority review [4].

Angiotensin II raises blood pressure in two ways. It binds the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor on the smooth muscle that lines blood vessels, which sets off a calcium-dependent signal that makes the muscle contract and the vessel narrow. It also signals the adrenal glands to put out more aldosterone, which in turn has the kidneys keep salt and water [2].

Most drugs used in shock, such as norepinephrine and epinephrine, work through adrenergic receptors, and vasopressin works through its own receptor. Angiotensin II acts through a separate pathway, which is why it is used as an add-on when those drugs are not enough on their own [4]. Doses are adjusted every few minutes against the patient's measured blood pressure, and the label caps how high they can go [2].

Yes. The FDA approved Giapreza in December 2017, and the approval rested on the ATHOS-3 trial [4]. The label covers adults in septic shock or other forms of distributive shock whose blood pressure needs to be brought up [2]. It carries no contraindications on the label, but it does carry a warning about blood clots [2].

sections.heading: What is angiotensin II prescribed for?

blocks.text: Angiotensin II is used for distributive shock, a state in which blood vessels widen so much that pressure falls too low to keep organs supplied with blood. Septic shock, caused by the body's response to a severe infection, is the most common form; neurogenic shock after spinal injury is another [2].

ATHOS-3 enrolled adults whose shock persisted despite more than 0.2 micrograms per kilogram per minute of norepinephrine or an equivalent dose of another vasopressor. Of the 321 who received a study drug, 114 of 163 (69.9%) on angiotensin II reached the blood pressure target at hour 3, against 37 of 158 (23.4%) on placebo. Organ failure scores for the heart and circulation improved more on the drug by 48 hours. Death by day 28 was 46% with angiotensin II and 54% with placebo, a gap that did not reach statistical significance [3].

rows: Reached blood pressure target at hour 3

blocks.text: Blood clots are the main risk. In ATHOS-3, clotting events in arteries or veins occurred in 12.9% of patients on angiotensin II and 5.1% on placebo, with deep vein thrombosis (a clot in a deep leg vein) accounting for much of the gap: 4.3% versus none. The label therefore directs that patients receive clot-preventing treatment at the same time [2].

Other reactions seen more often on the drug than on placebo included low platelet counts (9.8% versus 7.0%), fast heart rate (8.6% versus 5.7%), fungal infection (6.1% versus 1.3%), delirium (5.5% versus 0.6%), acidosis (5.5% versus 0.6%), high blood sugar and reduced blood flow to the limbs [2]. Because these patients are critically ill, many events in both groups reflect the shock itself.

name: AOD-9604
evidenceNote: AOD-9604 went through six placebo-controlled human trials, but only safety results were published in full. A 24-week trial of 536 people found no meaningful weight loss, and development stopped in 2007, so the human efficacy evidence is weak and negative.
summary: AOD-9604 is a modified piece of human growth hormone tested as an obesity drug. It failed to produce meaningful weight loss and was never approved.
keyTakeaway: AOD-9604 is a 16-amino-acid peptide based on the tail end of human growth hormone, first reported by Australian researchers around 2000 as a way to burn fat without growth hormone's other effects. It reduced weight gain in obese rats and mice. In people, an early 12-week trial hinted at a small benefit, but a 24-week trial in 536 adults did not show significant weight loss, and development was halted in 2007. It is not FDA-approved, the FDA lists safety concerns for compounded versions, and WADA names it as a banned growth hormone fragment.

blocks.text: AOD-9604 is a synthetic peptide of 16 amino acids [3]. It copies the last stretch of human growth hormone, the segment running from position 177 to 191, with one extra amino acid (tyrosine) added at the front [4]. The name stands for anti-obesity drug, and researchers at Monash University in Victoria, Australia, designed it in the hope of keeping growth hormone's fat-reducing action while leaving out the rest [1].

The Australian company Metabolic Pharmaceuticals took it into human trials as a weight-loss pill, and early animal work suggested it might work by mouth [1][4]. That program ended in 2007 [4]. The peptide later resurfaced in clinics and on research-chemical websites, usually as an injection, and it sits alongside the unmodified fragment sold as "Fragment 176-191".

Full-length growth hormone does several things at once. It breaks down stored fat (lipolysis), but it also raises blood sugar, lowers insulin sensitivity, and drives tissue growth through IGF-1. The idea behind AOD-9604 was that the fat-burning signal lives in the hormone's tail, so a fragment of that tail could keep the useful effect and drop the risky ones.

In obese mice, the peptide slowed weight gain, raised fat oxidation, and increased blood glycerol, a marker of fat being broken down [2]. Unlike growth hormone, it did not cause high blood sugar or reduce insulin release. It also did not bind the growth hormone receptor or make receptor-bearing cells multiply, so it seems to act through a different, still unidentified pathway [2]. In humans, it did not change IGF-1 levels or harm glucose tolerance [3].

No. AOD-9604 has never been approved by the FDA for any use. It was nominated for use by compounding pharmacies, and the FDA reviewed it among peptides that may carry significant safety risks. The nomination was later withdrawn [5]. In its summary, the agency flags a possible risk of immune reactions for some routes of use, difficulty characterizing the peptide and its impurities, too little safety data to judge harm, and serious adverse events that may be linked to it, although causation was not clear [5].

It was not on the agenda when the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee met in July 2026 to weigh seven other peptides for the compounding list [7]. For athletes, the World Anti-Doping Agency names AOD-9604 directly as a prohibited growth hormone fragment, banned in and out of competition [6].

The animal results were encouraging. Given by mouth to obese Zucker rats for 19 days, it cut their weight gain by more than half compared with untreated animals, without the loss of insulin sensitivity seen with growth hormone [1]. In obese mice on a two-week infusion it reduced weight gain and increased fat burning [2].

rows: Weight gain 15.8 g versus 35.6 g in controls [1]
Less weight gain, more fat oxidation, no rise in blood sugar [2]
2.6 kg lost on 1 mg a day versus 0.8 kg on placebo [4]
No significant weight loss; development stopped in 2007 [4]

blocks.text: The larger and longer trial is the one that counts, and it was negative. A 2013 review of obesity drug candidates lists AOD-9604 among those that failed to show efficacy in phase 2b testing [4]. The company's full efficacy data were never published in a peer-reviewed journal, which makes the early 12-week result hard to weigh.

The safety record is better documented. A company-authored paper pooled six randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials and reported side effects indistinguishable from placebo, no serious adverse events tied to the peptide, no antibodies against it in the people tested, and no effect on IGF-1 or blood sugar handling [3]. Those trials studied the oral and injected forms used in the original program, not the products sold today, and they were not designed to test long-term use.

AOD-9604 is widely sold as a research chemical and offered by some clinics for fat loss, often promoted with the animal results. Those products have not been reviewed by the FDA for identity, purity, or sterility, and the agency has listed impurity and immune-reaction concerns specific to compounded versions [5]. The claim that it melts fat in people rests on rodent data; the one large human trial did not find a meaningful effect [4].

name: Apraglutide
evidenceNote: One randomized phase 3 trial of 163 patients met its main goal, backed by small open-label studies. A second phase 3 trial is under way because the first delivered less drug than intended.
summary: Apraglutide is a once-weekly GLP-2 drug in phase 3 for short bowel syndrome. It cut IV nutrition needs in a trial but is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Apraglutide is a lab-made, long-lasting version of GLP-2, a gut hormone that helps the small intestine grow and absorb. It is being developed by Ironwood Pharmaceuticals for adults with short bowel syndrome who depend on intravenous nutrition and fluids. In the 163-patient STARS phase 3 trial, weekly injections cut the weekly volume of that support by 25.5 percent against 12.5 percent on placebo. It is not FDA-approved: the FDA asked for a confirmatory phase 3 trial after Ironwood found patients received less drug than planned, and that trial began recruiting in 2026.

blocks.text: Apraglutide is an experimental peptide drug that copies GLP-2 (glucagon-like peptide-2), a 33-amino-acid hormone released by the small intestine after meals. Natural GLP-2 helps the gut lining grow and absorb nutrients, but the body clears it within minutes, which makes it useless as a medicine on its own [1].

Apraglutide is being developed for short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure (SBS-IF), a condition in which so much intestine has been removed or lost that a person cannot absorb enough food and water by mouth. Many such patients rely on parenteral support, meaning nutrition and fluids given straight into a vein, often for many hours a night [5]. It is not the same drug as GLP-1 weight loss medicines such as semaglutide, which act on a different receptor.

Apraglutide carried the code FE 203799 early on, and a first trial in adults with lymphoma, sponsored by GlyPharma Therapeutics, was withdrawn for business reasons before it enrolled anyone [4]. The drug was later developed by VectivBio, which became part of Ironwood Pharmaceuticals [3]. Teduglutide, the only approved GLP-2 drug, has been on the market for short bowel syndrome since 2012 but needs a daily injection; apraglutide was engineered to last long enough for a weekly one [1].

items.text: Animal pharmacology published, showing very slow clearance compared with other GLP-2 drugs [1]
STARS phase 3 trial begins enrolling adults with SBS-IF [9]

blocks.text: Apraglutide binds the GLP-2 receptor about as strongly and selectively as natural GLP-2. What sets it apart is how long it stays in the body. In rats it was cleared roughly 100 times more slowly than natural GLP-2 and far more slowly than teduglutide or glepaglutide, another GLP-2 drug in development, and given less often it produced more growth of the small intestine than either [1].

In people, that growth shows up as better absorption. In a small 52-week study of nine patients whose colon was still connected, imaging showed the measured length of small bowel rising from about 30 to 41 centimeters, and fluid and energy absorption both improved [3]. The aim is intestinal adaptation: helping the remaining gut do more of the work that intravenous support does today.

No. Apraglutide has not been approved by the FDA or any other major regulator. Ironwood had planned to file for approval on the strength of the STARS results, but while preparing that application its pharmacokinetic analysis (a study of how much drug reached the blood) found that patients in STARS received a lower dose and exposure than planned, because of how doses were prepared and given. After discussing this with the FDA, the company announced in April 2025 that a confirmatory phase 3 trial would be needed [6].

That trial, STARS-2, is a 24-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study whose main measure is again the change in weekly intravenous support volume [7]. Its registry entry lists 124 planned adult participants and recruitment that opened in 2026 [8]. Until it reads out and the FDA reviews an application, apraglutide is available only inside clinical trials.

STARS is the largest trial completed to date in this condition. It randomized 163 adults with SBS-IF two to one between weekly apraglutide and placebo, split into people with a stoma (an opening that brings the bowel out through the abdominal wall) and people whose colon was still connected. At 24 weeks, weekly intravenous support volume fell 25.5 percent with apraglutide against 12.5 percent with placebo, and 43 percent of treated patients cut at least one day a week of support, against 27.5 percent [2].

rows: Change in weekly IV support volume, week 24, all patients
At least one day a week off IV support, week 24
Off IV support entirely, colon group, week 48

blocks.text: The results were strongest in patients with a stoma. In those with a connected colon, differences at 48 weeks in days off support and in reaching full independence from intravenous feeding did not reach statistical significance [2]. In the long-term extension, Ironwood reported that 27 patients on apraglutide reached that independence [6].

Earlier open-label studies support the same direction. In eight patients given weekly 5 mg injections for four weeks, absorption of fluid rose by about 741 grams a day and energy by about 1,095 kilojoules a day; the most common side effects related to the drug were changes in stoma output, stoma complications and nausea [10]. Across six placebo-controlled trials of GLP-2 drugs as a class, a 2025 meta-analysis found lower intravenous support needs and no rise in serious side effects, while noting the trials were few and early [5].

name: Aviptadil
evidenceNote: A large randomized, placebo-controlled trial (TESICO, 461 patients) exists, which places it in the moderate tier, but that trial found no benefit in critical COVID-19. Most other support is laboratory and animal work.
summary: A lab-made copy of the gut and nerve hormone VIP. Tested in critical COVID-19, where a large NIH trial found no benefit; not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Aviptadil is a lab-made copy of VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide), a small hormone released by nerves and immune cells that relaxes blood vessels and calms inflammation. It drew attention in 2020 as an IV drug for critical COVID-19. The FDA turned down emergency authorization in 2021, and TESICO, a randomized trial run by the NIH in 461 patients, was halted for futility after showing no gain in recovery or survival. No US approval exists for any condition. In the UK it is licensed only within a combination injection for erectile dysfunction.

blocks.text: Aviptadil is the drug name for a synthetic copy of vasoactive intestinal peptide, usually shortened to VIP. Natural VIP is a chain of 28 amino acids found throughout the brain, the gut, the lungs and the immune system, where nerve cells and immune cells release it as a signal [1][4].

As a drug it has gone by several names: RLF-100 at Relief Therapeutics and Zyesami at NRx Pharmaceuticals, the two companies that developed it for COVID-19 [6]. It has been given as an IV infusion and studied in inhaled form [9], and in the UK a low dose is combined with phentolamine in an injection for erectile dysfunction [7].

VIP was discovered in 1970 by Sami Said and Viktor Mutt, who purified it from pig small intestine. They noted that it widened blood vessels, lowered blood pressure, increased the heart's output and stimulated breathing, and that it was chemically distinct from glucagon and secretin [1]. Its name reflects that origin: vasoactive (acting on vessels) and intestinal.

items.text: VIP is isolated from the small intestine and described in Science [1].
NRx Pharmaceuticals applies to the FDA for emergency use authorization of IV aviptadil in critical COVID-19 [6].
The FDA declines the emergency authorization, citing insufficient data on benefits and risks, and also turns down a request for expedited development status [6].
The independent safety board stops the aviptadil arm of the NIH's TESICO trial for futility [5].
TESICO results are published: no improvement in recovery or survival at 90 days [5].

blocks.text: VIP acts through two receptors, VPAC1 and VPAC2, which sit on the surface of many cell types. Both belong to the large family of G protein-coupled receptors, and when VIP binds, they mainly switch on adenylyl cyclase, an enzyme that raises the cell's internal messenger cyclic AMP [2]. In blood vessels, that signal relaxes the muscle wall, which explains the flushing and drop in blood pressure seen when VIP is infused.

VIP also speaks to the immune system. T cells and macrophages carry VPAC receptors, and VIP signaling through them tends to restrain cell migration, multiplication and the release of inflammatory messengers [3][4]. In the lung, VPAC1 is found on alveolar type II cells, which make the surfactant that keeps air sacs open. That combination, protecting the cells that SARS-CoV-2 attacks while damping inflammation, was the rationale for trying it in COVID-19 [8].
Most of that picture comes from cell and animal work. A drug that behaves this way in a dish does not necessarily help a person in respiratory failure, which is the gap TESICO was designed to test.

No. The FDA has never approved aviptadil, for COVID-19 or anything else. Its COVID-19 product had received Fast Track status, which only speeds communication with the agency, but the emergency authorization request was declined in November 2021 [6]. ClinicalTrials.gov shows no aviptadil study currently recruiting [9].

VIP has also been nominated as an ingredient for compounding pharmacies. In the FDA's list of nominated bulk substances, updated in May 2026, it sits in category 1, meaning it is still under evaluation and the agency does not currently plan to act against pharmacies that compound with it under the usual conditions [10]. That is a temporary enforcement position, not a finding that VIP is safe or effective.

Outside the US, aviptadil has a narrow licensed role. Invicorp, an injection combining 25 micrograms of aviptadil with phentolamine, is licensed in the UK for erectile dysfunction. Health authorities in Wales recommended it in 2017 only for men whose erectile dysfunction had not responded to tablets such as sildenafil [7].

The strongest test is TESICO, an NIH-funded randomized trial at 28 US hospitals. Adults hospitalized with COVID-19 and acute respiratory failure received IV aviptadil as a 12-hour infusion on three days, or a saline placebo [5]. Nearly all were in intensive care, and about 40% were on a ventilator.

rows: Odds of a better recovery category [5]

blocks.text: The trial was stopped early because it had little chance of showing a benefit. Infusion-related effects were more common on aviptadil, including diarrhea, low blood pressure and facial flushing, which fits the drug's known action on blood vessels [5].

Outside COVID-19, the human evidence is thin. Interest in VIP for inflammatory and autoimmune disease comes mostly from cell and animal studies [4], and even reviews that favor the idea say that adequate clinical trials are still needed [8]. Products labeled VIP and sold online for research are outside any of this testing, and their contents are unverified.

name: Bacitracin
evidenceNote: Bacitracin is an FDA-regulated antibiotic sold over the counter as a first aid ointment and by prescription for eye infections. Its injectable form was withdrawn for safety reasons in 2020.
summary: A peptide antibiotic from Bacillus bacteria, sold over the counter as a first aid ointment. The injection was withdrawn in 2020 over kidney risks.
keyTakeaway: Bacitracin is a mix of ring-shaped peptides made by Bacillus bacteria, discovered in 1945 and now best known as a first aid ointment for minor cuts, scrapes, and burns. It kills mainly gram-positive bacteria by locking up a molecule they need to build their cell walls. It is FDA-regulated for skin and eye use, but the injectable form was withdrawn after a 2020 FDA request because of kidney damage and severe allergy. In a 922-patient trial after skin surgery, plain petrolatum worked as well for wound care, and bacitracin itself is a common cause of contact allergy.
