blocks.text: Bacitracin is an antibiotic made by strains of the Bacillus subtilis group of soil bacteria. It is not a single molecule but a mixture of related ring-shaped (cyclic) peptides, the main one being bacitracin A [5]. In medicine it is used as the zinc salt, applied to skin or eyes.

Most people meet it as a first aid ointment, on its own or in the triple antibiotic combination with neomycin and polymyxin B [1]. The over-the-counter ointment contains 500 units of bacitracin zinc per gram and is labeled to help prevent infection in minor cuts, scrapes, and burns [4].

Bacitracin was reported in 1945, during the first wave of antibiotic discoveries. Researchers recovered it from a strain of the B. subtilis group and found it worked mainly against gram-positive bacteria, cured streptococcal and gas gangrene infections in lab animals, and gave encouraging early results in people with streptococcal and staphylococcal infections [2].

Its use later narrowed. Given by injection, it could damage the kidneys, so that route was limited to one labeled use in infants [6]. Applied to skin it became a household staple, so common that a dermatology society journal named it allergen of the year in 2003 [8].

items.text: Bacitracin is described as a new antibiotic from a B. subtilis group organism [2].
A 922-patient trial finds plain petrolatum as good as bacitracin for clean surgical wounds [7].
Named allergen of the year in the American Contact Dermatitis Society journal [8].
FDA asks makers of bacitracin for injection to withdraw it from the market [6].
FDA withdraws the last remaining injectable approval, held by Xellia [6].

blocks.text: Bacteria build their cell walls using a fatty carrier molecule called undecaprenyl pyrophosphate, which ferries building blocks across the cell membrane and has to be recycled after each trip. Bacitracin grabs that carrier and, with the help of a zinc ion, wraps around its phosphate head so it cannot be reused [3]. Without a working carrier the wall cannot be built, and the bacterium dies.

This mechanism explains its spectrum. Bacitracin acts chiefly on gram-positive bacteria, such as hemolytic streptococci [2][5]. To cover a wider range of germs it is often paired with polymyxin B, and in the triple ointment also with neomycin [1][5].

Yes, for skin and eye use. Bacitracin zinc ointment is sold over the counter under the FDA's final monograph for first aid antibiotics, which sets the allowed uses and label warnings [4]. Prescription ophthalmic ointment combining bacitracin zinc with polymyxin B is approved for surface infections of the eye [5].

The injection is a different story. After an FDA advisory committee voted almost unanimously in April 2019 that its benefits no longer outweighed its risks, the FDA asked all makers on January 31, 2020 to withdraw bacitracin for injection, citing kidney toxicity and anaphylactic reactions [6]. Its only labeled use had been staphylococcal pneumonia and empyema in infants, for which safer drugs exist [6]. The request did not affect topical or eye products.

items: First aid for minor cuts, scrapes, and burns, to help prevent infection (over the counter) [4].
Surface infections of the conjunctiva and cornea, combined with polymyxin B (prescription eye ointment) [5].
Triple antibiotic ointment with neomycin and polymyxin B, for broader coverage of minor skin wounds [1].

blocks.text: Whether it adds much after clean surgery is doubtful. In a randomized, double-blind trial of 922 dermatologic surgery patients, infection rates were 0.9% with bacitracin and 2.0% with white petrolatum, a difference that was not statistically significant, and healing was the same [7]. Petrolatum caused no allergic reactions, while four bacitracin users developed contact dermatitis, leading the authors to favor petrolatum for routine wound care [7].

The main problem is allergy. Bacitracin has become one of the leading causes of allergic contact dermatitis, an itchy, red rash where the ointment was applied, and rare cases of near-fatal anaphylaxis have been reported [9]. The over-the-counter label tells users to stop and ask a doctor if a rash or other allergic reaction develops, or if the wound needs treatment for more than a week [4].

The label also says not to use it in the eyes, over large areas of the body, or for longer than a week without medical advice, and to check with a doctor first for deep or puncture wounds, animal bites, or serious burns [4]. The eye ointment can slow healing of the cornea, and long use may allow resistant organisms such as fungi to overgrow [5].

name: Balixafortide
evidenceNote: Balixafortide has been through one large randomized phase 3 trial, which places it in this tier, but that trial found no benefit and was stopped. The rest of the human data are phase 1 studies in breast cancer patients and healthy volunteers.
summary: Balixafortide is an experimental CXCR4-blocking peptide. Its phase 3 breast cancer trial failed in 2021; a small pancreatic cancer study is planned.
keyTakeaway: Balixafortide is a lab-made, ring-shaped peptide that blocks CXCR4, a receptor that helps keep stem cells in the bone marrow and helps some tumors spread. Given by vein with the chemotherapy drug eribulin, it shrank tumors in 30% of evaluable women in an early breast cancer study. The larger randomized phase 3 trial in 432 patients then found no improvement in progression-free survival and was halted. It is not FDA-approved. A small phase 1 study pairing it with an immunotherapy drug in pancreatic cancer is registered.

blocks.text: Balixafortide is an experimental drug made from a synthetic cyclic peptide, a short chain of amino acids joined into a ring for stability. It carried the code name POL6326 during development. The company Polyphor funded its early cancer trial [1], and its phase 3 trial was sponsored by Spexis AG [3].

The drug blocks a receptor called CXCR4. Researchers have tested it for two quite different jobs: pulling stem cells out of the bone marrow into the blood so they can be collected for transplant, and making chemotherapy work better against metastatic breast cancer [1][2]. It is given by intravenous infusion and has not been approved anywhere.

CXCR4 is a receptor found on blood-forming stem cells, many immune cells and a range of cancer cells. Its partner signal is CXCL12, also called stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1), a chemical messenger made in the bone marrow and other tissues. The pairing works like a tether, drawing cells toward places where CXCL12 is abundant and holding them there [1].

Cutting that tether has two uses. In the bone marrow, it releases stem cells into the bloodstream, where they can be gathered by apheresis, a process that filters cells from blood. In a dose-escalation study in healthy men, a single infusion raised circulating stem cells to levels that would let most donors give a standard transplant dose in one collection [2].

In cancer, the idea is that tumors use the same signal to shelter in protective tissue and to spread. Blocking CXCR4 strengthened several anticancer treatments in animal models, which is why balixafortide was paired with chemotherapy in breast cancer [1].

No. Balixafortide has not been approved by the FDA or any other regulator. Its most advanced program, a phase 3 trial in HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, was terminated in 2021 because it failed its primary endpoint [3].

The drug remains investigational. A single-center phase 1 study at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, registered in 2025, plans to test it with the immunotherapy antibody cosibelimab in people with metastatic pancreatic cancer that has progressed after standard chemotherapy [4].

A different CXCR4 blocker is approved for a related purpose. Motixafortide (Aphexda), also a peptide, was approved in 2023 to mobilize stem cells for collection in people with multiple myeloma, used together with the growth factor filgrastim [5]. That approval does not extend to balixafortide.

The breast cancer story began with an open-label phase 1 study at 11 sites in Spain and the US. It enrolled 56 women with HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer who had already received one to three chemotherapy regimens. They received balixafortide alongside eribulin, a standard chemotherapy. No dose-limiting toxicity was found, and 16 of 54 evaluable patients (30%) had a partial response, meaning their tumors shrank by a set amount [1].

Side effects were frequent, as expected in heavily treated cancer patients on chemotherapy. Fatigue affected 79%, low white blood cell counts 57%, and infusion reactions 48%. Serious adverse events occurred in 38%, and two patients died during treatment, one from septic shock and one from pneumonia [1].

Without a comparison group, the phase 1 study could not show whether balixafortide added anything to eribulin alone. The phase 3 trial, called FORTRESS, was designed to answer that. It randomly assigned 432 patients to eribulin with or without balixafortide [3].

rows: Hazard ratio for progression (lower favors balixafortide)

blocks.text: Adding balixafortide did not delay cancer growth or extend survival; the numbers were slightly, though not significantly, worse than chemotherapy alone. The study was halted early for failing its primary endpoint [3]. On the stem cell side, the human evidence stops at the healthy-volunteer phase 1 study, which found the drug well tolerated and effective at releasing stem cells [2].

name: Bivalirudin
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in December 2000 and backed by large randomized trials in coronary procedures, including the 4,312-patient BAT studies and the 3,602-patient HORIZONS-AMI trial.
summary: Bivalirudin is a 20-amino-acid IV blood thinner modeled on leech hirudin, FDA-approved since 2000 for use during coronary stenting and angioplasty.
keyTakeaway: Bivalirudin, a lab-made peptide of 20 amino acids sold as Angiomax and in generic forms, blocks thrombin, the enzyme at the heart of clot formation. Its design borrows from hirudin, the anticoagulant in leech saliva. The FDA approved it in 2000 as an IV blood thinner for percutaneous coronary intervention, including in people with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. In the HORIZONS-AMI heart attack trial it cut 30-day major bleeding from 8.3% to 4.9% compared with heparin plus a platelet blocker. Its main risks are bleeding and, in heart attack patients, early stent clotting.

atGlance.value: Approved December 2000 (Angiomax); generic versions also approved

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Binds thrombin at two sites, blocking both free and clot-bound thrombin; the effect wears off quickly

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Anticoagulation during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), including patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

blocks.text: Bivalirudin is a blood thinner made of 20 amino acids, produced by chemical synthesis rather than extracted from an animal [1]. It belongs to the direct thrombin inhibitors, drugs that attach straight to thrombin instead of working through a helper protein the way heparin does. It is sold in the United States as Angiomax and in several generic versions, and in Europe as Angiox [2].

It is a hospital drug. Cardiologists give it through a vein during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), the catheter procedure that opens narrowed heart arteries with a balloon or a stent [1]. It has no tablet form and is not used at home.

The medicinal leech feeds without its meal clotting because its saliva contains hirudin, a protein that shuts down thrombin. Hirudin became the template for a group of direct thrombin inhibitors [3]. Bivalirudin, first developed under the name Hirulog, is a short synthetic analog that keeps the parts of hirudin needed to grip thrombin while being far smaller [2][4].

The FDA approved Angiomax in December 2000 [6]. Early labeling covered angioplasty in people with unstable angina. Later trials tested it in elective stenting and in heart attacks, and the current label covers PCI broadly, including patients who cannot receive heparin because of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), an immune reaction that lowers platelets and paradoxically causes clots [1][2].

Thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin, the mesh that holds a clot together, and it also switches on platelets and other clotting factors. Bivalirudin latches onto thrombin at two places: the active site that does the cutting, and a separate docking site that thrombin uses to grab fibrinogen. Because it binds directly, it can disable thrombin floating in the blood and thrombin already trapped inside a clot [1][4].

The grip does not last. Thrombin slowly snips the bound drug apart and regains its function, and the body clears bivalirudin quickly. Its half-life is about 25 minutes in people with normal kidneys, and clotting tests return to baseline roughly an hour after the infusion stops [1]. Clearance slows in kidney disease, which is why the infusion rate is adjusted for poor kidney function. There is no antidote, though dialysis removes some of the drug [1].

Yes. Angiomax received FDA approval in December 2000, and generic bivalirudin products have since been approved [6]. The label lists it as an anticoagulant for patients undergoing PCI, including those with HIT or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis syndrome (HITTS) [1].

items.text: FDA approves Angiomax (bivalirudin) as an anticoagulant for coronary angioplasty [6].
Review summarizes the REPLACE-2 trial showing non-inferiority to heparin plus a platelet blocker with less bleeding [2].
HORIZONS-AMI reports lower bleeding and lower 30-day death rates in heart attack patients [5].

blocks.text: Bivalirudin keeps blood from clotting on catheters, wires, and fresh stents during PCI. Its short action suits a procedure that lasts an hour or two, and its predictable effect means doctors can check it with a bedside clotting test [1]. It is also a standard option for PCI in people with HIT, since it does not trigger the antibody reaction that heparin does. In a 51-patient study of people with HIT or HITTS, most reached the target clotting time and no major bleeding was reported [1].

The largest trials compared it against heparin combined with a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa blocker, a strong platelet-blocking drug. In HORIZONS-AMI, 3,602 people having emergency PCI for a heart attack were randomized to one approach or the other [5].

The earlier BAT trials in 4,312 people with unstable angina did not show bivalirudin to be superior to heparin on death, heart attack, or vessel closure, though event rates were similar between groups [1].
Bleeding is the main risk and the most common adverse reaction, as with any anticoagulant. In the BAT trials, 3.7% of patients on bivalirudin had a major bleed [1]. Other label warnings include:

items: Acute stent thrombosis (a clot forming in a new stent within hours) in heart attack patients: 1.2% on bivalirudin vs 0.2% on heparin in primary PCI, which is why monitoring for at least 24 hours is advised [1].
Higher risk of clotting during coronary brachytherapy (radiation inside the artery), including fatal cases [1].
More bleeding when combined with heparin, warfarin, clot-dissolving drugs, or platelet blockers, and in older adults [1].
Rare allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, reported after approval [1].

blocks.text: It should not be used in someone who is actively bleeding or who has had a serious allergic reaction to it [1]. Because there is no reversal agent, its short half-life is the main safety margin if bleeding occurs.

name: BPC-157
evidenceNote: Dozens of rat studies report faster healing, but almost all come from one lab in Zagreb. Human data amount to a 12-person retrospective knee report, a 2-person infusion safety check, and early bowel trials whose full results were never published.
summary: BPC-157 is a lab-made stomach-derived peptide that sped tissue healing in rats. Human evidence is tiny, and it is not FDA-approved for any use.
keyTakeaway: BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid peptide first described by a Croatian team as a fragment of a protein in gastric juice. In rats it repeatedly sped the healing of tendons, muscle, bone, and gut lining, but a 2025 systematic review found 35 animal studies and a single small human report. It is not FDA-approved. In late October 2026 HHS said it would not act against licensed pharmacies compounding it under strict conditions, which is not an approval. It is banned in sport, and online vials are unregulated.

atGlance.value: Not approved; compounding tolerated under an October 2026 HHS enforcement policy

blocks.text: BPC-157 is a short chain of 15 amino acids (a pentadecapeptide) with the sequence GEPPPGKPADDAGLV. Its developers describe it as a stable fragment of a larger protein found in human gastric juice, and the name stands for Body Protection Compound [3]. The version sold today is made synthetically in a lab.

Most of what is known about it comes from animal experiments. In those studies it has been given by injection, by mouth, and in drinking water, and it has been reported to protect the stomach lining and to speed repair of tendons, ligaments, muscle, and bone [1]. Clinicians and athletes have started using it despite the lack of approval, which is why it now draws regulatory and medical attention [1].

The compound grew out of decades of work by Predrag Sikiric at the University of Zagreb, who set out in the 1970s to find an anti-stress substance made by the stomach. His group screened gastric juice collected from hospitals and slaughterhouses, and in 1989 reported a protein from which the 15-amino-acid sequence was taken [5].

The Croatian drugmaker PLIVA developed the peptide in the 1990s and ran two early trials in ulcerative colitis in the early 2000s. The full results were never published, and the project was dropped after PLIVA's research arm was sold to GlaxoSmithKline in 2006 [5]. A small safety study in healthy volunteers was registered in 2015, but its status is listed as unknown and no results were posted [6].

Skeptics have raised basic questions. The full sequence of the parent protein was never published, no gene coding for the peptide has been identified, and no specific receptor for it has been confirmed [5].

No one has shown exactly how BPC-157 acts in the human body. The Zagreb group argues that it behaves as a cytoprotective agent, meaning it helps cells keep their integrity under stress, and that it steers two systems involved in repair: the growth of new blood vessels (angiogenesis) and nitric oxide signaling [4].

Across the animal and cell literature, reviewers list higher expression of growth hormone receptors on tendon cells, activation of pathways tied to cell growth and blood vessel formation, and lower levels of inflammatory signals [1]. In a 2003 rat study of a cut Achilles tendon, treated animals had stronger, more elastic tendons and better walking function than controls, and the peptide also protected cultured tendon cells from a toxic aldehyde [3].

These are plausible mechanisms drawn from rodents and dishes. They have not been confirmed in people, and the review authors note that the peptide is broken down in the liver with a half-life of under 30 minutes [1].

No. The FDA has never approved BPC-157 for any condition, and no company has filed for approval. For years the FDA placed it in Category 2 of its compounding list, a group of substances flagged for safety concerns. The agency cited a possible risk of immune reactions and the difficulty of characterizing peptide impurities, and said it had little or no safety information for the routes proposed [9]. The nominations were later withdrawn, and the FDA's April 2026 update lists BPC-157 among withdrawn substances [9].

On July 23, 2026, the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 6 to recommend adding BPC-157 to the list of bulk substances pharmacies may compound, with ulcerative colitis as the proposed use. FDA staff had argued against it, citing a lack of clinical evidence [14], and the vote is only advisory [10].

In late October 2026, HHS issued an interim enforcement discretion policy covering BPC-157 and five other peptides [13]. It says HHS does not intend to act against state-licensed pharmacies and physicians that compound BPC-157 for injection under the skin or into muscle, or for oral or topical use, provided they meet conditions such as sourcing from FDA-registered manufacturers, a certificate of analysis for each bulk lot, and a patient-specific prescription. The policy does not approve the drug or add it to the bulks list, and it lasts until the FDA finishes rulemaking [13][11].

The animal record is large and consistently positive, which is itself a caution. A 2019 review found that every published study reported prompt healing, that most used small rodent models, and that only a handful of research groups had studied the peptide in depth [2]. A 2026 investigation reported that the majority of the evidence still comes out of the Zagreb lab [5].

A 2025 systematic review searched for musculoskeletal studies and kept 36: 35 preclinical and one clinical [1]. The authors rated the whole body of evidence as low level and found no clinical safety data [1]. The human studies that do exist are small and uncontrolled:

rows: Retrospective knee report (described in a 2025 review)
7 reported relief lasting more than 6 months after one injection; no comparison group [1]
2 adults at a private Florida clinic
Infusions of 10 mg and 20 mg caused no changes in heart, liver, kidney, thyroid, or glucose tests [7]

blocks.text: The registered hamstring trial is the first placebo-controlled test of BPC-157 for a sports injury, with return to sport and MRI injury volume as its main measures [8]. Until results like these appear, claims about tendon, joint, or gut healing in people rest on animal data.

Vials and capsules sold as research chemicals are not covered by the HHS policy, which applies only to licensed pharmacies following its conditions [11]. Their purity and dose are not checked by any regulator, and the 2025 review warned that unregulated manufacturing and contamination could cause harm on top of the unknown safety of the peptide itself [1].
Athletes face a separate rule. Anti-doping rules list BPC-157 in WADA category S0, the class for non-approved substances, because no health authority anywhere has cleared it for human use [12].

name: Bremelanotide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2019 on the strength of two 24-week randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in about 1,267 premenopausal women. The measured gains were statistically significant but small, and an independent reanalysis questions how meaningful they are.
summary: An as-needed injection approved in 2019 for low sexual desire in premenopausal women. Gains in trials were small and nausea was common.
keyTakeaway: Bremelanotide is a synthetic peptide that acts on melanocortin receptors in the brain. The FDA approved it in 2019 as Vyleesi, an as-needed injection for premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) that is acquired and generalized. In two phase 3 trials, desire scores on a 1.2 to 6 scale rose by about 0.5 to 0.6 points with the drug against 0.2 with placebo, and the number of satisfying sexual events did not differ. Four in ten users had nausea, and blood pressure rises briefly after each dose. Vials labeled "PT-141" sold online are not the approved product.

blocks.text: Bremelanotide is a short, ring-shaped synthetic peptide built to resemble alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), a signaling molecule the body makes in the brain and skin [5]. It is the active ingredient in Vyleesi, a prescription injection for women who have lost interest in sex in a way that causes them distress [1].

The drug is used on demand rather than every day. Each prefilled pen holds one dose, and the label limits use to one dose in 24 hours and advises against more than eight a month [1]. Its maker describes it as the only FDA-approved treatment for this condition that is taken as needed rather than on a daily schedule [9].

Palatin Technologies first developed the compound under the code PT-141 as a treatment for erectile dysfunction. Early studies found that it produced erections in rats and monkeys and a dose-related rise in erectile activity in men [6]. A placebo-controlled study of a nasal spray version in men reported erections starting about 30 minutes after a dose, with flushing and nausea as the most frequent complaints [7].

The company later shifted the program to women, switched to an injection under the skin, and ran the two RECONNECT phase 3 trials from 2015 to 2016 [3]. Palatin licensed North American rights to AMAG Pharmaceuticals, which filed the application, and the FDA approved Vyleesi in June 2019 [2][5]. In December 2023 Palatin sold the product to Cosette Pharmaceuticals [9].

blocks.text: Bremelanotide switches on several melanocortin receptors, which are docking sites on cells that respond to alpha-MSH. It is not selective, but at the approved dose its effects at two subtypes matter most: MC4R, found on nerve cells across the brain, and MC1R, found on the pigment-making cells of the skin [1].

The label states plainly that the way it improves desire is not known [1]. The working idea, drawn from animal research, is that MC4R activity in the hypothalamus (a region at the base of the brain that governs drives such as hunger and sex) feeds into sexual response [5][6]. The action at MC1R explains a known side effect: patches of darker skin.

This is a different approach from flibanserin, the daily pill for the same condition, and from drugs such as sildenafil, which act on blood flow rather than on desire. Bremelanotide does not work on the genitals directly.

Yes. The FDA approved Vyleesi on June 21, 2019, for HSDD that is acquired and generalized, in women who have not reached menopause [2]. The approval rests on the two randomized, placebo-controlled RECONNECT trials [1][3].

The approval is narrow. It does not cover postmenopausal women, men, or use to enhance sexual performance [1]. Products sold online as "PT-141" for injection are not Vyleesi and have not been reviewed by the FDA for quality or dose.

Vyleesi is prescribed for low sexual desire that developed in a woman who previously had no such problem, occurs regardless of partner or situation, causes marked distress, and cannot be traced to a separate illness, a mental health condition, trouble in the relationship, or a drug [1]. The label says to stop after eight weeks if there is no improvement [1].

In the trials, 1,267 women with an average age of 39 were randomized to the drug or placebo for 24 weeks [3]. Both trials met their two main goals, a gain in desire and a drop in distress about low desire, but the size of the change was modest [1]. Far more women stopped early on the drug than on placebo, mostly because of side effects [1].

An independent reanalysis of the trial data published in 2023 found that several prespecified outcomes had gone unreported, that most showed effects ranging from none to small, and that the questionnaires used have limited evidence of validity in this group of women [4]. The authors concluded that the benefits are statistically modest [4].

Nausea is the main problem. It affected 40% of women on the drug against about 1% on placebo, 13% needed anti-nausea medicine, and 8% left the trials because of it, though it tended to ease with the second dose [1].

blocks.text: Each dose raises blood pressure for a few hours, by up to about 6 mmHg systolic and 3 mmHg diastolic, and slows the heart by up to 5 beats a minute, usually settling within 12 hours [1]. For that reason the label rules it out for anyone whose hypertension is not under control or who has established cardiovascular disease [1].

About 1% of trial users developed darker patches on the face, gums, or breasts, and in a separate study of daily dosing for eight days the figure was 38% [1]. The risk was higher in people with darker skin, and the patches did not always fade after stopping [1]. The drug can also slow stomach emptying and sharply lower blood levels of oral naltrexone, a medicine for alcohol and opioid dependence [1].

PT-141 is the old development code for the same molecule, and it is widely sold online as a powder for injection, often marketed to men and bodybuilders. These products are not Vyleesi. A forensic study of samples seized by Italian police alongside anabolic steroids identified both bremelanotide and its chemical relative melanotan II in black-market vials [8].

Unregulated vials carry no assurance of purity, sterility, or the amount of peptide inside. The blood pressure and skin darkening effects seen in the approved product apply to the molecule itself, and the trials never studied use by men or daily use [1].

name: Brilacidin
evidenceNote: Brilacidin has been through small phase 2 trials in skin infection, mouth sores from radiation, and COVID-19, but results sit mostly in trial registries rather than peer-reviewed papers, the COVID-19 trial was negative, and no phase 3 trial has been run.
summary: A lab-designed small molecule that mimics the body's defense peptides. Tested in phase 2 for infections and radiation mouth sores; never approved.
keyTakeaway: Brilacidin is a synthetic small molecule built to copy how the body's own antimicrobial peptides attack germs, though it is not itself a peptide. It has reached phase 2 trials for skin infections, for the painful mouth sores caused by head and neck radiation, and for hospitalized COVID-19. In the mouth sore trial, 9 of 21 patients on a brilacidin rinse developed severe sores against 15 of 25 on placebo. The COVID-19 trial showed no benefit. It is not FDA-approved, and no phase 3 trial has started.

blocks.text: Brilacidin is an experimental anti-infective drug designed from scratch to behave like host defense peptides, the short antimicrobial proteins such as defensins that the body uses as a first line of defense against germs [1]. Despite the comparison, it is not a peptide. It is an arylamide, a small molecule built on a non-protein scaffold, chosen because natural peptides break down quickly and are hard to manufacture as drugs [1][10].

It has been tested as an intravenous drip for skin infections, as an oral rinse for mouth sores caused by cancer radiation, and as an infusion for COVID-19 [3][4][5]. A tablet meant to release the drug in the colon has also been tried in healthy volunteers [6].

Brilacidin came out of research into compounds that could recreate the shape and charge of defense peptides on a small, stable frame, under the early code name PMX-30063 [1][2]. Its first clinical target was drug-resistant skin infection. The 2014 skin trial was sponsored by Cellceutix and the later trials by Innovation Pharmaceuticals, as the work broadened to oral mucositis and then COVID-19 [3][4][5].

blocks.text: Like natural defensins, brilacidin targets the membranes that wrap microbes. In the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus it depolarized the cell membrane, collapsing the electrical charge the cell needs to survive, to a degree similar to the antibiotic daptomycin [2]. The bacteria's genetic stress response looked much like their response to LL-37, a human defense peptide, pointing to damage to the cell wall and membrane [2].

In laboratory work it has also shown activity against viruses and fungi. In lung cells grown in culture it blocked SARS-CoV-2, apparently by damaging the virus and interfering with its entry into cells [7]. A second team found it also binds heparan sulfate, a sugar-coated molecule on the cell surface that several coronaviruses use to attach [8]. In fungi, it made existing drugs such as caspofungin work better, and the combination cleared Aspergillus lung infection in immunosuppressed mice [9]. None of these antiviral or antifungal effects has been shown in a human trial.

No. Brilacidin is an investigational drug and has not been approved by the FDA or any other major regulator for any use. All four of its studies listed on ClinicalTrials.gov are marked completed, the most recent in 2021, and none is a phase 3 trial [3][4][5][6].

Because it is a new chemical made only for clinical study, it is not a compounding ingredient and has no legitimate retail form. Anything sold online under the name has no connection to the trial material.

The oral mucositis trial is the most encouraging result. Oral mucositis is painful inflammation and ulceration of the mouth lining, common in people receiving radiation for head and neck cancer. In this phase 2 study, 61 patients rinsed with either brilacidin or water during radiation and chemotherapy [4]. Among those who received at least 55 Gy of radiation, severe mouth sores developed in 9 of 21 on brilacidin and 15 of 25 on placebo [4]. The gap was wider in patients given cisplatin every three weeks, 2 of 8 against 10 of 14, though those groups were very small [4].

blocks.text: The COVID-19 trial was clearly negative. Hospitalized patients received three or five days of brilacidin infusions or placebo on top of standard care, and the time to sustained recovery was about the same in every group [5]. The skin infection trial compared single doses and a three-day course of brilacidin with a week of daptomycin, but its results were never posted to the registry [3]. A 2017 review noted that brilacidin had completed two phase 2 studies in skin infection [1].

Everything else is preclinical. Activity against coronaviruses, Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, and dozens of fungal isolates comes from cell cultures and mice [7][8][9][10]. Several of these papers include authors who advise or work for the developer, which is common in early drug research but worth knowing [7][8][9].

name: Cagrilintide
evidenceNote: On its own, cagrilintide has one 26-week phase 2 randomized trial and a monotherapy arm inside a phase 3 trial; the much larger evidence base belongs to its combination with semaglutide.
summary: Cagrilintide is a once-weekly amylin analog from Novo Nordisk, in phase 3 trials alone and filed with the FDA in combination with semaglutide as CagriSema.
keyTakeaway: Cagrilintide is an injectable, long-acting copy of amylin, a fullness hormone the pancreas releases alongside insulin. In a 26-week phase 2 trial of 706 adults with obesity, the highest weekly dose produced 10.8% weight loss, against 3.0% on placebo and 9.0% on daily liraglutide. It is not FDA-approved. A standalone phase 3 trial began in late 2025, and the combination with semaglutide (CagriSema) has been under FDA review since December 2025. Vials sold online as research cagrilintide are unregulated and outside any trial.

blocks.text: Cagrilintide is an experimental weight management drug developed by Novo Nordisk. It is a modified version of amylin, a 37-amino-acid hormone that beta cells in the pancreas release together with insulin after a meal. Natural amylin lasts only minutes in the blood, so cagrilintide carries a fatty acid side chain that binds albumin and stretches its action to a single injection per week [1].

It is being developed two ways. As a single drug, it is in phase 3 testing for weight management [5]. Paired with semaglutide in one weekly injection, it forms CagriSema, which has finished its main phase 3 trials and is awaiting an FDA decision [2][3][4]. An older amylin drug, pramlintide, has been approved for diabetes since 2005, but it is injected before every meal and is not approved for weight loss.

Amylin acts on receptors in the brainstem and hypothalamus that register when the body has eaten enough. These amylin receptors are calcitonin receptors paired with helper proteins, and cagrilintide activates both the paired and unpaired forms [1]. The result is earlier fullness at meals. Amylin also slows the emptying of the stomach and dampens glucagon, the hormone that pushes blood sugar up after eating.

This pathway is separate from GLP-1, the target of semaglutide and tirzepatide. That is the rationale for combining the two: each signals fullness through a different receptor, and in trials the pair produced more weight loss than either alone [2]. Whether the combination also adds digestive side effects is one of the questions regulators are weighing.

No. Cagrilintide is an investigational drug in the United States, alone and in combination. Novo Nordisk submitted a new drug application for CagriSema, a fixed weekly dose of cagrilintide 2.4 mg and semaglutide 2.4 mg, on December 18, 2025, and the company said it expected the review to run through 2026 [4]. No decision had been announced as of early November 2026.

blocks.text: Cagrilintide is not an ingredient in any approved medicine. Products sold online as research cagrilintide have no FDA oversight of their purity, sterility, or actual content.

The single-drug evidence rests mainly on one phase 2 trial. Adults without diabetes were assigned to one of five weekly cagrilintide doses, daily liraglutide 3.0 mg, or placebo for 26 weeks. Every dose beat placebo, and weight loss rose with dose, from 6.0% at 0.3 mg to 10.8% at 4.5 mg, compared with 3.0% on placebo. The top dose also edged out liraglutide, which produced 9.0% [1].

blocks.text: REDEFINE 1 also included a small group on cagrilintide by itself, alongside groups on semaglutide alone and on placebo, so that the contribution of each drug could be separated [2]. The headline numbers in that trial describe the combination, not cagrilintide alone, which is easy to miss in coverage of the results.

Side effects follow the pattern of other appetite drugs. In phase 2, 41% to 63% of people on cagrilintide had digestive complaints, mostly nausea, constipation, and diarrhea, against 32% on placebo, and injection site reactions were also common [1]. With the combination, digestive effects were reported by 79.6% of participants in REDEFINE 1 and 72.5% in REDEFINE 2, mostly mild to moderate and short-lived [2][3]. There are no long-term safety data for cagrilintide alone.

sections.heading: What is the difference between cagrilintide and CagriSema?

blocks.text: Cagrilintide is the single amylin analog. CagriSema is a combination product that delivers cagrilintide and semaglutide together in one weekly injection [4]. Almost all of the phase 3 data and the FDA filing concern CagriSema. The standalone RENEW program is meant to show what cagrilintide does by itself over a longer period and in more people than the phase 2 trial could [5]. Until those results are out, any claim about cagrilintide by itself rests on 26 weeks of data.

class: Amylin analog plus GLP-1 agonist combination
evidenceNote: Several large phase 3 randomized trials, including REDEFINE 1 (3,417 adults) and REDEFINE 2 (1,206 adults with type 2 diabetes), have been published. It is under FDA review but not yet approved.

keyTakeaway: CagriSema is Novo Nordisk's weekly injection combining cagrilintide, a long-acting copy of the satiety hormone amylin, with semaglutide, the GLP-1 drug in Wegovy. In the 68-week REDEFINE 1 trial, adults without diabetes lost 20.4% of body weight against 3.0% on placebo. In a head-to-head trial it fell short of matching tirzepatide. Novo filed with the FDA in December 2025 and expects a decision in late 2026. It is not approved, and anything sold online under the name is not the real drug.

blocks.text: CagriSema is a fixed-dose combination of two peptides given together once a week: cagrilintide 2.4 mg and semaglutide 2.4 mg. Semaglutide is the GLP-1 receptor agonist already sold as Wegovy and Ozempic. Cagrilintide is a long-acting analog of amylin, a hormone the pancreas releases alongside insulin after a meal [1][3].

Novo Nordisk developed the pairing to test whether two satiety signals produce more weight loss than one. It is being studied for weight management in adults with obesity or overweight with related conditions, and separately in type 2 diabetes [4][6].

Amylin helps signal fullness after eating. In a 26-week phase 2 trial of 706 adults, cagrilintide alone produced weight loss of 6.0% to 10.8% depending on dose, against 3.0% on placebo, and its top dose edged out liraglutide, an older GLP-1 drug [1]. Nausea, constipation, and diarrhea were the most common side effects [1].

Semaglutide works on a different receptor. It mimics GLP-1, a gut hormone released after meals that raises insulin when blood sugar is high and dampens appetite. At 2.4 mg a week, semaglutide alone already has established weight-loss and cardiovascular benefits [3].

Because amylin and GLP-1 act through separate receptors, the idea is that their effects add up. Novo describes the combination as showing that cagrilintide adds weight loss beyond what GLP-1 biology achieves alone [5]. REDEFINE 1 included small single-drug arms to test that, alongside its main comparison with placebo [3].

No, not as of November 2026. Novo Nordisk submitted a new drug application to the FDA for CagriSema 2.4 mg/2.4 mg in adults with overweight or obesity, based on the REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 2 trials, which together enrolled more than 4,600 adults [2].

In its report for the first nine months of 2026, Novo listed a US decision as expected in the fourth quarter of 2026 and said it is preparing a US launch in early 2027, subject to approval [6]. Novo has also filed in China, where it expects a decision in the first half of 2028 [6].

blocks.text: REDEFINE 1 randomized 3,417 adults without diabetes who had a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with a weight-related condition. Over 68 weeks, on top of lifestyle advice, the combination group lost an average of 20.4% of body weight compared with 3.0% on placebo, a difference of 17.3 percentage points. More people on CagriSema reached each threshold the trial tracked, up to 30% weight loss [3].

REDEFINE 2 tested the same doses in 1,206 adults with type 2 diabetes. Weight fell 13.7% against 3.4% on placebo over 68 weeks, and 73.5% reached a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c, a three-month blood sugar average) of 6.5% or less, compared with 15.9% on placebo [4]. Weight loss was smaller than in the trial of people without diabetes.

blocks.text: The head-to-head comparison was a setback. In REDEFINE 4, 809 adults received CagriSema or tirzepatide 15 mg for 84 weeks with everyone aware of their assignment. If everyone stayed on treatment, weight loss was 23.0% with CagriSema and 25.5% with tirzepatide; counting everyone regardless of adherence, it was 20.2% and 23.6%. The trial failed to show CagriSema was no worse than tirzepatide [5].

Side effects are mainly digestive. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or abdominal pain affected 79.6% of people on CagriSema in REDEFINE 1 versus 39.9% on placebo, and 72.5% versus 34.4% in REDEFINE 2. Most episodes were mild to moderate and faded over time [3][4]. Longer and higher-dose trials are still running [6].

Because the product is not approved, no pharmacy can legally dispense genuine CagriSema in the United States. Vials marketed online as cagrilintide, or as cagrilintide blended with semaglutide, are research chemicals of unknown content and purity. The trial results above apply only to Novo Nordisk's product given at the studied doses under medical supervision [3].

name: Calcitonin-salmon
evidenceNote: Calcitonin-salmon has been FDA-approved since 1975. Its osteoporosis label is now a fallback use, because the FDA states that fracture reduction has not been demonstrated and a pooled analysis found more cancers in treated patients.
summary: Calcitonin-salmon is an FDA-approved hormone for Paget's disease, high blood calcium and, as a last resort, postmenopausal osteoporosis, with a cancer-risk caveat.
keyTakeaway: Calcitonin-salmon is a synthetic copy of the calcitonin hormone found in salmon, which acts on bone more strongly and for longer than the human version. The FDA approved it in 1975, and it is still sold as an injection for Paget's disease and high blood calcium, and as a nasal spray and injection for postmenopausal osteoporosis when other drugs are not suitable. A 5-year trial found 33% fewer new spine fractures at one dose, but the current label says fracture reduction has not been shown. A pooled analysis of 21 trials found cancers in 4.1% of treated patients against 2.9% on placebo.

blocks.text: Calcitonin is a peptide hormone released by specialized cells in the thyroid gland of mammals, and by a related gland in birds and fish. Calcitonin-salmon is a synthetic 32 amino acid peptide with the same sequence as the hormone found in salmon. It acts like human calcitonin, but it is more potent per milligram and its effect lasts longer, which is why the fish form became the drug [1].

It was one of the first peptide drugs for bone disease. The injection is sold as Miacalcin and as several generics, and the nasal spray is available as generic calcitonin salmon [1][2]. Over the last decade its role has narrowed sharply as better osteoporosis drugs arrived and safety reviews raised questions about cancer.

Bone is constantly rebuilt. Osteoclasts dissolve old bone, and osteoblasts lay down new bone. Calcitonin receptors have been found on both cell types. A single injection sharply but briefly suppresses bone breakdown, and with long-term use a smaller, lasting reduction remains, linked to fewer and less active osteoclasts [1]. It also has direct effects on the kidney and the gut, raising how much calcium, phosphate and sodium the kidneys pass into urine [1].

That explains its approved uses. In Paget's disease, bone turnover runs out of control in parts of the skeleton, and slowing osteoclasts calms it. In hypercalcemia (too much calcium in the blood), the drop in calcium is largest in people whose bone is being broken down quickly [1]. In osteoporosis, it slows bone loss, though more weakly than modern drugs. In the PROOF trial, a marker of bone breakdown (C-telopeptide) fell by only 12% to 14% compared with placebo [3].

Absorption depends on the route. About two thirds of an injected dose reaches the bloodstream whether it is given into muscle or under the skin [1]. The nasal spray delivers only about 3% to 5% as much as an injection into muscle [2]. That gap helps explain why the spray and the injection carry different approved uses.

Yes. Calcitonin-salmon was first approved in the United States in 1975, and both the injection and the nasal spray remain approved [1][2]. Its labels have been rewritten to reflect a much smaller place in treatment.

items.text: First US approval of calcitonin-salmon [1].
PROOF trial published: the 200 IU nasal spray dose cut new spine fractures by 33% over 5 years, while the 100 IU and 400 IU doses did not [3].
The EMA concludes that long-term calcitonin use carries a small rise in cancer risk and that its benefits in osteoporosis no longer outweigh that risk. The nasal spray is withdrawn in Europe [4].

Osteoporosis use limited to cases where alternatives are not suitable, with the statement that fracture reduction has not been demonstrated and a note to re-evaluate the need for continued therapy periodically [1][2].

blocks.text: The injection is approved for three uses: symptomatic Paget's disease of bone when other treatments are not suitable, hypercalcemia, and postmenopausal osteoporosis when other treatments are not suitable [1]. The nasal spray has a single approval, postmenopausal osteoporosis in women more than 5 years past menopause, again only when alternatives are unsuitable. Its label adds that the spray has not been shown to increase bone density in early postmenopausal women [2].

The evidence for fracture prevention comes mostly from PROOF, a 5-year, placebo-controlled trial in 1,255 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Only the middle dose reached significance, and fewer than half the women (511) completed 5 years, which makes the result harder to trust [3].

In Europe the picture is narrower still. Since 2012 the EMA has limited calcitonin to injection or infusion for Paget's disease in people who cannot use alternatives, for preventing sudden bone loss after immobilization (such as after a recent fracture), and for cancer-related hypercalcemia, with treatment kept as short as possible [4].

With the injection, the most common side effects are nausea with or without vomiting (about 10%), inflammation at the injection site (about 10%), and flushing of the face or hands (2% to 5%) [1]. With the nasal spray, the common ones are runny nose, nosebleeds and other nasal symptoms, back pain, joint pain and headache [2].

items: Cancer: in a pooled analysis of 21 randomized trials of the nasal spray and experimental oral forms, malignancies were reported in 4.1% of treated patients against 2.9% on placebo [2].
Serious allergic reactions, including bronchospasm, throat swelling and anaphylaxis, have been reported [1][2].
Low blood calcium, which can cause muscle cramps, twitching and seizures. Low calcium must be corrected before treatment begins [2].
Antibodies against calcitonin-salmon can develop and may make the drug stop working [1][2].

blocks.text: The EMA estimated the added cancer risk in long-term use at roughly 0.7% for the oral form studied in trials up to 2.4% for the nasal spray, while noting that absolute cancer rates in the trials were low [4]. That trade-off, a small cancer signal against a weak fracture benefit, is what moved regulators to push calcitonin to the back of the line for osteoporosis.

name: Carnosine
evidenceNote: Oral carnosine has a handful of small randomized trials, mostly measuring blood markers over a few months. Its skin claims rest on lab and donated-skin studies, plus one trial of a cream that also contained urea and arginine.
summary: Carnosine is a two-amino-acid peptide the body makes in muscle and brain. It is sold in skin creams and as a supplement; neither form is FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Carnosine is a dipeptide of beta-alanine and histidine that the body makes and stores in muscle and brain, where it buffers acid, binds metals and mops up reactive molecules. Cosmetic brands add it to creams for its antioxidant and anti-glycation effects, shown in lab and donated-skin models. Oral supplement trials are small: one 43-person trial found lower blood sugar after a glucose drink over 14 weeks. It is not an FDA-approved drug, and serum enzymes break swallowed carnosine down quickly.

atGlance.value: Not approved as a drug; sold as a cosmetic ingredient and a supplement

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Buffers acid, binds metals, neutralizes reactive molecules and blocks sugar damage to proteins

blocks.text: Carnosine is a dipeptide, a molecule made of two amino acids, in this case beta-alanine and L-histidine. It was identified in 1900 as an abundant compound in meat, and in people it is concentrated in skeletal muscle and other excitable tissues such as the brain [1].

The body builds carnosine itself, and diet adds more from meat and fish. Commercially it shows up in two places: in skin creams and serums as an antioxidant ingredient, and in capsules sold as a dietary supplement. Neither use goes through FDA drug approval [6][7].

Carnosine has four well-described chemical properties: it buffers acid, it binds metal ions such as copper and zinc, it acts as an antioxidant, and it helps prevent advanced glycation end products (AGEs), the damage sugars and fats do when they bond to proteins [1]. Most of this activity comes from the imidazole ring on histidine [1].

In muscle, the buffering role helps soak up acid during hard exercise. In skin, the interest is in AGEs and oxidative stress, both of which build up with sun exposure and age and contribute to stiffer, more lined skin. An important limit for oral use is serum carnosinase, an enzyme in human blood that splits carnosine back into its two amino acids, so swallowed carnosine does not survive long in circulation [1].

No. Carnosine is not an approved drug for any condition in the United States. In creams and serums it is a cosmetic ingredient, and FDA does not approve cosmetics or their ingredients before sale, apart from color additives; the maker is responsible for safety [6].

As a capsule or powder, carnosine is sold as a dietary supplement. FDA has no authority to approve supplements for safety or effectiveness, and a product that claims to treat or prevent a disease is legally a drug, even if it is labelled as a supplement [7]. Claims that carnosine treats diabetes, reverses ageing or heals skin disease are therefore not claims any carnosine product has been approved to make.

Skin evidence is mostly preclinical. In a study published in 2024 and co-authored by an ingredient supplier, pieces of donated human skin were kept alive in culture and exposed to simulated sunlight. Skin treated topically with 0.2% or 2% L-carnosine produced fewer reactive oxygen species and fewer AGEs, and showed smaller changes in a panel of 11 genes linked to sun damage [2]. That is a model of what light does to skin, not a measure of how people's skin looks over time.

The only controlled trial of a carnosine cream on human skin used a product that also contained urea and arginine. In 50 people with type 2 diabetes and severely dry feet, eight months of the combination cream improved dryness scores and hydration more than a glycerol cream, but the study was assessor-blinded rather than double-blind, and carnosine's own contribution cannot be separated out [3].

Less oxidative stress and AGE build-up with topical carnosine [2]

blocks.text: Oral trials are larger in number but still small. In a 2024 randomized trial, 43 adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes took 2 g of carnosine or placebo daily for 14 weeks; glucose was 1.31 and 1.60 mmol/L lower at 90 and 120 minutes into a glucose tolerance test, with no change in body composition [4]. A meta-analysis of nine trials found modest drops in some inflammation and oxidative stress markers but not others [5]. None of these trials measured skin.
Taken together, carnosine has a sound chemical rationale and some early human signals on blood markers, but no trial shows that a carnosine cream changes wrinkles, firmness or skin ageing in people.

The published summaries of the trials above report benefits but say little about harms, and the studies were too small and short to pick up uncommon effects [3][4][5]. There is no systematic safety record for long-term use of carnosine creams. Topical products also contain other ingredients that are more likely than carnosine to cause irritation, and supplements are not checked by FDA for contents before sale [7].

name: Cerebrolysin
evidenceNote: Randomized trials exist in stroke (7 trials, 1,773 people) and vascular dementia (6 trials, 597 people), so it sits in the moderate tier. Independent reviews rate the certainty low to moderate and find no survival benefit in stroke.
summary: A mixture of small peptides and amino acids extracted from pig brain, used by IV in many countries for stroke and dementia. Not FDA-approved; reviews find weak evidence.
keyTakeaway: Cerebrolysin is an extract of pig brain, broken down into short peptide fragments and single amino acids, and given by IV infusion in more than 50 countries for stroke, dementia and brain injury. It is not approved in the US. A 2023 Cochrane review of 7 stroke trials found it probably does not reduce deaths and may increase non-fatal serious adverse events. A Cochrane review in vascular dementia found modest gains in memory tests, but from small, high-risk studies, and judged the evidence weak. Animal studies show protective effects that human trials have not clearly confirmed.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Not approved in the US; used clinically in more than 50 other countries.

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Thought to mimic growth factors that protect neurons; the active parts of the mixture are not fully defined.

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Stroke trials: no effect on deaths. Vascular dementia: small cognitive gains, very low-certainty evidence.

atGlance.label: How it's taken
atGlance.value: A course of daily intravenous infusions, usually in hospital or clinic.

atGlance.value: Moderate research

blocks.text: Cerebrolysin is not a single molecule. It is what remains after proteins from pig brain are digested into small fragments: short peptide chains plus loose amino acids [1]. Because it is an extract, no one sequence defines it, which sets it apart from the synthetic peptides elsewhere in this library.

It is widely prescribed for acute ischemic stroke in Russia, Eastern Europe, China and other parts of Asia [1], and it is also used for vascular dementia, other neurodegenerative conditions and traumatic brain injury [2]. A 2021 review counted more than 50 countries where it is in clinical use, while noting that the US is not one of them [2]. It is given as a series of daily infusions into a vein [3].

The proposed mechanism is that some peptides in the mixture behave like neurotrophic factors, the natural growth signals that keep neurons alive and help them form connections. Reviews describe it as engaging signaling pathways involved in nerve repair and survival, although which components do the work has not been pinned down [2].

Most of the direct evidence comes from animals. In mice engineered to develop Alzheimer-like changes, cerebrolysin increased the number of new neurons forming in the hippocampus, a memory center, and reduced the death of the cells that give rise to them [4]. In rats with a crushed optic nerve, injections into the abdomen or the eye preserved more retinal nerve cells and better visual signals than saline, while injection directly into the nerve caused harm [5].
These are encouraging signals, but they come from controlled injuries in laboratory animals. The human trials below are the real test of whether the effect carries over to people.

No. Cerebrolysin has never been approved by the FDA for any condition, so US doctors cannot prescribe it as an approved medicine [2]. Its regulatory standing elsewhere varies by country, which is how it reaches patients in more than 50 of them [2].

Because it comes from animal brain tissue, its makeup depends on the extraction process rather than a fixed chemical recipe. Imported or online supplies outside a regulated pharmacy chain carry the added uncertainty of where they came from and how they were stored.

Stroke is where cerebrolysin has been tested most. The 2023 Cochrane review pooled seven randomized trials with 1,773 participants, six of cerebrolysin and one of a similar product called Cortexin. Treatment began within 48 hours of the stroke [1].

rows: Death or dependence, quality of life [1]

blocks.text: The reviewers also flagged weaknesses in the trials themselves: unclear methods of randomization in most, high dropout in four, and manufacturer support for three of the multicenter studies [1]. The increase in non-fatal serious events was most visible with a 10-day course of 30 mL a day [1].

For vascular dementia, a 2019 Cochrane review found six randomized trials with 597 people, mostly in China, Russia and Romania. Courses of IV cerebrolysin improved scores on cognitive tests and doctors' global ratings compared with placebo, with no excess of side effects [3]. But the authors rated the evidence very low quality, noted a high risk of bias, and warned that any benefit may be too small to matter in daily life [3].

A separate 2021 meta-analysis of animal-derived brain products across dementia types reached a similar view. Cerebrolysin produced a small improvement in cognition in the short term, with no rise in serious adverse events, but the effect was probably below what patients would notice and the certainty was low to very low [6]. The 2021 literature review describes the clinical results as inconsistent, with several studies finding no clear advantage over placebo [2].

name: Cetrorelix
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2000 after phase 3 trials in IVF, and the drug class is backed by a Cochrane review of 73 randomized trials with more than 12,000 participants.
summary: Cetrorelix (Cetrotide) is an injectable GnRH blocker used during IVF to stop the body from releasing eggs too early.
keyTakeaway: Cetrorelix is a synthetic peptide of ten amino acids that occupies pituitary GnRH receptors, so the hormone surge that triggers ovulation is quickly switched off. Sold as Cetrotide and approved by the FDA in 2000, it is injected under the skin during IVF so that eggs stay in place until the clinic retrieves them. In phase 3 studies, premature LH surges occurred in 0 to 1.9% of women. A Cochrane review found antagonists like it matched older agonist protocols on live birth while lowering the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

blocks.text: Cetrorelix is a synthetic decapeptide, a chain of ten amino acids, built on the structure of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). Five of its positions are replaced with modified amino acids, which turns a hormone that switches the pituitary on into one that switches it off [1]. It is sold as cetrorelix acetate under the brand name Cetrotide.

It is used in fertility clinics during in vitro fertilization (IVF) and related techniques. In these cycles, injected hormones stimulate the ovaries to grow several follicles at once, and cetrorelix keeps the body's own ovulation signal from firing before the eggs are ready to retrieve [1][2].

Before GnRH antagonists, clinics controlled ovulation with GnRH agonists, usually in a long protocol. Agonists first cause a flare of pituitary hormones and need a long period of down-regulation, with low-estrogen side effects along the way. Antagonists act directly and within hours, so they can be started at any point in the follicular phase [4].

items.text: European Commission authorizes Cetrotide to prevent premature ovulation during ovarian stimulation [2]
A French multicenter trial reports no LH surges in 115 women given a single 3 mg dose [3]
FDA approves Cetrotide (NDA 021197), covering 0.25 mg and 3 mg vials [5]

blocks.text: Normally the hypothalamus releases GnRH in pulses, and the pituitary answers with two hormones, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). A sharp rise in LH, called the LH surge, makes a mature follicle release its egg. Cetrorelix competes with natural GnRH for its receptors on pituitary cells, so LH and FSH release falls in proportion to the dose [1].

The effect is fast and reversible. LH suppression begins about two hours after a 0.25 mg injection, and ovulation is postponed rather than permanently blocked [1]. After a single 0.25 mg dose the drug's elimination half-life is about 5 hours, rising to about 20 hours with daily dosing [1].

That speed is what makes flexible scheduling possible. Trials of GnRH antagonists have used fixed daily injections from a set day of stimulation, flexible daily injections started once the lead follicle reaches a certain size, and a single larger injection later in the cycle [4].

Yes. The FDA approved Cetrotide on August 11, 2000. EMD Serono holds the application, and the 0.25 mg strength is the one still marketed in the US, while the 3 mg single-dose vial has been discontinued [5]. In Europe the medicine has been authorized since April 1999 and is held by Merck Europe [2].

The label limits its use to physicians experienced in fertility treatment, and pregnancy must be ruled out before the first dose [1]. It can be self-injected under the skin of the lower abdomen once a patient has been shown how [1].

It has one approved use: preventing an early LH surge in women whose ovaries are being stimulated for assisted reproduction [1]. The label's phase 3 program tested both the daily and single-dose regimens:

In the French trial behind the single-dose data, women on cetrorelix needed a shorter stimulation and less gonadotropin than those on a depot agonist, and had less ovarian hyperstimulation, though they produced fewer eggs and embryos [3].

The wider evidence comes from a 2016 Cochrane review of 73 randomized trials and 12,212 participants comparing GnRH antagonists with the long agonist protocol. It found no clear difference in live birth (odds ratio 1.02) and a lower rate of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with antagonists (odds ratio 0.61) [4].

The trade-offs run both ways. In the same review, cycles were cancelled less often for high hyperstimulation risk with antagonists (odds ratio 0.47) but more often for a poor ovarian response (odds ratio 1.32), and miscarriage rates did not differ [4].

Across 949 women in the clinical program, the most reported adverse events were ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (3.5%), nausea (1.3%), and headache (1.1%), along with mostly mild, short-lived redness or itching at the injection site [1]. Liver enzyme rises were seen in 1 to 2% of patients [1].

Allergic reactions, including anaphylactoid reactions on the first dose, have been reported since approval, so caution is advised for women with allergic conditions [1]. Cetrorelix must not be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, in severe kidney impairment, or by anyone allergic to cetrorelix, mannitol, or other GnRH-related peptides [1].

name: CJC-1295
alsoCalled: DAC:GRF; the no-DAC form is sold as modified GRF 1-29
evidenceNote: The human record is two short placebo-controlled dose studies and one follow-up in healthy volunteers, all measuring hormone levels. No trial has tested muscle, fat, recovery, or any other outcome people buy it for.
summary: CJC-1295 is an unapproved GHRH analog built to last for days. Short studies show higher growth hormone and IGF-1, but no proven benefit for muscle or fat.
keyTakeaway: CJC-1295 is a lab-made version of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) built to last for days rather than minutes. In healthy adults, one injection lifted average growth hormone 2- to 10-fold for six days or more and IGF-1 1.5- to 3-fold, but those studies measured hormones only. No controlled trial has tested muscle gain, fat loss, or recovery. It is not FDA-approved, FDA has recorded serious adverse events with it, it is not on any compounding list, and WADA bans it in sport at all times.

blocks.text: CJC-1295 is a synthetic peptide modeled on the first 29 amino acids of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), the hypothalamic hormone that switches on growth hormone output from the pituitary gland. The natural hormone is broken down within minutes. CJC-1295 carries amino acid swaps that slow that breakdown, and the original version adds a chemical linker called DAC (drug affinity complex) that lets it attach to albumin, the most common protein in blood [1][2].

Researchers studied it in the mid-2000s as a possible long-acting treatment for people whose pituitary still works but releases too little growth hormone [2]. It never reached approval. Today it circulates mainly through online "research peptide" sellers, often in two forms: the long-acting DAC version and a short-acting version without DAC, usually labeled modified GRF 1-29. Only the DAC version has published human data [1].

CJC-1295 binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary cells, the same target as the natural hormone. That prompts the gland to release more of its own growth hormone, which in turn drives the liver to make insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), the hormone that carries out many of growth hormone's effects on tissue [1].

Because the DAC version latches onto albumin after injection, it stays in circulation far longer than natural GHRH. In the first human studies its estimated half-life (the time for blood levels to fall by half) was 5.8 to 8.1 days [1]. A follow-up study in healthy men found that growth hormone still came in pulses after a single injection, as it does naturally, but the baseline level between pulses rose sharply [2]. The claim that this hormone rise builds muscle or burns fat is an inference from growth hormone biology, not something measured in CJC-1295 trials.

No. There is no approved CJC-1295 product for any condition, and no company is known to be pursuing approval. FDA lists CJC-1295 among substances whose nominations for use in pharmacy compounding were withdrawn, so it has no route into the 503A bulk substances program. On the same page, FDA notes it has identified serious adverse events tied to CJC-1295, including a raised heart rate and a body-wide blood vessel widening reaction, and that clinical data on it are limited [4].
In sport, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) names CJC-1295 in its list of growth hormone releasing factors, class S2.2.4, which is banned both in and out of competition [5].

The core human evidence comes from two randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind dose studies in healthy adults aged 21 to 61, run for 28 and 49 days. Participants received one injection or two to three injections spaced a week or two apart. No serious adverse reactions were reported, and the authors described the drug as relatively well tolerated at the two lower dose levels tested [1].

rows: Average growth hormone after one dose
Up 2- to 10-fold, lasting at least 6 days [1]
Above baseline for up to 28 days [1]
Trough growth hormone one week after a dose

blocks.text: These are hormone measurements over days to weeks. None of the studies tracked lean mass, fat mass, strength, sleep, injury healing, or aging markers, and none ran long enough to judge long-term safety. A separate long-acting GHRH product (a version of GHRH attached to polyethylene glycol, not CJC-1295) raised growth hormone in young and older volunteers but also impaired glucose tolerance in some older participants after repeat dosing, a reminder that pushing this hormone axis has metabolic costs [3].

The short-acting no-DAC peptide, which is what many online vendors actually sell, has not been studied in published controlled human trials. Neither has the common pairing of CJC-1295 with ipamorelin, a peptide that acts on a different receptor. Products sold as research chemicals are not checked by any regulator for identity, purity, or dose.

sections.heading: What is the difference between CJC-1295 with and without DAC?

blocks.text: The two products share the modified GHRH backbone but behave very differently in the body. The DAC version binds albumin and lingers for about a week, which is the version tested in the human studies above [1][2]. Without DAC, the peptide is expected to clear far faster, closer to natural GHRH, though its human pharmacology has not been published. Marketing often uses the name CJC-1295 for both, so a label alone does not say which molecule is in a vial or how long it acts.

name: Gonadorelin
evidenceNote: Pulsatile gonadorelin delivered by pump has solid human data in hypothalamic infertility. The way compounded gonadorelin is now marketed, as once or twice daily injections alongside testosterone, has no published controlled trial behind it.
summary: Gonadorelin is a lab copy of the brain hormone GnRH. Its approved brands were discontinued; compounded versions are sold to men on testosterone with little evidence.
keyTakeaway: Gonadorelin is a synthetic copy of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the brain signal that tells the pituitary to release LH and FSH. Delivered in pulses by a pump, it restored ovulation in more than 90% of women with hypothalamic amenorrhea in a 109-patient trial. Both FDA-approved brands, Factrel and Lutrepulse, are discontinued, so today it reaches patients only through compounding pharmacies. Its popular use, daily injections to protect fertility during testosterone therapy, has not been tested in controlled trials. It is banned in male athletes under the WADA code.

blocks.text: Gonadorelin is the drug name for a manufactured version of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), a ten-amino-acid peptide made by nerve cells in the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain. It has the same sequence as the hormone the body makes, which separates it from longer-acting GnRH drugs such as leuprolide or triptorelin that were chemically altered to last longer.

Two gonadorelin products once held FDA approval: Factrel, an injection of gonadorelin hydrochloride approved in 1982, and Lutrepulse, a gonadorelin acetate kit for pump delivery approved in 1989 with orphan drug status. Both are now listed by the FDA as discontinued [1][2]. The gonadorelin sold today is made by compounding pharmacies, which is why it appears in this library as compounded gonadorelin.

items.text: Primate experiments in Ernst Knobil's laboratory show that steady GnRH exposure shuts down LH and FSH release, while pulsed delivery sustains it [5].
FDA approves Factrel (gonadorelin hydrochloride injection) [1].
FDA approves Lutrepulse (gonadorelin acetate) for pump delivery, with orphan drug status [2].
A multicenter trial reports ovulation in more than 90% of women with hypothalamic amenorrhea on pulsatile Lutrepulse [3].
Both brands are discontinued; FDA lists each as no longer marketed [1][2].
Gonadorelin acetate appears on FDA's 503B Category 1 list of bulk substances under evaluation for outsourcing facilities [6].

blocks.text: GnRH travels a very short distance from the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland, where it binds receptors on the cells that make luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). LH drives testosterone production in the testes and ovulation in the ovaries; FSH supports sperm production and egg development.

Timing is the whole story. The brain releases GnRH in bursts, and the pituitary only keeps responding when the signal comes and goes. Classic primate work showed that a continuous supply sharply reduced LH and FSH output rather than raising it [5]. That is why the infertility studies of gonadorelin used portable pumps that deliver small, timed pulses around the clock instead of a single daily dose [3][7].

A 2026 review of peptide approaches for men on testosterone noted that steady GnRH exposure downregulates its receptor, and listed the need for pulsatile delivery as gonadorelin's main practical limitation [8]. Whether one or two injections a day behave more like pulses or more like steady exposure has not been settled in published human studies.

Not as any product that can be bought today. The molecule was approved twice, but both applications are marked discontinued in the FDA's Drugs@FDA database, and no current branded or generic version is on the market [1][2].

Because gonadorelin is an ingredient of drugs the FDA once approved, pharmacies can compound it under federal rules. The FDA's 503B list, last updated in March 2025, places gonadorelin acetate in Category 1 and flags it as a component of an approved drug, which means outsourcing facilities may use it while the agency evaluates it [6]. A compounded product is not reviewed by the FDA for safety, effectiveness, or quality before it is dispensed.
In sport, the 2026 WADA Prohibited List names gonadorelin under section S2.2.1, testosterone-stimulating peptides in males. It is banned at all times, in and out of competition [9].

The strongest data come from pump delivery in people whose brains do not make enough GnRH. In the multicenter trial behind Lutrepulse, 109 women with primary or secondary hypothalamic amenorrhea received intravenous pulses; 91% and 96% ovulated, respectively. Complications at the intravenous line averaged 7%, and 12% of pregnancies were multiples [3]. A Swiss cohort followed 66 women with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea treated by subcutaneous (under the skin) pump over 25 years and reported a live birth rate of 65.9% per treatment, with mostly single-follicle ovulation [7].

In men with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, a condition in which puberty never starts because GnRH is missing, a 2021 meta-analysis pooled seven studies covering 420 patients. Compared with gonadotropin injections, pulsatile GnRH was associated with larger testicular volume and sperm appearing about five months sooner, but sperm counts and pregnancy rates did not differ significantly. The included studies were comparative, not randomized, and the authors called for proper trials [4].

The use driving most compounded sales is different. Clinics prescribe gonadorelin injections to men on testosterone replacement, hoping to keep the testes producing sperm and testosterone of their own. A 2026 narrative review on this question found no clinical studies showing that gonadorelin preserves fertility or testicular size during testosterone therapy, and rated its clinical evidence as limited [8]. Until such trials exist, that use rests on physiology alone.

name: Tesamorelin (off-label)
class: GHRH analog used outside its approved indication
evidenceNote: Outside HIV, two randomized, placebo-controlled trials exist: 60 adults with abdominal obesity and 152 older adults tested for cognition. They are small and short next to the HIV program that won approval, and none tested anti-aging or muscle building.
summary: Tesamorelin is FDA-approved only for belly fat in HIV lipodystrophy. Wellness use for fat loss or aging rests on small trials.
keyTakeaway: Tesamorelin is a 44-amino-acid analog of growth hormone releasing hormone, approved by the FDA since 2010 as Egrifta to reduce excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV lipodystrophy. Wellness clinics also use it off-label for body composition and aging. Outside HIV, a 12-month trial in 60 obese adults cut visceral fat versus placebo, and a 20-week trial in older adults found modest cognitive gains. Because tesamorelin is licensed as a biological product, FDA rules leave no lawful path for compounded copies. It is banned in sport.
