blocks.text: Tesamorelin is a synthetic version of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH), the brain signal that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. It is a chain of 44 amino acids [1]. The approved drug, Egrifta, is made by Theratechnologies and is indicated only to reduce excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV who have lipodystrophy, an abnormal redistribution of body fat linked to HIV treatment [1].

This entry covers its use for other purposes: shrinking visceral fat, the fat packed around the organs, in people without HIV, and general body-composition or anti-aging goals. Prescribing an approved drug for an unapproved purpose is called off-label use. The approved product has its own entry in the library.

Tesamorelin binds GHRH receptors in the pituitary and prompts the gland to release more of its own growth hormone. That in turn raises IGF-1 and its binding protein IGFBP-3, the main messengers of growth hormone's effects in tissues [1]. The label describes growth hormone as having both anabolic (tissue-building) and lipolytic (fat-breaking) actions [1].
Its signature effect in trials is a selective drop in visceral fat with little change in the fat under the skin of the belly or limbs [3][5].

No. Tesamorelin itself has been FDA-approved since 2010, but only for one use. The label also states that it is not indicated for weight loss, that its long-term cardiovascular safety has not been established, and that it must not be used in pregnancy, with active cancer, or with a disrupted hypothalamic-pituitary axis [1].

Two versions are marketed, Egrifta SV and Egrifta WR. The WR form, labeled in March 2025, is an 11.6 mg vial that is mixed once and supplies daily doses for a week, and its label states that the two products differ in dose, mixing, and storage and are not interchangeable [2]. A doctor may legally prescribe either off-label, but no regulator has reviewed evidence for those uses.

The HIV evidence is solid. Among 404 randomized participants with HIV and excess belly fat, visceral fat fell 10.9% over six months on tesamorelin versus 0.6% on placebo, IGF-1 rose, and glucose measures did not change [3]. In an extension, the reduction held at about 18% through 52 weeks, but fat came back in people switched to placebo [4].
Off-label use rests on a much smaller set of trials:

rows: 60 abdominally obese adults without HIV with low growth hormone output; 12 months vs placebo
Visceral fat fell (treatment effect of 35 cm2), with lower triglycerides, CRP, and carotid wall thickness; no change in glucose [5]
152 adults aged 55 to 87, healthy or with mild cognitive impairment; 20 weeks vs placebo
Small improvement in executive function; body fat down 7.4%; IGF-1 up 117%; mild adverse events in 68% vs 36% on placebo [6]

blocks.text: These trials are encouraging for specific measures but do not test what wellness clinics often promise. The obesity trial enrolled people selected for low growth hormone secretion, and the cognition trial was short. Neither looked at muscle strength, longevity, or skin, and the HIV data show that the fat effect disappears once injections stop [4].

Side effects seen with the approved drug apply to any use. In the pooled 26-week HIV trials, injection site reactions occurred in 17% on tesamorelin versus 6% on placebo, and joint pain, muscle pain, and swelling in the limbs were also common [1]. The label warns about raised IGF-1, fluid retention, glucose intolerance, and allergic reactions [1].

Not lawfully, under current FDA policy. Tesamorelin is licensed as a biological product, under BLA 022505 [1], and the FDA states that biological products are not eligible for the exemptions that let 503A pharmacies and 503B outsourcing facilities compound drugs [7]. Compounded drugs in general are not FDA-approved, so their safety, strength, and quality are not checked before sale [7].

A 2026 clinical review lists tesamorelin among growth hormone axis peptides that turn up in online self-administration protocols, where product composition, dose, and stacking with other compounds are uncertain [9]. In competitive sport, the World Anti-Doping Agency's 2026 list names tesamorelin as a prohibited GHRH analog [8].

name: Copper tripeptide-1
evidenceNote: A handful of small randomized human trials exist, on diabetic foot ulcers, venous ulcers, and laser-treated skin, with mixed results. Most of the cosmetic claims rest on cell and animal work and on reviews written by the ingredient's commercial developers.
summary: Copper tripeptide-1 (GHK-Cu) is a copper-bound peptide used in skin care. Small human trials are mixed; most claims come from lab and animal work.
keyTakeaway: Copper tripeptide-1 is the skin-care name for GHK-Cu, a three-amino-acid peptide that grips a copper ion. Cell and animal studies show it can push skin cells toward making collagen and help wounds close. Human trials are few and small: a gel sped healing of diabetic foot ulcers in one 1994 trial, but a cream did no better than placebo on venous ulcers, and blinded raters saw no benefit after laser resurfacing. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug, and FDA has not cleared injectable GHK-Cu for compounding.

blocks.text: Copper tripeptide-1 is a tiny peptide of three amino acids, glycine, histidine, and lysine (written GHK), bound to a copper ion. GHK occurs naturally in human blood plasma, saliva, and urine, and its levels fall with age [1]. It holds copper about as tightly as albumin, the blood protein that normally ferries copper around the body, which is why GHK and GHK-Cu are usually discussed together [3].

In skin care it appears in serums, creams, and post-procedure products, often listed under its ingredient name copper tripeptide-1. Separately, GHK-Cu is sold online in vials for injection as a so-called research peptide. These are different uses with different risks, and almost all of the human data concern products applied to skin or wounds.

In laboratory studies, GHK-Cu acts like a repair signal. It prompts fibroblasts (the cells that build the skin's support layer) to make collagen, elastin, decorin, and glycosaminoglycans, the cushioning sugars of the dermis. It also adjusts the enzymes that break down that matrix and the inhibitors that restrain them, which suggests a role in remodeling tissue rather than simply adding more of it [1][3].

Other reported actions include drawing immune and blood-vessel cells to a wound, lowering markers of oxidative stress, and calming inflammation [3]. In mice with lung injury, GHK-Cu reduced the inflammatory signals TNF-alpha and IL-6 [8]. Analyses of public gene-expression databases suggest GHK shifts the activity of thousands of human genes [1][2]. These are computational and preclinical findings. They show what the molecule can do in a dish or an animal, not what a cream does on a human face.
No drug containing GHK-Cu is FDA-approved. In skin-care products it is used as a cosmetic ingredient, and cosmetics are not approved by FDA before sale.

Compounding is a separate question. Injectable GHK-Cu was nominated for pharmacy compounding and then withdrawn; FDA notes it may trigger immune reactions because the peptide can clump and carry impurities, and that human safety data are limited [10]. For routes other than injection, FDA moved GHK-Cu back into Category 1 (under evaluation) in May 2026 and says it plans to ask its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee about adding it to the 503A bulks list before the end of February 2027 [9].
The human record is short. Three randomized trials tested GHK-Cu on damaged skin, and they did not agree.

rows: Median plantar ulcer closure 98.5% with GHK-Cu gel vs 60.8% with vehicle; fewer infections
A 0.4% GHK-Cu cream was no better than placebo; silver sulfadiazine outperformed both
No difference in redness, wrinkles, or skin quality by blinded rating; patients using GHK-Cu rated their skin better (p = 0.04)

blocks.text: That positive ulcer trial did not lead to an approved GHK-Cu drug. Much of the wider literature on GHK-Cu as an anti-aging ingredient, including the most cited reviews, comes from one research group whose listed contact is a skin-care company [1][2]. Those reviews describe firmer skin, fewer fine lines, and better skin density in cosmetic testing, but independent, placebo-controlled trials of finished cosmetic products with blinded measurements are scarce [1].

Injection has been tested only in animals. In rats recovering from knee ligament reconstruction, weekly joint injections of GHK-Cu for four weeks made the knee tighter at six weeks, but the advantage had gone by twelve weeks, once treatment had stopped [7]. No human trial of injected GHK-Cu has been published.

The small topical trials did not report notable harms, and the diabetic ulcer study saw fewer infections with the gel than with vehicle [5]. That is not the same as a well-characterized safety profile. For injection, FDA's concern is immunogenicity, the chance that the body mounts an immune response to the peptide or to aggregated and impure material in a vial, and it notes there are limited human data to judge this [10].

name: Corticotropin
alsoCalled: ACTH gel, repository corticotropin injection (Acthar Gel, Purified Cortrophin Gel)
evidenceNote: Corticotropin gel has been FDA-approved since 1952. Its 2010 infantile spasms approval rests on controlled trials, while many of its older adult indications date from an era before modern trial standards.
summary: Corticotropin gel is a long-acting pituitary hormone injection, FDA-approved since 1952, used for infantile spasms, MS flares, and inflammatory disease.
keyTakeaway: Corticotropin, or ACTH, is the pituitary hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol. As a slow-release gel extracted from pig pituitaries, it has been FDA-approved since 1952 and is sold as Acthar Gel and Purified Cortrophin Gel. Acthar is the only one approved for infantile spasms, where a randomized trial found 13 of 15 infants responded to high-dose ACTH versus 4 of 14 on prednisone. Both are approved for multiple sclerosis flares and a long list of rheumatic, eye, skin, and kidney conditions. Side effects mirror long-term steroid use, including infection risk, high blood pressure, and mood changes.

blocks.text: Corticotropin, also called adrenocorticotropic hormone or ACTH, is a 39-amino-acid peptide made by the pituitary gland at the base of the brain. Its main job is to signal the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys, to release cortisol, the body's main stress and anti-inflammatory steroid [1].

As a medicine, corticotropin is given as a repository injection: the hormone is suspended in gelatin so that it is released slowly over hours after a shot into muscle or under the skin. Two products are sold in the United States. Acthar Gel is described in its label as a naturally sourced complex mixture of modified pig ACTH and related pituitary peptides [1]. Purified Cortrophin Gel, made by ANI Pharmaceuticals, is also derived from pig pituitaries and contains pig ACTH(1-39) with related peptides [2].
Both gels are distinct from cosyntropin, a synthetic ACTH fragment that has its own entry in this library.

items.text: Acthar Gel receives FDA approval [3].
Purified Cortrophin Gel receives FDA approval [6].
A randomized, blinded study finds high-dose ACTH far more effective than prednisone for infantile spasms [4].
FDA approves Acthar Gel as monotherapy for infantile spasms in children under 2 [5].
The Acthar Gel label, which now includes a single-dose SelfJect injector for adults, is updated with revised contraindications and hypersensitivity warnings [1].

blocks.text: Injected corticotropin acts like the body's own ACTH. It binds receptors on the adrenal cortex and drives the release of cortisol, corticosterone, aldosterone (a salt-regulating hormone), and weak androgens. With prolonged high doses, the adrenal glands enlarge and keep producing high levels of these hormones [1]. Its side effects come mainly from those released steroids [1].

ACTH is one of the melanocortin peptides, and the Acthar label notes that it also binds melanocortin receptors outside the adrenal glands [1]. What role those receptors play in treatment is not settled, and the label states plainly that its mechanism in infantile spasms is unknown [1].

Pure ACTH injected into a vein disappears from the blood within about 15 minutes. The gelatin depot stretches that out: in a study of 20 healthy volunteers given one intramuscular shot of Purified Cortrophin Gel, cortisol peaked at a median of 8 hours [2].

Yes. Acthar Gel has been approved since 1952 [3] and Purified Cortrophin Gel since 1954 [6]. Both are prescription-only and are given by injection into a muscle or under the skin; the labels forbid intravenous use [1][2].

The two products are not interchangeable on paper. Only Acthar Gel carries the infantile spasms indication, which the FDA added in 2010 under a separate application [5]. Purified Cortrophin Gel lists a set of adult inflammatory and autoimmune indications, including some, such as acute gouty arthritis and severe psoriasis, that do not appear on the Acthar label [2].
The Acthar Gel label lists these uses [1]:

items: Infantile spasms, a severe seizure disorder of babies, as the only treatment in children under 2 [1]
Acute flares of multiple sclerosis in adults [1]
Short-term add-on treatment in psoriatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis [1]
Flares of lupus and dermatomyositis [1]
Severe erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, serious skin reactions [1]
Serum sickness, an allergic reaction [1]
Severe inflammation of the eye, including uveitis, keratitis, and optic neuritis [1]
Symptomatic sarcoidosis [1]
Inducing remission of protein loss in certain types of nephrotic syndrome, a kidney disorder [1]

blocks.text: For infantile spasms, the strongest evidence is a 1996 randomized, blinded study of 29 infants. After two weeks, 13 of 15 infants given high-dose ACTH stopped having spasms and lost the chaotic brain wave pattern called hypsarrhythmia, compared with 4 of 14 given prednisone [4]. For multiple sclerosis, the label says controlled trials showed that ACTH speeds recovery from a flare but that there is no evidence it changes the long-term course of the disease [1].

Purified Cortrophin Gel's label covers a similar adult list but adds acute gouty arthritis, severe psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and allergic conjunctivitis, and it does not include infantile spasms [2]. For many of the adult conditions, both labels frame corticotropin as short-term or add-on treatment to carry a patient through a flare, with longer use reserved for selected cases [1][2].
Most side effects come from the steroid hormones corticotropin releases, and they grow with dose and length of treatment [1]. Warnings on the label include:

items: Higher risk of new infections and reactivation of hidden ones, such as tuberculosis, with symptoms that may be masked [1]
Cushing's syndrome with long use, and adrenal insufficiency (too little cortisol) if stopped suddenly [1]
Raised blood pressure, fluid retention, and low potassium [1]
Stomach ulcers, bleeding, or perforation [1]
Mood changes, insomnia, depression, and psychosis [1]
Worsened diabetes, cataracts, glaucoma, slowed growth in children, and bone loss [1]
Allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, especially in people sensitive to pig proteins [1]

blocks.text: In infants treated for infantile spasms with the recommended twice-daily regimen, the most common problems were infections (20%), high blood pressure (11%), and irritability (7%) [1]. Commonly reported effects after approval include injection site reactions, fatigue, swelling, insomnia, headache, and raised blood sugar [1]. Corticotropin is not used in people with scleroderma, osteoporosis, uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart failure, recent surgery, or peptic ulcer, among other conditions [1].

name: Cosyntropin
evidenceNote: FDA-approved as Cortrosyn for testing adrenal function, with generic versions on the market. Its role in diagnosis is backed by an Endocrine Society guideline and a patient-level meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy.
summary: Cosyntropin is a lab-made fragment of ACTH used in the short stimulation test that checks whether the adrenal glands can make enough cortisol.
keyTakeaway: Cosyntropin is a synthetic copy of the first 24 amino acids of ACTH, the pituitary hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol. It is FDA-approved, sold as Cortrosyn and as generics, and used almost entirely as a diagnostic: a clinician injects it and measures cortisol about 30 minutes later. A weak rise points to adrenal insufficiency, a condition in which the body cannot make enough cortisol. The Endocrine Society calls the 250 microgram short test the gold standard for diagnosing primary adrenal insufficiency. It is a one-off test drug, not a treatment, and serious reactions are rare.

blocks.text: Cosyntropin is a lab-built chain that copies the opening 24 of the 39 amino acids in natural ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone), the signal the pituitary gland sends to the adrenal glands. It is supplied as a freeze-dried powder that is mixed with saline just before use [1].

Its job is diagnostic. Doctors use it to find out whether the adrenal glands can respond to a strong signal by making cortisol, the hormone that helps the body cope with stress, illness and low blood sugar. A low resting cortisol level on its own is not enough to make the diagnosis, so a stimulation test with cosyntropin is used to show whether the glands can respond [1].

The part of ACTH that does the work sits at the front of the molecule. Research summarized in the label found that the first 20 amino acids are the minimum needed for full activity, while the tail end of natural ACTH is the part most likely to provoke an immune reaction. Cosyntropin keeps the active front segment and leaves off most of that tail, which is why allergic reactions to it are uncommon [1].

Once injected, cosyntropin binds the same receptors on the adrenal cortex (the outer layer of the adrenal glands) that ACTH does and drives them to release cortisol. According to the label, 0.25 mg of cosyntropin stimulates the adrenal cortex as fully as 25 units of natural ACTH [1]. Healthy glands respond quickly, so a blood sample taken about 30 minutes after the injection shows a clear rise. Glands that are damaged, or that have shrunk from long disuse, respond weakly or not at all [1].

Yes. Cosyntropin is approved in the United States as Cortrosyn, now marketed by Amphastar, and generic versions are also available. The approved use is as a diagnostic agent for people suspected of having adrenocortical insufficiency [1]. It is not approved as a long-term treatment for any condition.

Its main use is the ACTH stimulation test, which guidelines call the short corticotropin test [3]. A baseline blood sample is drawn, the drug is injected into a muscle or vein, and a second sample is drawn 30 minutes later to compare cortisol levels [1]. The label also describes a longer intravenous infusion over 4 to 8 hours, which gives the glands a bigger stimulus [1].

A poor result suggests adrenal insufficiency, and follow-up tests then sort out the cause. In primary insufficiency, known as Addison's disease, the adrenal glands themselves are damaged. In secondary insufficiency, the pituitary makes too little ACTH and the glands shrink from lack of use, a pattern seen for example after long courses of steroid medicines [1].

The Endocrine Society's 2016 guideline on primary adrenal insufficiency names the short test with 250 micrograms of cosyntropin as the gold standard for confirming the diagnosis. It also urges a low threshold for testing in acutely ill people and in pregnant women with unexplained persistent nausea, fatigue and low blood pressure [3].

For problems higher up the chain, in the pituitary or hypothalamus, the picture is less settled. A meta-analysis pooling patient-level data from 13 studies and 679 people found that a low-dose version of the test identified this form of insufficiency more accurately than the standard dose, with an area under the curve (a measure of diagnostic accuracy, where 1.0 is perfect) of 0.92 against 0.79. The authors noted the low-dose test has technical drawbacks [2].

columns: Diagnostic accuracy (area under the curve) for pituitary or hypothalamic insufficiency

blocks.text: Because cosyntropin is given once for a test, side effects are uncommon. The label describes rare allergic reactions, usually in people who already have allergies or who reacted to natural ACTH before, ranging from mild hives and blotchy redness at the injection site to rare cases of anaphylaxis, a severe whole-body allergic reaction [1].

Slow heart rate, fast heart rate, high blood pressure, swelling of the legs and rash have also been reported after the test, though a link to the drug has not been confirmed. The only listed contraindication is a previous adverse reaction to cosyntropin itself [1].

name: Cyclosporine
alsoCalled: Ciclosporin, cyclosporin A, Sandimmune, Neoral, Restasis
evidenceNote: Cyclosporine has been FDA-approved since 1983 on randomized transplant trials and decades of clinical use, with later approvals for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and dry eye. Its benefits and its kidney, blood pressure, and infection risks are both well documented.
summary: Cyclosporine is an 11-amino-acid ring peptide from a fungus that calms T cells, approved since 1983 for transplants, arthritis, psoriasis, and dry eye.
keyTakeaway: Cyclosporine is a ring-shaped peptide of 11 amino acids, made by a soil fungus, that blocks the T cells which drive organ rejection. Its 1983 FDA approval changed transplant medicine: in a Canadian kidney trial that year, one-year graft survival was 80% with cyclosporine against 64% with the older standard. It is now approved by mouth or vein for kidney, liver, and heart transplants, severe rheumatoid arthritis, and severe psoriasis, and as eye drops for dry eye. The pills carry boxed warnings for infection, cancer, kidney damage, and high blood pressure, and require blood-level monitoring.

blocks.text: Cyclosporine is a cyclic peptide: 11 amino acids joined head to tail in a closed ring, several of them unusual N-methylated forms that ordinary proteins do not contain [1]. It occurs in nature as a by-product of a fungus, which the label names as Beauveria nivea [1]. Unlike most peptide drugs, it works when swallowed, as a capsule or a drinkable solution, and it can also be given into a vein [1][2].

It is an immunosuppressant, a drug that dampens the immune system on purpose. Novartis sells the original capsule and injection as Sandimmune and a better-absorbed capsule and solution as Neoral [4][5]. A dilute eye emulsion, Restasis, treats one form of dry eye [3]. The two oral brands are not interchangeable milligram for milligram, because Neoral delivers more drug for the same dose [1][2].

Before cyclosporine, transplant patients relied mainly on azathioprine and steroids, and in the comparison arm of the trial below about a third of kidney grafts were predicted to fail within a year. A randomized trial across Canadian centers, published in 1983, put the new drug against that standard in 209 people receiving kidneys from deceased donors [7]. The same year, the FDA approved it as a new molecular entity with priority review [4].

items.text: Canadian trial reports one-year kidney graft survival of 80.4% with cyclosporine versus 64.0% with standard therapy [7].
The FDA approves Sandimmune for preventing organ rejection [4].
Researchers identify calcineurin as the enzyme that cyclosporine ultimately blocks [8].
Neoral, a formulation absorbed more reliably, is approved [5].
Restasis eye emulsion is approved for reduced tear production linked to eye inflammation [6].

blocks.text: Inside an immune cell, cyclosporine first grips a carrier protein called cyclophilin. That drug and protein pair then binds and disables calcineurin, an enzyme that relays the signal from the T-cell receptor to the cell nucleus [8]. Without that relay, T cells cannot switch on the genes for interleukin-2 and related messengers that recruit more immune cells.

The label describes the result as a specific, reversible block on lymphocytes early in their activation, with helper T cells the main target [1]. It suppresses cell-driven reactions such as graft rejection more strongly than antibody responses, and it does not suppress the bone marrow the way older drugs did [1]. The same brake on T cells explains its use in autoimmune skin and joint disease, and, applied to the eye, its effect on the surface inflammation that holds back tear production [3].

Yes. Sandimmune was approved in November 1983, Neoral in July 1995, and Restasis in December 2002 [4][5][6]. All are prescription only. The pills and injection carry boxed warnings stating that only doctors experienced in immunosuppression should prescribe them, in centers able to monitor blood levels, because both too much and too little drug can do harm [1][2].

items: Preventing rejection of kidney, liver, and heart transplants, and treating chronic rejection after other drugs [1][2]
Severe active rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded well enough to methotrexate, alone or alongside it (Neoral) [2]
Severe, widespread or disabling plaque psoriasis in adults with a healthy immune system when other treatments have failed (Neoral) [2]
Raising tear production in dry eye caused by inflammation of the eye surface (Restasis drops) [3]

blocks.text: The Canadian transplant trial gives the clearest picture of why the drug mattered. Besides better graft survival, predicted one-year patient survival was 96.6% on cyclosporine and 86.4% on standard therapy [7]. The same trial showed the cost: blood creatinine, a marker of kidney strain, was higher on cyclosporine at 90 days, and one patient developed lymphoma [7].

Because Sandimmune is absorbed erratically, patients on it need repeated blood-level checks, and switching to Neoral without adjusting the dose can push exposure too high or too low [1][2]. Grapefruit juice raises cyclosporine levels, and many common medicines, St. John's wort among them, raise or lower them [2].

The label lists kidney dysfunction, tremor, excess hair growth, high blood pressure, and overgrowth of the gums as the main adverse reactions [1]. In the randomized kidney transplant trials, rates on Sandimmune compared with azathioprine were [1]:

items: Kidney dysfunction: 32% versus 6% [1]
High blood pressure: 26% versus 18% [1]
Excess hair growth: 21% versus under 1% [1]
Tremor: 12% versus none [1]
Gum overgrowth: 4% versus none [1]

blocks.text: Kidney damage rises with dose and duration and can become structural and lasting if levels are not watched, and the drug can also harm the liver [2]. Suppressing the immune system raises the risk of serious infections, lymphoma, and other cancers, including squamous and basal cell skin cancers reported in psoriasis trials [2]. The intravenous form can cause anaphylaxis, so it is kept for people who cannot swallow capsules [1]. Restasis is far milder: the most common problem is burning in the eye, reported by 17% of users [3].

name: Dalbavancin / Oritavancin / Telavancin
evidenceNote: All three are FDA-approved for serious skin infections on the strength of large randomized phase 3 trials against vancomycin. Telavancin is also approved for certain hospital pneumonias.
summary: Dalbavancin, oritavancin and telavancin are FDA-approved IV antibiotics for serious skin infections, including MRSA. Two need only one dose.
keyTakeaway: Dalbavancin, oritavancin and telavancin are lipoglycopeptides: hospital antibiotics built on the same peptide core as vancomycin, with a fatty tail added. All three are FDA-approved by intravenous infusion for serious bacterial skin infections caused by Gram-positive germs such as MRSA. Dalbavancin and oritavancin last so long in the body that a single infusion can replace a week or two of daily drips; in phase 3 trials they matched vancomycin, with about 80 percent of patients responding early on either. Telavancin is given daily and carries a boxed warning about kidney harm and fetal risk.

blocks.text: Dalbavancin, oritavancin and telavancin are three related antibiotics grouped as lipoglycopeptides. Each is semisynthetic, meaning chemists start from a natural glycopeptide (a ring of amino acids decorated with sugars, the same family as vancomycin) and attach a lipid, or fatty, side chain [1][3][5]. That tail helps the drug cling to bacteria and, for two of the three, keeps it in the bloodstream for days.

They work only against Gram-positive bacteria, the group that includes Staphylococcus aureus and its drug-resistant form MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), as well as streptococci. They are given only as an infusion into a vein, by a clinician, and are not available as pills [1][3][5].

rows: Skin infections; hospital and ventilator pneumonia [5]

sections.heading: How does this drug class work?

blocks.text: Bacteria wrap themselves in a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, a mesh of sugar chains tied together by short peptides. Dalbavancin grabs the end of those peptide links, a pair of amino acids called D-alanyl-D-alanine, so the links cannot be cross-tied and the wall fails [1]. This is the same target vancomycin uses.

Oritavancin adds two more actions: it blocks a second step in wall building and it punches through the bacterial membrane, which kills the cell faster at higher concentrations [3]. Telavancin likewise binds wall precursors, including one called lipid II, and disrupts the membrane [5].

The practical difference is how long they last. Dalbavancin has a terminal half-life (the time for blood levels to halve) of about 346 hours, roughly two weeks, which is why one infusion can cover a full course [1]. Telavancin's half-life is about 8 hours, so it is dosed once a day [5].

sections.heading: Are dalbavancin, oritavancin and telavancin FDA-approved?

blocks.text: Yes. All three are FDA-approved prescription drugs. Telavancin came first, in 2009, for complicated skin infections, and was later approved for hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Dalbavancin followed in May 2014 and oritavancin in August 2014 [8]. In 2016 the FDA approved a single-infusion schedule for dalbavancin, and in 2021 it extended dalbavancin to children from birth onward [1][8]. A second oritavancin product, Kimyrsa, was approved in March 2021 with a shorter one-hour infusion [3][8].

items.text: Telavancin (Vibativ) approved for complicated skin infections [8]
Dalbavancin (Dalvance) approved as a two-dose course [8]
Oritavancin (Orbactiv) approved as a single infusion [8]
Single-dose dalbavancin regimen added [8]
Kimyrsa, a one-hour oritavancin product, approved [8]
Generic dalbavancin products appear on FDA labeling databases [2]

sections.heading: What are these drugs prescribed for?

blocks.text: Their shared approval is for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections, a category that covers cellulitis, large abscesses and infected wounds caused by susceptible Gram-positive bacteria [1][3][5]. Because a single dose of dalbavancin or oritavancin finishes treatment, they can let some patients avoid a hospital stay or a long-term IV line.

The evidence comes from large noninferiority trials, which test whether a new drug is not meaningfully worse than the standard. In the DISCOVER 1 and 2 trials of 1,312 adults, 79.7 percent on two weekly dalbavancin doses had an early response at 48 to 72 hours, against 79.8 percent on vancomycin followed by oral linezolid [6]. A later trial of 698 patients found one 1,500 mg dalbavancin infusion was not inferior to the two-dose schedule [7]. In SOLO I, a single oritavancin infusion produced an early response in 82.3 percent of patients against 78.9 percent on 7 to 10 days of twice-daily vancomycin [4]. For telavancin, the ATLAS trials in 1,867 patients reported cure in 88 percent against 87 percent on vancomycin [9].

rows: Dalbavancin 79.7 percent early response vs 79.8 percent on vancomycin and linezolid [6]
Single dalbavancin dose 81.4 percent vs two doses 84.2 percent, noninferior [7]
Single oritavancin dose 82.3 percent vs vancomycin 78.9 percent [4]
Telavancin 88 percent cure vs vancomycin 87 percent [9]

blocks.text: Telavancin's label reserves it for pneumonia patients when alternatives are not suitable, and its kidney warnings shape when it is chosen for skin infections too [5].

For dalbavancin, the most common side effects in adults were nausea, headache and diarrhea; warnings cover serious allergic reactions, a flushing reaction if infused too fast, liver enzyme rises and Clostridioides difficile diarrhea, a gut infection that can follow any antibiotic [1]. Oritavancin's most common effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, limb abscesses and diarrhea. It also falsely prolongs some blood clotting tests for up to five days, which matters for patients on the blood thinner heparin [3].

Telavancin has the heaviest warnings. Its boxed warning, the FDA's strongest, flags higher death rates in pneumonia patients with moderate or severe kidney impairment compared with vancomycin, new or worsening kidney damage, and possible harm to a developing fetus based on limb and skeletal malformations in animal studies [5]. Taste disturbance, nausea, vomiting and foamy urine were each reported by at least 10 percent of skin infection patients [5].

name: Daptomycin
evidenceNote: Daptomycin has been FDA-approved since 2003, based on two randomized skin infection trials with over 1,000 patients and a later randomized trial in Staph aureus bloodstream infection.
summary: An IV antibiotic for serious skin and bloodstream infections, including MRSA. FDA-approved since 2003; not used for pneumonia because lung fluid inactivates it.
keyTakeaway: Daptomycin is a hospital antibiotic given by IV once a day to treat complicated skin infections, as well as bloodstream infections with Staphylococcus aureus, right-sided heart valve infection included. It was the first approved drug in its class, the cyclic lipopeptides, and kills gram-positive bacteria such as MRSA by collapsing the electrical charge across their membranes. In a randomized trial of bloodstream infection it matched standard therapy, with 44% versus 42% success, and caused less kidney injury. It does not work for pneumonia, and muscle damage is the side effect doctors watch most closely.

blocks.text: Daptomycin is an antibiotic made from a compound produced by the soil bacterium Streptomyces roseosporus [1][6]. Chemically it is a cyclic lipopeptide, a ring of amino acids with a fatty tail attached, and it was the first drug of that class to reach patients [4]. It is given only into a vein.

It is used for serious infections caused by gram-positive bacteria, including strains that resist older drugs, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) [4][6]. Doctors also use it, outside the label, for vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) [6]. It was sold first as Cubicin and is now made by many generic manufacturers [2][7].

Daptomycin attaches to the outer membrane of bacterial cells and causes a rapid loss of the electrical charge across it, called depolarization [1]. Bacteria depend on that charge to run their machinery, so once it collapses they stop making DNA, RNA, and proteins and die [1]. Because it kills bacteria directly rather than only halting their growth, it is described as bactericidal.

That membrane-seeking behavior also explains its main blind spot. In the lungs, daptomycin binds to surfactant, the fatty film that lines the air sacs, and loses its activity there [5]. A clinical trial in severe community-acquired pneumonia failed to show it was as good as comparison drugs, which is why the label excludes pneumonia [5][1]. How bacteria become resistant is not fully understood, and no transferable resistance genes are known [1].

In healthy adults the drug has a half-life of about eight hours and leaves the body mostly through the kidneys, so people with poor kidney function receive doses spaced 48 hours apart instead of 24 [1].

Yes. The FDA first approved daptomycin, as Cubicin, on September 12, 2003, as a new molecular entity under priority review [2]. Its indications later grew to include Staph aureus bloodstream infections and use in children aged 1 to 17 [1][3].

The original Cubicin vials are listed as discontinued in the FDA's drug database [2], but daptomycin itself remains widely available: dozens of generic labels from manufacturers such as Fresenius Kabi, Camber, and NorthStar are listed on DailyMed [7]. A reformulated Cubicin RF label remains current [1].

items: Complicated skin and skin structure infections in adults and in children aged 1 to 17 [1].
Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections (bacteremia) in adults, including right-sided infective endocarditis, and in children aged 1 to 17 [1].
Not indicated for pneumonia or for left-sided endocarditis, and not recommended for children under 1 year [1].

blocks.text: Two randomized international trials compared it with standard antibiotics in 1,092 patients with complicated skin infections. Clinical success was 83.4% with daptomycin and 84.2% with the comparators, and most patients who did well on daptomycin needed only four to seven days of IV treatment [4].

rows: 246 patients with Staph aureus bacteremia or endocarditis
Kidney dysfunction 11.0% vs 26.3% with standard therapy [3]

blocks.text: The bloodstream trial is the reason for the second indication. Daptomycin was as effective as low-dose gentamicin plus an anti-staph penicillin or vancomycin, including in MRSA and right-sided endocarditis [3]. It caused less kidney damage, but microbiologic failure was more common (19 vs 11 patients), and in six of those daptomycin patients the bacteria became less susceptible to the drug [3].

Muscle injury is the signature risk. Daptomycin can cause myopathy and, rarely, rhabdomyolysis (rapid muscle breakdown), so the label calls for monitoring of CPK, a blood marker of muscle damage, and stopping the drug if it rises sharply with symptoms [1]. Other warnings include eosinophilic pneumonia, a lung reaction driven by a type of white blood cell; severe skin and organ reactions such as DRESS; kidney inflammation; nerve damage; and C. difficile diarrhea [1].

Common, milder effects in adults with skin infections included diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, abnormal liver tests, and raised CPK [1]. In children, vomiting, abdominal pain, itching, and fever were also reported [1]. Some laboratory clotting tests can read falsely high while a person is on daptomycin [1].

Kidney function also shapes how well it works. In the bacteremia trial, adults with moderately reduced kidney function (creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min) had lower success rates on daptomycin, a finding the label lists among its warnings [1].

name: Dasiglucagon
evidenceNote: Dasiglucagon was approved in 2021 on the strength of three randomized, placebo-controlled trials in adults and children with type 1 diabetes. FDA widened the pediatric label in 2026.
summary: Dasiglucagon (Zegalogue) is a ready-to-inject glucagon analog approved in 2021 for severe low blood sugar in people with diabetes.
keyTakeaway: Dasiglucagon is a modified form of glucagon, the hormone that tells the liver to release sugar. Unlike older glucagon kits that must be mixed before use, it is stable as a ready-to-inject liquid. In its main adult trial, half of treated patients had recovered within 10 minutes; on placebo that took 40. FDA approved it as Zegalogue in 2021 for severe hypoglycemia in diabetes, and in 2026 extended it to children weighing at least 20 kg. FDA's database now lists both Zegalogue presentations as discontinued. It is not approved for congenital hyperinsulinism.

blocks.text: Dasiglucagon is a glucagon analog: a 29-amino-acid peptide built to act like glucagon, the hormone that raises blood sugar [1]. It is used as a rescue medicine for severe hypoglycemia, a dangerous drop in blood sugar that can cause confusion, seizures or loss of consciousness, most often in people who use insulin.

Natural glucagon is unstable in liquid, so traditional emergency kits ship it as a powder that a caregiver must mix with water during the emergency. Dasiglucagon was designed to stay stable in an aqueous (water-based) solution, so it comes ready to inject [2]. It was sold as Zegalogue in a single-dose autoinjector and a prefilled syringe [1].

The liver stores sugar as glycogen, a chain of glucose molecules. Dasiglucagon binds glucagon receptors on liver cells, which triggers the breakdown of glycogen and the release of glucose into the bloodstream [1].

That mechanism has a built-in limit: it only works if the liver has glycogen to give. People who are starving, have adrenal insufficiency (underactive adrenal glands), or have had low blood sugar for a long time may not respond, and need glucose instead [1]. After injection under the skin, the drug reaches its highest level in about 35 minutes and has a half-life of about 30 minutes, and in adults blood sugar rose by an average of 168 mg/dL within 90 minutes [1].

Yes. FDA approved dasiglucagon as Zegalogue on March 22, 2021, as a new molecular entity. In June 2026, FDA approved a supplement that redefined the pediatric population by body weight rather than age, so the label now covers any adult with diabetes and any child with diabetes whose body weight is 20 kg or more [1][3].

Approval and availability are separate questions. As of late 2026, FDA's Drugs@FDA database lists the marketing status of both the autoinjector and the prefilled syringe as discontinued, even though the approval itself remains in place [3]. People who rely on a glucagon rescue product can confirm with a pharmacist which options are currently stocked.

items.text: FDA approves Zegalogue for severe hypoglycemia in diabetes, ages 6 and up [3].
Label updated to cover children who weigh at least 20 kg [1][3].

blocks.text: Dasiglucagon has a single approved use, as emergency treatment for severe low blood sugar in people with diabetes, covering adults and children of 20 kg or more. Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in children below that weight [1]. The label directs anyone giving it to call for emergency help right after the injection and, once the person responds, to give sugar by mouth [1].

Approval rested on three randomized, double-blind trials in type 1 diabetes, in which hypoglycemia was induced with insulin under medical supervision. The main measure was time until blood sugar rose by at least 20 mg/dL without rescue glucose [1][2].

Children aged 6 to 17, at least 20 kg
10 min vs 30 min with placebo; 10 min with standard glucagon [1]

blocks.text: Dasiglucagon has also been studied as a continuous infusion in children with congenital hyperinsulinism, a rare condition in which the pancreas releases too much insulin. A phase 3 trial in 32 children was completed in 2020 [4]. That use is not part of the approved label [1].

Stomach upset is the main side effect. In the two placebo-controlled adult trials, nausea occurred in 57% of people given dasiglucagon versus 4% on placebo, and vomiting in 25% versus 2%. Headache, diarrhea and pain at the injection site were less common. Children reported nausea, vomiting, headache and injection site pain [1].

The label lists two conditions in which it should not be used. In pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal gland, it can trigger a sharp rise in blood pressure. In insulinoma, an insulin-secreting tumor, it can raise blood sugar briefly and then provoke a rebound drop. Allergic reactions, including rare anaphylaxis, have been reported with glucagon products [1].

It can interact with other medicines. People taking beta-blockers may have a short-lived rise in pulse and blood pressure. Indomethacin can blunt its effect on blood sugar, and dasiglucagon may strengthen the blood-thinning effect of warfarin [1].

name: Davunetide
evidenceNote: Davunetide reached randomized, placebo-controlled human trials, including a 313-patient phase 2/3 study, so the evidence base is real. That pivotal trial was clearly negative, and the smaller positive signals in other conditions were never confirmed.
summary: Davunetide is an eight-amino-acid nasal spray peptide tested for brain diseases. Its main trial in progressive supranuclear palsy failed.
keyTakeaway: Davunetide, also called NAP, is an eight-amino-acid peptide taken from a brain-protecting protein called ADNP and given as a nasal spray. Lab studies suggested it steadies microtubules (the tubes that give nerve cells their shape) and limits harmful changes to the tau protein. Allon Therapeutics took it into human trials, but its largest study, a 313-patient phase 2/3 trial in progressive supranuclear palsy, found no difference from placebo on either main measure after a year. Small earlier trials in memory decline and schizophrenia were never confirmed. It is not FDA-approved, and no trials are currently recruiting.

atGlance.value: Not approved; development stopped, no trials active

blocks.text: Davunetide is a short peptide with the sequence NAPVSIPQ, eight amino acids long, and the lab name NAP comes from its first three letters [1]. It is a fragment of activity-dependent neuroprotective protein (ADNP), a protein the developing brain needs to form properly and that helps control hundreds of genes [1].

The company Allon Therapeutics developed it as a nasal spray under the codes AL-108 and AL-208, aiming at diseases where nerve cells lose their structure, especially those driven by the tau protein [2][4]. It was tested in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a rare movement and thinking disorder caused by tau buildup, and earlier in mild memory decline and schizophrenia [1][3].

Nerve cells rely on microtubules, long hollow tubes that give them shape and carry cargo along their length. The protein tau normally helps hold microtubules together. In tau diseases, tau becomes overloaded with phosphate groups, detaches, and clumps into tangles, leaving microtubules exposed.

Much of the case for davunetide came from mice. Animals with only half the normal amount of ADNP developed memory problems and tau changes, and giving NAP partly reversed those changes [1]. That made the peptide look like a way to replace a missing protective signal. The leap from a genetically altered mouse to a person with a decades-long brain disease is large, and this is where many brain drugs falter.

In cell and animal studies, davunetide protected microtubules from being cut apart when tau levels were low, and it reduced the death of nerve cells through survival signaling pathways [1]. In preclinical work it also lowered tau phosphorylation, which was the rationale for testing it in PSP [2]. These findings describe what happened in laboratory models. As the trials below show, they did not carry over into measurable benefit in patients.

No. Davunetide has never been approved for any condition by the FDA or any other major regulator. After its phase 2/3 trial in PSP failed, the lead program stopped. The ClinicalTrials.gov registry lists the PSP study and its earlier trials as completed, with none recruiting [4].
It is not sold as a medicine. Any product marketed online as NAP or davunetide has not been reviewed for safety, purity, or effect.

items.text: Allon begins trials in mild cognitive impairment; a university group starts a schizophrenia study [4].
Phase 2/3 trial in progressive supranuclear palsy starts across six countries [2][4].
Schizophrenia trial reports no effect on its main cognitive measure [3].
PSP results published: no benefit over placebo [2].

blocks.text: The deciding study was a randomized, double-blind trial at 48 centers in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the UK, and the US. It enrolled 313 people with PSP, who used davunetide spray twice daily or a placebo for 52 weeks [2]. The two primary measures were a PSP rating scale and a scale of everyday independence. On both, the groups changed by the same amount, and the investigators judged the drug ineffective for PSP [2].

rows: No difference from placebo on either primary endpoint [2]
63 people with schizophrenia on their usual medicines
No effect on the main cognitive battery; one functional skills test favored the drug [3]
Improved memory scores reported in early studies, not confirmed in larger trials [1]

blocks.text: Safety in the PSP trial was broadly similar between groups, with 54 serious adverse events in each arm, including 11 deaths on davunetide and 10 on placebo. Nose problems were more common on the drug: nosebleeds in 12% vs 8%, runny nose in 10% vs 5%, and nasal discomfort in 10% vs under 1% [2].

The schizophrenia study was small. Davunetide did not beat placebo on the MATRICS cognitive battery, its main measure, though a test of everyday functional skills reached significance across the groups [3]. The memory-decline results come from the developer's side and were never followed by a confirmatory trial [1]. Taken together, the human evidence does not show that davunetide helps any condition it was tested in.

sections.heading: What did the failed trial leave behind?

blocks.text: The PSP trial still mattered. It showed that a year-long, placebo-controlled study in a rare and fast-moving disease can be run across dozens of sites in six countries. The investigators argued that other tau-targeting drugs should be tested the same way [2].

For davunetide itself, the result means the lab rationale did not hold up in people with established disease. Earlier positive hints in memory decline and schizophrenia came from small or developer-linked studies and were never tested in a larger trial [1][3]. Without new randomized evidence, claims that the peptide protects the brain rest on animal work alone.

name: Degarelix
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2008 after a 12-month randomized phase 3 trial in 610 men with prostate cancer showed it kept testosterone at castration levels as reliably as leuprolide. A later randomized trial looked specifically at heart safety.
summary: A monthly injection that blocks the hormone signal driving testosterone, approved since 2008 for advanced prostate cancer.
keyTakeaway: Degarelix is a synthetic peptide that blocks the receptor for gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) in the pituitary, which shuts down testosterone production within days. The FDA approved it in 2008, sold as Firmagon, for advanced prostate cancer. In its pivotal trial, 97% of men kept testosterone at castration levels for a year, matching leuprolide, and most reached that level within three days with no initial hormone surge. Hot flashes and injection site pain are common. It is a cancer drug given by a health professional, with no role outside that setting.

blocks.text: Degarelix is a synthetic peptide used to lower testosterone in men with prostate cancer, a treatment known as androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) [1]. Many prostate cancers depend on testosterone to grow, so removing it slows the disease. Ferring Pharmaceuticals sells it as Firmagon [1].

It belongs to a small group called GnRH antagonists. Most older hormone drugs for prostate cancer, such as leuprolide, are GnRH agonists, which work in the opposite way at first [2]. That difference in mechanism is the main reason degarelix exists.

The hypothalamus, a region at the base of the brain, releases GnRH in pulses. GnRH tells the pituitary gland to release two hormones, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and LH in turn tells the testes to make testosterone. Degarelix attaches to the GnRH receptors on the pituitary and blocks them, so LH, FSH, and testosterone all fall [1].

GnRH agonists reach the same end point by a longer path. They first overstimulate the receptor, causing a surge in testosterone that can briefly worsen symptoms (a flare), and only after a couple of weeks does the pituitary stop responding [2]. Because degarelix blocks the receptor from the first dose, there is no surge, and the trial authors noted no need for extra anti-androgen pills to guard against a flare [2].

The speed difference is large. In the pivotal trial, testosterone reached castration levels (50 ng/dL or less) in 52% of men one day after the first dose and in 96% by day three. On leuprolide, no one had reached that level by day three and only 18% had by day 14 [1].

Yes. Degarelix was first approved in the United States in 2008 for patients with advanced prostate cancer [1]. The label posted by the maker was last revised in February 2020 to add a warning about harm to a developing fetus [1].

The approval rests on a one-year, open-label, randomized phase 3 trial that compared two degarelix schedules with monthly leuprolide injections [1][2]. Only one of the two degarelix maintenance schedules tested in that trial was approved [1]. It is given only by a health professional and is not sold or used outside prostate cancer care.

Degarelix is prescribed for advanced prostate cancer when lowering testosterone is part of the plan [1]. Treatment starts with two injections given the same day and continues with one smaller injection every 28 days, all into the belly [1].

The pivotal trial enrolled 610 men of any disease stage with a median age of 72 [2]. Its main question was whether degarelix would keep testosterone suppressed over a year at least as well as leuprolide. It did, and it brought both testosterone and PSA (prostate-specific antigen, a blood marker of prostate cancer activity) down faster [2].

rows: Testosterone at castration level, day 28 to day 364

blocks.text: The label cautions that the faster PSA drop has not been shown to translate into a clinical benefit such as longer survival [1]. Because people with prostate cancer often also have heart disease, the PRONOUNCE trial compared heart events on degarelix and leuprolide in 545 men with known cardiovascular disease. Major events occurred in 5.5% and 4.1% respectively, a difference that was not statistically significant, but the trial stopped early with fewer events than planned, so the question remains open [3].

The most common problems are reactions where the needle goes in and the effects of having very little testosterone. Most were mild or moderate, and severe reactions occurred in 1% of patients or fewer [1].

items: Injection site reactions such as pain, redness, or swelling: 35% versus under 1% with leuprolide [1]
Hot flashes: 26% versus 21% [1]
Raised liver enzymes: 10% versus 5% [1]
Weight gain: 9% versus 12% [1]
High blood pressure: 6% versus 4% [1]

blocks.text: Injection site reactions were mostly short-lived and tied mainly to the large starting dose, and fewer than 1% of patients stopped because of them [1]. Lowering testosterone for a long time can also thin the bones, reduce sex drive, and cause erectile problems, breast tissue growth, and smaller testes [1].

Hormone suppression can lengthen the QT interval (a measure of the heart's electrical recovery time), so the label advises weighing this in men with long QT syndrome, heart failure, or other QT-prolonging drugs [1]. Severe allergic reactions have been reported, and about 10% of patients develop antibodies to degarelix after a year, with no sign so far that this affects how well it works [1].

name: Desirudin
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2003 on two randomized, double-blind trials in more than 2,500 people having hip replacement, which compared it with heparin and with enoxaparin. The US product has since been discontinued.
summary: A lab-made copy of the leech anticoagulant hirudin, approved to prevent leg clots after hip replacement. The US product, Iprivask, is discontinued.
keyTakeaway: Desirudin is a recombinant version of hirudin, the anticoagulant in medicinal leech saliva, made in yeast. It blocks thrombin, the enzyme that turns blood into a clot. The FDA approved it as Iprivask in 2003 to prevent deep vein thrombosis after elective hip replacement. In the largest trial, 2,079 patients, it cut proximal clots to 4.5% against 7.5% with enoxaparin. Bleeding is the main risk, the label carries a boxed warning about spinal and epidural bleeding, and the US product is now listed as discontinued.

blocks.text: Desirudin is an anticoagulant, a medicine that slows blood clotting. It is a 65-amino-acid protein with three internal bridges that copies hirudin, the natural blood thinner found in the glands of the medicinal leech, Hirudo medicinalis [1]. It is made in yeast using recombinant DNA technology and differs from the leech's own molecule only by a missing sulfate group on one amino acid [1].

In the United States it was sold as Iprivask, a powder mixed with sterile liquid and injected under the skin [1]. In Europe the same drug was studied and sold under the name Revasc [2]. The FDA's drug database now lists Iprivask as discontinued [4].

Desirudin is produced in yeast rather than extracted from leeches [1]. Under the code CGP 39393, it was tested in European hip replacement trials in the mid-1990s against the two standard clot-prevention drugs of the time [2][3].

items.text: Double-blind trial in 445 hip replacement patients shows fewer clots than unfractionated heparin [2]
NEJM trial in 2,079 patients shows fewer clots than enoxaparin [3]
FDA approves Iprivask for clot prevention after elective hip replacement [4]
Latest revision of the US prescribing information [1]

blocks.text: Thrombin is the enzyme at the centre of clotting. It converts fibrinogen, a protein dissolved in blood, into fibrin strands that knit a clot together. Desirudin attaches directly to thrombin, one molecule to one molecule, and blocks it whether the enzyme is floating free or already trapped in a clot [1].

Its effect shows up as a longer aPTT, a standard clotting time test, which rose to about 1.4 times baseline on average with twice-daily injections [1]. After an injection under the skin the drug is cleared with a half-life of about two hours, mainly through the kidneys; 40 to 50% of a dose leaves in the urine unchanged [1]. In people with severe kidney impairment the half-life stretched to as long as 12 hours, which is why the label calls for lower doses and daily monitoring in that group [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Iprivask on April 4, 2003 [4]. The approval is for one use: preventing deep vein thrombosis, a clot in a deep leg vein that can travel to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism, in patients having elective hip replacement surgery [1].

The approval still stands on the record, but the product's marketing status in the FDA database is discontinued [4]. About 59% of trial patients were 65 or older, and their drop in clots was similar to that of younger patients, although they cleared the drug about 28% more slowly [1].

It was prescribed to prevent clots after hip replacement. In both pivotal trials, patients received 15 mg injected under the skin every 12 hours, with the first dose given shortly before surgery, and clots were checked by venography, an X-ray of the leg veins after dye injection [2][3].

rows: Any DVT 7% vs 23%; proximal DVT 3% vs 16%
Any DVT 18.4% vs 25.5%; proximal DVT 4.5% vs 7.5%

blocks.text: Against unfractionated heparin, desirudin cut proximal clots, those in the larger veins above the knee, by about four fifths, and all four pulmonary embolisms seen in follow-up occurred in the heparin group [2]. Against enoxaparin, a low-molecular-weight heparin, it lowered the proximal clot rate by about 40% with similar overall safety [3]. Neither trial needed routine lab monitoring at the fixed dose [2].

Bleeding is the main side effect, as with any anticoagulant. Across the hip replacement trials, some form of bleeding was recorded in 30% of desirudin patients, 22% on heparin, and 33% on enoxaparin, while major bleeding stayed under 1% [1].

items: Any bleeding: 30% on desirudin vs 22% heparin and 33% enoxaparin [1]
Serious bleeding: 3% vs 3% and 2% [1]
Lump at the injection site: 4% [1]
Wound oozing: 4%; anemia: 3%; nausea: 2% [1]
Allergic reactions: under 2% overall [1]

blocks.text: The label carries a boxed warning: patients given spinal or epidural anesthesia, or a spinal puncture, while on a thrombin blocker can develop a blood clot around the spinal cord that may cause long-term or permanent paralysis [1]. Desirudin is not used in people with active bleeding, irreversible clotting disorders, or a known allergy to hirudins [1]. Antibodies to hirudin have been found on re-exposure, and cross-reactions with other hirudin drugs cannot be ruled out [1].

name: Desmopressin
evidenceNote: Desmopressin has been FDA-approved since 1978 and is sold today as tablets and injection, with decades of clinical use in diabetes insipidus, bleeding disorders, and bedwetting.
summary: Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic form of the antidiuretic hormone vasopressin, approved since 1978 for diabetes insipidus, bedwetting, and some bleeding disorders.
keyTakeaway: Desmopressin is a modified version of vasopressin, the hormone that tells the kidneys to hold on to water. Two small changes to the molecule make it last longer and remove most of its effect on blood pressure. The FDA first approved it in 1978, and DDAVP tablets and injection remain on the market for central diabetes insipidus, bedwetting in children, and bleeding in milder forms of hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (type 1). Its key risk is low blood sodium from retained water, which can cause seizures. WADA bans it as a masking agent.

blocks.text: Desmopressin is a nine-amino-acid peptide based on arginine vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone, which the pituitary gland releases to control how much water the kidneys keep. Its chemical name, 1-deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin, describes the two changes from the natural hormone, and the initials of that name give the brand DDAVP [1][6].

It has been sold in many forms over the years: nasal sprays and drops, an injection, swallowed tablets, and low-dose tablets that dissolve under the tongue. In the United States, the DDAVP injection and tablets are still marketed, while the original DDAVP nasal products, the Noctiva nasal spray, and the Nocdurna under-the-tongue tablet have all been discontinued [4][5][8]. Generic desmopressin injection and tablets are available.

Desmopressin was developed as a purer antidiuretic than vasopressin, which also tightens blood vessels and the gut. Its second use came from an unexpected side effect on blood clotting. In 1977, Italian researchers reported that an infusion raised factor VIII, a clotting protein, two- to six-fold in people with mild hemophilia and von Willebrand disease, enough for some to have teeth pulled or major surgery without donated plasma [6].

items.text: First report of desmopressin raising factor VIII for surgery in hemophilia and von Willebrand disease [6].
DDAVP nasal solution approved by the FDA [4].
DDAVP injection approved [9].
DDAVP tablets approved [10].
Noctiva nasal spray and Nocdurna sublingual tablets approved for night-time urination in adults; both later discontinued [3][5][8].

blocks.text: Vasopressin acts on two main receptor types. V2 receptors in the kidney's collecting ducts open water channels so that water is pulled back into the blood, making urine smaller in volume and more concentrated. V1 receptors in blood vessel walls make them constrict. The structural changes in desmopressin extend how long it acts and shift its activity toward V2, so doses that control urine output usually stay below the level that affects blood pressure or the gut [1].

The bleeding effect comes from a separate action. Desmopressin releases stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from the cells lining blood vessels, raising factor VIII levels within 30 minutes and peaking at 90 minutes to two hours [1]. This only helps people who still make some of these proteins, which is why the label is limited to milder disease.

Yes. Desmopressin has been FDA-approved since 1978 in several forms [4]. The current DDAVP injection label carries a boxed warning for hyponatremia, meaning low blood sodium, which can become life-threatening [1]. The tablet label lists hyponatremia among its warnings and rules out use in anyone who has had it [2].

Desmopressin also appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency's 2026 list under diuretics and masking agents, prohibited at all times. By diluting urine, it can make other substances harder to detect in a sample [7].

items: Central diabetes insipidus, where the brain makes too little vasopressin and the kidneys pass large volumes of dilute urine; also short-term excess urination after head injury or pituitary surgery [1][2]. It does not work for the kidney form of the disease.
Primary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) in children, as tablets, alone or alongside alarm and behavioral methods [2].
Hemophilia A with factor VIII activity above 5%, to control bleeding during surgery or after injury, given intravenously [1].
Type 1 von Willebrand disease of mild to moderate severity, for the same purposes [1].

blocks.text: For night-time urination in adults caused by the kidneys making too much urine overnight, Nocdurna was studied in two 3-month trials. Women went from about 2.9 trips to the toilet a night to 1.5 fewer, against 1.2 fewer on placebo; men cut 1.3 trips against 0.9 [3]. The difference over placebo was modest, around a third of a trip per night, and the product has since left the market [8].

The central risk is water intoxication. Because desmopressin stops the kidneys from excreting water, drinking normally can dilute blood sodium. Early signs include headache, nausea, weight gain, fatigue, muscle cramps, and confusion; severe cases lead to seizures, coma, or breathing arrest [1][2]. Children and older adults are at highest risk, so fluid intake is restricted while it acts [2].

items: Headache, nausea, facial flushing, and mild stomach cramps, mostly at high doses [1][2].
Low or high blood pressure with a faster heart rate after injection [1].
Blood clots, and in type 2B von Willebrand disease, platelet clumping and thrombosis [1].
Severe allergic reactions, rarely [1].

blocks.text: It is not used in people with low sodium or a history of it, moderate to severe kidney impairment, excessive thirst and drinking, heart failure, or uncontrolled high blood pressure, or together with loop diuretics or steroid medicines [1]. In the Nocdurna trials, mildly low sodium was several times more common on the drug than on placebo, which shows why sodium checks are part of treatment even at low doses [3].

name: Difelikefalin
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in August 2021 on the basis of two randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in 851 hemodialysis patients with moderate to severe itch.
summary: Difelikefalin (Korsuva) is an IV peptide given after dialysis to ease kidney-related itch. FDA-approved in 2021 for adults on hemodialysis.
keyTakeaway: Difelikefalin is a small synthetic peptide that activates kappa opioid receptors while staying largely outside the brain. Given into the dialysis line three times a week, it is FDA-approved as Korsuva for moderate to severe itch caused by chronic kidney disease in adults on hemodialysis. In its first phase 3 trial, 49% of treated patients had at least a 3-point drop in itch scores against 28% on placebo. Dizziness, drowsiness, diarrhea, and falls are the main cautions. An oral version failed in a different itch condition in 2024.

blocks.text: Difelikefalin is a synthetic peptide built from four amino acids in their mirror-image (D) form, attached to a piperidine ring. The D-amino acids make it resistant to the enzymes that normally break peptides down. It is sold in the United States as Korsuva, a clear solution supplied in single-dose vials for intravenous use [1].

It treats a specific problem: chronic itch (pruritus) linked to kidney failure in people who depend on hemodialysis [1]. Cara Therapeutics developed the drug and licensed commercial rights to Vifor, now CSL Vifor, for the United States; it is sold as Kapruvia in other markets and was approved in Japan in 2023 through a separate partner [4].

The body has several families of opioid receptors. Mu receptors are the target of morphine and most painkillers; kappa receptors are a separate family considered important in controlling itch [2]. Difelikefalin is a selective kappa agonist designed to stay outside the brain and spinal cord, a property described as peripherally restricted [2].
The label is careful on this point: it identifies difelikefalin as a kappa opioid receptor agonist but states that how this activity produces the treatment effect is not known [1].

Its timing fits dialysis well. The kidneys of these patients do not clear the drug, so its half-life before dialysis is 23 to 31 hours, and a dialysis session removes 70% to 80% of it from the blood. That is why it is injected into the venous line after blood has stopped circulating through the dialyzer at the end of each session [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Korsuva (NDA 214916) on August 23, 2021, to treat moderate or severe itch caused by kidney disease in adults receiving hemodialysis [3]. The label notes it has not been studied in people on peritoneal dialysis and is not recommended for them [1].

blocks.text: Korsuva has one approved use: relieving moderate or severe kidney-related itch in adults who receive hemodialysis. The dialysis team gives it three times a week, with the amount set by the patient's target dry weight [1].

Two 12-week, placebo-controlled trials enrolled 851 hemodialysis patients whose average itch score was about 7 out of 10 [1]. In KALM-1, the main goal was a drop of at least 3 points on a 0 to 10 worst-itch scale: 49.1% of patients on difelikefalin reached it, versus 27.9% on placebo. Itch-related quality of life also improved on two questionnaires [2].

columns: At least 4-point itch improvement at 12 weeks

blocks.text: The benefit is real but partial. Even on treatment, most patients did not reach a 4-point improvement, and a meaningful share of placebo patients improved too. These were 12-week studies; the label's safety data include 400 patients treated for at least a year in uncontrolled extensions [1].
In the pooled 12-week trials, reactions that occurred at least 1 percentage point more often than with placebo were [1]:

The label's main warning groups dizziness, sleepiness, mental status changes, and walking problems including falls: 17.0% of treated patients had at least one, against 12.0% on placebo. Drowsiness was more common in people 65 and older. Combining it with sedating antihistamines, opioid painkillers, or other drugs that slow the brain may raise the risk, and patients are advised not to drive until they know how it affects them [1].
Only 2.6% of patients stopped treatment because of side effects, compared with 0.7% on placebo [1].

Cara Therapeutics also tested a tablet form for other itch conditions. In June 2024 the company ended its program in notalgia paresthetica, a nerve-related itch of the upper back, after the dose-finding part of the KOURAGE-1 study found no meaningful benefit over placebo at any dose. The company said the decision was not driven by safety concerns [4]. The approved product remains the IV injection for dialysis patients only.

name: Dihexa
evidenceNote: Every result comes from rats and cultured brain cells. The paper that proposed how dihexa works was retracted in 2025, and the main rat study carries a 2021 expression of concern. No study in people has been published, and the FDA says it has found no human exposure data.
summary: Dihexa is a lab-made fragment of angiotensin IV that improved maze learning in rats. It has never been tested in people and is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Dihexa is a small modified peptide built from angiotensin IV, designed by Washington State University researchers to reach the brain when swallowed. In rats with chemically induced or age-related memory loss it improved water maze performance and increased the number of connections between neurons. That is the whole evidence base: no human trial exists, the 2014 paper that explained its mechanism was retracted in 2025, and the 2013 rat study carries an expression of concern. It is not FDA-approved, it is not eligible for routine compounding, and the FDA says it has no human safety data. Products sold online are unregulated research chemicals.

blocks.text: Dihexa is a synthetic, chemically modified peptide fragment. Its full chemical name is N-hexanoic-Tyr-Ile-(6) aminohexanoic amide, which describes a two-amino-acid core (tyrosine and isoleucine) capped at each end with fatty chains. It was built in the laboratory of Joseph Harding at Washington State University as a drug candidate for dementia [1].

The starting point was angiotensin IV, a short fragment of the blood pressure hormone angiotensin. Earlier work had shown that some angiotensin IV relatives improve memory in animals, but they break down quickly and cannot cross from the gut into the blood or from the blood into the brain. The team trimmed the active part down to three amino acids, then modified the ends to resist digestion and pass those barriers. Dihexa was the most stable and brain-penetrant version they produced [1].
Dihexa is sometimes marketed as a nootropic (a substance claimed to enhance thinking). That marketing runs well ahead of the science, which has never moved beyond animals.

items.text: The Harding group reports that dihexa, taken by mouth, reverses memory deficits in rats given scopolamine and in aged rats [1].
A follow-up paper proposes that dihexa works by binding hepatocyte growth factor and strengthening its signaling through the c-Met receptor [2].
The journal retracts the 2014 mechanism paper [3]. The same year, a phase 2/3 trial of fosgonimeton, a different HGF-targeting drug, misses its main goals in Alzheimer's disease [7].
The FDA says its compounding advisory committee will review dihexa acetate at a meeting to be held before the end of February 2027 [5].

blocks.text: The proposed mechanism centres on hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), a signaling protein best known for tissue repair, and its receptor, c-Met. In the brain, this pair helps neurons grow dendritic spines, the small projections where synapses (the junctions between nerve cells) form. The 2014 study reported that dihexa binds HGF tightly and makes small amounts of it far more effective at switching on c-Met [2].

In that work, dihexa increased spine and synapse formation in cultured rat hippocampal neurons, and the effect disappeared when HGF was blocked or c-Met was silenced. Blocking HGF inside the brain also cancelled dihexa's benefit on a maze task in rats [2].

That paper has since been retracted [3], so the mechanism should be treated as unconfirmed. The earlier 2013 study, which showed the memory effect without explaining it, has not been retracted [1]. In 2021, though, the journal placed an expression of concern on it, as it did on the 2014 paper, over possible image manipulation [8][9]. Online claims about dihexa's potency compared with natural growth factors come from cell experiments, not from measurements in a living brain.
No. Dihexa has never been approved by the FDA or any other major regulator, and no clinical trial of it appears on ClinicalTrials.gov, the federal registry where human drug studies are listed.

Dihexa acetate was nominated for use by compounding pharmacies, and the FDA placed it in Category 2 of its interim policy, the group it flags for safety concerns. In its assessment the agency said it had not identified any human exposure data for any route of administration and lacked important information on whether the substance would harm people. The nomination was later withdrawn, which leaves dihexa outside the substances compounders may routinely use [4].

The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee is due to consider dihexa acetate at a meeting to be held before the end of February 2027 [5]. A committee vote is advice to the agency, not an approval. Dihexa was not among the six peptides covered by the October 2026 federal enforcement discretion policy.

The published research on dihexa itself is a small set of rodent and cell studies from one laboratory, and the journal has questioned the images in both key papers [8][9]. A 2026 review of peptides marketed for musculoskeletal and recovery uses grouped dihexa with other neuroactive peptides and noted the absence of clinical trials [6].

No published or registered study in people

blocks.text: The closest human evidence concerns a different molecule. Fosgonimeton is a small drug designed to enhance the same HGF and c-Met system. In the LIFT-AD trial, 287 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease received fosgonimeton or placebo for 26 weeks. The drug did not meet its primary or secondary endpoints, though it was generally well tolerated [7]. That result does not test dihexa directly, but it is the largest trial so far of the idea dihexa is built on.
Safety in people is unknown. In its review, the FDA said it had found no human exposure data for dihexa by any route and could not tell whether the substance would cause harm if given to humans [4].

Dihexa is sold by research chemical websites as capsules, powders, and creams, usually labeled not for human consumption. These products are not made under drug manufacturing rules, and their identity, purity, and dose are not verified by any regulator. Anyone taking them is using a compound whose effects in humans have never been measured, and whose mechanism rests on a retracted paper [3].

name: Dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate
evidenceNote: The only published human test of this peptide on its own is one small 4-week study with a placebo group. Other evidence is lab and computer modeling work, or studies of serums that mix it with several other actives.
summary: Syn-Ake is a cosmetic peptide modeled on a viper venom toxin and sold for expression lines. Human evidence is one small 4-week study.
keyTakeaway: Dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate, sold as Syn-Ake, is a small synthetic peptide that cosmetic makers modeled on waglerin-1, a toxin in the venom of Tropidolaemus pit vipers. The idea is that it blocks the muscle acetylcholine receptor, so facial muscles relax. One published 4-week study in 57 older women found less forehead frown-line area with a 4% preparation than with placebo. No large trial exists, and it is unproven that the peptide reaches muscle through skin. It contains no venom, is a cosmetic ingredient, and is not FDA-approved.
