sections.heading: What is dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate?

blocks.text: Dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate is the ingredient name (INCI) for a small synthetic peptide better known by its trade name, Syn-Ake. Its structure is H-beta-Ala-Pro-Dab-NH-benzyl, supplied as a diacetate salt, which is why it is sometimes also called tripeptide-3 [1]. Despite the name, it contains no venom. It is a lab-made molecule designed to imitate one property of a venom peptide.

It sits in the same family of so-called botox-like cosmetic peptides as acetyl hexapeptide-8 (Argireline), and the two are often combined in one product [1][2]. Products containing it include face creams, serums and eye patches [1].

The story starts with Tropidolaemus, a genus of pit vipers whose venom contains waglerin peptides, neurotoxins that paralyze prey. A 2017 study of the venom's genetics noted that these toxins have been used industrially as the template for skin creams designed to paralyze facial muscles and reduce wrinkles [3].

Waglerin-1 blocks the type of acetylcholine receptor found on mature skeletal muscle. In mouse experiments it suppressed nerve signals reaching adult muscle, but adult mice lacking the epsilon subunit of that receptor were resistant to it, which pinned down exactly where it acts [4]. Syn-Ake was designed as a much smaller molecule meant to copy that receptor-blocking action, and by 2020 it was being marketed by the ingredient maker DSM [1][3].

Muscles contract when a nerve releases acetylcholine and it binds receptors on the muscle cell. Those receptors are ion channels: when acetylcholine binds, sodium flows in and the muscle cell fires. Syn-Ake is described as a reversible antagonist of the muscle-type nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. By occupying the receptor, it is proposed to keep acetylcholine from binding, leave the channel closed, and let the muscle stay relaxed [1].

This is a different step from acetyl hexapeptide-8, which acts on the nerve side by interfering with acetylcholine release. Syn-Ake is meant to act on the muscle side, at the receiver [1]. Neither has been shown to reach facial muscles in meaningful amounts after being rubbed onto intact skin.

Lab and computer studies have suggested other possible actions. A 2024 modeling and cell study predicted binding to collagen-degrading enzymes (matrix metalloproteinases) and to SIRT1, and found antioxidant activity and no toxicity in cell and bacterial tests [5]. Those results describe what the peptide does in a dish or a simulation, not on a face.

No. Syn-Ake is a cosmetic ingredient, and cosmetic products and ingredients do not need FDA approval before they are sold, with color additives the only exception. Responsibility for safety rests with the companies that make and market them [6].

The FDA decides whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug by its intended use. Claims to beautify keep a product in the cosmetic category, while claims to affect the structure or function of the body make it a drug [7]. Marketing that promises a cream will relax muscles the way an injection does pushes against that line.

blocks.text: The 2021 study is the only one that tests this peptide alone against placebo in people. It is small, short and judged on the forehead frown lines, with the result reaching significance at p < 0.05 [8]. The 4% figure refers to a commercial preparation of the peptide, not 4% pure peptide.

A 2020 review of cosmetic peptides noted that most of the early support for Syn-Ake came from the supplier's own information, including a claim of up to 52% less visible wrinkling after 28 days, and that the authors could find no scientific papers describing clinical studies of it [1]. The 2026 serum study, run by researchers at the company behind the product, cannot separate this peptide's contribution from the four other actives in the formula, and its authors described the published research on this ingredient's anti-wrinkle effect as limited [2].

The human studies are too small and short to describe side effects with any confidence. The 2024 lab study found no toxicity to cells and no mutagenicity in a bacterial test [5], which is reassuring but thin. There is no large human safety dataset and, unlike acetyl hexapeptide-8, we found no published safety assessment of it by the US Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel. As with any new skin care ingredient, irritation or allergy in an individual is possible.

name: DSIP
evidenceNote: The human data are a handful of small studies from the 1980s and early 1990s, several uncontrolled. The two placebo-controlled insomnia studies, with 14 and 16 patients, disagree, and none tested the under-the-skin injections sold today.
summary: DSIP is a nine-amino-acid peptide first linked to deep sleep in rabbits in 1977. It is not FDA-approved, and its human sleep data are small and mixed.
keyTakeaway: DSIP (delta sleep-inducing peptide) is a nine-amino-acid peptide that Swiss researchers isolated from rabbit blood in 1977 and linked to deep sleep. Decades on, researchers still had not found a gene, precursor protein or receptor for it, and its role in natural sleep remains unproven. Small human studies in insomnia, chronic pain and drug withdrawal reported benefits, but a 16-patient double-blind trial found effects too weak to matter. DSIP is not FDA-approved. In July 2026 an FDA advisory committee voted 7 to 6 against allowing it in compounded drugs. Products sold online have no approved use and no tested safety record by injection.

atGlance.value: Unknown; no receptor or gene for DSIP had been identified as of the last major review

blocks.text: DSIP stands for delta sleep-inducing peptide, a chain of nine amino acids (a nonapeptide). Its name comes from delta waves, the slow brain rhythm of deep sleep seen on an EEG (a recording of the brain's electrical activity). FDA documents refer to it as emideltide, a common name rather than an official adopted drug name [8].

Despite the name, DSIP's link to sleep has never been firmly established. Its structure does not resemble any known peptide family, and its natural source and function in the body are still described by researchers as obscure [6]. Today it is sold online and by some clinics for sleep, stress and recovery, none of which is an approved use [8].

A team in Basel led by Guido Schoenenberger and Marcel Monnier isolated DSIP from venous blood draining the brains of rabbits [6], and reported in 1977 that a synthetic copy behaved like the original material [1]. The finding raised hopes that a natural sleep factor had been found.

Through the 1980s, European research groups gave DSIP intravenously to people with insomnia, chronic pain and alcohol or opioid withdrawal [2][3][4]. Interest faded after a 1992 double-blind trial found little benefit [5]. A 2006 review called DSIP a still unresolved riddle, noting that its proposed role as a sleep factor remained very poorly documented [6].

No one knows. Researchers have not isolated a gene, a precursor protein or a receptor for DSIP, which makes it hard to say how it could act or whether the body uses it at all [6]. Antibody staining finds DSIP-like material in hormone-secreting areas of the hypothalamus, regions not especially tied to sleep, which has led some scientists to suspect that a related, still unidentified peptide is responsible for the activity attributed to DSIP [6].

Early animal work suggested an interaction with opioid systems: in the withdrawal studies, injecting DSIP into deep brain structures produced slow-wave sleep that the opioid blocker naloxone reversed, which is why it was tried in addiction [4]. FDA reviewers in 2026 found the substance poorly characterized from a chemistry standpoint, with inconsistent naming and missing quality tests in the nominations [8].

No. DSIP is not part of any FDA-approved drug, has no United States Pharmacopeia monograph, and its nominators reported that it is not registered in other countries [8]. Two nominators asked the FDA to add it to the 503A bulks list, the roster of ingredients that compounding pharmacies may use, for insomnia, narcolepsy and opioid withdrawal by injection under the skin [7][8].

The FDA's review concluded that the evaluation criteria weighed against listing it [8]. At the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting on July 24, 2026, members voted 6 in favor and 7 against, with one abstention; those voting no pointed to weak, decades-old efficacy data, poor characterization and the availability of approved sleep medicines [9]. When HHS announced in October 2026 that it would not take enforcement action against compounding of six peptides while rulemaking proceeds, DSIP was not one of them [12][10].

blocks.text: Every human study used intravenous infusions, most were small, and several had no placebo group. In 1981, six middle-aged people with chronic insomnia slept longer and woke less after one infusion, with no daytime sedation [2]. A 1987 placebo-controlled study in 14 people with severe insomnia reported better night sleep and daytime alertness over a week of treatment [11].

The most careful test pointed the other way. In 1992, 16 chronic insomniacs were assigned to DSIP or a glucose placebo for three nights under double-blind conditions. Sleep efficiency and time to fall asleep looked slightly better on DSIP, but the authors judged the effects weak, possibly driven by chance changes in the placebo group, and saw no change in how well patients felt they slept. They concluded short-term DSIP was unlikely to be of major benefit [5].

Outside sleep, a 1984 pilot in seven patients with migraine, tinnitus and other chronic pain reported lower pain in six of them, but it compared patients only with their own history [3]. The same year, an open study gave DSIP to 107 inpatients in alcohol or opioid withdrawal and reported rapid improvement in most, judged by staff without a comparison group; headaches were the main complaint [4].

Better night sleep and daytime alertness [11]

blocks.text: No study has tested DSIP injected under the skin, the way it is sold now, and the FDA found no animal toxicity studies to draw on. The small intravenous insomnia studies reported no significant adverse effects, while the withdrawal studies noted passing headache, nausea and vertigo. The FDA judged that record insufficient to support safe use [8].

name: Dulaglutide
evidenceNote: Approved in 2014 on the AWARD trial program, with a later cardiovascular indication based on REWIND, a randomized trial of nearly 10,000 adults followed for a median of 5.4 years.
summary: Dulaglutide (Trulicity) is a once-weekly GLP-1 injection approved for type 2 diabetes and to lower heart attack and stroke risk in adults with diabetes.
keyTakeaway: Dulaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist injected under the skin once a week and sold by Eli Lilly as Trulicity. The FDA approved it in 2014 to lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, and its label now covers children from age 10 and the reduction of major cardiovascular events. In its first big trial it cut HbA1c by about 1.5 percentage points, and in REWIND it lowered heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death from 13.4% to 12.0%. It is not approved for weight loss and carries a boxed warning about thyroid tumors seen in rodents.

blocks.text: Dulaglutide is a long-acting copy of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a gut hormone released after meals. It is built from two GLP-1-like peptide chains, each attached by a short linker to part of a modified human antibody (the Fc portion of IgG4), and it shares about 90% of its amino acid sequence with natural GLP-1 [1].

Natural GLP-1 lasts only minutes in the blood. Fusing it to the antibody fragment slows clearance so much that dulaglutide has an elimination half-life of about five days, which is what makes a single weekly injection possible [1]. Eli Lilly markets it as Trulicity in prefilled single-dose pens.

Dulaglutide switches on the GLP-1 receptor on the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas. That raises a messenger molecule called cyclic AMP inside the cell, which makes the beta cell release insulin when blood glucose is high, but not when it is normal [1]. That glucose dependence means hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is uncommon when dulaglutide is used without other glucose-lowering drugs.

It also lowers glucagon, the hormone that tells the liver to release glucose, and slows the rate at which food leaves the stomach [1]. Together these effects lower both fasting glucose and the rise after meals, and an effect can be seen after the first dose [1]. Slower stomach emptying and effects on appetite also explain the nausea and modest weight loss seen in trials.

Yes. The FDA first approved Trulicity on September 18, 2014, under a biologics license held by Eli Lilly [5]. The current label, revised in March 2026, covers two uses: improving glucose control in type 2 diabetes from age 10 upward, and, for adults with type 2 diabetes plus heart disease or several risk factors, lowering the chance of heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death [1].

items.text: AWARD-1 reports HbA1c falls of 1.51 points on 1.5 mg dulaglutide, beating both placebo and twice-daily exenatide [2]. FDA approves Trulicity [5].
REWIND shows fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths than placebo over a median 5.4 years [3].
AWARD-11 shows that 3 mg and 4.5 mg weekly doses lower HbA1c and weight further than 1.5 mg [4].
The label adds a warning on severe gastrointestinal reactions [1].

blocks.text: Its first use is lowering blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, alongside diet and exercise. In AWARD-1, adults already on metformin and pioglitazone received dulaglutide, twice-daily exenatide or placebo. After 26 weeks HbA1c fell 1.51 points on 1.5 mg, 1.30 on 0.75 mg, 0.99 on exenatide and 0.46 on placebo, with no severe hypoglycemia on dulaglutide [2]. The label's dosing range runs from 0.75 mg up to a maximum of 4.5 mg once weekly, and in AWARD-11 the 4.5 mg dose lowered HbA1c by a further 0.24 to 0.34 points over 1.5 mg [1][4].

Its second use is cutting cardiovascular risk. REWIND randomized 9,901 adults aged 50 and over with type 2 diabetes, most of whom had cardiovascular risk factors rather than established heart disease, to dulaglutide 1.5 mg or placebo on top of usual care [1][3]. Only 31.5% had established cardiovascular disease when they joined, so most participants were at risk of a first event rather than a repeat one, and follow-up ran a median of 5.4 years [1].

rows: Heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death

blocks.text: Dulaglutide is not approved for weight loss. In AWARD-11, people with diabetes lost 4.6 kg on 4.5 mg against 3.0 kg on 1.5 mg over 36 weeks [4]. It is also not a substitute for insulin in type 1 diabetes.

Most side effects are digestive and most common when starting or increasing the dose. In pooled placebo-controlled trials, nausea affected 12.4% on 0.75 mg and 21.1% on 1.5 mg against 5.3% on placebo; vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain and loss of appetite followed the same pattern [1]. Severe digestive reactions were reported in 2.2% and 4.3% against 1.4% on placebo, and the label says it is not recommended in severe gastroparesis (very slow stomach emptying) [1].

items: Boxed warning: dulaglutide caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rats. It is unknown whether it does so in people, and it must not be used by anyone who has had medullary thyroid cancer, has a relative who had it, or has MEN 2, an inherited tumor syndrome [1].
Pancreatitis, including rare severe cases, has been reported with GLP-1 drugs [1].
Low blood sugar becomes more likely when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas [1].
Kidney injury can follow dehydration from vomiting or diarrhea [1].
In REWIND, diabetic eye complications occurred in 8.5% versus 6.2% among people who already had retinopathy [1].
Gallbladder disease, serious allergic reactions, and inhaling stomach contents during anesthesia or deep sedation are also listed [1].

blocks.text: In a trial of 150 children and teenagers aged 10 and older, the safety profile matched that seen in adults, apart from injection site reactions [1]. Its five-day half-life means a dose does not wear off quickly, so a reaction that starts after an injection can take days to settle [1].

name: Ecallantide
evidenceNote: FDA-approved in 2009 after two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (EDEMA3 and EDEMA4) in people having acute hereditary angioedema attacks.
summary: A recombinant protein injection that stops hereditary angioedema attacks by blocking plasma kallikrein. FDA-approved since 2009, with a boxed anaphylaxis warning.
keyTakeaway: Ecallantide, sold as Kalbitor, is a 60-amino-acid protein that blocks plasma kallikrein, the enzyme that floods the body with bradykinin during a hereditary angioedema attack. The FDA approved it in 2009 to treat acute attacks, now in patients 12 and older. In its first pivotal trial, patients rated their symptoms as clearly better four hours after the injection than those on placebo. Its main drawback is a boxed warning for anaphylaxis, seen in about 4% of patients, so it must be given by a healthcare professional. European regulators did not approve it.

blocks.text: Ecallantide is a protein of 60 amino acids that inhibits plasma kallikrein, an enzyme in the blood. It is made by recombinant DNA technology in Pichia pastoris, a yeast, and sold in the US as Kalbitor [1]. Dyax, the company that discovered it, developed it under the code DX-88; Takeda now markets it [1][4].

It is used for hereditary angioedema, or HAE, a rare inherited condition. People with HAE have repeated attacks of deep swelling in the skin, the gut wall or the throat. Abdominal attacks cause severe pain, and swelling of the larynx (voice box) can block the airway. Most attacks come on without any obvious trigger [4].

items.text: The FDA approves Kalbitor for acute HAE attacks in people 16 and older, the first under-the-skin HAE treatment approved in the US, with a risk management program for anaphylaxis [4].
The EDEMA3 trial results appear in the New England Journal of Medicine, showing faster symptom relief than placebo [2].
Dyax withdraws its European application after the EU's medicines committee concludes the benefits do not outweigh the risks [3].
The US label covers patients 12 years and older and keeps its boxed warning for anaphylaxis [1].

blocks.text: The European assessment raised two concerns: allergic reactions were more frequent on the drug, and it was unclear whether the fixed dose worked well enough in heavier patients [3]. In the US, approval came with a formal program to make sure prescribers understood the anaphylaxis risk and could tell an allergic reaction apart from an HAE attack [4].

HAE is caused by mutations that leave people short of working C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH), a protein that normally keeps plasma kallikrein in check. Without enough of it, kallikrein runs unchecked during an attack and cuts a large protein called high-molecular-weight kininogen into bradykinin [1].

Bradykinin widens blood vessels and makes them leaky, so fluid seeps into the surrounding tissue; that is the swelling, inflammation and pain of an attack. Ecallantide binds tightly and reversibly to plasma kallikrein and covers its active site, so the enzyme can no longer produce bradykinin [1]. It does not replace the missing C1-INH; it shuts down the step downstream of it. It clears quickly, with a half-life of about two hours, which suits treating a single attack rather than preventing them [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Kalbitor in December 2009 [4]. Its current label covers treatment of acute HAE attacks in people aged 12 and older, and it carries a boxed warning, the FDA's strongest, about anaphylaxis (a severe, whole-body allergic reaction) [1].

Because of that risk, the label states that only a healthcare professional with the means to treat anaphylaxis and HAE should give it. In practice, that means it is not a drug patients keep at home and inject themselves when an attack starts [1]. It is not approved in the European Union [3].

It has one approved use: stopping an HAE attack that is already under way, at any site in the body. It is not approved to prevent attacks. The label describes a 30 mg dose given as three separate injections under the skin of the abdomen, thigh or upper arm, with a second dose allowed within 24 hours if the attack continues [1].

Approval rested on two randomized trials, EDEMA3 and EDEMA4, covering 143 different patients with moderate or severe attacks, including attacks in the throat [1]. Patients scored their own symptoms using two scales designed for HAE.

rows: Median treatment outcome score (higher is better, top score 100) [2]
Median change in symptom severity score (more negative is better) [2]

blocks.text: No one in that trial died, had a treatment-related serious event, or left because of side effects [2].

Anaphylaxis is the main risk. Across 255 people with HAE treated in clinical studies, 10 (4%) had anaphylaxis, all within the first hour after dosing. Symptoms included chest discomfort, flushing, throat swelling, hives, wheezing and low blood pressure, which can look a lot like an HAE attack itself [1].

Because ecallantide is a foreign protein, the immune system can learn to recognize it. About 20% of patients developed antibodies against it over repeated use, and some developed allergy-type (IgE) antibodies; the label links antibody formation with a possibly higher risk of hypersensitivity [1]. Other reactions reported across the clinical program were:

items: Headache (16%), nausea (13%) and fatigue (12%) [1]
Diarrhea (11%) and vomiting (6%) [1]
Injection site reactions such as itching, redness, pain or bruising (7%) [1]
Upper respiratory infections and a sore, stuffy nose (6% to 8%) [1]
Itching (5%), fever (5%) and rash (3%) [1]

name: Echinocandins
evidenceNote: Four echinocandins are FDA-approved, each backed by randomized trials against standard antifungals, and US infectious disease guidelines rate them first-line for candidemia on high-quality evidence.
summary: Echinocandins are IV lipopeptide drugs that break down the fungal cell wall. They are first-line treatment for Candida bloodstream infections.
keyTakeaway: Echinocandins are large lipopeptide drugs that stop fungi from building beta-1,3-glucan, a core part of their cell wall that human cells do not have. Four are FDA-approved: caspofungin (2001), micafungin (2005), anidulafungin (2006), and once-weekly rezafungin (2023). All are given by IV infusion in hospital. In randomized trials they matched or beat amphotericin B and fluconazole for invasive candidiasis, and US guidelines name them the preferred first treatment for candidemia. Resistance in some Candida species is a growing caveat.

blocks.text: Echinocandins are a class of antifungal medicines. Chemically they are large lipopeptides: a ring of amino acids attached to a fatty side chain [1]. They are used to treat serious fungal infections, mostly those caused by Candida yeasts that have reached the bloodstream or internal organs [6].

Four echinocandins are sold in the US: caspofungin (Cancidas), micafungin, anidulafungin (Eraxis), and rezafungin (Rezzayo) [2][3][4][5]. They are absorbed poorly by mouth, so all of them are given only by intravenous infusion [1].

Caspofungin was the first of the class to be licensed, initially for invasive aspergillosis that had not responded to other drugs [1]. It gave doctors an alternative to amphotericin B, an older antifungal with substantially more toxic effects [1][6].

items.text: Caspofungin (Cancidas) receives initial US approval [2]
Caspofungin matches amphotericin B for invasive candidiasis in a randomized trial in the New England Journal of Medicine [6]
Micafungin receives initial US approval [3]
Anidulafungin (Eraxis) receives initial US approval [4]
Anidulafungin shown noninferior to fluconazole for invasive candidiasis [7]
Rezafungin (Rezzayo), dosed once a week, receives initial US approval [5]

blocks.text: The fungal cell wall is a rigid outer layer, and one of its main building blocks is a sugar polymer called beta-1,3-D-glucan. Echinocandins block the enzyme that makes it, glucan synthase, so the wall weakens and the cell cannot keep its shape [2]. Human cells have no cell wall and no equivalent enzyme, which is why the drugs cause relatively little harm to the patient [1].

Against most Candida species the effect is fungicidal, meaning it kills the yeast, while against Aspergillus molds it mainly halts growth. The class has little useful activity against Cryptococcus, Fusarium, or the molds that cause mucormycosis [1].

The drugs differ in how they are handled. Anidulafungin is not processed by the liver; it slowly breaks down on its own in the blood into an inactive form [4]. Rezafungin lasts long enough to be given once a week [5].

Yes. All four are approved prescription drugs, and generic micafungin is also on the market [3]. Rezafungin's approval is narrower than the others: it is indicated for candidemia and invasive candidiasis in patients 12 and older who have limited or no alternative options, and the label notes that the approval rests on limited clinical data [5].

Approved ages vary by drug. Caspofungin covers adults and children from 3 months old [2]. Micafungin covers adults and children from 4 months for most uses, and younger infants for candidemia without spread to the brain or eyes [3]. Anidulafungin is approved down to 1 month of age for candidemia, and its label warns that a solubilizing ingredient, polysorbate 80, has caused toxicity in low-birth-weight infants [4].

Their main use is candidemia, a Candida infection of the blood, and invasive candidiasis in sites such as the abdomen. The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends an echinocandin as the first treatment for candidemia in patients without low neutrophil counts, a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence [9]. Individual labels add other uses:

items: Caspofungin: candidemia and abdominal, peritoneal, or pleural Candida infections; esophageal candidiasis; invasive aspergillosis that is refractory or intolerant to other therapy; and empirical treatment of suspected fungal infection in feverish patients with low neutrophil counts [2]
Micafungin: candidemia and other invasive Candida infections, esophageal candidiasis, and prevention of Candida infection in people undergoing stem cell transplant [3]
Anidulafungin: candidemia and abdominal Candida infections in adults and children 1 month and older, and esophageal candidiasis in adults [4]
Rezafungin: candidemia and invasive candidiasis when alternatives are limited [5]

rows: Success in 73.4% vs 61.7%, with fewer drug-related adverse events on caspofungin [6]
Success at end of IV therapy in 75.6% vs 60.2% [7]
Rezafungin weekly vs caspofungin daily, ReSTORE (2023)
Day 14 cure 59% vs 61%; 30-day death or unknown status 24% vs 21%; noninferior on both [8]

blocks.text: ReSTORE, the rezafungin trial, ran at 66 hospitals in 15 countries. Patients on rezafungin received two to four weekly infusions, while the comparison group received daily caspofungin for up to four weeks. The trial was built to satisfy two regulators at once, using cure at day 14 for the European Medicines Agency and death at day 30 for the FDA [8].
Treatment is not free of limits. The IDSA guideline describes treatment failures caused by echinocandin-resistant strains of Candida glabrata, a trend that affects a minority of isolates [9].

Side effects are generally mild compared with older antifungals [1]. Labels list fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, low blood potassium, and raised liver enzymes among the most common [2][4][5]. Infusion reactions such as flushing, rash, itching, and low blood pressure can occur and are thought to be histamine-related, which is why infusions are given slowly [2][4].

All four labels warn about allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, and about liver effects ranging from abnormal tests to rare hepatitis or liver failure [2][3][4][5]. Caspofungin with the transplant drug cyclosporine raises liver enzymes [2]. Micafungin carries warnings for hemolysis (breakdown of red blood cells) and kidney effects [3]. Anidulafungin contains fructose and must not be given to people with hereditary fructose intolerance [4], and rezafungin carries a warning for sensitivity to light [5].

name: Efpeglenatide
evidenceNote: A phase 3 program of several large randomized trials, including a 4,076-person cardiovascular outcomes trial, plus a Korean phase 3 obesity trial. No US application has been announced.
summary: Efpeglenatide is a weekly GLP-1 drug that cut heart events 27% in a 4,076-person trial. It is unapproved in the US but was approved in South Korea in 2026.
keyTakeaway: Efpeglenatide is a once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist from Hanmi Pharmaceutical, built from an exendin-4 peptide joined to an antibody fragment. In the AMPLITUDE-O trial of 4,076 people with type 2 diabetes and heart or kidney disease, it lowered major cardiovascular events by 27% versus placebo. Sanofi, then its partner, ended funding for the wider diabetes program, and no FDA filing followed. In October 2026, South Korea approved it for weight management as Eppe after a local trial showed 9% weight loss at 40 weeks. It is not FDA-approved.

blocks.text: Efpeglenatide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist developed by the Korean company Hanmi Pharmaceutical under the code HM11260C. Most approved GLP-1 drugs, such as semaglutide, are modeled on human GLP-1. Efpeglenatide is instead based on exendin-4, a related peptide that also activates the GLP-1 receptor [1][5].

To make it last, the exendin-4 analog is chemically linked through a short polyethylene glycol spacer to the Fc fragment, the stem portion, of a human IgG4 antibody. Hanmi calls this platform LAPSCOVERY [5]. The result is a large molecule that circulates for days, designed for weekly or potentially less frequent injection.

items.text: The Sanofi-funded AMPLITUDE-O outcomes trial is published in the New England Journal of Medicine [1].
A phase 1b study finds weekly efpeglenatide slows stomach emptying about as much as daily liraglutide [7].
AMPLITUDE-M monotherapy results are published [3].
Three other AMPLITUDE glycemic trials are reported; all were ended early by the sponsor because of funding, not safety or efficacy [4].
South Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety approves efpeglenatide for chronic weight management as Eppe [6].

blocks.text: Efpeglenatide binds the GLP-1 receptor, the target shared by every drug in the class, which lowers blood sugar and body weight. In a randomized phase 1b study, weekly efpeglenatide delayed stomach emptying about as much as daily liraglutide and improved the insulin-producing beta cells' response to glucose [7]. Few people in its monotherapy trial had low blood sugar, consistent with the glucose-dependent way GLP-1 drugs raise insulin [3].

The antibody fragment is what sets it apart. Fc-containing proteins are recycled by a receptor called FcRn rather than broken down quickly, which keeps them in circulation. A 2025 pooled analysis of six studies estimated a very low clearance for efpeglenatide, similar to dulaglutide, another Fc-fused GLP-1 drug, and found exposure rose roughly in proportion to dose with weekly injection [5].

No. No FDA application for efpeglenatide has been announced. Its global diabetes program, funded by Sanofi, produced a positive outcomes trial [1], but three of its phase 3 glycemic trials were stopped early by the sponsor for funding reasons [4], and development since has been led by Hanmi with a focus on obesity [5].

Outside the United States, South Korea approved efpeglenatide in October 2026 for chronic weight management in adults without diabetes who have obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition. It is sold there as a weekly auto-injector under the name Eppe [6]. That approval does not make it legally available in the US.

Efpeglenatide has more randomized human data behind it than most unapproved peptides. The headline result is AMPLITUDE-O, run at 344 sites in 28 countries in people with type 2 diabetes plus either heart disease or reduced kidney function and another risk factor [1].

rows: 4,076 adults with type 2 diabetes and heart or kidney disease, median 1.8 years
Major cardiovascular events 7.0% vs 9.2% (hazard ratio 0.73); kidney composite 13.0% vs 18.4%
618 participants also taking an SGLT2 inhibitor
Benefit did not differ by SGLT2 inhibitor use
Type 2 diabetes on diet and exercise, 30 weeks
HbA1c down 0.5% to 1.0% more than placebo, depending on dose
Non-inferior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg on HbA1c; about 3 kg weight loss in all groups

blocks.text: Digestive effects were the main side effects. In AMPLITUDE-O, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, vomiting, and bloating were all more common on efpeglenatide than on placebo [1]. In the Korean obesity trial, diarrhea affected 17.6% and nausea 16.6% of treated participants [6].

Two caveats apply. The Korean obesity results were reported at a 40-week interim point, and the final 64-week average had not been disclosed when the drug was approved [6]. The weight loss is also smaller than reported for approved weight drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, though trial populations and designs differ [6].

sections.heading: How is efpeglenatide different from semaglutide?

blocks.text: Both are weekly injections that act on the same receptor, but they are built differently. Semaglutide is a modified human GLP-1 that shares 94% of the natural sequence and lasts about a week by binding albumin in the blood [8]. Efpeglenatide starts from exendin-4 and gets its long life from an attached antibody fragment, which makes it a far larger molecule that is cleared through the same recycling route as antibodies [5].

Their evidence also sits in different places. Semaglutide has outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, heart disease, and kidney disease, and holds FDA approval [8]. Efpeglenatide's outcomes trial, AMPLITUDE-O, enrolled a high-risk diabetes population and also cut a combined kidney endpoint (falling kidney function or heavy protein in the urine) from 18.4% to 13.0% of participants [1]. No head-to-head trial has compared the two drugs.

name: Elamipretide
evidenceNote: Elamipretide holds an accelerated FDA approval for one ultra-rare disease, granted on a muscle-strength measure from a 12-patient trial whose randomized phase missed its main goals. Its continued approval depends on a confirmatory trial, and a large trial in another mitochondrial disease was negative.
summary: Elamipretide (Forzinity) is a cardiolipin-binding peptide given under the skin, FDA-approved in 2025 to improve muscle strength in Barth syndrome.
keyTakeaway: Elamipretide, sold as Forzinity and long known in research as SS-31, is a four-amino-acid peptide that settles in the inner membrane of mitochondria and binds the lipid cardiolipin. The FDA granted it accelerated approval in September 2025 for Barth syndrome in patients weighing at least 30 kg. The evidence is thin: the randomized phase of its 12-patient trial did not beat placebo, and the strength gains appeared only in the open-label extension. A confirmatory trial is required. Vials sold online as "SS-31" are not the approved product.

blocks.text: Elamipretide is a short synthetic peptide built from four amino acids: D-arginine, a dimethylated tyrosine, lysine, and phenylalanine, with an amide cap at the end [1]. The unusual D form of arginine and the modified tyrosine make it resistant to the enzymes that normally break peptides down. In early research it went by the name SS-31. Stealth BioTherapeutics markets it in the United States as Forzinity [1].

It is designed to act on mitochondria, the compartments inside cells that turn food into usable energy. Its one approved use is Barth syndrome, an inherited disorder that disrupts a key mitochondrial lipid and causes weak muscles, heart failure, fatigue, and frequent infections. The condition is ultra-rare and affects mostly boys, with roughly 150 known patients in the United States [6].

The FDA label describes elamipretide as a mitochondrial cardiolipin binder. It collects in the inner mitochondrial membrane and, in laboratory work, improves the shape and function of mitochondria [1]. Cardiolipin is a fat molecule found almost only in that membrane. It acts as scaffolding for the protein complexes that make ATP, the cell's energy currency.

Early descriptions credited the peptide mainly with mopping up reactive oxygen species, the damaging by-products of energy production. A 2025 review argues that the binding to cardiolipin matters more. By sitting on that lipid, elamipretide appears to change the electrical charge at the membrane surface and help the energy-making proteins assemble correctly [5]. In Barth syndrome, a faulty gene leaves cardiolipin poorly remodeled, so the drug is aimed at the underlying defect rather than at a symptom. These mechanism findings come from cells and animals. They explain the rationale but do not by themselves show clinical benefit.

Yes, for one narrow use. On September 19, 2025, the FDA granted Forzinity accelerated approval for Barth syndrome. The label covers patients of any age with a body weight of 30 kg or more, and the stated goal is better muscle strength [2]. Accelerated approval lets the agency approve a drug for a serious condition on an intermediate measure, here knee extensor strength, that is thought likely to predict real benefit. The label states that continued approval may depend on a confirmatory trial [1].

items.text: Genetics in Medicine publishes the TAZPOWER extension data, covering 168 weeks of open-label treatment [3].
The FDA issues a complete response letter declining the first application [6].
After further talks with the agency, Forzinity receives accelerated approval for Barth syndrome [2].

blocks.text: Children under 30 kg are outside the label, and Stealth said it would keep providing the drug to them through expanded access [6]. Every other use studied so far, including eye disease and other mitochondrial disorders, remains investigational.

Its only approved indication is improving muscle strength in Barth syndrome. The pivotal study, called SPIBA-201 or TAZPOWER, enrolled 12 males at a single site. Its first part was a randomized, double-blind crossover, meaning each participant received the drug and a placebo in turn, for 12 weeks each [2]. Elamipretide did not beat placebo on either main goal, the 6-minute walk distance or a fatigue score, and knee strength did not improve in that phase [1].
The case for approval came from the open-label extension, in which everyone received the drug and knew it. Median knee extensor strength started near 124 newtons [2].

The published extension also reported a cumulative gain of 96.1 meters on the walk test by week 168 and trends toward better heart pumping volumes [3]. Without a comparison group, those gains cannot be pinned on the drug with certainty, a limit the label states directly [1]. Several of the extension's authors were company employees or received company funding [3].

Outside Barth syndrome, the strongest test so far was negative. MMPOWER-3, a phase 3 trial in 218 adults with primary mitochondrial myopathy, found no difference from placebo after 24 weeks on walk distance (3.2 meters, p = 0.69) or fatigue [4].
Reactions where the needle goes in are by far the most common problem. In the randomized phase, every participant on elamipretide had some local reaction, compared with two thirds on placebo [1].

items: Injection site redness: 100% on the drug versus 25% on placebo [1]
Injection site pain: 75% versus 42% [1]
Hardening and itching at the site: 67% each, versus 17% [1]
Bruising and hives at the site: 25% each, versus none on placebo [1]

blocks.text: The label also warns of serious allergic reactions that needed emergency treatment, which can begin minutes to months after starting. Anyone who has one should not be given the drug again [1]. The solution contains benzyl alcohol as a preservative, which has caused fatal reactions in newborns, so it is not approved for neonates and is not for intravenous use [1]. Blood eosinophil counts, a type of white cell, rose in longer studies and returned to baseline over time without symptoms [1]. Two patients in the extension stopped treatment because of hives [3].

Research-chemical sellers list elamipretide under its old SS-31 name, often marketed for energy or longevity. Those products are not Forzinity. They have not been checked by the FDA for identity, purity, or sterility, and the approved product's own benzyl alcohol and allergy warnings show that even the regulated version carries real risks [1]. No trial has shown that elamipretide improves energy, endurance, or aging in healthy people, and the only large trial in adults with a mitochondrial disease was negative [4].

name: Enfuvirtide
evidenceNote: Approved in 2003 on the strength of two randomized phase 3 trials, TORO 1 and TORO 2, in people with drug-resistant HIV. The brand was withdrawn from the US market in February 2025 for commercial reasons, not safety.
summary: Enfuvirtide (Fuzeon) is a 36-amino-acid peptide that blocks HIV from fusing with cells. FDA-approved in 2003, it left the US market in 2025.
keyTakeaway: Enfuvirtide, sold as Fuzeon, is an HIV fusion inhibitor: a 36-amino-acid synthetic peptide that stops the virus from merging with immune cells. Approved in 2003 for people whose HIV resisted other drug classes, it was injected under the skin twice a day. In the pooled TORO trials, 46% of people adding it to an optimized regimen cut their viral load at least tenfold by 48 weeks, against 18% without it. Nearly everyone had injection site reactions. Genentech stopped US distribution on February 28, 2025, citing reduced medical need, not safety.

blocks.text: Enfuvirtide is a synthetic peptide of 36 amino acids, with chemical caps on both ends to stabilize it. Its sequence is copied from part of gp41, a protein on the surface of HIV-1, the virus that causes AIDS [1]. It was developed under the code name T-20 and sold by Roche and its US affiliate Genentech as Fuzeon.

The FDA approved it in March 2003 under priority review as a new molecular entity [5]. It belongs to a class called fusion inhibitors: rather than acting on the virus's copying machinery inside an infected cell, it blocks the step where HIV enters the cell in the first place [1].

Because it is a peptide, it cannot be swallowed and has to be injected. Its label limited it to people whose HIV kept multiplying despite treatment, typically after resistance to the main drug classes had built up [1].

To infect a CD4 cell, a type of white blood cell, HIV has to merge its outer membrane with the cell's membrane. A viral envelope protein called gp41 drives that merger by changing shape, pulling the two membranes together so the virus's contents can pass inside [1].

Enfuvirtide binds to a region of gp41 called the first heptad repeat (HR1) and blocks the shape change. Without it, the viral and cell membranes cannot fuse, and the virus is stopped outside the cell [1]. In lab tests it was active against several HIV-1 subtypes [1].

Because it targets a different step than other HIV drugs, it worked even when a person's virus was resistant to the reverse transcriptase and protease inhibitors that formed standard treatment at the time [2].

Yes. The FDA approved Fuzeon on March 13, 2003, as a new molecular entity under priority review [5]. Its label covers use in combination with other antiretroviral drugs for HIV-1 infection in treatment-experienced patients who still have detectable viral replication despite ongoing therapy [1].

In August 2024, Genentech announced it would stop all marketing and commercial distribution of Fuzeon in the United States on February 28, 2025. The company cited changes in clinical practice and much lower medical need as newer HIV treatments arrived, and said the decision was not related to the drug's quality, safety, or effectiveness [4]. FDA records now list the product as discontinued [5].

items.text: FDA approves Fuzeon [5].
Full TORO 1 and TORO 2 results appear in the New England Journal of Medicine [2][3].
Genentech announces the end of US distribution [4].
US marketing and commercial distribution stop [4].

blocks.text: Enfuvirtide was used as one component of a combination regimen for HIV-1 in people who had already been treated with several drug classes and whose virus kept multiplying. Its pediatric use, in children weighing at least 11 kg, was supported by studies in children aged 6 and older [1]. Approval rested on two randomized, open-label phase 3 trials, TORO 1 in the Americas and TORO 2 in Europe and Australia. Participants had taken a median of 12 antiretroviral drugs over about 7 years [1].

rows: 501 patients at 48 sites in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil
Viral load fell 1.696 log10 copies/mL with enfuvirtide vs 0.764 with an optimized regimen alone
Viral load fell 1.429 log10 vs 0.648 log10

blocks.text: A drop of 1 log10 means roughly a tenfold fall in virus in the blood. In the pooled data at 48 weeks, 46% of people on enfuvirtide plus background therapy had at least that much reduction, compared with 18% on background therapy alone. About 23% versus 8% reached an undetectable level below 50 copies per milliliter [1]. Both trials also reported gains in CD4 cell counts [2][3].

Injection site reactions were almost universal. In the controlled trials, 98% of people had at least one, including pain, hardened skin, redness, nodules or cysts, itching, and bruising, often at several sites at once [1]. About 4% of participants stopped the drug because of them [1].

items: Bacterial pneumonia was more common with enfuvirtide in the phase 3 trials, with 6.7 events per 100 patient-years versus 0.6 in the control group; an observational study was later run to look at the link [1]
Systemic allergic reactions occurred in under 1% of people and could include rash, fever, nausea, chills, low blood pressure, and raised liver enzymes [1]
Using the needle-free Biojector 2000 device caused nerve pain lasting up to six months in some people, along with bruising [1]
People on blood thinners or with bleeding disorders had a higher risk of bleeding after injection [1]
Other common effects were diarrhea, nausea, and fatigue [1]

blocks.text: Like other HIV medicines, enfuvirtide could trigger immune reconstitution syndrome, an inflammatory flare as the recovering immune system reacts to hidden infections [1]. The only listed contraindication was a known allergy to the drug or its ingredients [1].

name: Enlicitide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in July 2026 on two 52-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trials with more than 3,200 participants combined. Whether it prevents heart attacks and strokes is still being tested in a separate outcomes trial.
summary: Enlicitide (Lipfendra) is the first PCSK9 inhibitor taken as a daily pill. It lowered LDL cholesterol by about 56 to 59% against placebo in phase 3.
keyTakeaway: Enlicitide is a ring-shaped peptide from Merck that blocks PCSK9, a protein that makes the liver clear less LDL cholesterol. Earlier drugs aimed at this target are all injections; enlicitide is a once-daily tablet, sold as Lipfendra since its FDA approval in July 2026. In the 2,904-person CORALreef Lipids trial, LDL fell 57% from baseline on the drug while it rose 3% on placebo, and side effects were about as common as with placebo. The tablet has to be taken on an empty stomach. It is not yet known whether it reduces heart attacks or strokes; that trial is still running.

blocks.text: Enlicitide is a prescription drug that lowers LDL cholesterol, the kind that builds up in artery walls. It belongs to the PCSK9 inhibitor class, which until 2026 consisted only of injected antibodies and an injected RNA drug. Enlicitide is instead a macrocyclic peptide (a chain of amino acids closed into a ring), small and stable enough to be swallowed as a tablet [2].

Merck developed it under the code MK-0616 and sells it in the United States as Lipfendra. Each film-coated tablet holds 20 mg of the drug, supplied as a salt called enlicitide decanoate [2]. The label lists no contraindications, meaning no group of patients in whom it is ruled out outright [2].

Liver cells carry LDL receptors that grab LDL particles from the blood and pull them inside. A circulating protein called PCSK9 attaches to these receptors and steers them toward breakdown, so fewer receptors remain to do the clearing. Enlicitide binds PCSK9 and stops it from latching onto the receptor, which leaves more receptors working and lowers the amount of LDL in circulation [2].

Getting a peptide through the gut is the hard part. Only about 1% of each dose reaches the bloodstream, helped by sodium caprate, an ingredient in the tablet that eases absorption across the intestinal wall [2]. Food gets in the way: taking the tablet 30 minutes after a meal cut blood levels roughly in half in the label's studies. For that reason the label directs patients to swallow it whole in the morning with water, black coffee or plain tea, then wait at least 30 minutes before eating [2]. Levels settle into a steady state after about a week of daily use [2].

Yes. Merck announced on July 16, 2026 that the FDA had approved Lipfendra as an add-on to diet and exercise for lowering LDL cholesterol in adults who have high cholesterol, the inherited heterozygous familial form among them [3]. Merck described it as the first PCSK9 inhibitor approved in pill form [3].

The approval rests on LDL lowering, a measurement, rather than on proof of fewer cardiovascular events. A third phase 3 trial, CORALreef Outcomes, had enrolled more than 14,500 people at the time of approval and is testing whether the drug reduces heart attacks, strokes and deaths. Until it reports, that benefit is unproven for enlicitide itself [3].

items.text: CORALreef Lipids results published in the New England Journal of Medicine [1]
Head-to-head CORALreef AddOn trial against other oral cholesterol drugs published in JACC [4]
FDA approval of Lipfendra announced by Merck [3]

blocks.text: Enlicitide is prescribed to bring down LDL cholesterol in adults whose levels stay too high, including people with the inherited condition HeFH, in which a gene variant keeps LDL elevated from birth [2]. In the pivotal trials it was added on top of existing treatment, mostly statins, in people who had already had a heart attack or stroke or were judged at raised risk of a first one [1].

In CORALreef Lipids, 2,909 adults were randomized two to one to enlicitide or placebo for 52 weeks. At week 24, LDL had fallen 57.1% from baseline on enlicitide and risen 3.0% on placebo, a gap of about 56 percentage points. Non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a), other markers tied to artery disease, also dropped more on the drug [1]. In the separate HeFH trial of 303 adults, the week-24 reduction against placebo was 59% [3].

CORALreef AddOn compared enlicitide directly with other cholesterol pills in 301 statin-treated adults over 56 days. LDL fell 64.6% with enlicitide, against 27.8% with ezetimibe, 6.3% with bempedoic acid and 36.5% with the two combined [4].

rows: 2,909 adults with or at risk of artery disease, mostly on statins
57.1% drop vs 3.0% rise on placebo at week 24 [1]
64.6% drop vs 36.5% for bempedoic acid plus ezetimibe at day 56 [4]

blocks.text: In the larger trial, side effects showed up at about the same rate on enlicitide as on placebo, and similar shares of each group stopped treatment because of one [2]. In the HeFH trial, the two reactions that appeared more often on the drug were dizziness (9% versus 4% on placebo) and diarrhea (7% versus 2%) [3].

The label advises stopping enlicitide once a pregnancy is recognized unless the benefit is judged to outweigh the risk. The reason is the mechanism: lowering cholesterol may also lower substances the fetus builds from cholesterol, and there are not enough human pregnancy data to judge the risk directly. Animal studies at many times the human exposure did not show harm to developing offspring [2]. The full prescribing information covers interactions and other details.

name: Epitalon
evidenceNote: Most of the work comes from cell cultures and rodents, largely from one research group in Saint Petersburg. Human data are small physiological and biomarker studies plus an older retinal study; no adequately powered randomized trial has tested it for any condition.
summary: Epitalon is a four-amino-acid peptide modeled on a pineal gland extract, studied for aging and sleep. It is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Epitalon is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) designed in Russia from the makeup of epithalamin, a cattle pineal extract. Cell studies report that it switches on telomerase and lengthens telomeres, and a mouse study reported a lifespan gain of about 13 percent, but human evidence is limited to small biomarker studies with no large randomized trial. It is not FDA-approved. In October 2026, HHS announced interim enforcement discretion that lets 503A pharmacies compound it under conditions while rulemaking runs, which is not an approval or a finding that it works.

blocks.text: Epitalon is a very short synthetic peptide made of just four amino acids: alanine, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and glycine, written Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly or AEDG. It is also spelled epithalon or epithalone. Researchers built it to copy the amino acid composition of epithalamin, a crude polypeptide extract taken from the pineal glands of cattle, so the two names refer to related but chemically different products [10].

The pineal gland is a small structure deep in the brain that makes melatonin, the hormone that signals night to the body. Because of that link, epitalon has been studied mainly as an anti-aging agent and as a way to restore day and night hormone rhythms in older animals [1]. It is not a hormone itself and is not the same thing as melatonin.

Epitalon comes out of decades of work by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology. The group first made tissue extracts from organs such as the thymus and pineal gland, then designed tiny peptides meant to reproduce each extract's effect. Their 2002 overview describes AEDG as a peptide designed for both the pineal gland and the retina, and frames the work within their own theory that aging stems from falling production of regulatory peptides [1].

Almost all of the early literature on epitalon comes from this one network of authors and was published in Russian or in a small number of journals. Independent replication has been slow, which is one reason recent reviews treat the findings with caution [5].

The mechanism is not settled. The originating group proposes that short peptides like AEDG reach the cell nucleus and change which genes are switched on, and that this explains effects seen in both pineal and retinal tissue [1]. In old rhesus monkeys, the same group reported that epitalon restored the nightly rise in melatonin and the daily rhythm of cortisol [1].

The claim that draws the most attention concerns telomeres, the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes that shorten as cells divide. In a 2003 experiment, adding epitalon to human fetal lung fibroblasts that normally lack telomerase (the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres) led to production of the enzyme's catalytic subunit, measurable enzyme activity and longer telomeres [2]. A 2025 study from an unrelated lab in the UK reported dose-dependent telomere lengthening in normal human cell lines, and found that breast cancer cell lines lengthened their telomeres through a separate route called alternative lengthening of telomeres [4].

These are laboratory findings in dishes of cells. Lengthening telomeres is not proven to slow aging in a person, and keeping telomeres long is also a feature of cancer cells, so the same property raises questions as well as hopes [5].

No. Epitalon has never been approved by the FDA for any use, and no company has completed the trials an approval would require. As of April 2026, the FDA's compounding safety page lists it among nominated substances that were withdrawn, and it notes concerns about immune reactions from peptide clumping and impurities, plus a lack of safety information for the proposed route [6].

The compounding picture moved quickly in 2026. FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted in July to recommend epitalon for the list of bulk substances that 503A pharmacies may use, against the advice of FDA staff reviewers, and the identified use under review was insomnia [7][11]. HHS then announced an interim enforcement discretion policy covering epitalon and five other peptides while the formal list goes through rulemaking [8]. The policy sets conditions such as sourcing from an FDA-registered facility, a certificate of analysis and adverse event reporting [9].

items.text: Founding group publishes its overview of pineal peptides, including AEDG [1]
FDA compounding safety page lists epitalon as a withdrawn nomination [6]
Advisory committee narrowly recommends adding epitalon to the 503A bulks list [7]
HHS announces interim enforcement discretion for six peptides, epitalon included [8]

blocks.text: Enforcement discretion means the government says it will not act against qualifying pharmacies for now. It does not mean the FDA has reviewed epitalon for safety or effectiveness, and compounded drugs are not FDA-approved products [8].

The animal results are the most cited. In female mice bred to carry the HER-2/neu breast cancer gene, injections of epitalon five times a week from the second month of life raised average lifespan by 13.5 percent and maximum lifespan by 13.9 percent, and fewer animals developed multiple breast tumors [3]. The founding group has reported longer lifespans in fruit flies and other rodent strains as well [1].

rows: Telomerase switched on and telomeres lengthened [2]
Average lifespan up 13.5 percent, fewer breast tumors [3]
Normal and breast cancer human cell lines
Telomeres lengthened in both, by different routes [4]

blocks.text: Human data are thin. A 2026 narrative review that weighed studies by design found that the human evidence consists of small physiological or biomarker studies plus an older controlled study in retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited eye disease, and that no adequately powered randomized trial has shown benefit for any condition [5]. The same review noted that dose ranging, pharmacokinetics (how the body absorbs and clears a drug) and long-term safety have not been worked out.

Many of the older human reports involve epithalamin, the cattle extract, rather than synthetic epitalon, so they cannot simply be carried over to the peptide sold today [5]. Claims that epitalon reverses aging in people have no trial behind them.

Epitalon is widely marketed online as a research chemical, usually as a powder in a vial. Those products sit outside the conditions of the 2026 HHS policy, which covers only licensed pharmacies and physicians using material from FDA-registered manufacturers with a valid certificate of analysis [9]. FDA reviewers flagged peptide impurities and aggregation as specific safety concerns for this substance, and those are the problems least likely to be checked in an unregulated vial [6].

name: Eptifibatide
evidenceNote: Eptifibatide was approved in 1998 on large randomized trials, including PURSUIT (10,948 patients) and later ESPRIT (2,064 patients). Its benefit and its main risk, bleeding, are both well measured.
summary: Eptifibatide is a hospital IV drug, modeled on rattlesnake venom, that stops platelets clumping in heart attacks and stenting. Approved in 1998.
keyTakeaway: Eptifibatide is a small ring-shaped peptide, modeled on a protein in pygmy rattlesnake venom, that blocks the receptor platelets use to stick together. It is given by IV drip in hospital to people with unstable angina or a non-ST-elevation heart attack and to people having a coronary stent placed. In the PURSUIT trial of 10,948 patients, it cut death or heart attack at 30 days from 15.7% to 14.2%. The FDA approved it in 1998 as Integrilin; the brand is now discontinued but generics remain. Bleeding is the main risk.

atGlance.value: Approved 1998 (Integrilin); sold today as generics

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Blocks the GP IIb/IIIa receptor so platelets cannot bind fibrinogen

atGlance.label: Approved for

blocks.text: Eptifibatide is a synthetic cyclic heptapeptide: six amino acids plus one modified residue, closed into a ring by a sulfur bridge [1]. It is an antiplatelet drug, meaning it stops platelets (the blood cells that start clots) from clumping. It is made by chemical peptide synthesis and supplied as a solution for infusion [1].

Its design traces back to snake venom. In 1991, researchers screening 62 venoms found that only one, from the southeastern pygmy rattlesnake, held a peptide that blocked the platelet clumping receptor without affecting related receptors on other cells [3]. That venom peptide, barbourin, carried an unusual lysine-glycine-aspartate (KGD) sequence, and the authors proposed it as a template for designing drugs [3]. Eptifibatide carries the same pattern, with a chemically modified lysine followed by glycine and aspartate [1].

When an artery's inner lining tears or a stent is pushed into place, platelets activate and display a surface receptor called glycoprotein (GP) IIb/IIIa. Fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, sticky blood proteins, bridge neighboring platelets through that receptor, and the clump grows into a clot that can block the vessel. Eptifibatide occupies the receptor and prevents those proteins from binding, which halts aggregation regardless of what triggered it [1].

The block is reversible. The drug's elimination half-life is about 2.5 hours, and platelet function largely recovers within hours of stopping the infusion, because the peptide detaches from the platelet [1]. At steady state, the standard regimen inhibits more than 90% of platelet aggregation in lab testing, while bleeding time rises less than fivefold [1]. In healthy people the kidneys handle about half of its clearance, so kidney function shapes how it is used [1].

Yes. The FDA approved it on May 18, 1998, as Integrilin [2]. The Integrilin brand has since been discontinued, and the FDA has determined that it was not withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness [2]. Generic eptifibatide injections from several manufacturers carry the same indications [1]. It is given only in hospital, and in its trials patients also received aspirin and heparin [1].

The label covers two settings [1]. The first is acute coronary syndrome without persistent ST elevation: unstable angina or a non-ST-elevation heart attack, whether the patient is managed with medicines or goes on to an artery-opening procedure. There it lowers the combined rate of death or a new heart attack. The second is percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), a procedure that opens a narrowed heart artery with a balloon or stent, where it lowers death, new heart attack, or the need for urgent repeat procedures.

rows: Death or heart attack at 30 days: 14.2% versus 15.7% on placebo [4]
Death, heart attack, urgent repeat procedure, or emergency rescue at 48 hours: 6.6% versus 10.5% [1]

blocks.text: PURSUIT's absolute benefit was modest, 1.5 percentage points, and it appeared within 96 hours and held through 30 days [4]. The effect was consistent in most subgroups but not in women in that trial [4]. In ESPRIT, by contrast, women did benefit at 48 hours [1]. Most of the long-term ESPRIT benefit came from fewer heart attacks [1].

Bleeding is the most common complication, and most major bleeds happen at the artery puncture site used for catheterization or in the gut or urinary tract [1]. Low blood pressure is the other reaction reported in at least 5% of patients and more often than with placebo [1]. In PURSUIT, the rates were [1]:

items: Major bleeding: 10.8% on eptifibatide versus 9.3% on placebo [1]
Minor bleeding: 13.1% versus 7.6% [1]
Needing a transfusion: 12.8% versus 10.4% [1]

blocks.text: PURSUIT did not find more hemorrhagic strokes on the drug [4]. A rarer danger is a sudden, deep fall in platelet count, sometimes caused by antibodies some people already carry, which requires stopping both eptifibatide and heparin [1]. The drug is not used in people with recent abnormal bleeding, a recent stroke or any past brain bleed, major surgery in the previous six weeks, very high uncontrolled blood pressure, dependence on dialysis, or another IV drug of the same type [1].

name: Etelcalcetide
evidenceNote: FDA-approved in 2017 after three randomized phase 3 trials in more than 1,700 dialysis patients, two against placebo and one against cinacalcet.
summary: Etelcalcetide (Parsabiv) is an FDA-approved IV peptide that lowers parathyroid hormone in adults on hemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism.
keyTakeaway: Etelcalcetide, sold as Parsabiv by Amgen, is a short synthetic peptide that makes the parathyroid glands more sensitive to calcium, so they release less parathyroid hormone (PTH). The FDA approved it in February 2017 for adults with chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis whose PTH runs too high, a condition that weakens bones and is linked to blood vessel calcification. It is injected into the dialysis line three times a week. In two placebo-controlled trials, about three in four treated patients cut PTH by more than 30 percent, against fewer than one in ten on placebo. Low blood calcium is its main risk.

blocks.text: Etelcalcetide is a synthetic peptide drug built on a chain of seven amino acids, all in their mirror-image D form, with one ordinary L-cysteine attached through a disulfide bond. It is supplied as a ready-to-use solution in single-dose vials under the brand name Parsabiv [1].

It belongs to a group of drugs called calcimimetics, which mimic the effect of calcium on the parathyroid glands. These four small glands in the neck make parathyroid hormone (PTH), which pulls calcium out of bone and into the blood. Etelcalcetide was the first calcimimetic given by vein; the older drug in the class, cinacalcet, is a daily pill [2].

The parathyroid glands decide how much PTH to release by sensing calcium through a protein on their surface called the calcium-sensing receptor. Etelcalcetide binds that receptor at a site separate from calcium and makes it respond more strongly to the calcium already present. The glands read this as a signal that calcium is plentiful and release less PTH [1].

In kidney failure, the body struggles to clear phosphate and make active vitamin D, and calcium balance is disturbed, so the parathyroid glands are driven to overwork. This is secondary hyperparathyroidism. Over time the excess PTH strips minerals from bone and is linked to calcium deposits in blood vessels and higher death rates [2].

In dialysis patients given three doses a week, blood levels reach a steady state after 7 to 8 weeks and build up to three to four times the level after a single dose. The effective half-life (the time for blood levels to halve) is 3 to 4 days, and most of the drug in the blood is bound to the protein albumin [1].

Yes. The FDA approved etelcalcetide on February 7, 2017, under the brand name Parsabiv, marketed by Amgen [4]. Its approval rests on three randomized phase 3 trials published together in JAMA in 2017 [2][3].

The approval is narrow. Only adults whose kidney disease has progressed to hemodialysis are covered. The label notes that the drug has not been studied in parathyroid cancer, in primary hyperparathyroidism (where the gland itself is the problem), or in kidney disease before dialysis, and is not recommended for those groups [1].

Etelcalcetide is used to lower PTH in adults on hemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism. It is given by the dialysis team as an injection into the dialysis circuit at the end of a session, three times a week, and the dose is adjusted over weeks based on regular blood tests for PTH and calcium [1]. Because it goes in during dialysis, it does not add another daily pill to what is often a long medication list.

Two identical placebo-controlled trials enrolled 1,023 patients with moderate to severe secondary hyperparathyroidism for 26 weeks. The main goal was a PTH drop of more than 30 percent. In trial A, 74.0 percent of patients on etelcalcetide reached it against 8.3 percent on placebo, and in trial B 75.3 percent against 9.6 percent [3]. About half the treated patients reached a PTH of 300 pg/mL or lower, compared with about 5 percent on placebo [3].

rows: 74.0 percent cut PTH by over 30 percent vs 8.3 percent on placebo [3]
68.2 percent on etelcalcetide vs 57.7 percent on cinacalcet [2]

blocks.text: The third trial compared etelcalcetide directly with cinacalcet in 683 patients, each receiving one active drug and a dummy version of the other. Etelcalcetide was not inferior and in fact met the bar for superiority: 68.2 percent reached a greater than 30 percent PTH reduction against 57.7 percent on cinacalcet, and 52.4 percent against 40.2 percent reached a greater than 50 percent reduction [2]. None of these trials was designed to show fewer fractures, heart events or deaths, and the authors called for studies of those outcomes [2][3].

The most common side effects reported in at least 5 percent of patients were a drop in blood calcium, muscle spasms, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, headache, low calcium symptoms and paresthesia (tingling or pins and needles) [1]. In the comparison with cinacalcet, reduced blood calcium was the most common effect, seen in 68.9 percent on etelcalcetide and 59.8 percent on cinacalcet [2].

The label's warnings center on hypocalcemia, which can be severe and cause muscle cramps, seizures, and changes in heart rhythm seen as QT prolongation on an ECG. It also warns of possible worsening heart failure, upper digestive tract bleeding in people already at risk, and adynamic bone disease, a low-turnover bone condition that can develop if PTH is pushed too low for too long [1]. Calcium is checked within a week of starting or changing the dose and every four weeks after that [1].

name: Exenatide
evidenceNote: Exenatide has been FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes since 2005, backed by placebo-controlled glucose trials and a 14,752-person cardiovascular outcomes trial.
summary: The first GLP-1 drug, copied from Gila monster venom. FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes since 2005; now sold mainly as a twice-daily generic pen.
keyTakeaway: Exenatide is a lab-made version of exendin-4, a peptide first found in Gila monster venom, and in 2005 it became the first GLP-1 receptor agonist approved by the FDA. It lowers blood sugar in type 2 diabetes: in 30-week trials the twice-daily pen cut HbA1c by up to 1 point more than placebo. A once-weekly version proved safe for the heart in a large outcomes trial but did not reduce events. AstraZeneca discontinued both brand products in 2024, and a generic twice-daily pen is now the main US form. Newer GLP-1 drugs beat it head to head on sugar and weight.

blocks.text: Exenatide is a 39 amino acid peptide used to lower blood sugar in adults with type 2 diabetes. It is the lab-made version of exendin-4, a molecule first isolated from the venom of the Gila monster, a lizard native to the southwestern United States and Mexico [3]. It belongs to the class called GLP-1 receptor agonists, the same family that later produced liraglutide, semaglutide, and the dual agonist tirzepatide.

In the United States exenatide was sold for years as Byetta, a pen injected twice a day, and later as a once-weekly extended-release product. Today the twice-daily form is available as a generic pen, labeled as an add-on to diet and exercise for glucose control in adults with type 2 diabetes [1]. It is not labeled for weight loss, and it has no role in type 1 diabetes.

Two lines of research met in exenatide. Scientists studying gut hormones had identified GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide 1) as a signal that boosts insulin after meals, but the natural hormone is broken down within minutes by the enzyme DPP-4, which made it impractical as a drug [3]. A separate survey of Gila monster venom turned up exendin-4, which shares about 53% of its structure with human GLP-1, binds the same receptor, and survives far longer in the body [3].

That stability is what made a medicine possible. The synthetic peptide, named exenatide, reached the US market in 2005 [2][3]. A once-weekly extended-release formulation followed and was compared head to head with the twice-daily pen in the DURATION-1 trial [6].

items.text: Byetta, twice-daily exenatide, receives its first US approval for type 2 diabetes [2].
DURATION-1 shows the once-weekly 2 mg form lowers HbA1c more than the twice-daily pen over 30 weeks [6].
The EXSCEL outcomes trial finds once-weekly exenatide safe for the heart but not protective [7].
AstraZeneca discontinues both Byetta and Bydureon BCise in the US [4].
FDA approves Amneal's generic exenatide pen, referencing Byetta [5].

blocks.text: Exenatide binds to and switches on the GLP-1 receptor, the docking site normally used by the body's own GLP-1 [1]. On pancreatic beta cells that signal increases insulin release, but only when blood glucose is raised, which is why the drug carries little risk of low blood sugar on its own. It also suppresses glucagon, a hormone that pushes the liver to release sugar, and it slows how quickly the stomach empties after a meal [3].

The twice-daily form has a short life in the blood: its mean terminal half-life is about 2.4 hours, and it is cleared mostly by the kidneys [1]. That is why it is injected within an hour before the two main meals of the day. Because the kidneys handle it, the generic label advises against use in people with severe kidney impairment or end-stage kidney disease [1].

Yes. Exenatide first gained FDA approval in 2005 [2]. The approval has never been withdrawn for safety reasons. What changed is the brand supply: AstraZeneca told the FDA it had discontinued Byetta on October 25, 2024 and Bydureon BCise on October 28, 2024 [4].

A month later, in November 2024, the FDA approved a generic exenatide pen from Amneal that references Byetta, which the company described as one of the first generic GLP-1 injectables in the country [5]. Its current label was revised in May 2026 [1]. A once-weekly exenatide product is no longer marketed by AstraZeneca in the US [4].

Exenatide carries a single labeled use: lowering glucose in type 2 diabetes in adults, used together with diet and exercise [1]. In 30-week placebo-controlled trials of the twice-daily pen, the 10 mcg dose lowered HbA1c (a measure of average blood sugar over about three months) by roughly 0.9 to 1.0 percentage point more than placebo when added to metformin, a sulfonylurea, or both [2]. Weight usually fell a little, by about 2 to 3 kg in the published trials [2].

rows: Adults on metformin, a sulfonylurea, or both
HbA1c fell up to 1.0 point more than placebo at 10 mcg twice daily [2]
Once weekly lowered HbA1c 1.9 points vs 1.5 for twice daily [6]
Major cardiac events 11.4% vs 12.2% on placebo; safe, not superior [7]

blocks.text: The heart question was settled by EXSCEL, which followed 14,752 people for a median of 3.2 years. Once-weekly exenatide met the safety bar, and the rate of heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death was slightly lower than with placebo, but the difference fell just short of statistical significance [7]. That sets exenatide apart from some later drugs in its class that did show a reduction.

Stomach symptoms dominate. In the twice-daily trials, nausea affected 44% of people on exenatide against 18% on placebo, and vomiting and diarrhea each affected 13% [1]. Feeling jittery, dizziness, and headache were each reported by about 9% of users [1]. These effects tend to be worst in the first weeks.

The label's warnings include acute pancreatitis, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea, kidney injury from dehydration after vomiting or diarrhea, severe gastrointestinal reactions, and gallbladder disease [1]. Some people form antibodies that blunt the drug's effect, and a rare immune reaction can destroy platelets, which is why a history of exenatide-linked low platelets rules out further use [1]. The twice-daily product carries no boxed warning [1].

sections.heading: How does exenatide compare with newer GLP-1 drugs?

blocks.text: Exenatide opened the class, but direct comparisons have mostly gone to its successors. In DURATION-6, daily liraglutide lowered HbA1c by 1.48 points against 1.28 for weekly exenatide, although exenatide caused less nausea (9% vs 21%) [8]. In SUSTAIN 3, weekly semaglutide cut HbA1c by 1.5 points and weight by 5.6 kg over 56 weeks, against 0.9 points and 1.9 kg for weekly exenatide [9].

Those results, together with the end of brand supply, explain why exenatide is now a minor option. It remains a reasonable reference point for how the class began and is still in use as a lower-cost generic, but it delivers smaller sugar and weight changes than semaglutide or tirzepatide.

name: Follistatin-344
evidenceNote: The only human data come from small, open-label gene therapy trials that delivered the follistatin gene into thigh muscles, not from injecting the protein. Nobody has published a controlled human trial of follistatin-344 as a peptide or protein product, which is how it is sold online.
summary: Follistatin-344 is a natural myostatin-blocking protein. Human data come only from small gene therapy trials in muscle disease, not from injected protein.
keyTakeaway: Follistatin-344 is one form of follistatin, a protein the body makes that binds myostatin and activin, two signals that hold muscle growth in check. Mice engineered to overproduce it grow much larger muscles. In people, the only studies used gene therapy: six men with Becker muscular dystrophy and six adults with inclusion body myositis had the follistatin gene injected into their thighs, and most walked farther afterward. No trial has tested the protein vials sold online. It is not FDA-approved for any use, and WADA bans follistatin in sport at all times.
