blocks.text: Follistatin is a protein found throughout the body. Its gene can be read in more than one way, a process called alternative splicing, and one of the resulting versions is 344 amino acids long. That version is follistatin-344, often shortened to FST-344 or FS344. After the body trims it, it circulates in the blood as a slightly shorter form called FS315 [2].

Interest in follistatin comes from its effect on muscle. It binds and neutralizes myostatin, a growth factor that tells muscle to stop growing. Blocking myostatin is one of the most studied ideas for treating muscle-wasting diseases, and follistatin is one of the body's own tools for doing it [1].

Follistatin-344 is not an approved medicine. In clinical research it has been delivered as a gene carried by a harmless virus, so that muscle cells make the protein themselves [3]. Products sold online as follistatin-344 peptide are a different thing entirely: vials of protein of unknown origin that have never been tested in a published human trial.

The story starts with myostatin. In 1997, researchers at Johns Hopkins described a new growth factor, then called GDF-8, that is made in skeletal muscle. Mice bred without the gene had individual muscles weighing two to three times more than normal, from both more and larger muscle fibers [1].

Four years later, the same group showed that follistatin could block myostatin from reaching its receptor. Mice engineered to make extra follistatin in their muscles grew muscle mass comparable to the mice that lacked myostatin altogether [4]. That result made follistatin a candidate treatment for diseases in which muscle wastes away.

items.text: Myostatin (GDF-8) is identified as a brake on muscle growth in mice [1].
Mice that overproduce follistatin in muscle show large gains in muscle mass [4].
First human gene therapy trial of FS344 reported in Becker muscular dystrophy [3].
A second small trial reports results in sporadic inclusion body myositis [5].

blocks.text: Myostatin slows muscle growth by docking onto a receptor on muscle cells called activin receptor type IIB. Follistatin grabs myostatin before it can dock, which lifts the brake. In lab experiments, follistatin blocked myostatin from binding that receptor [4].

Follistatin also binds activin, a related hormone that helps the pituitary gland release follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which is involved in fertility. That overlap raised a safety concern for human use. Researchers chose the FS344 version partly because its circulating form binds activin about ten times less tightly than another version, FS288, which was expected to limit effects outside muscle [2].

In the human trials, the follistatin gene was packaged in an adeno-associated virus (AAV), a virus that does not cause disease and is used to carry genes into cells. It was injected directly into the quadriceps, the large muscles at the front of the thigh, so the muscle itself produced follistatin [3].

No. The FDA has not approved follistatin-344 in any form, neither as a gene therapy nor as an injectable protein. The published human studies were small, early-stage research trials run by a single research team [3][5].

Follistatin is banned in sport. The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) lists myostatin-binding proteins, naming follistatin as an example, under its class of agents that prevent activin receptor IIB activation. The ban applies in and out of competition, and gene transfer used to enhance performance is separately banned as gene doping [6].

Animal work is consistent: removing myostatin, or adding follistatin, makes mice markedly more muscular [1][4]. Human evidence is much thinner and comes from two small trials by the same research team, both using gene therapy rather than injected protein.

The first enrolled six men with Becker muscular dystrophy, an inherited condition that weakens muscle over decades. Each received AAV-delivered FS344 into both thighs at one of two doses. The main measure was the six-minute walk test, which counts how far someone walks in six minutes. Four of the six walked farther afterward, by 29 to 125 meters, while two did not improve. Muscle biopsies showed less scar tissue and larger fibers, and no adverse effects were reported [3].

The second trial treated six adults with sporadic inclusion body myositis, a muscle disease that usually begins after age 50. Treated participants also followed an exercise program. Over about a year, their walking distance rose by a median of 56 meters, while eight untreated people matched by age and sex declined by about 26 meters. Four of the six gained 58 to 153 meters; two barely changed [5].

rows: 4 of 6 walked 29 to 125 m farther in six minutes; 2 showed no change [3]
Median gain of 56 m per year, versus a 26 m decline in 8 untreated comparison patients [5]

blocks.text: These results are encouraging for the diseases studied but limited. Neither trial had a placebo group, both were tiny, and participants knew they were treated. Neither tested healthy people, athletes, or the injectable protein marketed for muscle building. Whether a protein injected under the skin would reach muscle, how long it would last, and what it would do to fertility hormones are open questions.

Vials labeled follistatin-344 are sold as research chemicals for muscle growth. None of the published human data apply to them, because the trials delivered a gene rather than a protein, at a hospital, into specific muscles [3][5]. Buyers have no way to confirm what a vial contains, whether the protein is folded correctly, or whether it is active at all. Competitive athletes face a further risk, since WADA bans follistatin at all times [6].

name: Fragment 176-191
evidenceNote: Fat-loss effects come from rodent studies. The only human trials tested the related drug AOD-9604, were never fully published in peer review, and a 536-person trial failed to show meaningful weight loss.
summary: A short piece of the growth hormone tail sold online for fat loss. Rodent data only for the fragment; the related drug AOD-9604 failed a weight-loss trial.
keyTakeaway: Fragment 176-191 is a 16 amino acid piece cut from the tail end of human growth hormone, studied because it seemed to carry the hormone's fat-burning effect without its effects on blood sugar or growth. In obese rats and mice, versions of it slowed weight gain and raised fat burning. In people, the drug-development version, AOD-9604, produced about 2.6 kg of weight loss against 0.8 kg on placebo in a 12-week trial, then failed in a 536-person trial and was dropped in 2007. It is not FDA-approved, and WADA bans it in sport.

blocks.text: Human growth hormone is a protein of 191 amino acids. Fragment 176-191 is a synthetic copy of its last 16, the stretch at the far end of the chain known as the C-terminus. Researchers began studying these tail fragments decades ago to find out which part of the hormone handles fat and which part raises blood sugar [1][4].

The fragment was later developed as a drug candidate under the name AOD-9604 (anti-obesity drug 9604) by Metabolic Pharmaceuticals, built on the same tail segment [6]. Most published research on the idea used AOD-9604, so evidence about one is usually cited for the other. Online sellers now market both, often for fat loss in bodybuilding.

The theory is that the hormone's effect on fat sits in its tail. In rat fat tissue, a version spanning residues 177 to 191 blocked fat building (lipogenesis) as well as the whole hormone did, though it did not raise fat release in that test [1]. In obese mice, AOD-9604 increased fat burning and blood glycerol, a marker of fat breakdown [3].

What made the fragment interesting is what it did not do. Unlike full growth hormone, AOD-9604 left the growth hormone receptor alone, did not make cells multiply, and did not raise blood sugar in the mouse studies [3]. Its effects in mice appeared linked to more beta-3 adrenergic receptors on fat cells, though not routed directly through them [5].

The picture is not fully clean. An older rat study found that several tail fragments, including the 176 to 191 piece, briefly raised blood sugar and insulin, and some reduced insulin sensitivity [4]. Results depended on the exact length and shape of the fragment, which is a reason to be careful with products whose identity cannot be checked.

No. Neither Fragment 176-191 nor AOD-9604 has ever been approved by the FDA for weight loss or any other use, and development of AOD-9604 as an obesity drug ended in 2007 [6]. Vials sold online are not regulated medicines.

AOD-9604 was nominated for use by compounding pharmacies, but the nomination was withdrawn. FDA's safety page for nominated substances notes possible immune reactions to the peptide, impurity and identification problems, little safety information, and serious adverse events that may be linked to it, though cause was not established [7]. In February 2026 the health secretary announced that a group of restricted peptides, AOD-9604 among them, would be moved to the category that permits compounding [9], but the FDA's page still lists its nomination as withdrawn [7]. Even that move would not make it an approved drug [9].

For athletes the answer is simpler. The 2026 World Anti-Doping Agency list names growth hormone fragments, giving AOD-9604 and hGH 176-191 as examples, among substances banned in and out of competition [8].

The animal work is consistent but small. In genetically obese Zucker rats, a daily oral dose of AOD-9604 for 19 days cut weight gain by more than half compared with untreated rats, without the loss of insulin sensitivity seen with full growth hormone [2]. In obese mice given the fragment by pump for 14 days, weight gain slowed and fat burning rose [3]. Mice lacking the beta-3 receptor did not lose weight on long-term treatment [5].

rows: Weight gain reduced by over 50%, insulin sensitivity kept [2]
Less weight gain, more fat burning, no rise in blood sugar [3]
2.6 kg lost vs 0.8 kg on placebo [6]
No meaningful weight loss; program ended in 2007 [6]

blocks.text: Human data exist only for AOD-9604 and mostly reached the public through reviews rather than full trial reports. A 12-week randomized study reported 2.6 kg of weight loss against 0.8 kg on placebo, but a larger trial of 536 people over 24 weeks did not produce significant weight loss, and the company stopped development [6]. No trial has tested Fragment 176-191 as sold online, and there are no human studies of the injected doses people use for bodybuilding.

sections.heading: Is Fragment 176-191 the same as AOD-9604?

blocks.text: They are close relatives drawn from the same tail of growth hormone, and sellers often use the names interchangeably. AOD-9604 is the name of the version a company took into human trials as an oral obesity pill [2][6]. A product labeled Fragment 176-191 is usually injected, and without independent testing there is no way to confirm which peptide, or how much of it, a vial holds.
The practical point is the same for both. The best evidence for either is a failed weight-loss program, and the positive results come from rodents [2][3][6].

name: Ga-68 dotatate
evidenceNote: FDA approved the NETSPOT kit in 2016 as a diagnostic agent on the basis of three open-label imaging studies. It is a scan tracer given once, not a treatment.
summary: Ga-68 dotatate (NETSPOT) is a radioactive peptide tracer for PET scans that finds neuroendocrine tumors carrying somatostatin receptors. FDA-approved 2016.
keyTakeaway: Ga-68 dotatate is a diagnostic scan agent: a somatostatin-like peptide carrying a small amount of radioactive gallium, which lights up neuroendocrine tumors on a PET scan. FDA approved the NETSPOT kit in 2016 for adults and children. In a prospective study of 78 patients it matched or beat the older indium-111 scan in every case and changed treatment plans in 36%. Side effects are rare and mild. The same peptide carrying lutetium-177 instead becomes Lutathera, a treatment, so this scan often decides who is eligible for that therapy.

blocks.text: Gallium Ga 68 dotatate is a radiopharmaceutical, a drug that carries a radioactive atom to a specific target in the body so it can be imaged. It has two parts. Dotatate is a short peptide that resembles somatostatin, a natural hormone, fitted with a chemical cage called DOTA. Gallium-68 is a radioactive metal held inside that cage [1].

It is used for positron emission tomography (PET), a scan that detects radiation coming from a tracer and maps where the tracer has collected. The approved product, NETSPOT, is a kit: the hospital's nuclear pharmacy draws gallium-68 from a generator, adds it to the kit vial, and uses the dose within hours [1]. Gallium-68 decays quickly, with about half gone after an hour [1].

Its job is to find neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), cancers that arise from hormone-producing cells, most often in the gut, pancreas or lungs. Many NETs are studded with somatostatin receptors, and those receptors are what the tracer latches onto [1].

Somatostatin receptors come in several subtypes. Ga-68 dotatate has its strongest pull for subtype 2 (SSTR2), which many neuroendocrine tumor cells overproduce. After injection into a vein, the tracer circulates and collects wherever SSTR2 is dense [1].

Gallium-68 emits positrons, tiny particles that the PET camera detects indirectly. Tumors packed with receptors show up as bright spots. Some normal organs also carry the receptor, including the pituitary, thyroid, spleen, adrenal glands, kidneys and pancreas, so readers must tell normal uptake from disease. Little of the tracer reaches the brain or heart [1].

Because the scan reads receptor density, other drugs that occupy the same receptor can interfere. Long-acting somatostatin analogs such as octreotide compete for SSTR2, so the label advises imaging just before the next dose of those drugs [1].

Yes. FDA approved NETSPOT on June 1, 2016, as a new molecular entity under priority review, with orphan drug status for this rare-disease use [3]. It is approved for PET localization of somatostatin receptor-positive neuroendocrine tumors in both adults and children [1].

It is a diagnostic, not a therapy. The amount of peptide in each kit is tiny, 40 micrograms of dotatate, and the radiation dose is set for imaging [1]. The same dotatate peptide paired with a different isotope, lutetium-177, is the cancer treatment Lutathera, which is approved for somatostatin receptor-positive gut and pancreatic NETs [4].

sections.heading: What is Ga-68 dotatate used for?

blocks.text: Doctors order a Ga-68 dotatate PET scan, usually combined with CT, to find where a known or suspected neuroendocrine tumor is, to stage how far it has spread, and to check for recurrence. Because it shows whether tumors carry the receptor, it also helps decide whether someone could benefit from somatostatin analog drugs or from receptor-targeted radiation treatment [2][4].

FDA's approval rested on three open-label studies [1]. In the first, 97 adults with known or suspected NETs were scanned; among 50 patients whose tumors had been located on CT or MRI, the tracer was positive in 48, including 13 whose older indium-111 scan had been negative [1].

rows: 97 adults with known or suspected NETs
Agreed with CT or MRI in 74 of 78; positive in 48 of 50 CT- or MRI-confirmed tumors [1]
Correctly found tumor in 29 of 36 confirmed cases; negative in 61 of 68 without NET [1]
Readers found tumor in 22 to 23 of 29 confirmed recurrences [1]
78 patients with lung or gut NETs
Equal or better than indium-111 in all; changed treatment in 36% [2]

blocks.text: A prospective study published the same year as approval compared the new scan head to head with indium-111 pentetreotide, the older standard. Its authors concluded that Ga-68 dotatate gave better accuracy with a lower radiation dose and no significant toxicity [2].

Side effects are uncommon. Nausea, vomiting, and pain or burning at the injection site have been reported since approval. Hypersensitivity reactions, mostly rash and itching, have also occurred and usually resolved on their own or with routine care. The label lists no conditions in which it cannot be used [1].

Radiation is the main consideration. The scan adds to a person's lifetime radiation exposure, so patients are asked to drink water and empty the bladder often in the hours after injection. For 12 hours afterward, the label advises limiting close contact with infants and pregnant women, and breastfeeding mothers should pump and discard milk for that period [1].

There is also a risk of misreading. The tracer can collect in some tumors that are not NETs, in leftover spleen tissue after injury, and in normal spots such as part of the pancreas, so findings are interpreted alongside other imaging [1]. Repeated high doses of steroid medicines before the scan may also affect results [1].

name: Ganirelix
evidenceNote: FDA-approved since 1999 on the strength of controlled IVF trials, and supported by a Cochrane review of 73 randomized trials comparing GnRH antagonists with the older agonist protocols.
summary: Ganirelix is a daily IVF injection that blocks the brain's ovulation signal so eggs are not released early. FDA-approved since 1999.
keyTakeaway: Ganirelix is a synthetic ten-amino-acid peptide that blocks the receptor for gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) in the pituitary. During IVF it is injected under the skin once a day to stop a premature surge of luteinizing hormone, which could release eggs before retrieval. The FDA approved it in 1999. In a North American phase 3 trial, ongoing pregnancy rates were 30.8% with ganirelix and 36.4% with a long leuprolide protocol, with fewer injection days. Across many trials, antagonists like ganirelix lower the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. It must not be used during pregnancy.

blocks.text: Ganirelix acetate is a synthetic decapeptide, a chain of ten amino acids, built from the natural hormone GnRH with six of its positions swapped for altered amino acids [1]. Those changes turn a hormone that switches the pituitary on into a molecule that blocks it. It comes as a ready-to-use solution in prefilled syringes for injection under the skin [1].

It is used only in fertility medicine. Organon holds the original approval [4], and generic versions exist, including one sold by Sun Pharma under the brand name Fyremadel [5]. Treatment lasts days, not months: it runs for part of a single ovarian stimulation cycle and then stops.

The hypothalamus releases GnRH in pulses, and each pulse tells the pituitary to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Midway through a natural cycle, a large LH surge triggers ovulation. In IVF, doctors stimulate the ovaries to grow several follicles at once and then collect the eggs at a planned time. If the body launches its own LH surge first, the eggs can be released and lost before retrieval [1].

Ganirelix sits on the GnRH receptor and keeps the natural hormone from binding. LH falls more than FSH, and because it is a blocker rather than a stimulator, there is no initial burst of hormones before suppression begins [1]. Its effect is fast and reversible: LH and FSH return to normal within 48 hours of the last dose [1]. That speed lets it be started partway through stimulation, which is shorter than the older long agonist protocol, where drugs such as leuprolide first trigger a hormone flare and then need a long down-regulation period before stimulation can begin [3].

Yes. The FDA approved ganirelix acetate injection in July 1999 [4]. Its label covers one use: inhibiting premature LH surges in women undergoing controlled ovarian hyperstimulation [1]. The label states that it should be prescribed by physicians experienced in infertility treatment [1].

items.text: FDA approves Organon's ganirelix acetate injection [4].
North American phase 3 trial against leuprolide published [2].
FDA approves Sun Pharma's Fyremadel, a generic ganirelix [5].

blocks.text: Ganirelix is prescribed during IVF and related procedures, alongside FSH injections that grow the follicles. In the approval trials, it was started on day 6 of FSH and continued until follicles were large enough for the final trigger injection [1]. A dose-finding study in 332 patients found the highest pregnancy and implantation rates at the 250 mcg dose, which became the marketed strength [1].

The trial authors concluded that ganirelix gave similar pregnancy rates with a shorter course and fewer injections [2]. A 2016 Cochrane review pooled 73 randomized trials with 12,212 participants comparing GnRH antagonists against long agonist protocols. It found no clear difference in live birth rates, while antagonists lowered the odds of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a potentially serious overreaction of the ovaries, by roughly 40% [3].

The same review found no difference in miscarriage rates. Cycles run with an antagonist were less often cancelled because of a high OHSS risk, but more often cancelled because the ovaries responded poorly [3]. Those trade-offs are part of why clinics choose between protocols case by case rather than using one for everyone.

In the controlled trials, side effects were recorded from the first injection until pregnancy was confirmed, so they reflect the whole IVF cycle and not ganirelix alone. Events seen in at least 1% of the 794 treated women included [1]:

items: Gynecological abdominal pain (4.8%) [1]
Headache (3.0%) [1]
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (2.4%) [1]
Vaginal bleeding (1.8%) [1]
Injection-site reaction and nausea (1.1% each) [1]
Fetal loss (3.7%), which reflects early pregnancy outcomes in an IVF population [1]

blocks.text: Rare allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, swelling, and hives, have been reported after approval, sometimes with the first dose [1]. Ganirelix is contraindicated in known or suspected pregnancy and in people allergic to it or to other GnRH drugs [1]. A study of more than 1,000 newborns found birth defect rates similar to those after cycles using a GnRH agonist [1].

name: GHK-Cu
evidenceNote: Every result for injected GHK-Cu comes from cell cultures and rodents. The human studies that exist test creams on facial skin, are mostly summarized by the compound's own developer, and say nothing about injections.
summary: GHK-Cu is a copper-binding tripeptide found in blood. Creams use it for skin; injected use is unapproved and rests on animal studies only.
keyTakeaway: GHK-Cu is a three-amino-acid peptide (glycine, histidine, lysine) that carries copper and occurs naturally in human plasma, at levels that fall with age. Cosmetic creams have used it for decades. The injectable form sold for skin, hair, and healing is not an FDA-approved drug, and no controlled human trial has tested it. Its support comes from cell work, a rat ligament study whose benefit faded by 12 weeks, and a mouse lung injury model. In 2026 the FDA's compounding lists still treat injectable GHK-Cu as unsettled, with an advisory review expected by February 2027.

blocks.text: GHK is a tiny peptide made of three amino acids: glycine, histidine, and lysine. It grips copper ions tightly, and the copper-bound form is written GHK-Cu. The body makes it on its own; it circulates in plasma, saliva, and urine. A review by the researcher who first described it reports plasma levels of roughly 200 ng/mL at age 20, dropping to about 80 ng/mL by age 60 [1].

The peptide was first isolated in 1973 from human blood, where it appeared to push older liver tissue to make proteins the way younger tissue does [1]. It later became a familiar skin care ingredient, listed on labels as copper tripeptide-1. More recently, clinics and online sellers have offered it as an injection for skin quality, hair, and tissue repair. That injectable use is the subject of this page.

Most of what is known about the mechanism comes from cell cultures and animals. In those settings, GHK-Cu prompts fibroblasts (the cells that build connective tissue) to make collagen, elastin, and glycosaminoglycans, and it adjusts the enzymes that break down old matrix [2]. It also draws immune and blood-vessel cells toward a wound [1].

The developer's group has also run GHK through the Broad Institute's Connectivity Map, a database that compares how compounds shift gene activity in cultured cells. They report that it nudges thousands of genes, including ones tied to DNA repair, antioxidant defense, and nerve function, toward patterns they describe as healthier [1][3]. Those analyses describe gene readouts in cell lines, not effects measured in people. The authors of these reviews work in the research department of Skin Biology, a skin care company, which is worth knowing when weighing how broadly the claims are framed [2][3].

No. GHK-Cu has never been approved as a drug for any use. Creams that contain it are sold as cosmetics, which do not need FDA approval before sale as long as they make appearance claims rather than medical ones. Injections are a different matter, because anything injected to change the body is regulated as a drug.

Its standing with compounding pharmacies shifted during 2026. Injectable GHK-Cu had been nominated for the list of bulk substances that 503A pharmacies may use, then the nominations were withdrawn. The FDA's safety page now lists it among withdrawn nominations and notes a possible immune reaction risk from peptide clumping and impurities, adding that there are limited human data to judge safety [6]. In May 2026 the agency put the non-injectable form back under evaluation and said it plans to ask its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee about GHK-Cu before the end of February 2027 [7]. Until that process finishes, no route of GHK-Cu has a settled place on the compounding list.

items.text: Peptide activity isolated from human blood; later identified as GHK bound to copper [1].

blocks.text: For injected GHK-Cu, the evidence stops at animals. Two published studies show what that work looks like. In rats that had knee ligament reconstruction, weekly injections into the joint tightened the knee and stiffened the graft at 6 weeks, but by 12 weeks the treated and untreated knees no longer differed, and strength at failure, gait, and tissue scores never separated [4]. In mice given a bacterial toxin to inflame the lungs, GHK-Cu lowered inflammatory signals and reduced tissue damage [5].

rows: Weekly injections into the knee for 4 weeks
Less laxity at 6 weeks; no difference by 12 weeks [4]
GHK-Cu treatment in an acute lung injury model

blocks.text: Human data exist only for skin products. The developer's 2015 review describes several 12-week facial cream studies in women, mostly in their 50s, reporting improvements in fine lines, firmness, and skin thickness, with some comparing against placebo or other creams [1]. Those were topical products tested for appearance, and most of the details come from the same group that champions the peptide. None of them tells us whether injecting GHK-Cu under the skin is safe or does anything useful.

So the case for injections is an extrapolation from three places: cell experiments, short animal studies, and cosmetic cream data. The dose, purity, and long-term effects of injected copper peptide in people have not been studied in a controlled way.

sections.heading: How is the cream different from the injection?

blocks.text: The molecule can be the same, but the route changes almost everything about how it is judged. A cream sits on the skin, little of it is absorbed, and it is regulated as a cosmetic. An injection delivers the whole amount into tissue and bloodstream, so purity, sterility, and immune reactions matter in a way they do not for a face cream. That is why the FDA's safety note singles out the injectable route [6].

Products sold online as research peptides are not made under drug manufacturing standards, and their content is not checked by a regulator. Anyone weighing them is relying on a seller's label rather than on tested evidence.

name: GHRP-2
evidenceNote: Human data consist of short hormone-response studies and its use as a one-off diagnostic test. No randomized trial has tested repeated use for muscle, fat loss, recovery, or any other outcome people buy it for.
summary: A synthetic peptide that triggers a growth hormone surge. Used in Japan as a diagnostic test, never approved in the US, and banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: GHRP-2 is a small synthetic peptide that activates the ghrelin receptor, causing a sharp release of growth hormone and a rise in appetite. It came out of academic work at Tulane University and is used in Japan as a single-dose test of pituitary function, but it has never been approved by the FDA for any use. No controlled trial has shown that repeated use builds muscle or burns fat. The FDA lists it among substances outsourcing facilities may not compound, and WADA bans it at all times.

blocks.text: GHRP-2, short for growth hormone-releasing peptide-2, is a short lab-made peptide. It belongs to a family of small peptides created by Cyril Bowers and colleagues at Tulane University, designed to make the pituitary gland release growth hormone [3]. Its drug name is pralmorelin.

The Japanese company Kaken acquired the rights and developed it as a diagnostic agent, a single dose given to see whether the pituitary can still respond [3]. Other planned uses, including treatment of short stature in children and of growth hormone deficiency in the United States, did not reach approval, and the US program appears to have been dropped [3].

GHRP-2 mimics ghrelin, a hormone made mainly in the stomach that signals hunger. Both bind the growth hormone secretagogue receptor, also called the ghrelin receptor, which sits on growth hormone-producing cells in the pituitary and on appetite-related nerve cells in the brain [1][3].

The result is a fast, large pulse of growth hormone. In a small infusion study in healthy men, growth hormone exposure over four hours was more than ten times higher with GHRP-2 than with saline [1]. The same study showed the second effect of the receptor: when offered a buffet afterwards, every one of the seven men ate more, about 36% more on average [1].

Peptides in this family are not selective for growth hormone alone. A 2026 clinical review of these compounds lists raised prolactin and cortisol, swings in blood sugar, fluid retention, and joint and muscle aches among the effects reported with them [7].

No. GHRP-2 has never been approved by the FDA for treatment or diagnosis. In 2023 the FDA placed it, for injectable and nasal use, in Category 2 of its interim compounding policy for outsourcing facilities, the group of bulk substances it says raise significant safety concerns [5]. The agency cited a risk of immune reactions and serious adverse events reported with its use, while noting that cause and effect had not been established [5].

Japan is the exception. GHRP-2 is described in the scientific literature as the only peptide of its family to reach clinical approval, and Japanese guidelines recommend a GHRP-2 stimulation test as an alternative way to diagnose adult growth hormone deficiency [4][9]. That use is a single dose under medical supervision, not ongoing treatment.
For athletes, the World Anti-Doping Agency names GHRP-2 (pralmorelin) on its Prohibited List under growth hormone releasing factors, banned in and out of competition [6].

Almost all human research on GHRP-2 measures what happens to hormones in the hours after a dose. That makes it a useful tool for testing the pituitary, but it says nothing about long-term effects on body composition, healing, or aging.

rows: Food intake rose about 36% and growth hormone rose sharply versus saline [1]
The GHRP-2 test identified severe adult growth hormone deficiency with 85.5% sensitivity and 94.5% specificity against the insulin tolerance test [4]
65 patients aged 65 and over before pituitary surgery
Growth hormone response to GHRP-2 tracked adrenal function, supporting use as a gentler test in the elderly [2]

blocks.text: The diagnostic work is the strongest part of the record. Japanese researchers regard the GHRP-2 test as one of the safer stimulation tests for older patients [2], it performed close to the insulin tolerance test that has long been the reference [4], and its developers set a defined growth hormone cut-off for separating deficiency from normal function [3].

What is missing is any controlled trial of repeated GHRP-2 use in healthy adults. Claims about muscle gain, fat loss, better sleep, or faster recovery come from extrapolating short hormone spikes, from animal work, or from user reports. A 2026 review that sorted these peptides by evidence tier stressed the gap between published data and the self-dosing protocols circulating online [7].

GHRP-2 is widely sold as a powder labeled for research use. Anti-doping laboratories have found it in seized unlabeled vials [8], in tablets sold over the counter as a nutritional supplement [10], and have identified a modified version in a seized vial that appears designed to slip past doping tests [9].

None of these products is made to pharmaceutical standards, so purity, dose, and sterility are unknown. The appetite surge is a predictable effect of the molecule itself, and the hormonal side effects described for this class apply regardless of where the product came from [1][7].

name: GHRP-6
class: Growth hormone secretagogue, ghrelin receptor agonist
evidenceNote: Human data are limited to small, short studies in healthy volunteers that measured growth hormone, IGF-1, and drug levels in the blood. No randomized trial has tested GHRP-6 against a clinical outcome such as muscle, bone, or heart health.
summary: A six-amino-acid lab peptide that triggers growth hormone release through the ghrelin receptor. Never approved; studied mainly in animals and small hormone tests.
keyTakeaway: GHRP-6 is a small synthetic peptide, made in the early 1980s, that makes the pituitary release a burst of growth hormone by acting on the ghrelin receptor. In nine healthy men, a 34-hour infusion roughly doubled growth hormone output and raised IGF-1 by about a quarter. Beyond short hormone and blood-level studies, the human evidence is thin, and the heart-protection findings come from animals. It is not FDA-approved, the FDA has flagged safety concerns about compounding it, and it is banned in sport.

blocks.text: GHRP-6 stands for growth hormone-releasing peptide 6. It is a hexapeptide, a chain of six amino acids, with the sequence histidine, D-tryptophan, alanine, tryptophan, D-phenylalanine, lysine [1][3]. Two of those building blocks are D-forms, mirror images of the amino acids the body normally uses, which makes the peptide harder for enzymes to break down.

It is a growth hormone secretagogue, meaning a substance that prompts the body to release its own growth hormone rather than supplying the hormone directly [1]. GHRP-6 was never developed into a medicine. It remains a research compound, and versions sold online are made outside any approved manufacturing process.

Cyril Bowers and colleagues described the peptide in 1984. In pituitary tissue in the lab and in rats, monkeys, lambs, and calves, it released growth hormone without moving other pituitary hormones such as LH, FSH, TSH, or prolactin [1]. Young rats given it once or twice a day gained more weight than controls [1].

At the time nobody knew which receptor it used. The target was cloned in the 1990s and named the growth hormone secretagogue receptor, and its natural partner, the stomach hormone ghrelin, was found afterward [5]. GHRP-6 became the template for later compounds in the same family, including GHRP-2, hexarelin, and ipamorelin.

blocks.text: GHRP-6 binds GHS-R1a, the ghrelin receptor, which sits mainly in the hypothalamus and the pituitary [5]. Switching that receptor on makes pituitary cells release a pulse of growth hormone. In the first animal tests, levels rose within two minutes, peaked at 10 to 20 minutes, and were back to normal within about two hours [1].

It works alongside the body's main growth hormone signal, GHRH, rather than replacing it. During the 1993 infusion study, injections of GHRH produced larger growth hormone responses than usual, and the authors suggested GHRP-6 may partly work by blunting somatostatin, the hormone that holds growth hormone back [2]. Because ghrelin is a hunger hormone, activating its receptor is also linked to appetite.

Some actions may not involve growth hormone at all. Ghrelin receptors and other binding sites have been found in heart and blood vessel tissue [5]. A 2002 study of hexarelin, a closely related peptide, identified CD36, a protein on heart muscle and blood vessel cells, as one of these sites in rat hearts [4]. How much this applies to GHRP-6 in people is not known.
No. GHRP-6 has never been approved by the FDA for any use, and no company has a marketing application for it.

The FDA has also moved to limit compounding. Since September 29, 2023, GHRP-6 has sat in category 2 for outsourcing facilities (503B), the group of substances the agency says may present significant safety risks [7]. The FDA's reasons include possible immune reactions caused by clumping and impurities in compounded peptide products, effects on cortisol, and higher blood sugar from reduced insulin sensitivity [7].

For ordinary compounding pharmacies (503A), the FDA's nomination list dated May 14, 2026 places GHRP-6 in category 3, substances nominated without enough supporting information for the agency to evaluate them [9]. Neither listing allows routine compounding of the peptide, and products sold online as research chemicals are not regulated drugs.

The best human data are hormone studies. In 1993, nine healthy young men each received a 34-hour intravenous infusion of GHRP-6 and, separately, a saline infusion [2]. On GHRP-6, total growth hormone output roughly doubled, the height of each pulse rose, and IGF-1 (a growth factor made in response to growth hormone) climbed from about 252 to 312 micrograms per liter [2]. The number of pulses did not change, and the pituitary stayed responsive throughout [2].

rows: Growth hormone output about doubled; IGF-1 rose about 24%; TSH response smaller
Elimination half-life about 2.5 hours; blood levels rose with dose
Pigs with a blocked heart artery
Damaged heart mass 78% smaller than with saline

blocks.text: A 2013 study in Cuba gave nine healthy men single intravenous doses of 100, 200, and 400 micrograms per kilogram and measured the drug in their blood [3]. The peptide spread through the body within minutes and was cleared with a half-life of about 2.5 hours, and four of the nine men showed unexplained late spikes in blood levels [3]. The study measured blood levels, not benefits.

The heart findings are from animals. In pigs whose main heart artery was blocked for an hour, one dose of GHRP-6 cut the mass of dead heart muscle by 78% compared with saline, and the authors linked the effect to lower oxidative stress [6]. Reviews of ghrelin and its synthetic mimics describe protective heart effects in experimental models but note that the signaling is not fully understood [5]. No trial has tested GHRP-6 for muscle growth, fat loss, healing, or bone strength in people.

No. The World Anti-Doping Agency lists GHRP-6 by name among growth hormone secretagogues, which are prohibited both in and out of competition [8]. It sits in the same section of the list as GHRP-2, hexarelin, and other members of the family.

name: Glepaglutide
evidenceNote: One randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 106 adults with short bowel syndrome, plus open-label extension and absorption studies. Only the twice-weekly dose beat placebo, and the FDA asked for another trial before it would approve.
summary: An injectable GLP-2 analog for short bowel syndrome that cut IV nutrition needs in a phase 3 trial. Rejected by the FDA in 2024; recommended in the EU in 2026.
keyTakeaway: Glepaglutide is a lab-made version of GLP-2, a gut hormone that helps the intestinal lining grow and absorb more. It is being developed by Zealand Pharma for short bowel syndrome, where patients depend on intravenous nutrition and fluids. In its phase 3 trial, a twice-weekly injection cut weekly IV support by about 5.1 liters against 2.9 liters on placebo, while a once-weekly dose did not separate from placebo. The FDA declined to approve it in December 2024. Europe's medicines committee recommended approval in September 2026.

blocks.text: Glepaglutide is a synthetic, long-lasting copy of glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2), a hormone released by the lower intestine after meals [1]. It is unrelated in purpose to the GLP-1 drugs used for diabetes and weight loss, even though the names are similar. Zealand Pharma, the Danish company behind it, plans to sell it as Zeydovio [4].

Its target is short bowel syndrome (SBS), a rare condition in which a large part of the small intestine has been removed or does not work, so the body cannot absorb enough fluid and nutrients from food. Many patients with intestinal failure rely on parenteral support (nutrition and fluids given through a vein) several nights a week, often for years [1].

GLP-2 acts as a growth signal for the gut lining. Glepaglutide mimics it, increasing the thickness of the mucosa, the height of the absorptive cells, and the depth of the small pits (crypts) where new cells form [4]. It also raises blood flow to the intestine, lowers stomach acid, and slows how quickly contents move through the gut, all of which give the remaining bowel more time and surface to absorb [4].
Glepaglutide was engineered as a long-acting molecule, which is what allows it to be injected under the skin just once or twice a week in trials [1].

In a small open-label study that measured everything going in and out of the body, ten patients absorbed about 1,038 kJ (roughly 250 kcal) more energy per day after 24 weeks on a once-weekly dose, and by one year had cut their IV support by about 800 mL a day [2].

No. Zealand filed a New Drug Application, and on December 19, 2024 the FDA issued a complete response letter, its formal decision not to approve an application as submitted [3]. The agency said the data did not provide enough evidence of efficacy and safety for the dose intended for market, and recommended an additional clinical trial [3]. Zealand said it would run one more phase 3 trial to support a US resubmission [3].

Europe has moved further. On September 17, 2026, the European Medicines Agency's human medicines committee (CHMP) adopted a positive opinion recommending marketing authorization for adults with SBS who are stable after a period of intestinal adaptation following surgery [4]. A CHMP opinion is a recommendation; the European Commission makes the final decision.

blocks.text: The main evidence is EASE-1, a double-blind trial that randomized 106 adults with SBS and intestinal failure, all needing IV support at least three days a week, to glepaglutide 10 mg twice weekly, 10 mg once weekly, or placebo for 24 weeks [1]. IV volumes were lowered by protocol whenever a patient's urine output rose, which signals better absorption [1].

rows: Change in weekly IV support volume
At least one fewer IV day per week

blocks.text: The once-weekly arm, which reduced IV volume by about 3.1 liters a week, did not differ significantly from placebo on the main or key secondary outcomes [1][3]. That split matters because a once-weekly schedule is more convenient, and published coverage of the FDA's letter does not say which schedule Zealand sought to market [3].

The placebo group also improved by nearly 3 liters, a reminder that close monitoring and protocol-driven IV reductions help on their own. Investigators judged glepaglutide safe and well tolerated over the trial [1]. The side effects the EMA lists as most common are injection site reactions, problems at the stoma (the surgical opening in the abdomen) in patients who have one, abdominal pain and swelling, nausea, vomiting, and fluid retention [4].

Longer follow-up comes from extension studies. Reports from the EASE-2 extension describe more patients coming off IV support on both schedules, and an interim look at 43 patients in EASE-3, which uses an autoinjector once a week, found that reductions in prescribed IV support were mostly maintained [3]. These extensions have no placebo group.

name: Glucagon
evidenceNote: Glucagon has been an FDA-approved drug since 1960. Its newer ready-to-use forms were approved in 2019 after randomized crossover trials showed they raise blood sugar as reliably as the traditional mix-and-inject kit.
summary: The pancreatic hormone that raises blood sugar, approved as an emergency rescue for severe low blood sugar and as an aid for some X-ray exams.
keyTakeaway: The pancreas releases glucagon when blood sugar runs low, and the liver answers by turning stored sugar loose. As a drug it has been approved in the US since 1960 to treat severe hypoglycemia, dangerously low blood sugar, in people with diabetes, and some injectable forms are also approved to relax the gut during radiology exams. Newer products include a ready-to-inject pen (Gvoke) and a nasal powder (Baqsimi). In trials, nearly every patient's blood sugar recovered within 30 minutes. Nausea and vomiting are the most common side effects.

blocks.text: Glucagon is a hormone made by the pancreas that does roughly the opposite of insulin: when blood sugar falls, it signals the liver to release more. The drug form is a single chain of 29 amino acids identical to human glucagon, made by chemical synthesis [1].

It is best known as a rescue medicine for severe hypoglycemia, a drop in blood sugar so deep that a person cannot safely eat or drink to fix it, usually caused by insulin [1]. Because it also relaxes the muscle of the digestive tract, the traditional injectable form is approved as a diagnostic aid, used to keep the stomach and bowel still during X-ray imaging [3]. A related engineered drug, dasiglucagon, is covered separately.

Glucagon was first approved in the United States in 1960 [1]. For decades it came as an emergency kit of powder and liquid that a caregiver had to mix and draw into a syringe during a crisis, a step that is easy to get wrong under stress [4]. The newer products were designed to remove that step.

items.text: Initial US approval of glucagon [1]
Novo Nordisk's GlucaGen and Lilly's glucagon kit approved; both now listed as discontinued [7][8]
FDA approves Baqsimi, the first nasal glucagon [5]
FDA approves Gvoke, a premixed liquid in a pen or syringe [6]

blocks.text: Glucagon binds glucagon receptors on liver cells. That triggers glycogenolysis, the breakdown of glycogen (the liver's stored form of sugar) into glucose, which then pours into the blood [1]. After a 1 mg Gvoke injection in adults with diabetes, blood sugar rose by an average of 176 mg/dL at its peak [1].

The effect depends on having glycogen to release. People who are starving, have adrenal insufficiency, or have had long-running low blood sugar may have too little stored, and glucagon may not work for them; they need glucose instead [1]. The hormone is broken down quickly in the liver, kidneys, and blood, with a half-life of about half an hour [1][2].
On the gut, glucagon relaxes the smooth muscle of the stomach, duodenum, small bowel, and colon, which is why radiologists use it to reduce movement blur [3].

Yes. Several glucagon products are approved and on the market. Gvoke from Xeris is a premixed liquid in an auto-injector or prefilled syringe for patients aged 2 and older [1][6]. Baqsimi is a 3 mg nasal powder for patients aged 4 and older, originally from Lilly and now held by Amphastar [2][5]. Fresenius Kabi sells a powder-and-diluent injection, which also carries the diagnostic aid approval [3].
Some older brands are gone. Lilly's original glucagon kit and Novo Nordisk's GlucaGen are both listed as discontinued in the FDA's database [7][8].

Its main use is as a rescue drug for people on insulin, usually given by someone else during a severe low, followed by a call for emergency help and carbohydrates by mouth once the person responds [1][2]. The newer forms were tested by deliberately lowering blood sugar with an insulin drip in a clinic, then comparing them with the traditional kit.

blocks.text: Success in these studies meant blood sugar climbing to at least 70 mg/dL, or by at least 20 mg/dL, within 30 minutes [1][4]. Both new forms met the preset bar for being no worse than the standard injection, though each took a few minutes longer on average [1][4]. As a diagnostic aid, the injectable form is given just before an X-ray exam of the stomach or bowel [3].

Nausea and vomiting are the most common. In adult Gvoke trials, 30% had nausea and 16% vomited within 12 hours, and 7% had swelling at the injection site [1]. With the nasal powder, the common effects were headache, irritation of the nose and throat, and watery or itchy eyes, reported by more than half of adults when asked directly [2]. In the Rickels trial, head or face discomfort was reported at 25% of nasal visits against 9% for injections [4].

Not used with insulinoma, a tumour that can release excess insulin and cause a later crash [1]
Allergic reactions, rarely including anaphylaxis, have been reported [1]
A skin rash called necrolytic migratory erythema has followed continuous infusions [1]
When used for imaging, it can raise heart rate and blood pressure, and blood sugar in people with diabetes [3]

name: Glutathione
evidenceNote: Several small randomized trials exist for skin tone, Parkinson's disease, cystic fibrosis, and body glutathione levels, but most are short, involve fewer than 160 people, and give mixed or modest results.
summary: Glutathione is a three-amino-acid antioxidant the body makes itself, sold as a supplement and compounded injection, with small trials on skin tone and Parkinson's.
keyTakeaway: Glutathione is a tripeptide (three linked amino acids) that every human cell makes and uses as its main internal antioxidant. Small randomized trials suggest oral doses of 250 to 500 mg a day can modestly lighten sun-exposed skin over 4 to 12 weeks, and a 6-month trial found that oral supplements raise glutathione stores in blood. It is not an FDA-approved drug. It sells as a dietary supplement, and as of May 2026 it remains in the FDA's category 1 for compounding while under evaluation. Trials in Parkinson's and cystic fibrosis missed their main goals.

atGlance.value: Not an approved drug; compounding allowed under category 1 while FDA evaluates it

atGlance.label: What it is
atGlance.value: A tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine made in every cell

atGlance.value: Small randomized trials on skin tone, Parkinson's, cystic fibrosis, and body stores

blocks.text: Glutathione is a small peptide built from three amino acids: glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. The body makes it in nearly every cell, and it is the most abundant antioxidant produced inside the body [7]. The active form is called reduced glutathione, or GSH. When it neutralizes a reactive molecule, two GSH units join into oxidized glutathione, and enzymes then recycle it back.

Outside the body, glutathione is sold in three main forms: oral capsules marketed as supplements, intravenous drips offered at wellness and aesthetic clinics, and inhaled or topical preparations used in research. In parts of Asia it is widely marketed as a skin-lightening product [4]. Because the peptide is broken down in the gut, whether swallowed glutathione reaches the blood intact was long debated.

Its main job is defense against oxidative stress, the damage done by reactive oxygen molecules produced during normal metabolism. Glutathione donates an electron to neutralize them, helps recycle vitamins C and E, and is used by liver enzymes to bind and clear drugs and toxins. It is depleted in the fluid lining the lungs of people with cystic fibrosis [8], and its role against oxidative damage in the brain led researchers to test it in Parkinson's disease [5].

The skin effect is thought to work through melanin, the pigment that colors skin. Pigment cells can make dark eumelanin or lighter pheomelanin, and glutathione appears to tilt production toward the lighter form [3]. This is a proposed mechanism drawn largely from lab work, and it does not mean the effect in people is large or lasting.
No. Glutathione is not an FDA-approved drug for any condition. Oral glutathione reaches the market as a dietary supplement, a category the FDA does not review for effectiveness before sale.

Injectable glutathione is made by compounding pharmacies. The FDA lists glutathione in category 1 of substances nominated for its 503A bulk drug list, meaning it is under evaluation and pharmacies may keep compounding it in the meantime [1]. That listing was still in place in the FDA's May 2026 update. Category 1 is a holding position, not an approval, and it says nothing about whether an IV drip does what clinics advertise.

For athletes, glutathione itself is not on the World Anti-Doping Agency list. The method matters, though: intravenous infusions or injections of more than 100 mL in any 12-hour period are prohibited outside hospital care, which covers a typical clinic drip [9].

The human evidence is a collection of small randomized trials, not a single large program. Results are strongest for the narrow question of whether supplements raise body levels, mixed for skin tone, and weak for the diseases tested.

rows: At 1,000 mg a day, glutathione in red cells, plasma, and lymphocytes rose 30 to 35%; levels fell back within a month of stopping [7]
Skin melanin fell at all six sites measured, but beat placebo at only two, the face and a sun-exposed forearm [2]
The combination lightened skin and shrank dark spots more than placebo; glutathione alone did not match it [3]
No significant difference in symptom scores against placebo [5]
No improvement in lung function, flare-ups, or quality of life [8]

blocks.text: A 2019 systematic review of the skin studies found only four trials in healthy people, and concluded that the whitening effect was inconclusive because of study quality and inconsistent results, though there was a trend toward lighter sun-exposed skin [4]. None of the skin trials ran longer than 12 weeks, and none tested the high-dose IV drips sold by clinics.

In Parkinson's disease, a 2021 meta-analysis pooled seven randomized trials with 450 participants and found a small improvement in motor scores, with no difference in other symptom scales [6]. Many of the included trials were small and published in Chinese databases, and the one US pilot of IV glutathione found no significant benefit [5].

Side effects in these trials were uncommon and mild. The trials were short, though, and the original skin study authors noted that long-term safety had not been established [2]. Injected products also carry the usual compounding risks of contamination and dosing error, which trials of pharmaceutical-grade glutathione do not capture.

For years the common view was that swallowed glutathione is digested into its amino acids and does nothing a protein meal would not. The 6-month Penn State trial challenged that: blood and tissue glutathione rose in a dose-dependent way and dropped again after a washout month, and natural killer cell activity more than doubled in the high-dose group at 3 months [7]. Raising a blood level is not the same as treating a disease, and that trial measured biomarkers, not health outcomes.

name: Goserelin
evidenceNote: Goserelin has been FDA-approved since 1989, with controlled trials in prostate cancer, breast cancer, endometriosis, and endometrial thinning behind its label.
summary: Goserelin (Zoladex) is a GnRH agonist implant that shuts down sex hormones, used since 1989 for prostate and breast cancer and endometriosis.
keyTakeaway: Goserelin is a synthetic version of the brain hormone GnRH, delivered as a small dissolving implant under the skin of the abdomen. After a brief surge, it switches off the pituitary signal to the testes or ovaries, dropping testosterone in men to castrate levels within 2 to 4 weeks. First approved by the FDA in 1989, Zoladex is now labeled for prostate cancer, advanced breast cancer before menopause, endometriosis, and thinning the uterine lining before ablation. In trials it matched surgical removal of the testes or ovaries. In sport, WADA bans it in men.

atGlance.value: Approved as Zoladex since 1989 (3.6 mg and 10.8 mg implants)

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Overstimulates then shuts down pituitary signals to the testes or ovaries

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Prostate cancer, advanced premenopausal breast cancer, endometriosis, endometrial thinning before ablation

blocks.text: Goserelin is a ten-amino-acid peptide modeled on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the hypothalamic hormone that tells the pituitary gland to drive the testes and ovaries. Two of its amino acids are changed from the natural sequence, which makes it far more resistant to breakdown [1]. It is sold as Zoladex.

Unlike most peptide drugs, goserelin is not given as a liquid. The drug is dispersed in a rod about 1 mm wide made of a lactic and glycolic acid polymer, the same kind of material used in dissolving stitches. A healthcare provider injects the rod under the skin of the lower abdomen with a wide needle, and it releases goserelin steadily as it dissolves [1]. The 3.6 mg implant lasts 28 days; a 10.8 mg implant, approved for prostate cancer only, lasts 12 weeks [2].

Natural GnRH arrives in pulses. A constant supply has the opposite effect to a pulse. In the first days, goserelin pushes the pituitary to release a burst of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and testosterone rises. With continued exposure, the pituitary's receptors stop responding, LH and FSH fall, and testosterone drops to the range seen after surgical castration, about 2 to 4 weeks after starting [1].

The suppression holds for as long as the implants are renewed. In trials with more than two years of follow-up, testosterone stayed at castrate levels throughout treatment [1]. Animal studies before approval showed the drug shrinking hormone-sensitive breast and prostate tumors in rats, the early signal that it could stand in for surgery [1].

In women, the same shutdown lowers estradiol to postmenopausal levels [1]. That is the basis for every approved use: prostate cancer and hormone receptor positive breast cancer are fed by sex hormones, endometriosis tissue grows under estrogen, and a thin uterine lining makes ablation easier. The early surge explains the tumor flare warning, a temporary worsening of cancer symptoms in the first weeks.

Yes. Zoladex was first approved in the United States in 1989 and remains on the market, now from TerSera Therapeutics [1]. The 3.6 mg implant carries five uses across men and women; the 10.8 mg implant is limited to prostate cancer [1][2]. The label was updated in September 2025 to add a warning about severe skin reactions [1].

Every approved use requires a prescription and an in-office injection. For athletes, the World Anti-Doping Agency lists goserelin among the GnRH agonists prohibited in men at all times, because the initial surge raises testosterone [4].

items: Locally confined prostate cancer, together with the antiandrogen flutamide and radiation [1].
Advanced prostate cancer, as long-term palliative treatment [1][2].
Advanced breast cancer in women before or around menopause [1].
Endometriosis, for a course of up to 6 months [1].
Thinning the uterine lining before endometrial ablation for abnormal uterine bleeding [1].

rows: Local failure at 4 years 16% with goserelin, flutamide, and radiation, against 33% with radiation alone [1]
Premenopausal women with advanced receptor-positive breast cancer
Response 22% against 12% for removal of the ovaries; median survival about 33 months in both arms [1]
At least half of lesion extent cleared in 62 to 63% on goserelin, against 42 to 51% on danazol [1]
Premenopausal women with node-positive early breast cancer
Matched CMF chemotherapy for survival in estrogen receptor positive disease; worse in receptor negative disease [3]

blocks.text: In advanced prostate cancer, controlled studies comparing goserelin with removal of the testes found similar hormone responses, tumor responses, and survival [1]. The ZEBRA trial, followed for a median of 7.3 years, tested goserelin as adjuvant treatment after surgery for early breast cancer. That adjuvant use is not one of the indications on the US label [1][3].

Most side effects follow from low sex hormones. In men, hot flashes, sexual dysfunction, and reduced erections are the most common, each in more than 10% [1]. In women, hot flushes affected 96% in the endometriosis trials, with vaginal dryness and inflammation, headache, mood changes, lower libido, sweating, and acne also frequent [1].

items: Bone loss: women lost an average of 4.3% of spinal bone density over 6 months, recovering only partly, which is why endometriosis courses are capped [1].
Tumor flare in the first weeks, including rare spinal cord compression or urinary blockage in men with advanced cancer [1].
Higher blood sugar and diabetes risk, and reports of heart attack, sudden cardiac death, and stroke in men on GnRH drugs [1].
QT prolongation on the heart tracing, depression, injection site and blood vessel injury, and severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome [1].

blocks.text: Goserelin is not used in pregnancy except for advanced breast cancer, and pregnancy must be ruled out before treating benign gynecological conditions [1]. Adding back low-dose estrogen or progestin during endometriosis treatment can reduce bone loss and hot flushes without weakening the effect on pain [1].

sections.heading: How does goserelin compare with other GnRH agonists?

blocks.text: Goserelin belongs to a family of GnRH agonists that includes leuprorelin (leuprolide), triptorelin, histrelin, nafarelin, buserelin, and deslorelin [4]. All of them work the same way, with an early hormone surge followed by shutdown, so the choice between them often comes down to how they are delivered and how often. Goserelin comes as a small solid rod placed under the abdominal skin from a preloaded syringe, releasing drug over 4 or 12 weeks [1][2].

Because the 3.6 mg and 10.8 mg implants are not interchangeable in their approved uses, the strength matters: only the 3.6 mg implant carries the breast cancer and gynecological indications [1][2]. The longer-acting implant means four clinic visits a year instead of thirteen for men on continuous treatment.

name: Hexapeptide-9
evidenceNote: Human data are thin: one 56-day randomized trial of about 90 women tested a chemically cyclized version, not the standard peptide, and a delivery study included only a small clinical test. Both came from cosmetic-industry or engineering groups.
summary: Hexapeptide-9 is a six-amino-acid collagen fragment used in anti-wrinkle creams. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug, and human evidence is limited.
keyTakeaway: Hexapeptide-9 is a short synthetic peptide (Gly-Pro-Gln-Gly-Pro-Gln) that copies a repeating pattern found in collagen. It is added to serums and creams on the theory that collagen fragments signal skin cells to make more matrix. The best human data come from a 2025 trial in which a stabilized, ring-shaped version reduced wrinkle counts and area more than retinol over 56 days in about 90 women. The ordinary linear form breaks down quickly in lab tests. As a cosmetic ingredient it never needs FDA approval, and it cannot legally be sold as treating anything.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Cosmetic ingredient; cosmetics do not need FDA approval

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Mimics a collagen fragment that may prompt skin cells to build new matrix

atGlance.label: Topical form
atGlance.value: Serums and creams, often at very low concentrations

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Lab work plus one small randomized trial of a modified (cyclized) version

atGlance.label: Evidence strength
atGlance.value: Limited research

blocks.text: Hexapeptide-9 is the cosmetic ingredient name for a chain of six amino acids: glycine, proline, glutamine, glycine, proline, glutamine. That pattern echoes the repeating units in collagen, the protein that gives skin its firmness, which is why it is described as a collagen peptide [1].

It belongs to a broad group often called signal peptides: short fragments of skin proteins that are thought to act as messages to skin cells rather than as building material. A 2026 safety review from Procter and Gamble scientists found that a related form, caffeoyl hexapeptide-9, shares sequence with skin matrix proteins such as collagen and showed no toxin or allergen signals in screening tools [3].

The theory behind signal peptides is that small collagen fragments act as feedback, telling fibroblasts (the cells that make collagen) to produce more. Hexapeptide-9 is designed to imitate such a fragment. A 2025 laboratory and animal study described it as a peptide that promotes collagen production and reported that, delivered with a skin-penetration enhancer, it reduced UV-induced oxidative stress, inflammation, and the loss of collagen and elastic fibers in animal skin [2].

The obstacle is getting it where it is needed. Peptides are relatively large and water-loving, so they cross the outer skin barrier poorly. In the same study, an ionic liquid made from GABA and lactic acid raised hexapeptide-9 penetration about 5-fold and its retention under the skin about 8-fold over 12 hours compared with no enhancer [2].

Stability is the second problem. Researchers at a Shanghai cosmetics company reported that, in their internal tests, the ordinary linear peptide was completely broken down by a collagen-digesting enzyme, while a version closed into a ring (cyclized) survived [1]. That suggests the form in a given product matters, and most labels do not say which form they use.

No, and it does not need to be. In the United States, cosmetic products and their ingredients, apart from color additives, can be sold without FDA approval [4]. Hexapeptide-9 is used as a cosmetic ingredient, so no regulator has reviewed whether it works.

The line between a cosmetic and a drug depends on what a product claims to do. A product intended to affect the structure or function of the body is legally a drug, even if it is marketed as a cosmetic [4]. That is why hexapeptide-9 creams talk about the look of fine lines rather than rebuilding collagen or reversing aging.

The most rigorous human study is a 2025 randomized, double-blind trial in healthy adults aged 30 to 55 with signs of skin aging. Ninety-one completed the study, and all but three were women. They applied a serum twice daily for 56 days containing 0.002% cyclized hexapeptide-9, 0.002% retinol, or no active ingredient [1].

The cyclized peptide reduced the number, area, and roughness of both crow's feet and forehead lines compared with the plain serum. Retinol at the same low concentration improved fewer of those measures, and the peptide's effect was larger than retinol's on every outcome except crow's feet roughness. No treatment-related side effects were reported in any group [1].

rows: Cyclized hexapeptide-9 vs retinol vs plain serum, 91 adults, 56 days
Fewer and smaller wrinkles than plain serum; larger effect than 0.002% retinol [1]
Linear hexapeptide-9 with a GABA and lactic acid enhancer; cells, animals, small clinical test
Better skin penetration; less UV damage in animal skin [2]
Computer screening of cosmetic peptides including caffeoyl hexapeptide-9
Matrix protein similarity, no toxin or allergen flags [3]

blocks.text: These results need careful reading. The trial tested a modified, more stable molecule, compared it with a very low retinol concentration, and its authors work for cosmetics companies, though they reported no conflicts [1]. No independent trial has tested the standard linear hexapeptide-9 found in most products, and nothing shows that it builds new collagen in human skin.

In the 56-day trial, no treatment-related side effects were reported in any arm, though the authors noted this does not prove the peptide is safer than retinol [1]. Bioinformatic screening found no sequence signals pointing to toxicity or allergy for a related hexapeptide-9 derivative [3]. Safety data for long-term use of the standard linear form in people have not been published.

name: Hexarelin
evidenceNote: Human studies of hexarelin are small, mostly single-dose hormone tests from the 1990s. They show it releases growth hormone, but no trial has tested a health outcome such as muscle, bone or heart function over time.
summary: Hexarelin is an unapproved synthetic peptide that triggers growth hormone release. Human data are short hormone tests; it is banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: Hexarelin is a six amino acid synthetic peptide from the GHRP family that makes the pituitary release a burst of growth hormone. Small studies in the 1990s showed a single injection released about twice as much growth hormone as GHRH, the body's own releasing hormone. When given twice daily for 16 weeks, the response faded and blood IGF-1, body fat, lean mass and bone density did not change. It was never approved anywhere as a medicine, has no FDA approval, and is prohibited at all times under anti-doping rules.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Not FDA-approved; never approved as a medicine

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Activates the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) in the brain and pituitary, releasing growth hormone; also binds CD36 in the heart

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Short human hormone studies and small acute heart studies; no outcome trials

atGlance.label: Sport

atGlance.label: Evidence strength
atGlance.value: Low research

blocks.text: Hexarelin is a synthetic hexapeptide (six amino acids) with the sequence His-D-2-methyl-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2 [2]. It belongs to the growth hormone-releasing peptides, or GHRPs, a family of man-made peptides that make the pituitary gland release growth hormone [4].

In the 1990s it was tested in healthy volunteers as a possible way to test or boost growth hormone secretion, and its developers judged it could be clinically useful [1][3]. It never reached approval. Today it appears mainly as a research chemical sold online and on anti-doping lists, where it is named by its official name, examorelin [7].

Hexarelin activates the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R1a), the same receptor used by ghrelin, the body's hunger hormone. This receptor sits mostly in the hypothalamus and pituitary, and switching it on releases a pulse of growth hormone [5]. It acts on a different receptor from GHRH, so the two add together. In healthy men, giving hexarelin with GHRH produced a larger growth hormone response than either alone, and somatostatin, the body's brake on growth hormone, blunted the hexarelin response [2].

Hexarelin also binds CD36, a receptor on heart muscle cells and the cells lining small blood vessels. In isolated rat hearts, activating CD36 with hexarelin raised coronary pressure, an effect missing in hearts from mice without CD36 [4]. That finding is the root of interest in hexarelin for the heart, though it shows a mechanism in animal tissue rather than a benefit in people.

No. Hexarelin has never been approved by the FDA or by any other major regulator. It does not appear on the FDA's list of peptides placed in the safety-risk category for compounding, but that does not make it legal to compound or sell for human use [8]. Products sold online are research chemicals with no FDA oversight of their purity, strength or sterility. Without approval there is no label, no defined dose, and no formal safety monitoring for anyone using it.
For athletes, the anti-doping list in force from January 2026 names examorelin (hexarelin) among the growth hormone-releasing peptides banned at all times [7].

Most human data on hexarelin are acute hormone tests from the 1990s, each in about a dozen people. They show clearly that hexarelin releases growth hormone in people, and how that response behaves. Almost none of it measures a clinical outcome.

rows: 1 mcg/kg into a vein released about twice the growth hormone of the same dose of GHRH. About 77% of an injection under the skin was absorbed, against under 5% by nose and 0.3% by mouth.
Growth hormone rose with dose and peaked about 30 minutes after injection, with the response near its ceiling at 2 mcg/kg.
Adults given twice-daily injections for 16 weeks
The growth hormone response shrank over time, then recovered 4 weeks after stopping. IGF-1, body fat, lean mass and bone density did not change.
Patients with coronary artery disease under anesthesia
One IV dose raised the heart's ejection fraction and output within 10 minutes for up to 90 minutes, while GHRH, growth hormone and placebo had no effect.

blocks.text: The long-term study is the most telling for anyone weighing claims about muscle or bone. Repeated dosing produced a partial and reversible tolerance, and the authors concluded that the effect on the growth hormone and IGF-1 system was minimal [6]. The heart findings are intriguing but are acute, short and small, with no study testing whether hexarelin changes outcomes for people with heart disease [9][5].

Much of the enthusiasm for hexarelin's heart effects comes from animal work. A 2006 review described ghrelin and synthetic secretagogues protecting heart muscle from ischemia (loss of blood flow) and acting on blood vessels in experimental models, with some supporting acute measurements in humans, and noted that the signaling pathways behind these effects were not fully mapped [5]. Animal protection from a controlled injury is a long way from showing a benefit in people living with heart disease.
Nothing in the published record establishes safe long-term use. The human studies ran for hours to a few months and were not designed to find uncommon side effects.

sections.heading: How does hexarelin compare with other growth hormone peptides?

blocks.text: Hexarelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and ipamorelin all act on the ghrelin receptor. The FDA has placed GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and ipamorelin in its category of substances that raise significant safety risks when used in compounding [8]. Hexarelin is not named on that list, which reflects which substances were nominated for review, not evidence that it is safer. All four are banned in sport, where examorelin sits on the same line of the list as the other GHRPs [7]. None has outcome data in people showing gains in muscle, bone or heart health.

name: Histrelin
evidenceNote: Supprelin LA is approved for central precocious puberty on two open-label trials in 47 children that measured hormone suppression. Vantas was approved for advanced prostate cancer on a 138-man trial and is no longer made.
summary: Histrelin is a GnRH agonist delivered by a small implant in the upper arm for 12 months. It is FDA-approved to pause early puberty in children.
keyTakeaway: Histrelin is a synthetic, more potent version of the brain hormone GnRH. Delivered continuously from a small implant placed under the skin of the upper arm, it shuts down the pituitary signals that drive puberty and sex hormone production. As Supprelin LA it is FDA-approved for central precocious puberty in children aged 2 and older; in its pivotal trial, peak LH fell into the suppressed range within one month and stayed there for a year. A sister implant for prostate cancer, Vantas, was discontinued in 2021.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Approved: Supprelin LA (2007); Vantas approved 2004 but discontinued

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Constant GnRH stimulation desensitizes the pituitary, lowering LH, FSH and sex hormones

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Central precocious puberty (Supprelin LA)

atGlance.label: How it's taken
atGlance.value: One 50 mg implant under the skin of the inner upper arm, replaced every 12 months
