atGlance.value: FDA approved

blocks.text: Histrelin is a synthetic nonapeptide (a chain of nine amino acids) modelled on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the brain signal that tells the pituitary gland to release the reproductive hormones LH and FSH. It is more potent than the natural hormone [1].

What sets histrelin apart from other GnRH agonists is how it is given. Supprelin LA is a thin, flexible tube about 3.5 cm long containing 50 mg of histrelin acetate inside a hydrogel reservoir. Once placed under the skin, it releases about 65 mcg a day for 12 months, so a child needs no daily or monthly injections [1].

Natural GnRH arrives at the pituitary in pulses, and the pulses are what keep LH and FSH flowing. A steady, unbroken supply has the opposite effect. After a short initial burst of stimulation, the pituitary becomes desensitized, LH and FSH fall, and the ovaries or testes stop making much estrogen or testosterone [1].

That early burst is real and can be seen. In the first days, LH, FSH and sex hormones rise, and a child's puberty signs can briefly get worse or new ones appear [1]. In men with prostate cancer, testosterone climbed in the first week before dropping below the castrate threshold of 50 ng/dL by week 4 in a monitored subgroup [2]. In children, the label says sex hormone output is suppressed within four weeks and puberty signs then recede [1].

Yes. Supprelin LA, made by Endo, is approved and marketed for central precocious puberty [6]. The label records the first US approval of histrelin as 1991, when an injectable form came first; the yearly implant followed in 2007 [1][6].

items.text: Histrelin first approved in the United States [1].
Vantas, a 50 mg implant for advanced prostate cancer, is approved [5].
Supprelin LA is approved for central precocious puberty; the pivotal trial is published the same year [6][3].
After a manufacturing problem it could not fix, Endo tells FDA it has stopped making Vantas [4].
The Supprelin LA label adds a warning on severe skin reactions [1].

blocks.text: Drugs@FDA now lists Vantas as discontinued, while Supprelin LA remains a prescription product [5][6].

Supprelin LA treats central precocious puberty (CPP), meaning puberty that starts too early because the brain's GnRH system has switched on ahead of time: before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys [1]. Untreated, children with CPP often have a markedly advanced bone age, which can leave them shorter as adults [1]. The implant is not approved for children under 2, and the label suggests stopping around the age puberty would normally begin, roughly 11 for girls and 12 for boys [1]. While the implant is in, LH, FSH and sex hormones are checked one month after insertion and every six months after that, with height and bone age every 6 to 12 months [1].

The main trial enrolled 36 children (33 girls, 3 boys) at nine US centers, 20 of them new to treatment [3]. In the newly treated children, peak LH after a stimulation test fell from 28.2 to 0.8 mIU/mL within one month, estradiol dropped from 24.5 to 5.9 pg/mL, and suppression held for the full year [3].

rows: All newly treated children by month 1, maintained to month 12 [1]
Suppression maintained in all three previously treated boys [1]

blocks.text: Vantas used the same 50 mg design at a slightly lower release rate for palliative treatment of advanced prostate cancer, meaning to control the disease rather than cure it [2]. Before it was discontinued it cost roughly a ninth of Supprelin LA, and some doctors used it off label for early puberty to spare families the higher price [4].

Most problems come from the implant procedure. In the two pediatric trials, 51.1% of the 47 children had an implant site reaction, such as bruising, soreness, swelling or itching, and about 6% each had keloid or other scarring or a stitch problem [1]. Implants have broken during removal, and placing the implant too deep makes it harder to find and take out [1].

items: A temporary worsening of puberty signs, or new ones, in the first week or so while hormones briefly rise [1].
Mood changes, including crying, irritability and aggression, and rare reports of depression with suicidal thoughts in children on GnRH agonists [1].
Seizures, mostly in children with a history of seizures or other risk factors [1].
Pseudotumor cerebri (raised pressure around the brain), signalled by headache and vision changes [1].
Severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, added to the label in 2025 [1].

blocks.text: In men treated with Vantas for prostate cancer, the profile was that of testosterone loss: hot flashes affected 65.5% of trial patients [2].

name: Human chorionic gonadotropin
evidenceNote: hCG is an FDA-approved prescription hormone with decades of use in fertility care and male hypogonadism. Its use for weight loss is the exception: the FDA says no hCG product is approved for it.
summary: hCG is an FDA-approved pregnancy hormone that acts like LH. It treats some male hypogonadism, undescended testes and infertility, but not obesity.
keyTakeaway: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is the hormone the placenta makes in pregnancy. As a drug it stands in for luteinizing hormone (LH), switching on testosterone production in the testes and triggering ovulation. It is FDA-approved, by prescription, for undescended testes in boys, hypogonadism caused by low pituitary output in men, and ovulation induction. In a 282-man randomized trial, hCG raised testosterone about as well as clomiphene. The labels state that hCG has not been shown to help with obesity, the FDA calls homeopathic hCG diet products illegal, and anti-doping rules ban it in male athletes.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Approved, prescription only (Pregnyl and generics)

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Acts almost exactly like LH, telling the testes to make testosterone and the ovary to release an egg

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Undescended testes, male hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, ovulation induction

atGlance.label: Sport

blocks.text: hCG is a hormone produced by the placenta. It is made of two parts, an alpha subunit that is essentially the same as the one in LH, FSH and thyroid-stimulating hormone, and a beta subunit that gives it its specific action [1]. It is the hormone that home pregnancy tests detect.

Most medical hCG is extracted from the urine of pregnant women and standardized by a biological assay. It is sold as Pregnyl and as generic chorionic gonadotropin [1][2]. A recombinant version made in cell culture is used in fertility clinics, and a Cochrane review of trials comparing the two found no clear difference in pregnancy or live birth rates when either was used to trigger egg maturation [3].

sections.heading: How does human chorionic gonadotropin work?

blocks.text: hCG binds the same receptor as LH, the pituitary hormone that controls the sex glands, and its effects are virtually identical, with a small amount of FSH-like activity as well [1][2]. In males, it stimulates Leydig cells in the testes to make testosterone. In females, it can take the place of the mid-cycle LH surge that triggers ovulation, and it supports the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone early in pregnancy [2].

This is why hCG behaves differently from testosterone itself. Testosterone given as a drug signals the pituitary to stop making LH, so the testes shrink and sperm production falls. hCG works around the pituitary and drives the testes directly, which keeps them producing both testosterone and sperm. That makes it useful when the problem is a lack of pituitary signal rather than a failure of the testes. The labels also state plainly that hCG has no known effect on fat mobilization, appetite or the way body fat is distributed [1].

Yes. hCG is an FDA-approved prescription drug given by injection into muscle [1][2]. The FDA has never approved any hCG product for weight loss, and it considers over-the-counter products claiming to contain homeopathic hCG to be illegally marketed, unapproved and misbranded drugs [4].

In sport, hCG is listed among the testosterone-stimulating peptides banned in males at all times, in and out of competition, under the anti-doping list in force from January 2026 [7]. The ban applies to men because hCG raises their own testosterone output.

sections.heading: What is human chorionic gonadotropin prescribed for?

items: Prepubertal cryptorchidism (undescended testes) when nothing is physically blocking descent. The label notes that descent after hCG is often temporary and that treatment usually happens between ages 4 and 9 [2].
Selected cases of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in males, meaning low testosterone caused by too little signal from the pituitary [2].
Induction of ovulation and pregnancy in women whose lack of ovulation is not due to primary ovarian failure, after pretreatment with menotropins (FSH and LH preparations) [2].

blocks.text: The male hypogonadism evidence is reasonably consistent. A randomized trial in 282 men with low testosterone who wanted to protect their fertility compared clomiphene, hCG injections twice weekly, and both together for 3 months. Testosterone rose in all three groups and the researchers judged the treatments equally effective at restoring it, with the combination improving symptom scores the most [5]. A 2021 systematic review pooled five hCG studies covering 196 men and found average total testosterone roughly doubled after treatment, from about 285 to 566 ng/dL [6]. Those pooled studies were mostly uncontrolled, so the review shows direction more than precise size.
Giving hCG alongside testosterone therapy to keep the testes active is an off-label use. None of the approved indications on the labels covers it [2].

The label lists headache, irritability, restlessness, depression, fatigue, fluid retention, breast enlargement in males (gynecomastia), early puberty in boys, and pain at the injection site [2]. Because hCG raises androgen levels, it can bring on puberty too soon when used for undescended testes, which is one reason the dose and length of treatment are tightly managed [2].

In fertility treatment, the serious risks come from ovarian stimulation: ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (sudden ovarian enlargement with fluid in the abdomen or chest), ruptured ovarian cysts, multiple pregnancy and blood clots in arteries. Allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with urine-derived products [2]. hCG must not be used in early puberty, prostate cancer or other androgen-dependent tumors, or after a prior allergic reaction to it [2].

The hCG diet pairs hCG injections or drops with a very low calorie diet. The hCG labels carry a statement in capital letters that hCG has not been shown to be effective for obesity, does not add to the weight lost from cutting calories, does not create a more attractive fat distribution, and does not reduce the hunger of a restricted diet [1][2].

The FDA has warned that people on very low calorie diets face higher risks of gallstones, electrolyte imbalances and heart rhythm problems, and that such diets should only be used under medical supervision [4]. Drops and sprays sold as homeopathic hCG are not approved drugs, and the agency has stated that all of them are illegally marketed [4].

name: Humanin
evidenceNote: Every treatment result comes from cells, worms, rats or mice, often using a lab-made analog rather than humanin itself. Human data are limited to measuring natural blood levels, and no trial has ever given humanin to a person.
summary: Humanin is a small peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA. It protects cells in lab and animal studies, but it has never been tested as a treatment in people.
keyTakeaway: Humanin is a 24-amino-acid peptide coded by a gene inside mitochondria, discovered in 2001 because it kept nerve cells alive in Alzheimer's-type lab experiments. In rodents, humanin and a stronger synthetic version improved insulin action and some markers of healthy ageing, and natural blood levels tend to fall with age. All of that is preclinical or observational: no human trial has given humanin as a treatment. It is not FDA-approved, and vials sold online are untested research chemicals.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Not approved; no human treatment trials

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Binds cell-surface receptors and blocks cell-death proteins such as BAX

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Cell, worm and rodent studies; human blood-level studies only

atGlance.label: Sold online
atGlance.value: Research-labelled vials with no tested human dose

atGlance.label: Evidence strength
atGlance.value: Low research

blocks.text: Humanin is a short peptide, usually 24 amino acids long, that the body makes from a small stretch of genetic code inside the mitochondria (the structures in cells that produce energy) [2]. Most of the body's proteins are coded in the nucleus, so humanin belongs to a newer group called mitochondrial-derived peptides, alongside MOTS-c.

It is found in blood and in many tissues, and its levels can be measured. Falling levels with age made it a marker of interest in ageing research [2]. Synthetic humanin is now also sold online as a longevity peptide, even though no human treatment study exists [6].

Japanese researchers found humanin in 2001 by screening genes for anything that could stop nerve cells dying. The gene they pulled out encoded a short peptide that, once secreted, blocked the cell death caused by several inherited Alzheimer's disease genes and by amyloid beta, the protein that clumps in Alzheimer's brains [1]. The authors suggested it as a lead for future Alzheimer's drugs.

Over the next two decades the research widened from the brain to metabolism, the heart and ageing in general. A potent variant called HNG, in which one amino acid is swapped, became the usual tool in animal work, which means many headline findings are about the analog rather than natural humanin [2][4].

Humanin seems to act both outside and inside the cell. Outside, it binds receptors on the cell surface, including one called FPRL1 and a three-part receptor built from CNTFR, gp130 and WSX-1. Binding the second switches on the JAK2 and STAT3 signalling pathway, which supports cell survival [2].

Inside the cell it binds BAX, a protein that triggers programmed cell death, and holds it inactive. It also interacts with IGFBP-3, a growth factor binding protein linked to the same death pathways [2]. In rats, humanin delivered into the brain improved the body's response to insulin through STAT3 signalling in the hypothalamus, suggesting part of its metabolic effect runs through the brain rather than directly on the liver [3].

No. Humanin is not approved for any use in the United States, and no company has filed for approval. Searches of the ClinicalTrials.gov registry turn up studies that measure natural humanin levels in blood, for example after heart surgery or in kidney injury, but none that gives humanin to people as a treatment [6].
Synthetic humanin sold online is labelled for research use. With no human study, there is no tested dose, no safety record, and no information on how long an injected dose lasts in the body.

The original 2001 work was done in cultured nerve cells, where humanin blocked several forms of Alzheimer's-linked cell death [1]. Later lab work found that astrocytes (support cells in the brain) release humanin, that their output fell in rats after removal of the ovaries, and that humanin protected cultured hippocampal neurons from glutamate damage to their synapses [5].

Metabolic findings come from rodents. Humanin infused into rat brains improved insulin sensitivity, a single dose of a potent analog lowered blood sugar in diabetic rats, and humanin levels in several tissues fell with age in rodents [3]. The same paper reported lower circulating levels in older people, which is an observation, not a treatment effect [3].

rows: Blocked cell death from Alzheimer's genes and amyloid beta [1]
Better insulin action in rats; lower blood levels with age in people [3]
Astrocytes release humanin; it protected synapses from glutamate [5]
Longer life in worms; healthier metabolism in mice on HNG; higher levels in children of centenarians [4]

blocks.text: The ageing case rests mostly on one 2020 study. Extra humanin lengthened lifespan in roundworms, and middle-aged mice injected twice a week with HNG showed better metabolic health markers and less inflammation [4]. In people, the study found higher circulating humanin in the children of centenarians than in matched controls, and lower levels in Alzheimer's disease and in a mitochondrial disorder called MELAS [4]. Two of its senior authors disclosed consulting and stock ties to a company developing mitochondrial peptides [4].

A 2023 systematic review summed up the field: humanin protects cells under stress in many lab models, but its mechanisms are not fully worked out, and the human evidence consists of association studies [2]. Whether raising humanin in a person changes any health outcome has simply never been tested.

name: Icatibant
evidenceNote: FDA-approved in 2011 on the basis of three controlled trials in adults having acute hereditary angioedema attacks, including the placebo-controlled FAST-3 trial.
summary: A self-injected 10-amino-acid peptide that blocks bradykinin to stop hereditary angioedema attacks. FDA-approved since 2011; generics are available.
keyTakeaway: Icatibant, first sold as Firazyr, is a synthetic peptide of 10 amino acids that blocks the bradykinin B2 receptor, the switch that drives swelling during a hereditary angioedema attack. The FDA approved it in 2011 for acute attacks in adults, and patients can inject it themselves under the skin once trained. In the FAST-3 trial, symptoms eased by half in a median of 2 hours, compared with almost 20 hours on placebo. Nearly everyone gets a short-lived reaction where the needle went in; serious side effects were not seen in trials.

atGlance.value: Approved in 2011 as Firazyr; generic versions also approved.

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Sits on the bradykinin B2 receptor so bradykinin cannot trigger leaky, swollen blood vessels.

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Treating a hereditary angioedema attack as it starts, in adults.

atGlance.value: One prefilled syringe injected under the skin of the abdomen; patients can self-inject.

atGlance.value: FDA approved

blocks.text: Icatibant is a lab-made peptide of 10 amino acids, five of which do not occur in natural proteins. It was designed to mimic bradykinin, a small hormone of the blood vessel lining, and binds bradykinin's main receptor with about the same strength [1]. It is sold as Firazyr by Takeda and as generic icatibant injection by several other makers [1][4].

It treats hereditary angioedema, or HAE, an inherited condition in which people suffer sudden episodes of deep swelling of the skin, the intestine or the throat. Swelling of the gut wall causes intense abdominal pain, and swelling in the throat can close the airway [1].

Most people with HAE lack enough working C1-esterase inhibitor, a protein that keeps the kallikrein system under control. When that brake fails, the body produces too much bradykinin. Bradykinin binds to B2 receptors on the lining of blood vessels and makes them widen and leak, so fluid escapes into the tissue and causes swelling and pain [1].

Icatibant is a competitive antagonist of the B2 receptor: it occupies the receptor about as strongly as bradykinin does but does not switch it on, so the bradykinin already circulating has nowhere to act [1]. Where ecallantide stops bradykinin being made, icatibant blocks it at the point of action. Under the skin it is almost completely absorbed, peaks in the blood in about 45 minutes, and has a half-life of roughly an hour and a half [1].

Yes. The FDA first approved icatibant, as Firazyr, in 2011 for acute attacks of HAE in people aged 18 and older [1]. Europe had authorized it earlier, in July 2008, and the European label now also covers adolescents and children from age 2, with doses based on body weight [3]. In the US, its safety and effectiveness below age 18 have not been established [1].

Generic versions are now on the US market under the same indication, sold as prefilled syringes by companies such as Teva [4]. The drug has no listed contraindications (situations where it must never be used) [1].

Icatibant is used to stop an HAE attack once it has begun; it is not a preventive medicine. After training from a healthcare professional, patients may inject it themselves as soon as they recognize an attack, which matters for a condition where swelling can build over hours. The label limits use to three injections in any 24-hour period [1].

Because a throat attack can block breathing, the label tells patients who have treated a laryngeal attack to get emergency care straight away as well [1]. Efficacy was established in three controlled trials covering 223 adults [1]. The clearest comparison with placebo came from FAST-3, which treated 88 patients with moderate to very severe skin or abdominal attacks [2].

rows: Median time to 50% drop in symptom severity (main goal) [2]
Median time to first relief of the main symptom [2]
Median time to almost complete relief [2]

blocks.text: No patient on icatibant in FAST-3 needed rescue medication before their symptoms began to ease. Ten patients with throat attacks also received the drug openly, outside the placebo comparison [2].

The defining side effect is a reaction at the injection site. In the placebo-controlled trials, 97% of people on icatibant had one, against 33% on placebo. It can include redness, swelling, burning, itching, warmth, bruising or numbness where the needle went in, and it typically settles on its own [1]. In FAST-3, every treated patient had such a reaction, but none had a serious adverse event [2].
Other reactions reported more often than with placebo were less common [1]:

items: Fever (4%) [1]
A rise in liver enzymes on blood tests (4%) [1]
Dizziness (3%) [1]
Rash (reported in more than 1% of patients) [1]

blocks.text: Animal studies found that repeated daily dosing in young male rats delayed the maturation of the testes, an effect attributed to blocking the B2 receptor. The label notes that this was not seen in dogs dosed twice weekly for nine months [1]. In a dedicated heart rhythm study in healthy volunteers, it did not lengthen the QT interval to a level of regulatory concern [1].

name: IGF-1 DES
evidenceNote: Everything known about IGF-1 DES comes from cell cultures and rodents, mostly from one Australian research group in the late 1980s and 1990s. No human study of it has been published.
summary: IGF-1 DES is a shortened form of the growth factor IGF-1 that escapes its binding proteins. It has only been tested in cells and rats.
keyTakeaway: IGF-1 DES is a trimmed version of the growth factor IGF-1, with three amino acids removed from the front of the chain. Without them it barely binds the carrier proteins that usually restrain IGF-1, so in cell cultures it was about ten times as potent as the full hormone. In rats it improved nitrogen balance and slowed muscle breakdown. It has never been tested in people, it is not FDA-approved, and IGF-1 analogs are banned in sport. Online products are unregulated, and the approved IGF-1 drug carries warnings about low blood sugar.

atGlance.value: Not approved for any use

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Activates the IGF-1 receptor while largely evading IGF binding proteins

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Cell and rat studies only; no published human trials

blocks.text: IGF-1 DES, written in research papers as des(1-3)IGF-I, is a slightly shortened version of IGF-1, short for insulin-like growth factor 1. IGF-1 is a hormone made mainly in response to growth hormone, and it drives growth in bone, muscle, and many other tissues. The DES form lacks the first three amino acids of the chain, glycine, proline, and glutamate [2].

It is not purely a lab invention. Researchers isolated the truncated form from cow colostrum, human brain, and pig uterus, and believe the body makes it by trimming full IGF-1 after the protein is built [2]. The versions sold online are synthetic or recombinant copies.

In the blood and tissues, most IGF-1 is held by a family of IGF binding proteins. They act as carriers and also as brakes, because bound IGF-1 cannot easily reach its receptor on cells. In a 1989 study, these binding proteins blocked the effects of IGF-1 and IGF-2 on cultured cells but had no effect on des(1-3)IGF-1, and the more weakly each form bound the proteins, the more potent it was [1].

The missing glutamate at position 3 is what weakens binding protein attachment. As a result, the truncated form is generally about ten times as potent as IGF-1 at making cultured cells grow and divide [2]. It still works through the same type 1 IGF receptor as the full hormone [1], so it carries the same broad growth signal rather than a muscle-specific one.
Part of that extra potency survives in living animals, where the clearest effects were seen in gut tissue [2]. Animal results like these have never been checked in a human body.

No. IGF-1 DES has never been approved by the FDA, and no company has developed it as a medicine. The only approved IGF-1 drug in the US is mecasermin (Increlex), which is the full-length hormone. It is approved for children with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, a rare cause of short stature, and is not a substitute for growth hormone [6].

Mecasermin's label shows what IGF-1 activity can do in the body. It warns of severe low blood sugar, including seizures, and requires the drug to be given with a meal or snack. It also lists raised pressure inside the skull, enlarged tonsils and adenoids, hip problems in growing children, and reports of cancers, and it is not to be used by anyone with a malignancy [6]. None of these risks has been studied for IGF-1 DES, which is more potent in the lab.

The research base is small and old. Most of it comes from a group in Adelaide, Australia, that studied the variant in cell lines and rats. Writing in 1996, the same researchers noted that clinical uses for des(1-3)IGF-I had not yet been evaluated, and suggested catabolic states and bowel disease as areas to explore [2].

blocks.text: In the kidney study, full IGF-1 and the DES form both improved growth in rats with impaired kidneys, and neither changed overall body composition. The DES form stood out for slowing muscle protein breakdown [3]. These were short experiments in young animals given continuous infusions by pump, not tests of muscle building in healthy adults.

A 2026 review of growth hormone and IGF-1 axis peptides sold as research compounds includes IGF-1 analogs such as IGF-1 LR3 among products with no regulatory approval for physique or performance use. It lists disturbed blood sugar, fluid retention, and a plausible but unproven risk of promoting abnormal growth, and notes that the content and dose of products in unregulated supply chains are uncertain [4].

sections.heading: Is IGF-1 DES allowed in sport?

blocks.text: No. The World Anti-Doping Agency's 2026 Prohibited List bans insulin-like growth factor 1 and its analogues under the growth factor section of S2, and IGF-1 DES falls in that class as a modified form of the hormone [5].

name: IGF-1 LR3
evidenceNote: There are no published human studies of IGF-1 LR3. Everything known about it comes from cell culture and animal experiments, so claims about muscle growth in people are extrapolation.
summary: A modified IGF-1 built to dodge the proteins that normally hold IGF-1 in check. Never tested in humans, not FDA-approved, and banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: IGF-1 LR3 is a laboratory variant of insulin-like growth factor 1, the hormone that carries out much of growth hormone's effect on tissues. Two changes, an arginine swapped in at position 3 and an extra stretch added to the front, stop it binding the proteins that usually restrain IGF-1, which made it two to three times more potent at restoring growth in diabetic rats. No study has tested it in people. It is not FDA-approved for any use, and IGF-1 and its analogs are prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.

atGlance.value: Not approved. The only approved IGF-1 drug is mecasermin (Increlex), for rare childhood growth failure.

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Activates the IGF-1 receptor while largely escaping the binding proteins that limit natural IGF-1.

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Cell and animal studies only; no peer-reviewed human studies.

atGlance.value: Low research

blocks.text: IGF-1 LR3 is an engineered version of IGF-1, short for insulin-like growth factor 1. Natural IGF-1 is made mainly by the liver in response to growth hormone and drives much of growth hormone's effect on bone, muscle and other tissues. The LR3 version differs in two ways: the glutamic acid at position 3 is replaced with arginine (the R3 in its name), and an extra run of amino acids is added to the front of the chain (the L, for long) [1][2].

It began as a laboratory variant for studying how IGF-binding proteins control IGF-1 [1]. Today it is sold online as a 'research chemical' and promoted in bodybuilding circles for muscle growth and fat loss, a use that has no clinical testing behind it [2].

IGF-1 acts on the IGF-1 receptor, a protein on the cell surface with a built-in enzyme (a tyrosine kinase). When IGF-1 binds, the receptor switches on two main signaling routes inside the cell, the PI 3-kinase pathway and the MAP kinase pathway, which push cells to multiply, mature and survive [3].

In the blood, almost all natural IGF-1 is held by a family of IGF-binding proteins, which control how much reaches the receptor and for how long. The LR3 modifications sharply reduce that binding [1][2]. More of the molecule is therefore free to act, which explains its higher potency in animals. In a rat wound model, LR3 also left tissue fluid faster than ordinary IGF-1 and appeared more readily in the bloodstream and urine, because fewer binding proteins were holding it in place [4].

IGF-1 shares structure with insulin and can lower blood sugar. That effect is the most frequently described problem in informal reports of LR3 use, and it is the main warning on the label of the approved IGF-1 drug, mecasermin [2][5].

No. Neither the FDA nor any other regulator has approved LR3 for a medical use [2]. Products sold online as LR3 come from unregulated supply chains, so their identity, purity and strength are not verified [2].

The approved relative is mecasermin, sold as Increlex since 2005. Mecasermin is recombinant human IGF-1, identical to the body's own 70-amino-acid hormone, and it is approved only for growth failure in children aged 2 and over with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or a growth hormone gene deletion [5]. Its label warns of severe low blood sugar that can cause seizures, raised pressure inside the skull, and enlarged tonsils, and it must not be used by children with cancer or a history of cancer [5].
In sport, the World Anti-Doping Agency's Prohibited List names IGF-1 and its analogs among banned substances, a category that takes in LR3 [2].

The useful studies are in animals. In diabetic rats, LR3 and another binding-protein-resistant variant restored growth two and a half to three times more potently than ordinary IGF-1 and raised muscle protein production, although none of the IGF-1 forms corrected the high blood sugar [1].

A 2019 mouse study of cancer-related muscle wasting gives a sharper warning. LR3 limited the loss of muscle mass in tumor-bearing mice, but the tumors grew faster [6]. That fits the biology: the same receptor signals that build muscle also help cells survive and divide [3].

A 2026 review of performance-enhancing peptides placed IGF-1 LR3 in its lowest evidence tier. It found no peer-reviewed human studies, no documented half-life in people, and no published human dosing; claimed benefits rest on animal extrapolation and user accounts [2]. The review described the cancer concern as theoretical but clinically relevant, since long-term risk cannot be judged from short-term use [2].

name: Insulin analogs
alsoCalled: lispro, aspart, glulisine, glargine, detemir, degludec, icodec, efsitora (related human insulins: regular, NPH)
evidenceNote: Insulin has been regulated by FDA for over 80 years, and each analog is approved on its own label after controlled trials against human insulin or another analog.
summary: Insulin analogs are re-engineered insulins that act faster or last longer than human insulin. All are FDA-approved for diabetes and given by injection or pump.
keyTakeaway: Insulin analogs are versions of human insulin with a few amino acids swapped, or a fatty acid attached, so they reach the blood faster or linger for a day or more. The first, lispro (Humalog), was approved in 1996. In a 756-person trial, long-acting glargine matched NPH insulin on HbA1c but let more people reach target without a night-time low. Low blood sugar is the main risk with every insulin. In 2026 FDA approved the first two once-weekly insulins, for type 2 diabetes only. WADA bans insulins in sport.

atGlance.value: Approved; regulated as biologics since March 2020

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Activates the insulin receptor, moving glucose into muscle and fat and holding back liver glucose output

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes in adults and children (varies by product)

atGlance.label: Sport

blocks.text: Insulin is a two-chain peptide hormone made by the pancreas. An insulin analog is a lab-made insulin whose structure has been changed slightly to alter how it behaves after injection, without changing the job it does. In insulin lispro, for example, two neighboring amino acids near the end of one chain (positions B28 and B29) trade places, and the result starts working sooner and wears off sooner than regular human insulin [2]. In insulin detemir, one amino acid is removed and a 14-carbon fatty acid is attached, which makes it bind albumin and act for up to 24 hours [4].

Analogs fall into broad groups by speed. Rapid-acting analogs such as lispro, aspart, and glulisine are taken around meals. Long-acting or basal analogs such as glargine, detemir, and degludec provide steady background insulin [1][2][4]. Since 2026, once-weekly basal insulins have joined them [6][7]. Regular insulin and NPH are human insulins rather than analogs, but they remain on the market and are the usual comparison.

Insulin was among the first peptide drugs. Animal-derived extracts came first, then genetically engineered human insulin, and from the mid-1990s analogs designed to fix the timing problems of human insulin.

items.text: Banting and Best study pancreatic extracts; clinical tests in January 1922 show lower blood sugar [1].
The Insulin Amendment requires FDA to certify every batch [1].

sections.heading: How does an insulin analog work?

blocks.text: Every insulin and analog lowers blood glucose the same basic way. It switches on insulin receptors so that skeletal muscle and fat take up glucose, and it tells the liver to release less glucose. It also slows the breakdown of fat and protein and supports protein building [2]. A unit of lispro lowers glucose as much as a unit of regular human insulin; the difference is timing, with a quicker start and a shorter run [2].

The structural tweaks change how the molecule leaves the injection site and how long it stays in circulation. Detemir lasts longer because its molecules cluster together under the skin and because the attached fatty acid binds albumin in the blood, slowing its spread into tissues [4]. Because the body's response to any insulin can vary a lot from person to person, and from day to day in the same person, labels treat timing figures as guides rather than guarantees [2].

Yes. Each analog is FDA-approved on its own label, and Humalog, the first, has been approved since 1996 [2]. Insulin products were originally approved as drugs. On March 23, 2020, under the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act, their approvals were deemed biologics licenses, which made it possible for other companies to win approval for biosimilar and interchangeable versions [5]. The first interchangeable biosimilar, a version of insulin glargine, followed in July 2021 [1].
In sport, the 2026 WADA Prohibited List bans insulins and insulin-mimetics at all times under its metabolic modulators class, S4.4.2 [9].

sections.heading: What are insulin analogs prescribed for?

blocks.text: Insulin analogs are approved to improve blood sugar control in diabetes. People with type 1 diabetes make little or no insulin and depend on it. In type 2 diabetes, insulin is usually added when other treatments are not enough. Humalog, for example, is labeled for adults and children with diabetes, given under the skin by injection or pump, or into a vein [2].

Basal analogs were developed largely to cut night-time lows. In the Treat-to-Target trial, 756 adults with type 2 diabetes on tablets added bedtime glargine or NPH and adjusted the dose toward a fasting glucose goal [3].

rows: Reached 7% or lower with no documented night-time low

blocks.text: The weekly insulins icodec and efsitora are approved only for type 2 diabetes. Lilly states that efsitora is not for people with type 1 diabetes because of a higher risk of severe low blood sugar [6][7].

Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is the central risk of every insulin and can be severe. Labels list it alongside allergic reactions, injection-site reactions, lipodystrophy (lumps or dents in fat where injections are repeated), itching, and rash [2]. Rotating injection sites lowers the risk of lipodystrophy and of localized cutaneous amyloidosis, a buildup of insulin-derived protein under the skin that can disrupt absorption [2].

Insulin can also cause hypokalemia (low blood potassium), which can be life-threatening. Used with thiazolidinedione diabetes pills, it can cause fluid retention and heart failure. Mix-ups between insulin products are a recognized cause of dosing errors and low blood sugar, and the label states that pens, cartridges, and syringes must never be shared between people [2].

name: Ipamorelin
evidenceNote: Ipamorelin reached randomized, placebo-controlled human trials, but only for gut recovery after bowel surgery, where the published trial found no benefit. For muscle, fat loss, or anti-aging, the human data are limited to short hormone studies in healthy men.
summary: Ipamorelin is a lab-made peptide that triggers growth hormone release. Its only human trials, in post-surgery gut recovery, did not show benefit.
keyTakeaway: Ipamorelin is a five-amino-acid peptide designed by Novo Nordisk in the 1990s to make the pituitary gland release growth hormone, without the cortisol rise seen with older compounds. In healthy men it produced a single short pulse of growth hormone. Its one published efficacy trial, in 114 bowel surgery patients, found no meaningful difference from placebo. It is not FDA-approved for any use, FDA advisers voted against letting pharmacies compound it, and it is banned in sport. Muscle and anti-aging claims rest on animal work.

blocks.text: Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide, a chain of five amino acids (Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2), that belongs to a family of drugs called growth hormone secretagogues. A secretagogue is a substance that makes a gland release a hormone, and in this case the gland is the pituitary at the base of the brain [1].

Chemists at Novo Nordisk identified it in the 1990s while refining an older peptide called GHRP-1. They reported it as the first growth hormone releaser of its type that was selective, meaning it raised growth hormone without also raising other pituitary hormones or the stress hormones ACTH and cortisol [1]. It was later developed for a hospital use, restarting the gut after abdominal surgery, but that program did not lead to approval [5][6].

Ipamorelin mimics ghrelin, a hormone made mostly in the stomach, by binding the same receptor on pituitary cells. That receptor is separate from the one used by growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH), which is why the drug's effect was not blocked by GHRH antagonists in the original lab work [1]. In pigs, doses more than 200 times the amount needed for growth hormone release still did not raise cortisol, a key difference from GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 [1].

In healthy men given a 15-minute intravenous infusion, ipamorelin produced one burst of growth hormone that peaked at about 40 minutes and then faded to negligible levels. The drug itself had a terminal half-life of about 2 hours, and blood levels rose in proportion to the dose across five dose levels [2].

Because the ghrelin receptor is also found in the gut, the compound speeds bowel movement in animals. In rats that had abdominal surgery, repeated intravenous doses increased stool output, food intake, and weight gain compared with salt water [4].

No. Ipamorelin has never been approved by the FDA, and no company is seeking approval. The FDA placed ipamorelin acetate in Category 2, its group of compounding substances with possible safety risks. It cited a risk of immune reactions, unnatural amino acids that make impurities hard to characterize, and a published report of serious adverse events, including death, when ipamorelin was given intravenously [7].

Ipamorelin was one of four substances the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee reviewed at its October 29, 2024 meeting, where the question was whether to add it to the 503A bulks list for growth hormone deficiency and post-surgical ileus (a stalled bowel) [8]. It has not been added. The FDA's 2026 update moves the 503A nomination to the withdrawn section but notes that ipamorelin acetate stays in Category 2 for outsourcing facilities [7]. It is also not among the six peptides in the October 2026 HHS enforcement discretion policy [12][11].

Most of the evidence is from animals. In adult female rats given a steroid that weakens bone and muscle, three months of ipamorelin injections alongside the steroid preserved calf muscle strength and raised the rate of new bone formation about fourfold compared with the steroid alone [3]. No similar study has been done in people.

The human record is narrow. Early studies in healthy volunteers measured blood levels and growth hormone responses over hours, not body composition, strength, or aging [2]. The only completed efficacy trials tested intravenous ipamorelin for gut recovery after bowel resection:

rows: 114 adults after bowel resection, randomized to ipamorelin or placebo for up to 7 days
Median time to a tolerated solid meal 25.3 vs 32.6 hours; not statistically significant [5]

blocks.text: In the published trial, side effects were common in both groups, reported by 87.5% on ipamorelin and 94.8% on placebo, which reflects recovery from major surgery rather than the drug [5]. A 2026 review of growth hormone axis peptides sold to the public notes that online use for physique or performance has no regulatory approval and that product contents and doses in that supply chain are uncertain [10].

No. The World Anti-Doping Agency's 2026 Prohibited List names ipamorelin among the growth hormone secretagogues in section S2, alongside ibutamoren (MK-677) and ghrelin itself [9]. The ban covers the substance in any form, including compounded or online products.

name: Kisspeptin-10
evidenceNote: Several small controlled human studies show kisspeptin-10 raises LH and testosterone for hours, mostly given by vein in a clinic. None ran longer than a few days or tested a clinical outcome, and the brain and desire studies used a different form, kisspeptin-54.
summary: Kisspeptin-10 is a short fragment of a reproductive hormone that raises LH in small human studies. It is unapproved and on FDA's compounding safety list.
keyTakeaway: Kisspeptin-10 is the smallest active piece of kisspeptin, the hormone that switches on the reproductive axis. In small studies of healthy men, an intravenous dose roughly tripled luteinizing hormone (LH) within 30 minutes, and longer infusions lifted testosterone. Healthy women in the early part of the cycle showed no response. No trial has tested it for fertility, libido, or low testosterone as a treatment. It is not FDA-approved, FDA has placed it in its compounding safety-risk category, and WADA bans it in male athletes.

blocks.text: Kisspeptins are a family of peptides cut from a single precursor protein made by the KISS1 gene. The longest natural form has 54 amino acids (kisspeptin-54). Kisspeptin-10 is the final ten amino acids of that chain, and it is the shortest piece that still fully activates the kisspeptin receptor [1].

Interest in the family took off after people born with faulty kisspeptin signaling were found to go through no puberty, which showed that the hormone is a required trigger for human reproduction [8]. Academic groups in the UK and elsewhere have since given kisspeptin-10 to volunteers to study how it shapes reproductive hormones. Outside research, it is sold online as an unregulated "research peptide," often marketed to men for testosterone and libido.

Kisspeptin acts upstream of the hormones most people know. It binds receptors on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons in the hypothalamus, which then release GnRH in pulses. GnRH in turn prompts the pituitary to release LH and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which drive the testes and ovaries [8]. In men, kisspeptin-10 increased both the number and the size of LH pulses, and a long infusion raised testosterone [1].

The response depends heavily on sex and timing. Healthy men responded at low doses, while healthy women in the follicular phase (the first half of the menstrual cycle) showed no hormone change even at much higher doses. Women in the days just before ovulation did respond [2]. Kisspeptin is also found in parts of the brain that handle emotion and sexual cues, which has led to research on desire and mood, though that work used kisspeptin-54 rather than kisspeptin-10 [6][7].

No. No kisspeptin product is approved for any use in the United States. FDA places kisspeptin-10 in Category 2 of its 503A bulk substance list, the group of compounding ingredients that raise significant safety concerns, and this listing was still in place in FDA's May 2026 update [9]. FDA's stated concern is a risk of immunogenicity (the body forming an immune response against the peptide) for some routes of use, along with little safety information for the routes proposed [10].
In sport, the 2026 WADA Prohibited List bans kisspeptin and its agonist analogs in males, under the testosterone-stimulating peptides in class S2.2.1, both in and out of competition [11].

Every published human study of kisspeptin-10 is small and short, and most gave it into a vein in a research unit. They show that the peptide moves reproductive hormones. They do not show that it treats any condition.

A 1 mcg/kg bolus raised LH from 4.1 to 12.4 IU/L at 30 minutes; a 22.5-hour infusion raised testosterone from 16.6 to 24.0 nmol/L
Healthy men and women, 4 to 5 per group
LH rose in men and in women before ovulation; no change in follicular-phase women
In 4 men given an 11-hour infusion, LH climbed about fivefold (3.9 rising to 20.7 IU/L) and testosterone by about a third (8.5 rising to 11.4 nmol/L); there was no placebo arm

A 12-hour infusion restarted LH pulses and raised estradiol

blocks.text: The better-known kisspeptin trials, including brain-scan studies in healthy men and a randomized crossover trial in 32 women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder (persistently low sexual desire that causes distress), gave kisspeptin-54 by infusion [6][7]. Those studies reported changes in brain activity during erotic images, not changes in sexual behavior, and they cannot be read across to a kisspeptin-10 injection bought online. A 2024 review from the field's leading group describes kisspeptin's therapeutic uses as still in development [8].

Two practical gaps matter when weighing online claims. First, the hormone effects in these studies came from carefully timed doses, mostly by vein, under supervision; how repeated self-injection over weeks behaves has not been reported. Second, more is not necessarily better: in the 2011 dose-response study, the highest bolus tested gave a smaller LH rise than the one below it [1].

Vials sold as kisspeptin-10 for "research use" are not made or tested under drug manufacturing rules, so their content, purity, and sterility are unknown. FDA's safety listing reflects exactly this gap: there is little information on what repeated injection of the compounded peptide does in people [10]. The published studies were run by endocrinology teams who measured hormones every few minutes, a very different setting from self-dosing at home.

name: KPV
evidenceNote: KPV has calmed colitis in mice and lowered inflammatory signals in cultured human cells, but no study in people has been published or registered. The FDA has said it found no human exposure data for KPV by any route.
summary: KPV is a three-amino-acid fragment of α-MSH that reduced gut inflammation in mice. It is untested in people and not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: KPV is a tripeptide (lysine, proline, valine) taken from the tail of α-MSH, a hormone with anti-inflammatory effects. Taken by mouth in mice, it reduced colitis, and in human gut cells it damped NF-κB, a master switch for inflammation. No clinical trial exists, and the FDA says it has no human safety data. It is not FDA-approved. Since October 2026, a federal enforcement discretion policy lets 503A pharmacies compound KPV for oral and topical use on prescription while rulemaking continues. That policy is not an approval and does not establish that KPV works.

atGlance.value: Not approved; compounding tolerated under an interim HHS policy since October 2026

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Enters gut and immune cells through the PepT1 transporter and dampens NF-κB inflammatory signaling

blocks.text: KPV is a peptide made of just three amino acids: lysine (K), proline (P), and valine (V). It matches the last three positions, numbers 11 to 13, of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), a 13-amino-acid hormone cut from a larger precursor protein called proopiomelanocortin [1].

α-MSH is best known for darkening skin, but researchers found it also reduces inflammation in animal models of dermatitis, arthritis, asthma, and bowel disease. Reviewing this work in 2007, Thomas Luger and Tomasz Brzoska concluded that most of α-MSH's anti-inflammatory activity could be traced to its final three amino acids, KPV [1].

Most KPV research has focused on inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the group of conditions that includes ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. KPV is also sold online for skin and gut health, well ahead of any human data.

Full-length α-MSH acts through melanocortin receptors, especially MC1R. KPV seems to work largely without them. In mice engineered to lack a working MC1R, KPV still protected against chemically induced colitis, which suggests a separate route [2].

That route appears to be PepT1, a transporter that normally carries small peptides from digested food into cells. PepT1 is found mainly in the small intestine, but it becomes more abundant in the colon during IBD. A 2008 study showed that human intestinal cells and human T cells take KPV in through PepT1. Once inside, nanomolar amounts of KPV blocked the activation of NF-κB and related signaling pathways and cut the release of inflammatory cytokines (immune signaling proteins) [3].

Getting an intact peptide to the inflamed colon is a delivery problem, so later studies have packed KPV into nanoparticles built to release it there and to be taken up by gut lining cells and macrophages (immune cells that drive much of the inflammation) [4].

No. KPV has never been approved as a drug in the United States, and no company has reported a human trial. In its compounding safety assessment, the FDA said it had not identified any human exposure data on products containing KPV by any route of administration and lacked important information on whether it would harm people [5].

Its compounding status changed in 2026. In July, the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 6, with one abstention, to recommend adding KPV to the 503A bulks list, the list of substances pharmacies may use to compound prescriptions, even though FDA staff had argued against it [6][9]. In late October, HHS issued an interim policy saying it would not take enforcement action against pharmacies or physicians that compound KPV and five other peptides while the formal listing is worked out through rulemaking [7][8]. For KPV, that policy covers topical and oral dosage forms only [8].

The policy itself notes that compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and that the FDA does not review their safety or effectiveness before they are sold. It can be revisited if a safety or quality problem appears [7].

items.text: FDA advisory committee recommends KPV for the 503A bulks list by a narrow vote [6].
HHS enforcement discretion policy covering KPV and five other peptides is published in the Federal Register [7].

blocks.text: All published efficacy data come from mice and cell cultures. The main studies used chemically induced colitis, in which an irritant such as dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) damages the colon lining, and a transfer model in which immune cells provoke colitis.

rows: Mice with DSS colitis and T-cell transfer colitis
Faster recovery, regained weight, less tissue inflammation; protected mice lacking MC1R
Human gut and T cells; mice with two colitis models
KPV entered cells via PepT1, reduced NF-κB activity, and lowered colitis when given in drinking water
KPV in colon-targeted nanoparticles sped mucosal healing and lowered TNF-α

blocks.text: These results are consistent with each other, and the mechanism is plausible. But mouse colitis models do not reliably predict what happens in people with IBD, and no one has measured how KPV is absorbed, how long it lasts, or what dose would matter in humans. The FDA's advisory committee recommended the peptide for compounding over the objections of agency scientists, who cited the lack of clinical evidence [6][9].
Side effects in people are unknown because no one has formally studied them. Products sold online as research chemicals carry additional risks of contamination and mislabeled content.

name: Lanreotide
evidenceNote: FDA-approved since 2007, with each of its three uses backed by randomized trials, including the CLARINET trial in neuroendocrine tumors and a placebo-controlled carcinoid syndrome study.
summary: Lanreotide (Somatuline Depot) is a long-acting somatostatin analog injected monthly for acromegaly, neuroendocrine tumors, and carcinoid syndrome.
keyTakeaway: Lanreotide is a synthetic eight-amino-acid version of somatostatin, the body's own brake on growth hormone and gut hormones. Given as a deep injection under the skin every four weeks, it has been FDA-approved since 2007 for acromegaly and later for gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and carcinoid syndrome. In the CLARINET trial, 65.1% of people with these tumors were alive without progression at two years on lanreotide versus 33.0% on placebo. Common side effects are diarrhea, abdominal pain, and gallstones. Brand Somatuline Depot and several lanreotide injections from other makers are available by prescription.

blocks.text: Lanreotide is a synthetic octapeptide (a chain of eight amino acids) with biological activity similar to somatostatin, a natural hormone that switches off the release of many other hormones [1]. Somatuline Depot is a prolonged-release formulation: the drug is injected deep under the skin as a concentrated solution and released slowly, which allows one dose every four weeks [1].

The brand product, Somatuline Depot, is made by Ipsen and comes in prefilled syringes of 60, 90, and 120 mg [1]. Other lanreotide acetate injections, including ones marketed by Cipla and Amneal, carry the same three indications [5][6].

Octreotide and pasireotide are related somatostatin analogs with their own entries in this library. The class is used mainly for two kinds of problems: too much growth hormone, and tumors of hormone-producing cells in the gut and pancreas [1].

Somatostatin works through five receptor types, numbered SSTR1 to SSTR5. Lanreotide binds most strongly to SSTR2 and SSTR5 and much more weakly to the other three [1]. Activating SSTR2 and SSTR5 on pituitary cells is thought to be the main way it reduces growth hormone (GH) and, downstream, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) [1].

Like somatostatin, lanreotide also dampens endocrine, exocrine, and local signaling in the gut and pancreas [1]. CLARINET enrolled only people whose tumors carried somatostatin receptors, and in that group lanreotide slowed tumor growth [2]. In carcinoid syndrome, it reduces the flushing and diarrhea caused by hormones the tumors release, measured as fewer days needing rescue medication [1].

The same broad braking effect explains several of its side effects. It slows gallbladder emptying, which can lead to gallstones, and it can push blood sugar up or down by changing insulin and glucagon release [1].

Yes. The FDA first approved Somatuline Depot in August 2007 for acromegaly, then added two more indications in later years [3]. Other lanreotide products approved since then list 2007 as the drug's initial US approval and carry the same uses [5][6].

items.text: Somatuline Depot approved for long-term treatment of acromegaly [3].
CLARINET trial results published [2].
Approval extended to GEP-NETs to improve progression-free survival [3].
Approval extended to carcinoid syndrome [3].
Label adds a warning on steatorrhea and fat malabsorption [1].

items: Acromegaly, a condition caused by too much growth hormone, in people who did not respond well enough to surgery or radiation or cannot have them. The goal is to bring GH and IGF-1 back to normal [1].
Adults with gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs) that cannot be removed surgically and are well or moderately differentiated, to delay tumor progression [1].
Adults with carcinoid syndrome, the flushing and diarrhea caused by hormones from some neuroendocrine tumors, where it reduces the need for short-acting rescue injections [1].

blocks.text: For acromegaly, the label describes a one-year randomized study of 108 patients. In its four-week placebo-controlled phase, 63% of people given a single lanreotide injection had their average growth hormone level cut by more than half, against none of the 25 on placebo. By the end of the study, about 58% had a normal IGF-1 level for their age, up from 8% at the start [1]. A separate 48-week open-label study of 63 patients found that 43% reached a normal IGF-1 level [1].

The tumor approval rests on CLARINET, a randomized, double-blind trial in people with advanced, nonfunctioning GEP-NETs of grade 1 or 2 that showed somatostatin receptors on scans. Lanreotide 120 mg every four weeks roughly halved the risk of progression or death compared with placebo [2].

rows: Hazard ratio for progression or death [2]

blocks.text: CLARINET did not show a difference in overall survival or quality of life [2]. For carcinoid syndrome, a 16-week placebo-controlled trial of 115 patients found that people on lanreotide needed rescue octreotide on 34% of days, against 49% on placebo [1]. In a prospective analysis of that trial, the benefit on rescue use and symptoms was clearest in patients who had never taken a somatostatin analog before [4].

The most common side effects differ a little by condition. In acromegaly they include diarrhea, gallstones, abdominal pain, nausea, and injection site reactions. In GEP-NETs, the most frequent were abdominal pain, muscle and joint pain, vomiting, headache, injection site reactions, high blood sugar, high blood pressure, and gallstones. In carcinoid syndrome, headache, dizziness, and muscle spasm stood out [1].

items: Gallstones and gallbladder sludge, sometimes with complications such as inflammation of the gallbladder or pancreas; among 167 people with acromegaly given routine ultrasounds, 12% developed new gallstones [1]
High or low blood sugar, which may require changes to diabetes treatment [1]
A slower heart rate [1]
Reduced thyroid function [1]
Fatty, pale, or loose stools and weight loss, signs of reduced fat absorption that may point to pancreatic exocrine insufficiency [1]
Allergic reactions, including angioedema and anaphylaxis, in rare cases; a known allergy to lanreotide is the only contraindication [1]

blocks.text: Gallbladder problems are the side effect most specific to this drug class. Across clinical studies of 416 people with acromegaly, gallstones or gallbladder sludge were reported in 20%. Pancreatitis was reported in less than 1% of patients across the pooled studies [1]. The label advises periodic monitoring and stopping the drug if gallstone complications are suspected [1].

name: Larazotide acetate
evidenceNote: Tested in several randomized, placebo-controlled trials in celiac disease, including a 342-patient phase 2b study. Results were mixed: one low dose helped symptoms while higher doses did not, and the phase 3 trial was halted when an interim analysis showed it would need far more patients.
summary: Larazotide is an oral peptide built to tighten the gut lining in celiac disease. Its phase 3 trial stopped in 2022 and it is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Larazotide acetate is an eight-amino-acid peptide taken by mouth that was designed to close the gaps between intestinal cells, which gluten pries open in celiac disease. In a 342-person phase 2b trial, only the lowest 0.5 mg dose reduced symptoms more than a gluten-free diet alone, and the higher doses did no better than placebo. A phase 3 trial was stopped in 2022 after an interim analysis showed it would need an impractically large number of patients, and the sponsor moved its money to other programs. Larazotide is not FDA-approved for any use, and the only proven treatment for celiac disease remains a strict gluten-free diet.

blocks.text: Larazotide acetate is a short, single-chain peptide of eight amino acids, developed as a pill for celiac disease [1]. Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition in which gluten, a protein in wheat, barley and rye, triggers an immune attack on the lining of the small intestine. The only established treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet [3].

Larazotide was meant to work alongside that diet, not replace it. Recurring symptoms are common even on a gluten-free diet, and no nondietary treatment had been approved or proven when the drug was tested [2]. It was developed for celiac disease by Innovate Biopharmaceuticals, which later merged to form 9 Meters Biopharma [1].

The cells lining the intestine are sealed to one another by protein complexes called tight junctions, which control what slips between cells into the tissue below. In celiac disease, fragments of gluten (gliadin) trigger signals that loosen those seals, letting more gluten reach immune cells and keeping the inflammation going [1].

Larazotide is thought to act as an antagonist of zonulin, a protein that increases intestinal permeability, and to help rearrange tight-junction proteins and the cell's internal actin scaffolding so the seals close [1]. Later lab work linked it to inhibition of myosin light chain kinase, an enzyme that pulls on actin filaments; easing that tension may help the junctions shut [1]. Most of this mechanism comes from cell and animal studies, including mice and pigs [1].

No. Larazotide has never been approved by the FDA or any other major regulator. Its phase 3 trial, CeDLara, began in 2019 and was terminated by the sponsor in 2022 after enrolling 307 participants [5].

In June 2022, 9 Meters reported that an independent statistician had run a planned interim analysis on roughly the first half of the 525-patient target, solely to re-estimate how many patients would be needed to show a statistically significant effect. The answer was too large to justify continuing, and the company redirected its resources to other programs [4].

items.text: Phase 2b trial in 342 adults: 0.5 mg dose meets primary endpoint, higher doses do not [2]
Phase 3 CeDLara trial starts [5]
Interim analysis does not support continuing; trial stopped [4][5]
Academic phase 2a trial in long COVID completes; no results posted [6]

blocks.text: The largest completed trial tested larazotide in 342 adults who had followed a gluten-free diet for at least a year but still had symptoms. Participants took capsules of 0.5, 1 or 2 mg three times a day, or placebo, for 12 weeks while staying on their diet [2]. The 0.5 mg dose met the primary goal, a lower celiac-specific gastrointestinal symptom score than placebo. It also cut days with celiac symptoms by 26% and eased headache and tiredness [2].

The catch was the dose pattern. The 1 mg and 2 mg doses did no better than placebo on any measure, so the benefit appeared only at the lowest dose [2]. A drug that works at a low dose and stops working at higher ones is harder to trust, because it raises the question of whether the low-dose result was chance. The authors themselves described the results as mixed [2].

A 2022 meta-analysis pooled four randomized trials with 626 patients. Larazotide did not change the lactulose-to-mannitol ratio, a urine test of gut leakiness and the measure most directly tied to its proposed mechanism. In patients deliberately given gluten, it improved symptom scores and reduced gluten-related diarrhea compared with placebo, but in patients on a gluten-free diet the symptom scores did not differ significantly. Side effects were similar to placebo [3].

rows: 342 adults with symptoms despite a gluten-free diet
0.5 mg improved symptoms; 1 mg and 2 mg no better than placebo [2]
No change in gut permeability test; symptom benefit only under gluten challenge [3]

blocks.text: Researchers at Massachusetts General Hospital have also tested larazotide outside celiac disease. A small trial in children with MIS-C, a severe inflammatory illness after COVID-19, was terminated after 12 participants because cases of the illness declined [7]. A randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial in children and adults with long COVID finished in June 2026, but no results had been posted at the time of writing [6].

name: Leuprolide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in several brands and depot strengths for advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, fibroid-related anemia and central precocious puberty, each backed by its own clinical studies.
summary: Leuprolide is a synthetic GnRH agonist that shuts down sex hormone production. It treats prostate cancer, endometriosis and early puberty.
keyTakeaway: Leuprolide is a lab-made version of GnRH, the brain hormone that switches on the testes and ovaries. Given continuously, it does the opposite of the natural pulses: after a brief surge, the pituitary stops responding and testosterone or estrogen falls to very low levels. It is FDA-approved under brands such as Lupron Depot and Eligard for advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, fibroid-related anemia and early puberty in children. In a pediatric trial, a 3-month injection suppressed the puberty hormone LH in 78 to 95% of children. Hot flashes, the initial flare, and bone loss with longer use are the main trade-offs.

blocks.text: Leuprolide (called leuprorelin outside the United States) is a synthetic peptide modeled on gonadotropin-releasing hormone, or GnRH. GnRH is made in the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain, and tells the pituitary gland to release the two hormones that drive the testes and ovaries: luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) [2].

Most leuprolide is given as a depot, a slow-release injection that keeps working for weeks or months. AbbVie's Lupron Depot comes in strengths that last 1, 3, 4 or 6 months for prostate cancer [2]. Tolmar sells Eligard, injected under the skin, for the same cancer [6], and separate pediatric products exist for early puberty [4].

Leuprolide grew out of a race to decode the brain's control of the pituitary. Andrew Schally and Roger Guillemin, working in rival laboratories, each isolated the hypothalamic releasing hormone for LH in 1971, an effort that took hundreds of thousands of pig brains. The work earned them a share of the 1977 Nobel Prize [1].

The same year the hormone was isolated, Schally's group showed that it could also suppress gonadotropin release, and experiments in monkeys showed that a constant supply of the hormone desensitized its receptors on the pituitary. That paradox, a stimulating hormone used to switch the system off, opened the way to synthetic analogs. Schally ran the first clinical studies in Mexico in 1972, and the first study of an agonist in prostate cancer was published in 1982 [1].

The body releases natural GnRH in short pulses. Leuprolide binds the same receptor on the pituitary but stays active far longer. In the first days, this triggers a surge of LH and FSH, and testosterone in men can climb about 50% above baseline [2]. With continuous exposure, the pituitary stops responding, LH and FSH fall, and the testes or ovaries largely stop making sex hormones. The label notes the effect reverses once the drug is stopped [2].

That shutdown is the point. Prostate cancer growth is fueled by testosterone, endometriosis tissue by estrogen, and early puberty by hormones switching on too soon. In the main prostate cancer study of the 1-month depot, testosterone dropped into the castrate range (50 ng/dL or lower) within 30 days in 94% of men [2].

Yes. Leuprolide is FDA-approved in several brands and strengths, each with its own label. Lupron Depot at 7.5, 22.5, 30 and 45 mg treats advanced prostate cancer [2]. The 3.75 mg monthly Lupron Depot treats endometriosis and, with iron, anemia caused by uterine fibroids before surgery [3]. Lupron Depot-PED treats central precocious puberty [4], and Eligard is approved for advanced prostate cancer [6]. Generic leuprolide acetate is also available.

items: Advanced prostate cancer, to lower testosterone that drives tumor growth [2]
Endometriosis, to relieve pain and shrink lesions, often paired with norethindrone acetate to limit bone loss [3]
Anemia from uterine fibroids, together with iron, to improve blood counts before surgery [3]
Central precocious puberty, when puberty starts unusually early because the brain's signal switches on too soon [4]

blocks.text: In children with precocious puberty, a phase 3 trial gave a 3-month depot of 11.25 mg or 30 mg to 84 children. The puberty hormone LH stayed suppressed from months 2 to 6 in 78.4% of the lower-dose group and 95.2% of the higher-dose group, and growth rates and side effects were similar between doses [5].
For endometriosis, the label limits total treatment with the 3.75 mg depot plus add-back hormone therapy to 12 months because of concerns about bone density [3].

Most side effects follow from low sex hormones. In men with prostate cancer, common reactions reported in more than 10% included hot flashes and sweats, general pain, injection site reactions, digestive complaints, swelling and urinary symptoms [2]. In women treated for endometriosis, hot flashes, headache, vaginal inflammation, mood changes, weight change, nausea, lower libido and dizziness were each reported by more than 10% [3].

The early testosterone surge can briefly worsen prostate cancer symptoms, including bone pain and, rarely, spinal cord compression [2]. Labels also warn of metabolic changes such as raised blood sugar and lipids, a reported increase in heart attack and stroke risk in men, effects on heart rhythm, seizures, and severe skin reactions [2]. In women, bone mineral density loss limits how long it can be used, and it can harm a pregnancy [3]. Children may have emotional swings and, early on, a flare of puberty signs [4].

name: Linaclotide
evidenceNote: Linaclotide was approved in 2012 after several large placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in IBS with constipation and chronic constipation, and its label has since been extended to children on further trials.
summary: Linaclotide (Linzess) is a 14-amino-acid capsule that draws fluid into the gut to treat IBS with constipation and chronic constipation. FDA-approved since 2012.
keyTakeaway: Linaclotide is a small peptide taken as a daily capsule that acts on the lining of the intestine and is barely absorbed into the blood. It switches on a receptor called guanylate cyclase-C, which pulls water into the bowel and calms gut pain nerves. In a 26-week trial in IBS with constipation, 33.7% of patients met the FDA's combined pain and bowel goal against 13.9% on placebo. The FDA approved it as Linzess in 2012 for adults, later extending it to children aged 2 and older. Diarrhea is the main side effect, and it is ruled out under age 2.

atGlance.value: Approved August 2012 (Linzess), prescription only

atGlance.label: How it works

blocks.text: Linaclotide is a peptide of 14 amino acids, six of them cysteines that pair up into three internal sulfur bridges [1]. Those bridges fold it into a compact, stable shape. It is related to two hormones the gut makes for itself, guanylin and uroguanylin, which help control how much water moves into the intestine [1].

AbbVie sells it as Linzess, a capsule [2]. Unlike most peptide drugs, it is meant to stay inside the digestive tract. After an oral dose, the amounts reaching the blood are too small to measure, so it has no conventional half-life [1]. That local action is the reason a peptide can work as a pill here: it does its job on the inner surface of the gut, where it lands.

Linaclotide and its active breakdown product bind guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C), a receptor on the cells that line the intestine [1]. Activating it raises a messenger molecule called cyclic GMP (cGMP) inside and outside those cells. Inside, cGMP opens the CFTR channel, the same channel that is faulty in cystic fibrosis, which releases chloride and bicarbonate into the gut [1]. Water follows the salt, stool softens, and transit speeds up.

The cGMP that escapes the cells appears to act on nearby nerves. In animal models of gut pain, linaclotide quieted the pain-sensing nerves and reduced abdominal muscle contractions [1]. That second effect is why it was tested for irritable bowel syndrome, where abdominal pain is as central as constipation, and not only for constipation alone.

Yes. The FDA approved Linzess on August 30, 2012 [2]. Later actions added a lower-dose capsule in 2017, a new indication for functional constipation in children in 2023, and further pediatric age groups in 2025 and 2026 [2]. It is prescription only.

items.text: Approved for adults with IBS with constipation and with chronic idiopathic constipation [2].
A new, lower dosing regimen is approved [2].
Functional constipation in children is added as a new indication [2].
Use expands to IBS with constipation from age 7 and functional constipation from age 2 [1][2].

blocks.text: The current label lists three uses [1]. In irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C), where belly pain travels with infrequent, hard stools, it is approved for adults and for children from age 7. In chronic idiopathic constipation, long-lasting constipation with no identified cause, it is approved for adults. In functional constipation, the common childhood form with no structural cause, it is approved from age 2.

rows: FDA responder endpoint met by 33.7% versus 13.9% on placebo [3]
Pain responders 48.9% versus 34.5%; bowel movement responders 47.6% versus 22.6% [3]
Primary endpoint reached by 16.0% to 21.3% on linaclotide versus 3.3% and 6.0% on placebo [4]

blocks.text: The FDA's IBS-C endpoint is demanding: a patient had to report at least 30% less abdominal pain and at least one extra complete bowel movement in the same week, for at least six of twelve weeks [3]. About one in five additional patients met it on linaclotide compared with placebo, which the authors expressed as five people treated for one extra responder [3]. Bloating, straining, and stool form also improved [3].

The pediatric evidence is newer and smaller. In a 12-week trial of 328 children aged 6 to 17 with functional constipation, those on the lowest capsule strength went from about one spontaneous bowel movement a week to roughly 3.8, a gain of 2.6 per week against 1.3 on placebo [1]. The improvement showed up in the first week and held for the rest of the trial [1].

The capsule is taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before a meal, at about the same time each day [1]. For people who cannot swallow it, the label allows the capsule to be opened and the contents taken in applesauce or water, but not crushed or chewed [1].
Because it works by moving water into the bowel, its main side effect is too much of that. In the two pivotal adult IBS-C trials, the reactions seen more often than with placebo were [1]:

items: Diarrhea: 20% versus 3% [1]
Abdominal pain: 7% versus 5% [1]
Gas: 4% versus 2% [1]
Bloating (abdominal distension): 2% versus 1% [1]
Viral gastroenteritis and headache, each a point or two above placebo [1]

blocks.text: Severe diarrhea affected about 2% of adults, and about 5% of IBS-C patients stopped the drug because of it [1]. The boxed warning concerns very young children: a single adult-equivalent dose killed newborn mice through dehydration, so linaclotide is contraindicated under age 2 [1]. It is also not used when a mechanical blockage of the bowel is known or suspected [1].

name: Liraglutide
evidenceNote: Liraglutide has been FDA-approved since 2010, and its main uses rest on large randomized trials, including a 9,340-patient cardiovascular outcomes trial and a 3,731-patient weight trial. Generic versions of both brands are now approved.
summary: Liraglutide is a once-daily GLP-1 drug, approved as Victoza for type 2 diabetes and as Saxenda for weight management. Generics exist for both.
keyTakeaway: Liraglutide is a once-daily injected copy of the gut hormone GLP-1, made by Novo Nordisk and approved in the United States as Victoza (type 2 diabetes, 2010) and Saxenda (weight management, 2014). In its main weight trial, people on the 3 mg dose lost 8.4 kg over 56 weeks against 2.8 kg on placebo. In people with diabetes and heart disease, it cut major cardiac events by 13%. Nausea is the most common side effect, and the label carries a boxed warning on thyroid tumors seen in rodents. FDA-approved generics of both brands reached the market in 2024 and 2025.
