blocks.text: Liraglutide is a lab-made version of GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1), a hormone the gut releases after a meal. Its amino acid sequence matches the human hormone at 97% of positions, and a fatty acid chain is attached to it [1]. That chain lets the molecule bind to proteins in the blood and resist breakdown, so one injection lasts about a day instead of a few minutes.

Novo Nordisk sells it under two brand names at different doses. Victoza treats type 2 diabetes in adults and in children aged 10 and older, and also lowers the risk of heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death in adults with diabetes and established heart disease [1]. Saxenda is the higher-dose product for long-term weight management in adults and in adolescents aged 12 and older [2]. Both are injected subcutaneously (under the skin) with a prefilled pen.

Novo Nordisk designed liraglutide so that slow absorption, protein binding, and resistance to enzymes would stretch its action across a full day, making it suitable for a single daily shot [1]. Over the following decade it gathered new indications, and it became one of the first drugs in its class to be sold as a generic.

items.text: The FDA approves Victoza as a new molecular entity for type 2 diabetes [3].
Saxenda, the higher-dose version, is approved for chronic weight management [4].
The LEADER trial reports fewer cardiovascular events with liraglutide than with placebo [5].
New indications follow: cardiovascular risk reduction and diabetes in children for Victoza, and adolescent weight management for Saxenda [3][4].
The FDA approves the first generic referencing Victoza, citing an ongoing shortage [7].
The first generic referencing Saxenda is approved [8].

blocks.text: Liraglutide switches on the GLP-1 receptor. In the beta cells of the pancreas, that raises insulin release, but only when blood sugar is high, and the effect fades as glucose returns to normal [1]. It also lowers glucagon, a hormone that pushes blood sugar up, and slows the emptying of the stomach [1]. Because the insulin effect depends on glucose, liraglutide alone rarely causes low blood sugar, although the risk rises when it is combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea.

The weight effect runs largely through the brain. GLP-1 receptors sit in brain areas that regulate appetite, and in animal studies liraglutide reached appetite centers such as the hypothalamus [2]. People taking it generally feel full sooner and eat less. The natural hormone survives only 1.5 to 2 minutes in the blood, while liraglutide has a half-life of about 13 hours, which is what allows once-daily use [2].

Yes. Victoza was approved in 2010 and Saxenda in 2014, both by prescription only [3][4]. In December 2024 the FDA approved Hikma's generic referencing Victoza and said it had prioritized the review because liraglutide was in shortage [7]. In August 2025 it approved Teva's generic referencing Saxenda, the first generic in the class indicated for weight [8]. Generic versions carry the same indications and the same boxed warning as the brands.

As Victoza, it is used alongside diet and exercise to lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, and to reduce major cardiovascular events in adults with diabetes and known heart or vascular disease [1]. As Saxenda, it is used with a reduced-calorie diet and more activity in adults with obesity, in adults with overweight and at least one related health problem, for example hypertension or abnormal blood fats, and in adolescents aged 12 and older who weigh more than 60 kg and have obesity [2]. The two brands should not be combined, since both contain the same drug.

rows: 9,340 adults with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, median 3.8 years
Heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death in 13.0% versus 14.9% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.87); cardiovascular death 4.7% versus 6.0% [5]
3,731 adults with obesity or overweight, no diabetes, 56 weeks
Average loss of 8.4 kg versus 2.8 kg; 63.2% versus 27.1% lost at least 5% of body weight [6]

blocks.text: In the weight trial, a third of people on liraglutide lost more than 10% of their starting weight, against about one in ten on placebo [6]. Everyone in these trials, including the placebo group, was coached to cut about 500 calories a day and to exercise at least 150 minutes a week, so the placebo result shows what that counseling achieved on its own [2]. Roughly a quarter of the liraglutide group stopped the drug before the end of the 56-week trials [2].
Stomach and bowel complaints dominate, especially in the first weeks as the dose is raised. In the pooled Saxenda weight trials, the most frequent problems compared with placebo were [2]:

items: Nausea: 39.3% versus 13.8% [2]
Diarrhea: 20.9% versus 9.9% [2]
Constipation: 19.4% versus 8.5% [2]
Vomiting: 15.7% versus 3.9% [2]
Indigestion, fatigue, dizziness, and abdominal pain at lower rates [2]

blocks.text: About 10% of people on Saxenda in the 56-week trials stopped because of a side effect, compared with 4% on placebo [2]. The boxed warning concerns thyroid C-cell tumors, which liraglutide caused in rats and mice. Whether it does the same in humans is unknown, and the label rules it out for anyone who has had medullary thyroid cancer, or whose relatives have, and for people with the MEN 2 syndrome [1].

Other labeled risks include pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea, kidney injury from dehydration after vomiting or diarrhea, allergic reactions, and food entering the lungs during anesthesia because the stomach empties slowly [1][2]. Resting heart rate rose by 2 to 3 beats per minute on average in the weight trials [2].

name: Lixisenatide
alsoCalled: Adlyxin; in Soliqua with insulin glargine
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in July 2016 on the basis of placebo- and active-controlled diabetes trials, with a 6,068-patient cardiovascular safety trial behind it.
summary: Lixisenatide is an FDA-approved once-daily GLP-1 drug for type 2 diabetes. In the US it is now found mainly in Soliqua, with insulin glargine.
keyTakeaway: Lixisenatide is a 44-amino-acid peptide that activates the GLP-1 receptor, raising insulin after meals, lowering glucagon and slowing stomach emptying. The FDA approved it in 2016 as Adlyxin, a once-daily injection for adults with type 2 diabetes, and as part of Soliqua, a daily mix with insulin glargine. It is short-acting, with a half-life of about 3 hours, and nausea affected about a quarter of users in trials. In the 6,068-patient ELIXA trial it neither raised nor lowered heart attack and stroke risk. Today the FDA's active label listings for lixisenatide cover only Soliqua.

blocks.text: Lixisenatide is a synthetic peptide drug for type 2 diabetes. It is a chain of 44 amino acids that mimics GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1), a hormone the gut releases after eating [1]. It belongs to the same family as exenatide, liraglutide and semaglutide, but it is one of the shortest-acting members.
Sanofi developed it and markets it in the US as Adlyxin. It also comes premixed with the long-acting insulin glargine as Soliqua 100/33, given as one daily injection [1][2].

Lixisenatide binds the GLP-1 receptor and does three things. It makes the pancreas release more insulin when blood glucose is high, a glucose-dependent effect that limits the risk of low blood sugar on its own. It reduces glucagon, a hormone that tells the liver to release glucose. And it slows gastric emptying, the rate at which food leaves the stomach [1].

That last effect matters more for lixisenatide than for the long-acting drugs in its class. Its terminal half-life in people with type 2 diabetes is about 3 hours, so a single morning dose has its largest effect on the glucose rise after breakfast [1]. Slowed stomach emptying can also delay the absorption of pills, which is why the label addresses timing for medicines such as antibiotics, acetaminophen and oral contraceptives [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Adlyxin on July 27, 2016, and Soliqua 100/33 on November 21, 2016 [3]. The Adlyxin approval remains on file, and its label was last revised in November 2024 to add a class warning about inhaling stomach contents during anesthesia or deep sedation [1][3].

items.text: ELIXA cardiovascular outcomes trial published [4]
Adlyxin approved as a once-daily injection for type 2 diabetes [3]
Soliqua 100/33, combining insulin glargine and lixisenatide, approved [3]
Adlyxin label updated with the aspiration warning [1]

blocks.text: Approval and availability are not the same thing. FDA's database of current drug labels now carries Soliqua as the only lixisenatide product with an active label, which means the combination with insulin glargine is the form in current US use [6].

Its one approved use is lowering blood glucose in adults who have type 2 diabetes, on top of diet and exercise. It is not for type 1 diabetes, has not been studied in people with chronic pancreatitis, and is not recommended for people with gastroparesis, a condition in which the stomach empties too slowly [1].

Its clinical program tested it alone, with oral diabetes pills and with basal insulin. In a 12-week monotherapy trial of 241 adults, HbA1c (a measure of average blood sugar over about three months) fell 0.65 percentage points more than with placebo, and 44 percent reached an HbA1c below 7 percent against 24 percent on placebo [1]. In a head-to-head study, it lowered HbA1c less than twice-daily exenatide [1].

ELIXA was its cardiovascular safety trial. It enrolled 6,068 people with type 2 diabetes who had had a heart attack or a hospital stay for unstable angina within the previous six months, and followed them for a median of about 25 months. Major cardiovascular events occurred in 13.4 percent on lixisenatide and 13.2 percent on placebo, a hazard ratio of 1.02, which ruled out added harm but showed no benefit [4].

blocks.text: In the pooled placebo-controlled trials, nausea was reported by 25 percent of people on lixisenatide against 6 percent on placebo, vomiting by 10 percent against 2 percent, plus headache, diarrhea and dizziness [1]. Low blood sugar was more likely when it was combined with insulin or with sulfonylureas, pills that push the pancreas to release insulin [1].

The label warns of serious allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, pancreatitis, acute kidney injury in people who become dehydrated from vomiting or diarrhea, gallbladder disease, antibodies to the drug that can blunt its effect, and aspiration during anesthesia [1]. It is not recommended in end-stage kidney disease [1].

sections.heading: What about lixisenatide and Parkinson's disease?

blocks.text: Lixisenatide drew new attention in 2024 when a French phase 2 trial tested it in 156 people diagnosed with Parkinson's disease within the previous three years. After 12 months, motor scores were essentially unchanged on lixisenatide but worsened by about 3 points on placebo [5]. Nausea affected 46 percent of treated participants. The authors called for longer and larger trials, and Parkinson's disease is not an approved use [5].

name: LL-37
evidenceNote: Several small randomized trials have tested LL-37 on the skin and by mouth, which meets the bar for moderate. The largest, a 148-patient leg ulcer trial, found no benefit overall, and no trial has tested the injected product sold online.
summary: LL-37 is the only human cathelicidin, an immune peptide that kills microbes. Topical trials for leg ulcers were mixed. It is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: LL-37 is a 37-amino-acid peptide the body makes as part of its first-line defense against bacteria, viruses and fungi. As a drug it has been tested in small randomized trials, mostly as a topical treatment for chronic leg and foot ulcers: a 34-patient trial showed faster healing at lower doses, but a 148-patient follow-up found no overall benefit. It is not FDA-approved for any use and is not on the list of substances pharmacies may compound. The injectable vials sold online have never been studied in a trial, and FDA has flagged animal findings on male fertility and tumor growth.

blocks.text: LL-37 is a naturally occurring human peptide, named for the two leucines that start its chain and its length of 37 amino acids. It is the only member of the cathelicidin family in people. Cells first make a larger precursor protein called hCAP18, and enzymes cut LL-37 free from its tail end [1].

White blood cells called neutrophils store it, and skin, gut and airway linings release it when they sense infection or injury [1]. In the lab, LL-37 has also been shown to bind siderophores, small molecules that bacteria use to steal iron from their host, which may be another way it limits microbial growth [2]. Synthetic LL-37 is the same sequence made in a lab, and it is sold online in vials, usually for injection.

LL-37 is positively charged and folds into a spiral shape with one oily face. That structure lets it stick to the negatively charged membranes of bacteria and open pores in them, which kills the cell [1]. It also acts as an alarm signal: it draws immune cells to a site, tunes inflammation up or down, and in lab studies supports new blood vessel growth and skin cell migration during wound repair [1].

Vitamin D is one switch that controls how much LL-37 the body makes. When immune cells called macrophages detect bacteria, they activate vitamin D, which then turns on the cathelicidin gene and helps the cells kill tuberculosis bacteria [3].

Its immune effects cut both ways. In psoriasis, LL-37 binds fragments of the body's own DNA and carries them into immune cells, which then treat the DNA as if it came from a virus and drive inflammation [4]. In rosacea, people's facial skin carries abnormally high levels of cathelicidin, processed into fragments that inflamed mouse skin when injected [5]. More of this peptide is not automatically better.

No. LL-37 has not been approved by the FDA for any condition, and no LL-37 drug has completed a phase 3 trial. It is also not on the 503A bulks list, the roster of substances that compounding pharmacies may use, and it was not among the six peptides covered by the interim compounding policy HHS announced in October 2026 [12][11].

As of April 2026, FDA's compounding safety page lists cathelicidin LL-37 among nominations that were withdrawn. The agency wrote that it lacks enough safety information to judge whether the peptide would harm people, and pointed to animal and lab findings suggesting harm to male reproduction and possible promotion of tumor growth in some tissues [6].

Most human research has applied LL-37 directly to chronic wounds. The first trial in people enrolled 34 patients with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers, wounds caused by poor blood return in the leg veins. Over four weeks of twice-weekly applications, the 0.5 mg/mL concentration healed about six times faster than placebo, while the highest concentration did no better than placebo [7].

A larger phase 2b trial called HEAL LL-37 then tested the two lower concentrations alongside compression bandaging in 148 patients. Across the whole group, LL-37 did not improve healing compared with placebo. A post hoc look (an analysis decided after the results were in) suggested benefit in patients with wounds of at least 10 square centimeters, a finding that needs its own trial to confirm [8].

blocks.text: Two other randomized trials point in a positive direction but have limits. In a diabetic foot ulcer study from Jakarta, an LL-37 cream raised a measure of healthy healing tissue at every weekly check, though it did not lower bacterial counts or inflammatory markers [9]. A Chinese trial gave hospitalized COVID-19 patients an oral product made from bacteria engineered to produce LL-37, and reported faster viral clearance, but the study was open label (patients and doctors knew who got what) and run at one center [10].

Nothing in this record covers the way LL-37 is usually used outside trials. No published trial has injected synthetic LL-37 under the skin, so its effects, dosing and safety by that route are unknown. Claims about injected LL-37 for immunity, chronic infections or gut health rest on lab and animal work.

name: LTX-315
evidenceNote: Every human study so far has been open-label and uncontrolled, the largest a 92-person phase 2 trial in basal cell carcinoma reported mainly through company releases. Placebo-controlled phase 3 trials are planned but have not reported.
summary: A nine amino acid peptide injected into tumors to burst cancer cells and rouse the immune system. In trials for basal cell skin cancer; not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: LTX-315, now named ruxotemitide, is a lab-designed nine amino acid peptide that is injected straight into a tumor, where it ruptures cancer cell membranes and releases signals that draw in immune cells. In a 39-person phase 1 trial in advanced solid tumors, about 29% of injected tumors shrank by at least 30%. Its lead use is basal cell carcinoma, where an open-label phase 2 trial reported complete clearance under the microscope in about half of treated lesions. It is not FDA-approved, and the placebo-controlled phase 3 program agreed with the FDA has yet to report.

blocks.text: LTX-315 is an oncolytic peptide, a short chain of amino acids that kills cancer cells by breaking them open. It is nine amino acids long and was designed from scratch by Lytix Biopharma, using structure studies of host defense peptides, the natural antibiotics found in many animals, starting from a bovine peptide called lactoferricin [1][2]. It is meant to be injected directly into tumors.

In dermatology the program is licensed to Verrica Pharmaceuticals, which holds worldwide rights for skin cancers and calls the drug VP-315 [4]. Its international name is ruxotemitide [6]. The first target is basal cell carcinoma, a non-melanoma skin cancer, with squamous cell carcinoma also named as a focus [4]. Lytix continues to test it in other cancers, including melanoma and sarcoma [7][8].

The peptide acts on cell membranes [3]. In human melanoma cells in the lab it disrupted the outer membrane and killed cells within two hours; at lower doses it entered the cell and gathered near the mitochondria, the cell's power units, which then lost their charge and changed shape [2]. Within minutes the dying cells released danger signals such as ATP and HMGB1 [2].

Those signals matter more than the direct kill. They alert dendritic cells, the immune system's scouts, which then train T cells to recognize the tumor, a process called immunogenic cell death [3][9]. The hope is that a few injected tumors can teach the immune system to attack tumors that were never injected, known as an abscopal effect [1]. In patients, treated tumors filled with CD8+ killer T cells, and new T-cell clones appeared in the blood [1].

No. LTX-315 is an investigational drug available only in clinical trials. The FDA accepted Verrica's application to start US trials in basal cell carcinoma in November 2021 [4]. In November 2025 the company said the FDA had agreed with its plan for two placebo-controlled phase 3 studies of about 100 people each, with complete clearance at week 14 as the main goal, which it expects could support an approval filing [6].

items.text: Phase 1 results in 39 people with advanced solid tumors are published [1].

blocks.text: The first published human data came from a dose-ranging phase 1 trial in 39 people with advanced solid tumors that could be reached with a needle. About 29% had a shrinkage of 30% or more in the injected tumor, but no one met formal criteria for a partial response across all disease [1]. The most common side effects were brief drops in blood pressure (46%), flushing (28%), and injection site reactions (38%); four people (10%) had serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis [1].

rows: 29% had 30% or more shrinkage of injected tumors; no formal partial responses [1]
92 adults with basal cell carcinoma; 93 lesions
51% of lesions fully cleared on biopsy; average tumor size down 86% [5]
Best response was stable disease for 208 days [7]

blocks.text: In basal cell carcinoma the numbers look stronger, but the design is weaker than it sounds. The phase 2 trial was open-label and non-randomized, with no placebo group [8]. Preliminary results released by the company found that 51% of 93 treated lesions showed no tumor cells on biopsy, and that overall tumor size fell by about 86% on average, with no dose-limiting toxicities and mostly mild to moderate skin reactions [5]. These figures come from company announcements rather than a full peer-reviewed report [5][6].

Elsewhere the evidence is thinner still. In a pilot study of six heavily treated people with metastatic sarcoma, LTX-315 followed by T-cell therapy was safe and produced tumor-reactive T cells, but the best outcome was disease that stopped growing for a while [7]. No randomized trial of LTX-315 has yet been completed in any cancer [8].

Basal cell tumors sit on the skin surface, so they can be injected directly and biopsied afterward, which makes them a practical test for a drug that has to be placed inside a tumor [4]. The trial measured clearance on biopsy rather than by eye, a stricter test [5]. If the effect holds up in controlled trials, it would be given as an injection straight into each lesion [4][6].

The planned phase 3 trials will compare the injection with placebo and count how many lesions are completely cleared at 14 weeks [6]. Until those results are public, it is not known how LTX-315 compares with existing treatments, or how often treated lesions come back.

name: Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate
evidenceNote: FDA approved Lutathera in 2018 based on the randomized phase 3 NETTER-1 trial and a large Dutch expanded-access cohort, and extended it to children 12 and older in 2024. A second randomized phase 3 trial, NETTER-2, tested it as a first treatment.
summary: Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate (Lutathera) is a radioactive peptide that delivers radiation into neuroendocrine tumors. FDA-approved in 2018.
keyTakeaway: Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate is radioligand therapy: a somatostatin-like peptide that carries radioactive lutetium into neuroendocrine tumors and irradiates them from inside. In the NETTER-1 trial of 229 people with advanced midgut tumors, 65% were alive without progression at 20 months, against 11% on high-dose octreotide. The final analysis found no significant difference in overall survival. FDA approved it as Lutathera in 2018 for gut and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and for children 12 and older in 2024. Risks include low blood counts, kidney injury, and a small rate of later blood cancers.

blocks.text: Lutetium Lu 177 dotatate, marketed as Lutathera, is a cancer treatment that combines a targeting peptide with a radioactive atom. The peptide, dotatate, mimics somatostatin, a natural hormone. The atom, lutetium-177, gives off radiation that damages cells at close range. Together they form what is called a radioligand or peptide receptor radionuclide therapy [1].

It treats gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs), slow-growing cancers that start in hormone-producing cells of the stomach, intestines or pancreas. It only works on tumors whose cells carry somatostatin receptors, which is checked with a receptor scan before treatment [1][5].
It is a close relative of the scan agent Ga-68 dotatate. Both use the same peptide; swapping the gallium-68 used for imaging for lutetium-177 turns a diagnostic tracer into a therapy [1][5].

sections.heading: How does lutetium Lu-177 dotatate work?

blocks.text: After infusion, the drug circulates and binds somatostatin receptors, with the strongest attraction to subtype 2 (SSTR2). Tumor cells that carry the receptor pull the drug inside. Lutetium-177 then emits beta particles, which create free radicals that damage the tumor cell and the cells immediately around it [1].

Lutetium-177 has a physical half-life of about 6.6 days, so it keeps delivering radiation for some time after each dose. It also gives off a small amount of gamma radiation, which allows imaging of where it went [1]. The kidneys clear the drug and receive a meaningful radiation dose, so an infusion of amino acids is given before, during and after treatment to help protect them [1].

Yes. FDA approved Lutathera on January 26, 2018, as a new molecular entity under priority review, with orphan drug status [4]. In April 2024 the indication was extended to children aged 12 and older, based on adult efficacy data plus safety and dosing data from a pediatric study called NETTER-P [1].

NETTER-2 results published, testing it as a first treatment for grade 2 to 3 tumors [3].

sections.heading: What is lutetium Lu-177 dotatate prescribed for?

blocks.text: Lutathera is approved for adults and children 12 and older with somatostatin receptor-positive GEP-NETs, including tumors of the foregut, midgut and hindgut. It is given as four infusions eight weeks apart, alongside long-acting octreotide, a somatostatin drug that controls hormone symptoms [1].

The pivotal trial, NETTER-1, enrolled 229 people with advanced, progressing midgut NETs that had grown despite standard octreotide. They were randomly assigned to Lutathera plus octreotide or to a high dose of octreotide alone. At 20 months, an estimated 65% of the Lutathera group were alive without progression, versus 11% of the control group [2].

rows: Risk of progression or death cut by 79% (hazard ratio 0.21) vs high-dose octreotide [1]
No statistically significant difference in overall survival [1]
226 patients with newly diagnosed grade 2 to 3 GEP-NETs

blocks.text: The final overall survival result matters for honest interpretation. Lutathera clearly delayed tumor growth, but in the long-term NETTER-1 analysis people in the two arms did not live significantly different lengths of time [1]. NETTER-2 later tested it as a first treatment in faster-growing tumors and found progression-free survival extended by about 14 months [3].

Nausea and vomiting are the most frequent complaints, reported by 65% and 53% of patients in NETTER-1, and the label calls for anti-nausea medicine before the protective amino acid infusion. Fatigue, abdominal pain, diarrhea and reduced appetite were also more common than on octreotide alone [1]. The most frequent severe lab changes were low lymphocyte counts (44%) and raised liver enzymes [1].

Radiation affects the bone marrow. Low platelet and white cell counts can occur, so blood counts are monitored and doses can be held or reduced. Over the longer term, a small share of patients develop myelodysplastic syndrome, a bone marrow disorder, or acute leukemia: 2.3% developed myelodysplastic syndrome in NETTER-1, and in the large ERASMUS cohort the median time to onset was 29 months for that condition and 55 months for leukemia [1].

The kidneys can be injured, which is why hydration and the amino acid infusion are used and kidney function is tracked. The label also warns of liver toxicity, allergic reactions, and hormonal crisis, a sudden release of tumor hormones causing flushing, diarrhea or low blood pressure. It can harm a fetus and may cause infertility, and breastfeeding is not advised [1].

summary: Pluvicto carries radioactive lutetium-177 to prostate cancer cells that display PSMA. FDA-approved for PSMA-positive metastatic prostate cancer.
keyTakeaway: Pluvicto pairs a homing molecule for PSMA, a protein abundant on prostate cancer cells, with the radioactive metal lutetium-177, so radiation is delivered straight to the tumor. The FDA approved it in 2022 after the VISION trial, where adding it to standard care extended median survival from 11.3 to 15.3 months in men whose cancer had spread after hormone therapy and chemotherapy. Approvals in 2025 and 2026 moved it earlier in treatment. Patients are selected with a PSMA PET scan. Common effects include fatigue, dry mouth, nausea, and low blood counts.

sections.heading: What is lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan?

blocks.text: This drug is a radioligand: a targeting molecule with a radioactive atom attached. The targeting part, vipivotide tetraxetan (also known in research as PSMA-617), is a small peptide-like molecule that latches onto PSMA, a protein heavily displayed on most prostate cancer cells. The radioactive part is lutetium-177 [1][2]. Novartis sells it as Pluvicto.

It is a cancer treatment for men whose prostate cancer has spread beyond the prostate (metastatic disease). Because it is radioactive, it is given only by staff trained and licensed to handle radiopharmaceuticals, and patients follow radiation safety steps at home for several days after each infusion [2].

sections.heading: How does lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan work?

blocks.text: Once infused, the drug travels through the blood and binds to cells carrying PSMA. Lutetium-177 then decays, giving off beta particles, a form of radiation that travels only a short distance in tissue. That radiation breaks DNA in the cancer cell and in nearby cells, which can kill them [2]. The approach concentrates radiation where the tumors are while sparing much of the rest of the body.

The treatment only works if the tumors carry the target. Before treatment, patients have a PSMA PET scan, an imaging test using a related tracer, to confirm that their cancer lights up for PSMA [2]. In the trials, men qualified only if their tumors took up more tracer than the normal liver [2].

Yes. The FDA approved Pluvicto in March 2022 as a new molecular entity, first for men whose PSMA-positive cancer had progressed after hormone-pathway drugs and taxane chemotherapy [3]. Two efficacy supplements have since widened its use [3].

blocks.text: The current label covers adults with PSMA-positive metastatic prostate cancer in two broad situations [2]. The first is cancer that has stopped responding to an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (a newer hormone-blocking pill such as abiraterone or enzalutamide), either before or after chemotherapy. The second, added in 2026, is metastatic cancer that has not been treated with, or is still responding to, hormone-pathway therapy, where Pluvicto is given together with one of those pills [2].

blocks.text: In VISION, serious adverse events of grade 3 or higher were more common with the drug (52.7% vs 38.0%), but quality of life was not worse [1]. The trial was funded by Endocyte, a Novartis company [1].
Across 1,320 patients in the three trials, the most frequent problems were laboratory changes and symptoms tied to radiation reaching healthy tissue [2]:

items: Low lymphocytes (86%) and low hemoglobin (68%) [2]
Fatigue (51%) [2]
Dry mouth (46%) [2]
Nausea and low neutrophils (35% each), and low platelets (33%) [2]

blocks.text: The label carries warnings for bone marrow suppression, which can be severe, and for kidney damage, so blood counts and kidney function are checked during treatment [2]. It can harm a developing fetus and may cause temporary or permanent infertility [2]. Because patients give off radiation for a time, the label sets out precautions after each dose, such as limiting close contact with others for 2 days and with children and pregnant women for 7 days [2]. Long-term cumulative radiation also adds to lifetime cancer risk [2].

sections.heading: How is it different from Lutathera?

blocks.text: Pluvicto and Lutathera (lutetium Lu 177 dotatate) share the same radioactive payload, lutetium-177, and the same basic idea of a targeting molecule carrying radiation to a tumor. What differs is the target. Lutathera carries a somatostatin analog that binds somatostatin receptors, especially subtype 2, and it was first approved in 2018 for somatostatin receptor-positive neuroendocrine tumors of the gut and pancreas [4]. Pluvicto binds PSMA instead and is used only in prostate cancer [2].

That difference is why each drug is matched to its own target before treatment. A tumor has to carry somatostatin receptors for Lutathera to bind it [4], and has to show PSMA on a PSMA PET scan for Pluvicto [2]. Pairing a diagnostic scan with a treatment built on a related molecule is often called theranostics.

class: GLP-1 and glucagon receptor dual agonist
evidenceNote: Several large randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, pooled in a 2026 meta-analysis of nine trials and 2,292 people. Almost all participants were Chinese, and long-term and heart safety data are still missing.
summary: A weekly injection that acts on GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. Approved in China for weight and diabetes in 2025, not approved in the US.
keyTakeaway: Mazdutide is a weekly injectable peptide that activates two hormone receptors at once: GLP-1, the target of semaglutide, and glucagon. Developed by Eli Lilly with Innovent Biologics, it was approved in China in 2025 for weight management and then for type 2 diabetes. In the GLORY-2 trial, adults on the 9 mg dose lost about 16.7% of body weight over 60 weeks against 1.5% on placebo. It is not FDA-approved, and nearly all trial data come from Chinese adults. Gastrointestinal side effects were the main drawback.

blocks.text: Mazdutide is a synthetic peptide given as a once-weekly injection for obesity and type 2 diabetes. It was developed by Eli Lilly, where it carried the code LY3305677, together with the Chinese company Innovent Biologics, which calls it IBI362 [1].

It belongs to a newer group of weight loss drugs that act on more than one hormone receptor. Mazdutide's two targets are the receptor for GLP-1, the same one semaglutide acts on, and the receptor for glucagon [1][5]. In China it is sold under the brand name Xinermei [1].

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) is a gut hormone that helps regulate appetite and how much people eat, and its receptor is found in brain areas that control hunger [5]. Drugs that activate it lower calorie intake and help the pancreas release insulin, and hold back glucagon, when blood sugar is high [5]. That arm of mazdutide is the same mechanism used by semaglutide.

Glucagon is usually known for raising blood sugar, which makes it an unexpected partner for a diabetes drug. Mazdutide deliberately activates the glucagon receptor as well, and in trials it still lowered HbA1c (a three-month blood sugar average) in people with type 2 diabetes [1][4]. It also improved waist size, blood fats, liver enzymes, and uric acid, changes that fit the interest in pairing the two hormones for metabolic health beyond weight alone [4].

How much the glucagon component adds beyond GLP-1 alone has not been settled by a head-to-head trial against a weight loss drug of similar strength. Against dulaglutide, an older GLP-1 drug, mazdutide lowered both weight and HbA1c more in people with type 2 diabetes [4].

No. Mazdutide has not been approved by the FDA. Its first approval anywhere came in China in June 2025, for long-term weight management alongside diet and exercise in adults with a BMI of 28 or more, or 24 or more with at least one weight-related condition [1]. In September 2025 China added approval for blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes [1].
Mazdutide is also being studied for fatty liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and alcohol use disorder [1]. Anything sold online as mazdutide in the US is not an approved product.

blocks.text: Two phase 3 obesity trials carry most of the weight. GLORY-1 randomized 610 Chinese adults with overweight or obesity to 4 mg, 6 mg, or placebo, and measured its main outcomes at 32 weeks [3]. GLORY-2 tested a higher 9 mg dose in 461 adults with a BMI of 30 or more over 60 weeks, about one in six of whom had type 2 diabetes [2].

blocks.text: GLORY-2 participants were young for an obesity trial, with an average age of 34 and an average starting weight of 94 kg, and about two thirds were women [2]. In that trial the injections were added to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity [2]. GLORY-1 counted every participant in the group they were assigned to, even if they stopped the drug or started another weight treatment, which gives a more conservative estimate than counting only those who stayed on it [3].

Side effects followed the pattern of GLP-1 drugs. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and other gastrointestinal complaints were more common on mazdutide, while serious adverse events and the rate of stopping treatment were similar to comparators [2][4].

The limits are clear. The meta-analysis rated the certainty of the weight loss evidence in people without diabetes as very low, largely because there were few trials and results varied, and it called for longer studies in more diverse populations that also measure heart safety [4]. Nearly all participants so far have been Chinese adults, so results may not carry over directly to other groups.

name: Mecasermin
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2005 for a rare growth disorder, based on pooled data from five studies in 71 children, mostly open-label, in which growth speed nearly tripled in the first year. Long-term follow-up and a European registry have since confirmed the height gains.
summary: A lab-made copy of the growth factor IGF-1, approved for children who stay very short because their bodies cannot respond to growth hormone.
keyTakeaway: Mecasermin is recombinant human IGF-1, the growth factor that growth hormone normally tells the liver to make. Sold as Increlex, it was approved in 2005 for children aged 2 and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, such as Laron syndrome, whose growth hormone works but their bodies cannot respond. In the pooled studies, growth speed rose from 2.8 to 8.0 cm a year in the first year. Low blood sugar is the main risk, reported by 42% of trial children. It is not a substitute for growth hormone and is not approved for adults.

blocks.text: Mecasermin is a recombinant (lab-made) form of human insulin-like growth factor-1, or IGF-1. It is a chain of 70 amino acids with three internal bridges, identical in sequence to the IGF-1 the body makes, and it is produced by E. coli bacteria that carry the human IGF-1 gene [1].

It is sold as Increlex, an injection for children with a rare cause of short stature [1]. It is a different product from IGF-1 LR3 and other modified IGF-1 versions sold online as research chemicals, which are not approved drugs and are covered separately.

Children with growth hormone insensitivity make plenty of growth hormone, but a defect in the hormone's receptor or signaling means their bodies do not respond to it, so IGF-1 stays low and they grow very slowly. Extra growth hormone cannot fix that [2]. Researchers began giving these children recombinant IGF-1 directly, and a collaborative study group followed 76 of them for up to 12 years [2].

blocks.text: Normally, growth hormone binds receptors in the liver and other tissues, which then make IGF-1. IGF-1 in turn activates the type 1 IGF receptor, a close relative of the insulin receptor, on target cells [1]. At the growth plates near the ends of long bones, this drives cartilage cells to divide and then harden into bone, which lengthens the skeleton until the plates fuse after puberty [1].

Mecasermin skips the broken step. Instead of relying on a growth hormone signal the child cannot answer, it supplies IGF-1 directly [1]. Because IGF-1 also lowers blood sugar, by cutting the liver's glucose output and pushing tissues to take up glucose, the drug can cause hypoglycemia, which is why doses are timed around a meal or snack [1]. In children with severe deficiency, the half-life after an injection under the skin was about 5.8 hours [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Increlex on August 30, 2005, and it remains on the market as a prescription product [3]. The current label, revised in July 2025, lists Eton Pharmaceuticals as the manufacturer [1].

The approval is narrow. Severe primary IGF-1 deficiency is defined by a height score and a baseline IGF-1 score both at least three standard deviations below average, with normal or high growth hormone [1]. The label states that mecasermin is not a substitute for growth hormone and is not for IGF-1 deficiency caused by growth hormone deficiency, malnutrition, an underactive thyroid, or long-term steroid treatment [1]. Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in children under 2 [1].

It is prescribed for children aged 2 and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, or with a deletion of the growth hormone gene who have developed antibodies that neutralize growth hormone treatment [1]. Most children in the approval studies had Laron syndrome, the most severe form, caused by defects in the growth hormone receptor gene [1][4].

The FDA pooled five studies, four open-label and one placebo-controlled, covering 71 children who received 0.06 to 0.12 mg/kg twice daily [1]. Before treatment they averaged 6.7 years old, grew 2.8 cm a year, and stood more than six standard deviations below average height [1].

The biggest jump comes in the first year, with smaller gains afterward [2]. The long-term US cohort found the response depended on dose and stayed above baseline for up to eight years [2]. Data from 346 children in a European and US registry confirm that most gain height, and that starting younger predicts a better response [4].

Low blood sugar is the most common problem. In the approval studies, 42% of children had at least one episode, five had severe episodes needing help, and four had seizures or lost consciousness [1]. Episodes were most frequent in the first month and in younger children, and were generally avoided when the child ate within about 20 minutes of the injection [1].

items: Enlarged tonsils in 15%, sometimes needing surgery [1]
Fat lumps at injection sites (lipohypertrophy) and bruising [1]
Ear fluid, ear infections, and hearing changes [1]
Raised pressure inside the skull in three children [1]
Slipped hip growth plate and worsening of existing scoliosis [1]

blocks.text: Cancers have been reported after marketing in children treated with Increlex, mostly in those with genetic conditions that already raise cancer risk or who received higher than recommended doses; whether the drug caused them is unknown [1]. It is not used in children with active cancer or once the growth plates have closed, and because it contains benzyl alcohol it is not recommended for infants [1].

name: Mechano growth factor
evidenceNote: No human trial has ever given MGF to people. The evidence is cell culture and animal work, plus muscle biopsy studies that measured the body's own MGF gene activity, and an industry replication attempt found no effect on muscle cells.
summary: Mechano growth factor is a synthetic peptide from the tail of an IGF-1 variant, studied only in cells and animals and banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: Mechano growth factor (MGF) is the name given both to a muscle-made variant of the IGF-1 gene and to a 24-amino-acid synthetic peptide copied from its tail. Lab studies reported that the peptide made muscle stem cells multiply, but a 2014 attempt by two drug companies could not reproduce the effect, and no one has shown the body actually produces the peptide. It has never been tested in a human trial. It is not FDA-approved, the FDA has placed it in category 3 for compounding, and WADA bans it at all times.

blocks.text: The IGF-1 gene, which encodes the growth hormone partner insulin-like growth factor 1, can be spliced (cut and rejoined) in different ways to produce slightly different messages. One of these variants, called IGF-1Ec in humans and IGF-1Eb in rodents, rises in muscle after mechanical stress such as heavy exercise or injury. Researchers named it mechano growth factor for that reason [1][3].

The product sold today is something narrower. It is a synthetic peptide made of the last 24 amino acids of that variant's E domain, the tail that differs from ordinary IGF-1 [1][5]. Online sellers also offer PEG-MGF, the same peptide with a polyethylene glycol chain attached to slow its breakdown. The name MGF is therefore used for two different things, a gene message in muscle and a lab-made fragment, and studies of one do not automatically apply to the other [5].

The proposed idea is a two-step repair signal. After muscle damage, the MGF version of the gene is switched on early and is linked to activation of satellite cells, the stem cells that sit on muscle fibers and divide to repair them. The standard IGF-1 version rises later, when those cells fuse into mature fibers [5]. On this model, the MGF tail peptide would act as a separate signal telling stem cells to multiply before they fuse.

That model has a gap. A 2010 review noted that no MGF peptide matching the synthetic product has ever been isolated from cells, culture fluid, animal tissue, or body fluids [5]. The gene message clearly exists. Whether the body ever cuts it into the 24-amino-acid peptide that is sold has not been shown.

No. MGF is not an approved drug, and no company has run a clinical trial of it. In the FDA's list of substances nominated for compounding under section 503A, mechano growth factor sits in category 3, the group nominated without adequate supporting information, as of the May 2026 update [6]. Substances in that category get no enforcement discretion, so pharmacies have no basis to compound it.

In sport, the 2026 World Anti-Doping Agency list names mechano growth factors under S2, growth factors and growth factor modulators, prohibited both in and out of competition [7]. Vials sold online as MGF or PEG-MGF are labeled for research use, have no regulatory oversight of content or sterility, and have no safety data in people.
Every piece of evidence comes from cells, animals, or biopsies. None involves giving MGF to a person and measuring what happens.

blocks.text: The 2003 biopsy study is often cited as human evidence, but it measured the body's own gene activity after exercise. It found that older muscle failed to raise MGF in response to loading, which the authors read as an age-related loss of sensitivity to mechanical stress [3]. It says nothing about injecting the synthetic peptide.

Several of the positive studies involved Geoffrey Goldspink, whose laboratory first described MGF [1][3]. The Kandalla study suggested the peptide could help counter age-related muscle loss without the cancer concerns linked to full IGF-1 [1], but that was a hypothesis drawn from cultured cells. When scientists at two pharmaceutical companies tried to repeat the core findings at concentrations up to 500 ng/mL, neither native nor stabilized MGF changed muscle cell growth, fusion, or a signaling marker in heart cells. They concluded that a physiological role for the peptide was in doubt [4].

No human safety data exist. Because the peptide is pitched as an IGF-1 relative, the theoretical concerns that apply to growth factors, such as effects on blood sugar or on tissue growth, cannot be ruled in or out. PEG-MGF has even less published research than the unmodified peptide.

name: Melanotan I
evidenceNote: The molecule has several small randomized human trials for tanning and two randomized trials for a light-sensitivity disease, but all used pharmaceutical-grade material. Injectable vials sold online for cosmetic tanning have never been tested in a trial.
summary: A lab-made tanning hormone. Approved only as afamelanotide implants for a rare light disorder; injectable Melanotan I sold online is unapproved.
keyTakeaway: Melanotan I is a synthetic version of alpha-MSH, the hormone that tells skin cells to make melanin. Under the drug name afamelanotide, it is FDA-approved only as a 16 mg implant, placed by a clinician, for adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, a rare light-sensitivity disorder. In small randomized studies, injections darkened fair skin and cut sunburn damage, raising melanin by about 41% in people who burn easily. Vials sold online as Melanotan I for cosmetic tanning are not approved, are not quality checked, and are a separate thing from the regulated implant.

blocks.text: Melanotan I is a 13 amino acid peptide built to mimic alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), the body's own signal for darkening skin. Two swaps in its sequence, norleucine at position 4 and a mirror-image phenylalanine at position 7, set it apart from the natural hormone [5]. University researchers tested this highly potent version in the 1990s as a way to tan skin without ultraviolet light [1].

The same molecule later became a regulated medicine under the name afamelanotide, sold as Scenesse [5]. The name Melanotan I now mostly refers to powder in vials sold online for cosmetic tanning. That product is not the approved drug, even though the label on the vial may name the same peptide. It should also not be confused with Melanotan II, a different peptide in the same family.

Pigment cells in the skin, called melanocytes, carry a receptor named MC1R (melanocortin 1 receptor). When alpha-MSH or afamelanotide binds it, the cell raises its levels of a messenger molecule called cAMP, which drives the cell to make more melanin, the pigment that colors skin [6]. The result is a tan that develops without sun exposure.

Given as an injection under the skin, the peptide is fully absorbed, but taken by mouth it does not reach the blood at all [2]. In a small three-person study its half-life in the blood was between about 0.8 and 1.7 hours, yet the skin darkening it caused peaked about a week after the last dose and was still visible three weeks later [2]. The approved product gets around the short half-life with a slow-release implant [5].

Not as a tanning product. The only FDA-approved form is Scenesse, a 16 mg afamelanotide implant first approved in 2019 [5]. A healthcare professional inserts it under the skin above the hip every two months, and it is labeled only to increase pain-free light exposure in adults who have had phototoxic reactions from erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), an inherited disorder that makes sunlight painful [5].

No product is approved for cosmetic tanning, and injectable Melanotan I sold online falls outside FDA oversight of drug quality. Laboratory testing of related tanning vials bought from websites found impurities of 4% to 6% and less than the stated amount of peptide, between about 43% and 88% of what the label claimed [7]. The FDA has also flagged the related compound Melanotan II for impurity risks and serious adverse event reports [8].

The early human work was small but controlled. In a 1991 double-blind trial of 28 white men, ten injections over 12 days darkened skin in both poor and good tanners, while no one on saline changed; the color peaked one to three weeks after the course ended [1]. A larger trial of 65 fair-skinned volunteers then tested three 10-day cycles over three months against placebo [3].

rows: Skin darkened in all skin types on the peptide, none on placebo [1]
Melanin up 41% in burn-prone skin; sunburn cells cut by over half [3]
168 adults with EPP in the EU and US
More pain-free sun time, e.g. 69 vs 41 hours over 6 months in the US arm [4]

blocks.text: The 2006 trial found the largest gains in the palest skin, where melanin rose about 41% on average against 12% in people who tan more easily [3]. After a measured dose of UV light, treated volunteers who burn easily had less than half the sunburn cells, and a marker of DNA damage at the base of the outer skin layer fell by 59% [3]. That points to real photoprotection, not just a color change.

The strongest data come from the medical use. Two randomized, placebo-controlled trials of the implant in 168 people with EPP showed longer pain-free time in sunlight, fewer phototoxic reactions in the European study, and better quality of life, with mostly mild side effects [4]. Later testing found no neutralizing antibodies against the drug after long-term use [6].

sections.heading: What are the known side effects?

blocks.text: In the early injection studies, side effects were mostly occasional stomach upset and facial flushing [2]. The approved implant's label lists implant site reactions (21% vs 10% on a dummy implant), nausea (19% vs 14%), and a smaller rise in fatigue, cough, and dizziness [5]. It also warns that the drug darkens existing moles and freckles, and it asks for a full skin check twice a year [5].

That mole effect is the main open question for cosmetic use. A tan from this peptide does not replace sunscreen, and darkened moles can be harder to monitor for changes. None of these safety findings were gathered with unregulated online vials, whose dose and purity cannot be confirmed [7].

name: Melanotan II
evidenceNote: Human data are limited to a three-man pilot study from 1996, a ten-man erection study from 1998, and a growing file of case reports of harm. No trial has tested it for tanning in a controlled way, and no product has ever gone through FDA review.
summary: Melanotan II is an unapproved tanning and libido peptide. Human data are a few tiny 1990s studies plus case reports of new moles, melanoma and priapism.
keyTakeaway: Melanotan II is a lab-made copy of a skin-darkening hormone, first tested in people in the 1990s. In a three-man pilot study it darkened skin after five low injections and caused nausea, yawning and spontaneous erections. That is close to the whole human trial record. It is not FDA-approved, its nomination for compounding was withdrawn, and FDA lists safety concerns including melanoma and priapism in published case reports. Online vials are unregulated. Its relatives are different drugs: afamelanotide (Scenesse) and bremelanotide (Vyleesi) are approved.

blocks.text: Melanotan II, or MT-II, is a synthetic peptide modeled on alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), the hormone that tells pigment cells in the skin to make melanin. It is a short ring-shaped chain of seven amino acids, a design its developers described as far more potent than the natural hormone [1].

It was developed as a possible sunless tanning agent. Early testing showed it also triggers erections, which led to a separate line of research [1][2]. It never became a medicine. Today it circulates as an unlicensed product bought online, mainly by people who want a tan without the sun [3].

Melanocortin receptors are a family of switches that respond to alpha-MSH. The MC1 receptor sits on melanocytes, the skin's pigment cells, and turning it on makes them produce darker melanin. MC3 and MC4 receptors work mainly in the brain, where they influence appetite and sexual function.

Melanotan II is not selective. It activates several of these receptors at once, which is why the same injection can darken skin, reduce appetite, and cause nausea, yawning and erections [1][2]. That spread of effects is the core problem with the molecule: the tanning effect cannot be separated from the others.

Approved drugs in the same family were designed to be more targeted. Afamelanotide acts mainly on MC1, the pigment receptor [7]. Bremelanotide was built for its action on MC4, the receptor tied to sexual desire [8].

No. The FDA has never approved Melanotan II for any use. It was nominated for use by compounding pharmacies and placed in FDA's category of bulk substances that may present significant safety risks; the nomination was later withdrawn by the nominator. FDA's notice points to a risk of immune reactions from impurities and to published case reports of melanoma, a brain swelling syndrome called posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, a stimulant-like toxic reaction, and priapism [6].

Two related peptides did reach approval, which is a common source of confusion. Afamelanotide, once called Melanotan I, was approved in 2019 as a slow-release implant (Scenesse) to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, a rare light-sensitivity disorder [7]. Bremelanotide (Vyleesi) was approved in 2019 for low sexual desire in premenopausal women [8]. Neither approval covers Melanotan II.

The first human study, published in 1996, gave Melanotan II to three healthy men by subcutaneous injection (under the skin) every other day, alternating with saline. Two of them showed darker skin on the face, upper body and buttocks a week after dosing ended. Nausea occurred at most doses, one man had marked drowsiness and fatigue at the highest dose, and the men had spontaneous erections lasting one to five hours, often after bouts of stretching and yawning [1].

A 1998 study tested it in ten men with erectile dysfunction that had no physical cause. In this double-blind crossover design, each man received both drug and placebo on different days. Eight of ten developed visible erections on the drug, and the time spent with firm rigidity averaged 38 minutes versus 3 minutes on placebo. Nausea, yawning and reduced appetite were more common with the drug [2].

rows: Darker skin in 2 of 3; nausea, drowsiness and spontaneous erections [1]
Erections in 8 of 10; 38 vs 3 minutes of firm rigidity [2]

blocks.text: Those thirteen men are the controlled human record. There is no published randomized trial of Melanotan II for tanning, for skin cancer prevention, or for safety over months of use. What has accumulated since is a series of case reports from people using it on their own.

A 40-year-old man with a history of melanoma developed crops of new, atypical moles after injecting a synthetic alpha-MSH product, and his existing moles darkened; they faded after he stopped [3]. A British case described moles erupting after melanotan injections [4]. A 20-year-old woman who combined a few weeks of Melanotan II with sunbed use was diagnosed with melanoma three months later [5]. Case reports cannot prove cause, but they are the reason FDA lists melanoma among its concerns [6].

sections.heading: What about Melanotan II sold online?

blocks.text: Melanotan II is sold online as powder for injection and as nasal sprays, usually labeled for research only. These products are not made under drug-quality standards, so the dose, purity and sterility of any vial are unknown. FDA has flagged peptide-related impurities and aggregation as specific concerns for this molecule [6].

The case literature also shows that the drug's effects on the skin are not limited to an even tan. Changes to existing moles and new atypical ones have been reported, which can make skin checks harder for people at higher risk of melanoma [3][4][5]. Because it acts on the same brain receptors that trigger erections, priapism (a painful erection that will not subside) is another reported harm [6].

name: MK-677 (ibutamoren)
evidenceNote: Several randomized, placebo-controlled trials exist, including a 2-year study in older adults and a 563-person Alzheimer's trial. They show reliable rises in growth hormone, IGF-1, and lean mass, but no gain in strength, function, or disease outcomes, plus a heart failure signal that ended one trial early.
summary: MK-677 is an oral pill that mimics ghrelin to raise growth hormone. It was never approved, the FDA flags safety risks, and it is banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: MK-677, also called ibutamoren, is a small-molecule pill (not a peptide) that copies the hunger hormone ghrelin and makes the pituitary release more growth hormone. Merck tested it in randomized trials: in healthy adults aged 60 to 81 it added about 1.1 kg of lean mass in a year, yet strength and function did not improve, while weight, fasting glucose, and appetite rose. A 563-patient Alzheimer's trial found no benefit, and a hip fracture trial stopped early over heart failure cases. It is not FDA-approved, sits on the FDA's compounding safety-risk list, and is prohibited in sport at all times.

blocks.text: MK-677 is a drug candidate that Merck developed to raise growth hormone with a daily pill. Its generic name is ibutamoren, and the salt used in trials is ibutamoren mesylate [2]. Although it is often sold alongside peptides, it is a small synthetic molecule, which is why it survives digestion and works when swallowed.

Merck studied it in older adults losing muscle, in people recovering from hip fracture, and in Alzheimer's disease [1][2][3]. None of those programs led to an approved product. Today it circulates mainly through online sellers that label it as a research chemical or a supplement, and it is popular with people seeking more muscle, better sleep, or a bigger appetite.

The stomach hormone ghrelin does two jobs: it signals hunger, and it tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. MK-677 binds the same receptor, so it does both. Growth hormone then prompts the liver to make IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1), the messenger behind many of growth hormone's effects on muscle and bone.

In a 2-year trial, a daily 25 mg dose lifted growth hormone and IGF-1 in people over 60 into the range typical of young adults [1]. In the Alzheimer's trial, IGF-1 was about 60% higher at 6 weeks and 73% higher at a year [2]. The same mechanism explains its main side effects: ghrelin drives appetite, and extra growth hormone raises blood sugar and makes the body hold fluid.

No. Ibutamoren has never been approved for any condition, and it is not a lawful dietary supplement, since it was studied as a drug. The FDA places it in Category 2 for both 503A and 503B compounding, meaning the agency considers it a bulk substance that raises significant safety risks. The stated reason is the potential for congestive heart failure in certain patients, drawn from the hip fracture trial that was stopped early [4]. The agency's May 2026 update of the 503A lists still shows ibutamoren mesylate in Category 2 [5].

In sport, the World Anti-Doping Agency lists growth hormone secretagogues and their mimetics under section S2, and names ibutamoren (MK-677) among them. The substance is banned in and out of competition [6].

items.text: Two randomized trials published: a 2-year study in healthy older adults and a 12-month Alzheimer's study [1][2].
Hip fracture trial reported; it was ended early after heart failure cases [3].

blocks.text: Unlike many compounds sold online, MK-677 has genuine randomized human trials. What they show is a gap between lab numbers and real-world benefit. The drug moves hormones and body composition, but the outcomes that matter to people did not follow.

rows: Lean mass up 1.1 kg vs down 0.5 kg on placebo; no change in strength or function [1]
563 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease
IGF-1 rose, but no difference from placebo on any of four clinical scales [2]
123 older adults recovering from hip fracture
Gait speed improved, most function tests did not; stopped early for heart failure cases [3]

blocks.text: In the older-adult trial, body weight climbed 2.7 kg on MK-677 against 0.8 kg on placebo, and limb fat rose more on the drug. Fasting glucose went up by about 5 mg/dL and insulin sensitivity fell. The most common complaints were a surge in appetite that eased after a few months, mild swelling of the lower legs, and muscle pain [1]. Cortisol also rose modestly.

The hip fracture study pushed the safety question further. Patients on the drug had higher IGF-1 and walked somewhat faster, yet showed no improvement on several other performance measures. The investigators halted it after a small number of patients developed congestive heart failure, and concluded the drug had an unfavorable safety profile in that population [3].

No trial has tested MK-677 for the goals it is marketed for online, such as building muscle in young adults, sleep quality, or recovery from training. Those uses are extrapolated from the hormone changes, not demonstrated.

Products sold as MK-677 capsules or liquids are not made under drug manufacturing standards, and no regulator checks what they contain. The trials above used a pharmaceutical-grade compound with medical monitoring of blood sugar and fluid status. People buying online get neither, and the known effects on glucose, insulin sensitivity, and fluid retention are the ones most likely to matter for anyone with diabetes risk or heart disease [1][3]. Athletes in tested sports also face a doping violation regardless of the source [6].

name: Motixafortide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in September 2023 on the strength of GENESIS, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 122 people with multiple myeloma.
summary: Motixafortide (Aphexda) is an injected peptide that releases stem cells from bone marrow so they can be collected for transplant in multiple myeloma.
keyTakeaway: Motixafortide is a synthetic cyclic peptide that blocks CXCR4, the receptor that anchors blood-forming stem cells in bone marrow. Given once with the growth factor filgrastim, it pushes those cells into the bloodstream so they can be harvested before an autologous (own-cell) transplant. In the GENESIS trial, 67.5% of myeloma patients reached the collection target in up to two sessions after one dose, versus 9.5% on placebo. The FDA approved it as Aphexda in 2023. Allergic reactions, including rare anaphylactic shock, require premedication.

blocks.text: Motixafortide is a synthetic peptide of 14 amino acids, several of them unusual building blocks such as citrulline and naphthylalanine, closed into a ring by a disulfide bond. It is sold as Aphexda, a powder that is dissolved and injected under the skin [1].

It has one job: helping people with multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow, give up enough of their own blood-forming stem cells for a transplant. An autologous stem cell transplant, using the patient's own stored cells, improves survival in myeloma, but many people cannot collect enough cells when a growth factor injection is used alone [2].

Stem cells stay in the marrow partly because of a molecular tether. A chemokine called SDF-1 alpha (also known as CXCL12) binds the CXCR4 receptor on stem cells, guiding them home to the marrow and helping hold them to the surrounding matrix [1].

Motixafortide occupies CXCR4 and blocks SDF-1 alpha from binding. With the tether released, stem and progenitor cells spill into the circulating blood, where an apheresis machine can filter them out. White blood cell counts rise at the same time, an effect seen in mice, rats, dogs, and people [1].

It is paired with filgrastim (G-CSF), a growth factor that boosts stem cell production over several days. Filgrastim fills the marrow; motixafortide opens the door. The GENESIS investigators described it as having extended activity in the body, and reported that it preferentially mobilized more primitive stem cells [2].

Yes. The FDA approved Aphexda (NDA 217159) on September 8, 2023, and approved a supplement to the application in March 2026 [3]. The label limits its use to mobilizing stem cells, together with filgrastim, for collection and later autologous transplantation in patients with multiple myeloma [1].

items.text: GENESIS phase 3 results published in Nature Medicine [2].
FDA approves Aphexda for stem cell mobilization in multiple myeloma [3].
FDA approves a supplement to the application; the current label dates from 2026 [1][3].

blocks.text: It is used in transplant centers for adults with multiple myeloma who are preparing for an autologous stem cell transplant. In the trial and on the label, patients first receive filgrastim daily for four days; motixafortide is then injected the evening before the first collection, with a second dose possible before a third collection if the target has not been met [1].

GENESIS enrolled 122 patients at 18 sites in five countries and randomized them 2 to 1 to motixafortide or placebo, both with filgrastim. The goal was to collect at least 6 million CD34+ cells (a marker of stem cells) per kilogram of body weight [2]. The median age was 63, and 70% had already been treated with lenalidomide, a common myeloma drug [1].

rows: Target reached in up to 2 collections
Minimum of 2 million cells/kg in 1 collection

blocks.text: The published paper reports higher figures, 92.5% versus 26.2% for the primary goal [2]; the label's numbers come from a central-laboratory analysis limited to a single dose [1]. Both analyses point the same way. Time to blood count recovery after transplant and the durability of the graft were similar between groups [1].
Reactions at the injection site and allergy-type reactions dominate. Among 92 patients given motixafortide in GENESIS, the most common were [1]:

The most serious risk is anaphylactic shock, which occurred in 0.7% of 407 patients across clinical studies, within 5 to 30 minutes of the dose. Hypersensitivity reactions affected 7.6% of patients in GENESIS. The label calls for premedication before every dose with an antihistamine, an acid-reducing H2 blocker, and a leukotriene blocker, plus a pain reliever for injection site reactions, and for dosing only where emergency treatment is available [1].

Other warnings: it may mobilize leukemia cells and should not be used in leukemia; it raises white blood cell counts, which need monitoring; tumor cells could be released from the marrow and collected with the graft, with unknown consequences; and it can harm a developing fetus [1].

name: MOTS-c
alsoCalled: Mitochondrial open reading frame of the 12S rRNA-c
evidenceNote: The metabolic and exercise benefits come from mouse studies. In people, there are only observational measurements of the body's own MOTS-c and one four-week trial of a modified analog in 20 adults; MOTS-c itself has no published human treatment data.
summary: A 16-amino-acid peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA that improved metabolism in mice. Untested as a treatment in people and banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: MOTS-c is a short peptide made from instructions in the DNA of mitochondria, the cell's energy units. In mice it improved insulin sensitivity, prevented diet-induced weight gain, and extended running capacity in old age. In people, exercise raises the body's own MOTS-c, but no published trial has given MOTS-c itself to humans. It is not FDA-approved. Since October 2026, an interim HHS policy lets 503A pharmacies compound it without enforcement action, which is not an approval. WADA bans it at all times.

blocks.text: MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide encoded not in the main genome in the cell nucleus but in the separate, much smaller set of DNA carried by mitochondria [1][2]. Its name describes where the code sits: a short open reading frame inside the gene for the mitochondrial 12S ribosomal RNA [1].

It was described in 2015 by a team that included Pinchas Cohen, as part of a small family of mitochondrial-derived peptides that also includes humanin [1]. Levels of MOTS-c circulate in the blood and appear to fall with age, which drew interest from longevity researchers [2].

Synthetic MOTS-c is now sold online as an injectable research peptide, often marketed for fat loss, endurance, and healthy aging. Those claims run ahead of the evidence, which in people is close to nonexistent.

The original study found that MOTS-c acts mainly on skeletal muscle. Inside muscle cells it blocks the folate cycle, which slows the production of purines (building blocks of DNA). The resulting change in cell chemistry switches on AMPK, an enzyme that senses low energy and pushes cells to take up glucose and burn fuel [1].

Under metabolic stress, MOTS-c can also move from the cytoplasm into the nucleus and change which nuclear genes are switched on, including genes involved in metabolism and protein quality control [2][4]. That makes it an unusual case of the mitochondria sending instructions back to the nucleus.

Exercise appears to be one natural trigger. In human volunteers, a hard bout of exercise raised MOTS-c in muscle and in the blood, which is why researchers have proposed it as an exercise-sensitive signal [3][4]. Whether regular training changes MOTS-c over the long run is less clear, and studies disagree [3].

No. MOTS-c is not approved for any use. On its compounding safety page, the FDA lists it among bulk peptides whose nominations were withdrawn, and states it had found no human exposure data for MOTS-c by any route and lacked key information on whether it could cause harm [6]. The agency also flagged a possible risk of immune reactions and difficulties in characterizing peptide impurities [6].

That position shifted in late October 2026. After an FDA advisory committee voted in July to back adding six peptides to the 503A bulks list, HHS announced an interim policy under which it will not take enforcement action against 503A compounding pharmacies that make products from MOTS-c, BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, semax, or TB-500 [10][7][8]. FDA's own scientific staff had recommended against adding these peptides [11][8].

The policy is not an approval and does not establish that MOTS-c is safe or effective [10][8]. It requires a patient-specific prescription and quality-tested ingredients, has no fixed end date, and can be revisited if a safety signal appears [10][8]. For athletes, WADA lists MOTS-c as a prohibited metabolic modulator, banned in and out of competition [5].

blocks.text: Most of what is known comes from mice. Injected MOTS-c prevented both the insulin resistance that comes with aging and the weight gain that comes with a high-fat diet [1]. A later study found it improved running performance in young, middle-aged, and old mice, and that treatment started late in life, three times a week, increased physical capacity [4].

rows: Prevented diet-induced obesity and age-related insulin resistance [1]
Better physical performance at all ages tested, including late-life treatment [4]
Natural MOTS-c rose in muscle and blood after hard exercise [3][4]
20 adults with obesity and fatty liver
Liver enzymes and glucose fell versus placebo; liver fat fell similarly in both groups [9]

blocks.text: The only controlled human dosing data come from CB4211, a modified version of MOTS-c developed by CohBar, a company founded by Cohen [9]. In a four-week placebo-controlled study of 20 adults with obesity and fatty liver, it lowered the liver enzyme ALT by about 21% from baseline against 4% on placebo, and glucose by 6% [9]. Liver fat fell by almost the same amount on placebo, body weight showed only a trend, and the results came from a company press release rather than a peer-reviewed paper [9].

CB4211 is not the same molecule as the MOTS-c sold online, so even these small results do not transfer directly. A 2023 review noted that no effective way to use MOTS-c in the clinic had yet been developed [2]. No human study has tested the endurance, fat loss, or anti-aging effects seen in mice.

name: Murepavadin
evidenceNote: Published human data are limited to a phase 1 safety study in healthy men. Both phase 3 pneumonia trials were stopped early over kidney injury before producing efficacy results, and the inhaled program has been discontinued.
summary: Murepavadin is an experimental antibiotic built on a protegrin peptide scaffold to kill Pseudomonas. Phase 3 stopped over kidney injury; it is not approved.
keyTakeaway: Murepavadin is a lab-designed antibiotic modeled on protegrin I, a natural antimicrobial peptide. It kills Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a hospital germ that often resists many drugs, by jamming LptD, a protein the bacterium needs to build its outer membrane. A phase 1 study in healthy men found it well tolerated. But in 2019 its intravenous phase 3 pneumonia trials were halted after 56% of treated patients in one trial developed acute kidney injury, above the 25% to 40% expected. A later inhaled version for cystic fibrosis is listed as discontinued. It is not FDA-approved.

atGlance.value: Not FDA-approved; no active development
