blocks.text: Murepavadin is a synthetic antibiotic designed to treat infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ behind many hospital pneumonias and lung infections in people with cystic fibrosis. It is a peptidomimetic, a molecule shaped like a peptide but built to be more stable and selective. Researchers in Zurich derived it from protegrin I, a natural antimicrobial peptide, through several rounds of chemical optimization [1].

Its unusual feature is how narrow it is. Murepavadin was highly active against Pseudomonas species at very low concentrations but largely inactive against other bacteria [1]. Its developer, Polyphor, described it as the first of a new antibiotic class, the outer membrane protein-targeting antibiotics, and took it into phase 3 for hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia [2][3].

The need it was meant to fill is real. Pseudomonas is naturally hard to treat because few drugs get through its membrane, and multidrug-resistant strains have become more common, especially in intensive care units where patients are on ventilators [2]. A drug that worked against those strains by a new route would have given doctors an option where current antibiotics are failing.

Gram-negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas are wrapped in an outer membrane whose outer layer is made of lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The bacterium has to ferry LPS from inside the cell to that outer surface, and the last step relies on a barrel-shaped protein called LptD. Biochemical and genetic work identified LptD as the target of the original compound, and showed that it kills bacteria without bursting their membranes, unlike most natural antimicrobial peptides [1].

That mechanism matters for drug resistance. Pseudomonas resists many antibiotics because its membrane is hard to cross and it pumps drugs back out. A drug acting on an outer membrane protein at the cell surface sidesteps part of that defense, which is why reviewers saw murepavadin as a promising answer to multidrug-resistant strains [2]. In mice, the lead compound protected against bloodstream infection with Pseudomonas [1].
No. Murepavadin has not been approved by the FDA or any other regulator, and no program is currently moving it toward approval.

items.text: The protegrin-based peptidomimetic family and its LptD target are described in Science [1].
Phase 1 results in healthy men published; intravenous murepavadin is in phase 3 for Pseudomonas pneumonia [2][3].
Polyphor halts enrollment in both phase 3 trials, PRISM-MDR and PRISM-UDR, after a higher than expected rate of acute kidney injury [5].
Both phase 3 trials are terminated, citing safety data review, after enrolling 41 and 2 patients [4].
An inhaled form for cystic fibrosis, partly funded by the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, completes preclinical laboratory studies and is then listed as discontinued [6].

blocks.text: The only full human study in the published record is a phase 1 trial in healthy men. Part A tested single rising doses in 10 groups of 6 men, 4 given murepavadin and 2 given placebo in each group; Part B tested repeated doses in 3 groups. The drug's half-life ranged from about 2.5 to 5.3 hours, its levels rose in proportion to dose, side effects were mild and short-lived, and no dose-limiting toxicity appeared [3].

Healthy volunteers, though, are not critically ill patients. The phase 3 program enrolled people with pneumonia in intensive care, a group already prone to kidney problems. In PRISM-MDR, kidney injury occurred in 56% of patients on murepavadin, while the company had expected 25% to 40% based on published data and the comparison arm [5]. Polyphor and the independent data monitoring committee stopped enrollment, and both trials were then terminated [4][5]. No efficacy results from phase 3 have been published.

rows: Terminated after 41 patients; 56% kidney injury on murepavadin

blocks.text: Moving to an inhaled form was a logical way to put the drug in the lung while keeping blood levels, and kidney exposure, low. The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation's pipeline lists that program as discontinued after preclinical work, with no active development in cystic fibrosis [6].

sections.heading: Why does murepavadin still come up?

blocks.text: Murepavadin remains a reference point for antibiotic research. It showed that a protein on the bacterial surface can be hit selectively by a peptide-like drug, and its LptD target pointed antibiotic research toward the machinery that builds the bacterial outer membrane [1][2]. Its failure was about safety in very sick patients, not about whether it killed bacteria. It is not something that can be obtained or used outside a trial, and no supplier can legitimately sell it for human use.

name: NAD+
evidenceNote: Two randomized, placebo-controlled trials from one Chinese hospital found small gains in heart pumping function after a week of low-dose IV NAD+. No outcome trial has tested IV or injected NAD+ for the anti-aging and wellness uses it is sold for.
summary: A coenzyme every cell uses to make energy, sold as IV drips and injections for aging. Not FDA-approved; human evidence is small heart trials.
keyTakeaway: NAD+ is a coenzyme, a helper molecule found in every living cell, not a peptide. It carries electrons in energy production and feeds enzymes involved in DNA repair, and its levels fall with age. Wellness clinics sell it as IV infusions and injections, but a 2026 systematic review found no outcome trials of IV or injected NAD+ for anti-aging. The best human data are two small Chinese trials in heart patients, where a week of IV NAD+ raised ejection fraction by about 3 points. It is not an FDA-approved drug, and the FDA is still evaluating it for compounding.

blocks.text: NAD+ stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide. It is a coenzyme, a small molecule that enzymes need in order to work, and it is present in every cell [1]. It is built from two nucleotides, the same kind of units that make up DNA and RNA, not from amino acids, so it is not a peptide even though it is often sold alongside peptides.

Interest in NAD+ comes from studies showing that its levels in tissues and cells decline with age, in rodents and in people [1]. That finding has driven sales of NAD+ infusions, injections, and oral precursors such as nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which the body converts into NAD+ [2]. Commercial clinics now offer IV NAD+ despite limited evaluation of its safety and effectiveness [3].

NAD+ has two main jobs. First, it carries electrons in the redox reactions that turn food into usable energy, which places it at the centre of metabolism [1]. Second, it is consumed as fuel by enzymes that do not use it for energy at all: sirtuins, which influence metabolism and how DNA is packaged; PARPs (poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases), which take part in DNA repair; and CD38, another enzyme that consumes it [1].

Because so many processes draw on it, falling NAD+ has been linked in animal studies to age-related problems such as metabolic disease, muscle loss, and cognitive decline, and restoring it reversed some of these in rodents [1][2]. Whether topping it up does the same in older people is the open question [1].

Infused NAD+ does not simply circulate. In a 2019 pilot study, a six-hour IV infusion produced no rise in blood NAD+ or its breakdown products for the first two hours, meaning the body cleared it rapidly and completely at first [4]. Later, NAD+ itself and a breakdown product, methylnicotinamide, appeared in urine [4].
No. NAD+ is not an FDA-approved drug for any condition, and IV or injectable NAD+ has never been through an FDA review for safety or effectiveness.

Its compounding status is unresolved. On the FDA's list of substances nominated for use by 503A compounding pharmacies, updated May 14, 2026, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its reduced form NADH sit in category 1, substances still under evaluation [5]. A separate entry, beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, is in category 3, substances nominated without adequate support [5]. Category 1 placement does not mean the FDA has found NAD+ safe or effective.

The strongest human evidence comes from the heart. A research group at the University of Science and Technology of China ran two randomized, placebo-controlled trials giving 10 mg of IV NAD+ a day for seven days alongside standard care [6][7]. Ejection fraction, the share of blood the left ventricle pumps out with each beat, was the main measure in both.

rows: 180 adults with heart failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy
Ejection fraction 45.4% vs 42.4% at 1 month; 6-month major events 14.6% vs 24.7%, not significant
120 adults after primary angioplasty for STEMI
Ejection fraction 56.3% vs 53.4% at 30 days; no difference in 6-month events
Clinic clients given 500 mg IV daily for 4 days, compared with IV NR
Moderate to severe stomach upset, faster heart rate, and chest pressure during NAD+ infusions

blocks.text: Both heart trials reported gains of about three percentage points in ejection fraction, a modest change in a surrogate measure [6][7]. Neither found a significant difference in deaths, heart attacks, strokes, or hospital stays, and both were single-centre studies too small to settle those questions [6][7].

For anti-aging and wellness, the evidence is missing rather than negative. A 2026 systematic review of 113 studies found that oral NR and NMN reliably raise NAD-related molecules in blood, but their effects on function and health outcomes were mixed and often null, and it found no eligible outcome trials of IV or injected NAD+ for these uses [2]. A retrospective review at a commercial wellness chain found that IV NAD+ often caused stomach symptoms, a racing heart, and chest pressure, so infusions took an average of 97 minutes against 37 for IV NR [3]. The authors of that review were employed by the clinic chain [3].

name: Nafarelin
evidenceNote: Approved in 1990 as a nasal spray, supported by double-blind trials against danazol and leuprolide in endometriosis and by pediatric studies in central precocious puberty.
summary: Nafarelin (Synarel) is a GnRH agonist nasal spray, FDA-approved for endometriosis in adult women and for central precocious puberty in children.
keyTakeaway: Nafarelin is a synthetic version of the brain hormone GnRH, given as a nasal spray and sold by Pfizer as Synarel. Used every day, it switches off the pituitary signals that drive the ovaries and testes, creating a temporary low-estrogen or low-testosterone state. The FDA approved it in 1990 and it treats endometriosis and early puberty. In its pivotal endometriosis trial it shrank disease as well as danazol did without danazol's harmful cholesterol changes, but it reduces bone density, so adult courses are limited to six months.

blocks.text: Nafarelin is a decapeptide (a chain of ten amino acids) designed as a long-lasting, more potent copy of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the hypothalamic signal that controls the reproductive hormones LH and FSH [1][5]. Pfizer sells it as Synarel, a nasal solution containing 2 mg per mL, with each spray delivering about 200 mcg [1].

Most drugs in this class are injected or implanted. Nafarelin is one of the few given through the nose, which avoids needles but means it has to be used every day, and only about 3% of a dose reaches the bloodstream [5].

The pituitary responds to GnRH only when it arrives in pulses. Nafarelin, applied twice a day, keeps the GnRH receptor occupied instead. At first this stimulates the pituitary, so LH, FSH and sex hormones briefly rise; with continued use the pituitary stops responding, and by about four weeks the ovaries or testes produce far less estrogen or testosterone [5].

Endometriosis tissue, which grows outside the uterus, depends on estrogen, so the low-estrogen state shrinks it and eases pain [5]. In children with central precocious puberty, the same shutdown pauses sexual development and slows bone maturation. The effect wears off after stopping: in all 69 children followed for a year after treatment, puberty restarted [5].

Yes. The FDA first approved Synarel on February 13, 1990, and Drugs@FDA lists it as an active prescription product held by Pfizer [4]. The label covers two uses: management of endometriosis, including pain relief and shrinking lesions, in women 18 and older for up to six months; and central precocious puberty in children of both sexes [1].

The six-month limit in endometriosis reflects bone loss. The label says retreatment cannot be advised because no safety data exist for a second course, and that bone density should be checked before any further treatment is considered [1].

For endometriosis, the key trial randomized 213 women with surgically confirmed disease to nasal nafarelin at 400 or 800 mcg a day or oral danazol at 800 mg a day for six months, with matched placebos keeping it double-blind [3]. More than 80% in every group had less disease on repeat laparoscopy (a camera inspection of the pelvis), and the share with severe pain fell from about 40% to between 5% and 10% [3].

rows: Abnormally low HDL cholesterol at end

blocks.text: At the end of six months on 400 mcg a day, 60% of women were symptom free and 32% had only mild symptoms [5]. Relief faded in some: six months after stopping, half of those who had been symptom free still were [5]. A separate trial found the 400 mcg daily spray comparable to monthly injections of leuprolide depot 3.75 mg for endometriosis pain [5].

Central precocious puberty is puberty that begins too early, before about age 8 in girls or 9 in boys, because the brain's GnRH system has switched on ahead of schedule [1]. In trials, LH responses fell to prepubertal levels within a month, breast development stopped or regressed in 82% of girls, and genital development stopped or regressed in all boys [5].

In adult women the side effects are mostly those of low estrogen. In the danazol trial, women on nafarelin more often reported hot flashes and lower libido, while danazol worsened their cholesterol [3]. After six months, bone density in the spine had fallen by an average of 8.7% on one scan method and 3.2% on another, with only partial recovery six months after stopping [2].

items: Ovarian cysts in the first two months, mostly in women with polycystic ovaries [1].
Depression that starts or worsens, and mood swings such as crying, irritability and anger [1].
Seizures, mainly in people with existing risk factors [1].
Rare pituitary apoplexy (sudden bleeding into the pituitary), usually in people with an undiagnosed pituitary tumor [2].
Severe skin reactions and, in children, raised pressure around the brain (pseudotumor cerebri) [1].

blocks.text: In 155 children treated for an average of 41 months, most side effects came in the first six weeks from the drug's initial stimulating effect. Rhinitis affected 5%, hot flashes 3% and vaginal discharge 3%, and about 3% left the trials because of side effects [2]. Nafarelin is contraindicated in pregnancy, and because it does not reliably prevent ovulation, the label calls for non-hormonal contraception during use [1].

name: Nangibotide
evidenceNote: Randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trials exist in septic shock (355 patients) and severe COVID-19 (219 patients), which places it in the moderate tier. The sepsis trial missed its main goal, and the positive signals come from subgroups or a trial stopped early.
summary: An experimental IV peptide that damps the TREM-1 inflammation amplifier in septic shock. Phase 2b missed its main goal; a biomarker-guided phase 3 is planned.
keyTakeaway: Nangibotide is a 12-amino-acid peptide from the French company Inotrem, given by IV infusion in intensive care. It blocks TREM-1, a receptor on immune cells that amplifies inflammation during septic shock. In the 355-patient ASTONISH trial, it did not improve organ failure scores at day 5 in the group it was meant to help. The developer reports benefit in patients with the highest levels of the blood marker sTREM-1 and has agreed a biomarker-selected phase 3 with the FDA. It is not approved anywhere.

atGlance.value: Not approved. Phase 3 (ACCURATE) agreed with the FDA but not yet registered as started.

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Acts as a decoy for the TREM-1 receptor, damping an amplifier of the immune response in sepsis.

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Phase 2b in septic shock missed its main goal; benefit was seen only at high sTREM-1 levels.

blocks.text: Nangibotide is a synthetic peptide of 12 amino acids, developed by Inotrem and earlier called Motrem. Its sequence comes from a natural protein called TREM-like transcript-1 (TLT-1). In animal studies, researchers mostly used LR12, a matching peptide suited to the species being tested [1].

It is being developed for septic shock, the most severe form of sepsis. Sepsis is the body's runaway response to an infection; in septic shock, blood pressure collapses and organs begin to fail despite fluids and drugs to support the circulation. The peptide is given as a continuous infusion into a vein in intensive care, and it breaks down in the blood within minutes once the infusion stops [1][2].

TREM-1 (triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 1) sits on neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages, the white blood cells that respond first to infection. It works alongside the Toll-like receptors that detect bacteria, turning up the strength of the inflammatory response. In septic shock it is among the most strongly activated pathways, and that amplified response is thought to help drive organ damage [1].

Nangibotide acts as a decoy. It mops up the molecule that would normally switch TREM-1 on, so the receptor is activated less, rather than shutting down the immune system entirely [1]. In rodents with abdominal sepsis, the matching peptide lowered inflammatory markers and improved bacterial clearance and survival, and in pigs it reduced the need for drugs to hold up blood pressure [1].

A soluble form of the receptor, sTREM-1, can be measured in the blood and tracks how active the pathway is. It offers a way to pick out the patients whose sepsis runs through this pathway. That idea, testing the drug only where its target is busy, now shapes the whole program [3][6].
No. Nangibotide is not approved by the FDA, the European Medicines Agency, or any other regulator, and there is no legitimate source of it outside clinical trials.

items.text: First study in 27 healthy volunteers finds no safety concerns up to the highest dose and no antibodies against the drug [1].
Phase 2a in 49 septic shock patients finds no excess of side effects; organ failure scores fall more in treated patients, but not significantly [2].
Phase 2b ASTONISH (septic shock) and phase 2 ESSENTIAL (COVID-19) are published [3][4].
Inotrem reports agreement with the FDA on a single phase 3 trial, ACCURATE, of about 1,300 patients selected by high sTREM-1 [5].
Inotrem publishes a biomarker-based analysis of ASTONISH and says the approach is agreed with US, European and Japanese regulators [6].

blocks.text: The planned ACCURATE trial will measure the share of patients alive and off organ support at day 29, using a Roche blood test for sTREM-1 that is meant to become the companion diagnostic [5]. As of late 2026, ClinicalTrials.gov lists no phase 3 study of nangibotide; the registered studies are the earlier phase 1 and phase 2 trials [7].

The key trial is ASTONISH, a randomized, double-blind phase 2b study in 355 adults with septic shock across 42 hospitals in seven countries. Patients received a low or high dose of nangibotide or placebo, started within 24 hours of needing blood pressure drugs. The main goal was a bigger drop in SOFA score, a 24-point measure of organ failure, by day 5 in patients with sTREM-1 of at least 400 pg/mL [3].

rows: Main goal missed: no significant SOFA difference at day 5 in either the high-sTREM-1 group or overall
219 adults with COVID-19 on breathing support
Deaths by day 28: 16% vs 28% on placebo; trial stopped early for slow recruitment
Septic shock patients with the highest sTREM-1
SOFA score 2.5 points better than placebo by day 5, as reported by Inotrem

blocks.text: Read plainly, ASTONISH did not show that nangibotide helps the population it was designed for, and the low-dose group had numerically more deaths, though the trial was not powered to judge survival [3]. What it did find was a pattern: the higher a patient's starting sTREM-1, from about 532 pg/mL upward, the more the high dose seemed to improve organ scores. A pattern discovered after the fact, at a cutoff chosen from the data, is a hypothesis to test, and that is exactly what the phase 3 is for [3][5].

Safety so far looks unremarkable. In ASTONISH, adverse events affected about 95% of patients in every group, which is expected in septic shock, and serious adverse events were similar between treated and placebo patients [3]. The COVID-19 result is encouraging but rests on a trial that ended early with 219 patients, so its size limits how much weight it can carry [4].

name: Nesiritide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2001 after randomized trials showed faster relief of breathlessness and lower heart filling pressures. A 7,141-patient outcome trial later found no effect on death or readmission, and the brand is now discontinued in the US.
summary: Nesiritide (Natrecor) is a recombinant version of BNP, a heart hormone, once infused in hospital for acute heart failure. It is now discontinued in the US.
keyTakeaway: Nesiritide is BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) produced by recombinant technology. BNP is a hormone the heart uses to relax blood vessels and shed fluid. The FDA approved it as Natrecor in 2001 as an IV drip for people hospitalized with acutely decompensated heart failure. It lowered heart filling pressures faster than nitroglycerin, but pooled data raised safety questions, and the 7,141-patient ASCEND-HF trial found no effect on death or rehospitalization, only a small effect on breathlessness and more low blood pressure. Drugs@FDA now lists Natrecor as discontinued.

blocks.text: Nesiritide is a laboratory-made (recombinant) version of human B-type natriuretic peptide, or BNP [5]. BNP is one of the heart's own hormones. Its name comes from natriuresis, the loss of sodium in urine, which is one of the effects that helps the body get rid of excess fluid.

It was sold by Scios under the brand Natrecor, as a powder in 1.5 mg vials for intravenous use [1]. It was meant for one situation: people admitted to hospital with acutely decompensated heart failure, meaning a sudden worsening in which fluid backs up and breathing becomes hard even at rest [2].

Nesiritide was the first drug in a new class designed for acute heart failure and was well received at launch. Meta-analyses suggesting more deaths and kidney problems appeared four to five years later, and an expert panel issued new guidance on its use [7].
In practice its use spread beyond the hospital ward. A 2009 review describes it being given as repeated outpatient infusions and around the time of surgery, as well as in single hospital courses [7].

items.text: FDA approves Natrecor (NDA 020920) [1]
The VMAC trial in 489 hospitalized patients is published in JAMA [2]
A pooled analysis in JAMA suggests a possible rise in 30-day deaths [3]
ASCEND-HF, with 7,141 patients, finds no effect on death or rehospitalization [4]
Drugs@FDA lists Natrecor as discontinued [1]

blocks.text: Nesiritide acts as a balanced vasodilator, relaxing both the arteries and the veins, and it also dampens the hormone systems that make the body hold on to salt and water [6]. Some researchers describe heart failure as a state in which the body has too little BNP or responds poorly to it, which was part of the rationale for giving more [6].

The practical effect is lower pressure inside the heart. In the VMAC trial, three hours of nesiritide reduced pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, a catheter measure of how congested the heart and lungs are, by an average of 5.8 mm Hg, compared with 3.8 mm Hg for nitroglycerin and 2 mm Hg for placebo [2].

Yes, but it is no longer sold in the US. The FDA approved Natrecor on August 10, 2001, under new drug application 020920, and the label was last updated in January 2019. Drugs@FDA now lists the product's marketing status as discontinued [1].
The approved use was early relief of shortness of breath in acute heart failure [4]. The FDA record does not give a reason for the discontinuation [1].

Nesiritide was given as an intravenous infusion to hospitalized adults with acutely decompensated heart failure who were short of breath at rest [2]. Two large randomized trials define what it does and does not do:

rows: 489 inpatients; nesiritide vs nitroglycerin vs placebo, added to standard care
Lower wedge pressure than either comparator at 3 hours; less breathlessness than placebo but not than nitroglycerin [2]
7,141 inpatients; nesiritide vs placebo for 24 to 168 hours
Death or heart failure readmission at 30 days 9.4% vs 10.1% (not significant); breathlessness gains too small to meet the trial's threshold [4]

blocks.text: VMAC's 24-hour results were more modest. Wedge pressure had fallen by 8.2 mm Hg on nesiritide against 6.3 mm Hg on nitroglycerin, yet patients reported no significant difference in breathlessness between the two drugs and only a small gain in overall clinical status [2].

In ASCEND-HF, the share of patients reporting moderately or markedly better breathing at 24 hours was 68.2% on nesiritide and 66.1% on placebo [4]. The investigators concluded that the drug could not be recommended for routine use across the broad population of people with acute heart failure [4]. A 2015 review still described a role as add-on therapy for patients who remain symptomatic despite optimal IV diuretics [5].

The clearest adverse effect is low blood pressure. ASCEND-HF found more hypotension with nesiritide than with placebo [4]. Because the drug relaxes blood vessels, the effect follows directly from how it works.

Two other concerns shaped its reputation. A 2005 pooled analysis of three randomized trials found that 7.2% of patients given nesiritide died within 30 days, compared with 4.0% on control therapy, a difference that fell just short of statistical significance [3]. Earlier meta-analyses had also raised the possibility of kidney harm [4]. ASCEND-HF, designed partly to settle both questions, found no difference in death at 30 days (3.6% vs 4.0%) and no significant difference in worsening kidney function (31.4% vs 29.5%) [4].
The original label also cautioned that nesiritide binds heparin, so it was not to be infused through heparin-coated central catheters [8].

name: NNZ-2591
alsoCalled: cyclo-L-glycyl-L-2-allylproline; an analog of cyclic glycine-proline
evidenceNote: The human efficacy data are small open-label phase 2 studies in children with rare genetic syndromes, with no placebo group. A randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial began in late 2025 and has not reported.
summary: NNZ-2591 is an oral, investigational analog of an IGF-1 breakdown product, in phase 3 testing for Phelan-McDermid syndrome. It is not approved.
keyTakeaway: NNZ-2591 is an oral drug candidate from Neuren Pharmaceuticals, modeled on cyclic glycine-proline, a small molecule the body makes when it breaks down IGF-1. In an open-label trial of 18 children with Phelan-McDermid syndrome, clinicians rated 16 of them improved after 13 weeks, but there was no placebo group, so expectation effects cannot be ruled out. A 160-child placebo-controlled phase 3 trial started in November 2025. NNZ-2591 is not FDA-approved, is not sold as a medicine, and as an unapproved substance it falls under WADA's S0 ban.

blocks.text: NNZ-2591 is a small ring-shaped molecule (a diketopiperazine) made of two amino acids, glycine and a modified proline. It is a synthetic relative of cyclic glycine-proline (cGP), which forms naturally when insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is broken down. The natural compound was altered to improve its bioavailability, and in rats the modified version stayed stable in blood and reached the brain [3].

Neuren Pharmaceuticals is developing it as a medicine taken by mouth for rare genetic conditions that affect brain development [1][5]. The lead target is Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS), a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder for which no treatment is approved [1]. Unlike many peptides on this site, it is not marketed as a wellness product; the only human use on record is inside registered clinical trials [1][5][6][7].

The idea starts with IGF-1, a growth factor that protects brain tissue in animal studies. Using IGF-1 itself as a brain drug is hard: it is a large protein, enters the brain poorly, and can spur cell growth elsewhere [4]. The researchers who first studied cGP propose that it helps regulate how much IGF-1 is available to act, and that small, stable analogs could deliver some of IGF-1's protective effects without those drawbacks [4].

In rats, NNZ-2591 crossed the blood-brain barrier after an injection under the skin, reduced brain damage after an injury that cut off blood and oxygen supply, and improved movement and sensation over the following weeks [3]. How it might act in genetic syndromes such as PMS has not been established in people; the rationale comes from animal work and from the proposed link to IGF-1 signaling [4].

No. NNZ-2591 is an investigational drug and is available only inside clinical trials. A randomized, quadruple-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in children aged 3 to 12 with PMS started in November 2025 and plans to enroll about 160 participants. Its two primary measures are a PMS-specific clinician rating of change and the receptive communication score on the Vineland-3 scale of daily skills, with primary completion estimated for October 2027 [5]. An open-label extension for children who finish that trial is also recruiting [8].
In sport, any substance with no current approval by any government health regulator for human use falls under class S0 of the WADA Prohibited List and is banned at all times [9].

The only peer-reviewed human efficacy results come from an open-label phase 2 trial in PMS. Eighteen children aged 3 to 12 took NNZ-2591 by mouth twice daily for 13 weeks, with the dose raised over the first six weeks. Safety and drug levels were the main goals; 14 symptom measures were secondary [1].

rows: 16 of 18 children rated improved; mean score 2.4, where lower is better [1]

blocks.text: These numbers need careful reading. Without a placebo group, improvement can reflect natural change, extra attention from study visits, and the hopes of families and clinicians, especially on ratings of global impression. Children with higher drug exposure tended to improve more, which is encouraging but also unconfirmed [1]. The journal later issued a correction to the paper [2].

Neuren also ran open-label phase 2 studies in Pitt Hopkins syndrome and Angelman syndrome, both completed in 2024, again without placebo groups [6][7]. A planned study in Prader-Willi syndrome was withdrawn before enrolling anyone [10]. The placebo-controlled phase 3 trial will be the first real test of whether the effects seen so far hold up [5].

name: Nonapeptide-1
evidenceNote: Its activity has been shown only in receptor assays, cultured skin cells, and formulation experiments. No controlled study of nonapeptide-1 in people has been published in a peer-reviewed journal.
summary: Nonapeptide-1 is a lab-made α-MSH blocker used in skin brightening products. It reduced melanin in cultured cells but lacks published human trials.
keyTakeaway: Nonapeptide-1, also traded as Melanostatine 5, is a lab-made chain of nine amino acids that blocks the receptor α-MSH uses to tell pigment cells to make melanin. It was discovered in a 1994 screen of more than 31,000 peptides, where it blocked the receptor at nanomolar strength. In cultured human pigment cells it cut melanin and the enzymes that make it. No published, controlled human trial shows it fades dark spots. As a cosmetic ingredient it needs no FDA approval, but a product claiming to reduce melanin production is legally a drug.

atGlance.value: Cosmetic ingredient; not reviewed or approved by the FDA

blocks.text: Nonapeptide-1 is the cosmetic ingredient name (INCI name) for a synthetic peptide of nine amino acids: Met-Pro-D-Phe-Arg-D-Trp-Phe-Lys-Pro-Val, with an amide cap on the end. Two of its building blocks, the phenylalanine in position 3 and the tryptophan in position 5, are D-amino acids, the mirror-image forms of the usual building blocks. It is also sold under the trade name Melanostatine 5 [2].

Its sequence is modeled on part of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), the skin's main signal for producing melanin, the pigment that gives skin its color. PubChem catalogs it as a modified version of α-MSH positions 5 to 13 [2]. By resembling the natural hormone closely enough to occupy its receptor without switching it on, nonapeptide-1 acts as a blocker.
Skin care brands add it to serums and creams sold for dark spots and uneven tone. It is studied and sold as a topical ingredient only; it is not a medicine [5].

The peptide was first described in a 1994 study searching for compounds that could block the α-MSH receptor. The researchers built a library of 31,360 peptides based on the α-MSH(5-13) sequence and screened about 40% of them. The most potent blocker they found had exactly the sequence now sold as nonapeptide-1, with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of about 11 nanomolar, meaning very small amounts were enough to blunt the receptor's response [1].

That study was basic pharmacology, aimed at understanding which parts of α-MSH matter. It found that the D-tryptophan and the phenylalanine beside it were crucial to the peptide's blocking action, and that the D-phenylalanine near the front made it more potent [1]. The cosmetic industry later adopted the molecule as a pigment-control ingredient, and it now carries an official cosmetic ingredient name [2].

When skin is exposed to ultraviolet light, keratinocytes (the main cells of the outer skin) release α-MSH. The hormone binds to melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) on melanocytes, the pigment cells, which raises cyclic AMP inside them and switches on MITF, a master regulator of the genes for tyrosinase and other melanin-making enzymes [3].

Nonapeptide-1 competes with α-MSH for MC1R. In a 2022 study of UVA-exposed human keratinocytes and melanocytes, adding nonapeptide-1 lowered melanin content, tyrosinase activity, and levels of MITF and related proteins, and it reduced MC1R levels too. It did not change how much α-MSH the cells made, which fits a receptor blocker rather than a hormone suppressor [3].

A 2024 formulation study attached nonapeptide-1 to silica nanoparticles carrying the green tea antioxidant EGCG, describing the peptide as interfering with melanin transfer and reducing melanin in treated skin [4]. That work tested a combined product, so it cannot isolate how much the peptide itself contributed.

No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. In the United States, cosmetic products and their ingredients, other than color additives, generally reach the market without FDA approval [5]. The FDA has not evaluated whether nonapeptide-1 is effective.

There is a catch in how products are worded. The FDA defines a product by its intended use, and it specifically lists claims to increase or decrease the production of melanin in the skin as drug claims, even when the product is sold as a cosmetic [5]. A cream marketed with nonapeptide-1 can describe a brighter or more even look, but a label promising to block or reduce melanin production would make it an unapproved drug.

blocks.text: The lab data make the mechanism plausible. What is missing is the step that matters to anyone using it: evidence that enough intact peptide penetrates human skin from a cream to block MC1R on melanocytes, and that this produces a visible change compared with an identical product without it. Cell studies apply the peptide directly to bare cells in a dish, which skips the skin barrier entirely.
Commercial brightening products usually combine several active ingredients, so any results reported for a finished product cannot be credited to nonapeptide-1 alone.

No published study has measured irritation or allergy rates for nonapeptide-1 in people. As with any topical ingredient, a product containing it can cause irritation or contact allergy, either from the peptide or from other ingredients in the formula.

Cosmetic ingredients are not reviewed by the FDA before they are sold [5], so no regulator has assessed nonapeptide-1's safety for long-term use on the face. The cell studies used the peptide on bare cells for a few days, which says little about years of daily application [3].

name: Octreotide
evidenceNote: FDA-approved since the late 1980s in injectable, monthly depot and oral capsule forms for acromegaly and hormone-secreting tumors. A placebo-controlled trial (PROMID) also showed slower tumor growth, a use not on the US label.
summary: Octreotide is a long-acting copy of somatostatin that switches off excess hormone release, used for acromegaly and diarrhea from neuroendocrine tumors.
keyTakeaway: Octreotide is an eight-amino-acid ring peptide built to act like somatostatin, the body's general brake on hormone release, but for hours rather than minutes. It is FDA-approved as Sandostatin injection, Sandostatin LAR monthly depot and Mycapssa oral capsules for acromegaly, and the injectable forms also treat severe diarrhea and flushing from carcinoid and VIP-secreting tumors. In the PROMID trial, the monthly depot extended median time to tumor progression in midgut tumors to 14.3 months, against 6 months on placebo. Gallstones and sludge are the most frequent problem with long-term use.

blocks.text: Octreotide is a cyclic octapeptide, a chain of eight amino acids closed into a ring by a sulfur bridge, designed to mimic the natural hormone somatostatin [1]. Somatostatin acts as a brake on many glands at once, but it breaks down in one to three minutes. Octreotide does the same job with a plasma half-life of about 1.7 to 1.9 hours, long enough to be useful as a drug [1].

Novartis markets it as Sandostatin, a short-acting injection, and Sandostatin LAR Depot, a monthly injection into the buttock muscle [1][2]. Mycapssa, sold by Chiesi, puts octreotide into delayed-release capsules taken by mouth [3]. Generic injectable octreotide is also available.

Octreotide binds somatostatin receptors on hormone-producing cells and turns down their output. According to its label, it suppresses growth hormone, glucagon and insulin even more strongly than somatostatin itself. It also lowers the release of serotonin, gastrin, vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), secretin, motilin and pancreatic polypeptide, dampens the pituitary's response to GnRH, and reduces blood flow to the gut [1].

Those effects map onto its uses. In acromegaly, a pituitary tumor makes too much growth hormone, and lowering it brings down IGF-1, the hormone that drives much of the overgrowth. Carcinoid tumors release serotonin and other substances that cause flushing and diarrhea, and VIP-secreting tumors cause large-volume watery diarrhea; suppressing those secretions controls the symptoms [1].

The forms differ mainly in how long one dose lasts. The short-acting injection is absorbed quickly and completely from under the skin, reaching peak blood levels in well under an hour [1]. The LAR depot is a suspension that a healthcare provider mixes and injects into the gluteal muscle every four weeks, and its label limits it to people already known to respond to and tolerate the short-acting injection [2]. The capsules are enteric-coated, meaning they pass the stomach intact before releasing the drug [3].

Yes. Sandostatin injection is approved to lower growth hormone and IGF-1 in acromegaly when surgery, radiation and bromocriptine have not worked or cannot be used, and to treat symptoms of metastatic carcinoid tumors and VIP-secreting tumors [1]. Sandostatin LAR Depot covers the same three uses for people who have already responded to and tolerated the short-acting injection [2]. Mycapssa is approved for long-term maintenance in acromegaly for people who have responded to octreotide or lanreotide injections [3].

The Sandostatin label states plainly that its own trials did not show shrinkage or slower growth of tumors, adding that those trials were not designed to detect such effects [1]. The PROMID trial described below later tested that question directly.

items: Acromegaly, to bring growth hormone and IGF-1 levels down [1]
Severe diarrhea and flushing episodes caused by metastatic carcinoid tumors [1]
Profuse watery diarrhea caused by VIP-secreting tumors (VIPomas) [1]
Long-term acromegaly maintenance by mouth, with Mycapssa, after a response to injections [3]

blocks.text: The PROMID trial asked whether octreotide could also slow tumor growth. It randomized 85 previously untreated patients with well-differentiated metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumors to monthly 30 mg octreotide LAR or placebo. Median time to tumor progression was 14.3 months on octreotide and 6 months on placebo, a hazard ratio of 0.34. After 6 months, disease was stable in 66.7% on octreotide against 37.2% on placebo. Too few deaths had occurred to draw conclusions about survival [4].
The oral form needs careful timing. The Mycapssa label directs that capsules be swallowed with water on an empty stomach, at least an hour before or two hours after a meal [3].

Gallbladder problems are the most common issue with long-term use. In clinical trials of the injection, mainly in people with acromegaly or psoriasis, 63% developed biliary tract abnormalities: 27% gallstones, 24% sludge without stones and 12% widened bile ducts [1].

In acromegaly, other reactions seen in more than 10% of patients included slow heart rate, diarrhea, loose stools, nausea, abdominal discomfort, high blood sugar and an underactive thyroid [1]. The label also warns of low blood sugar, heart conduction problems (including complete heart block with high intravenous doses during surgery), fatty stools from poor fat absorption, and lower vitamin B12 levels with long use [1]. The oral capsules carry the same set of warnings [3].

name: Oligopeptide-1
evidenceNote: Recombinant EGF has randomized evidence for healing diabetic foot ulcers, but its cosmetic use rests on small pilot and open-label studies, mostly without a placebo group. A 2021 systematic review judged the aesthetic evidence insufficient to establish efficacy.
summary: Oligopeptide-1 is what skincare labels call lab-made human epidermal growth factor (EGF), used in anti-aging serums. Skin evidence is small and early.
keyTakeaway: Oligopeptide-1 is the label name for recombinant human epidermal growth factor (EGF), a natural signal protein that tells skin cells to divide. It appears in serums sold for wrinkles, texture, and recovery after procedures. Randomized trials show recombinant EGF helps diabetic foot ulcers heal, but the cosmetic data are small: pilot studies of 6 to 29 people, mostly without a placebo. It is sold as a cosmetic, which needs no FDA approval, and any claim that it regenerates skin would make it an unapproved drug. EGF's link to cell growth is the reason long-term safety deserves more study.

blocks.text: Oligopeptide-1 is the name used on skincare labels for epidermal growth factor (EGF) made by genetic engineering. EGF is a small protein the body makes to signal skin and other surface cells to multiply. Stanley Cohen found it while studying mouse salivary gland extract, which made newborn mice open their eyes and grow teeth early, and he shared the 1986 Nobel Prize for the discovery [1].

Cosmetic EGF is made by engineered organisms rather than extracted from people. One open-label study, for example, used an EGF-like protein grown in barley [5]. A 2026 pilot study used the name oligopeptide-1 for its recombinant EGF serum and compared it against a serum built from human-derived growth factors [4].

EGF works by docking onto the EGF receptor on the surface of target cells. The receptor then adds phosphate groups to tyrosine building blocks on its own inner tail, a step that relays the signal into the cell and switches on protein production, DNA copying, and cell division [1]. In skin, that drives the outer layer (epidermis) to renew and helps wounds close. EGF also stimulates fibroblasts, the cells that make collagen in the deeper skin layer [1].

The open question for cosmetics is delivery. EGF is a protein, and the outer layer of healthy skin is a barrier to large molecules, so the studies on intact facial skin are the weakest part of the evidence. Its benefit is clearest where the barrier is broken, in wounds [3], and clinics also use it on freshly treated skin: one split-face study included an EGF gel in the standard aftercare for fractional CO2 laser [9].

No. EGF is sold in the United States as a cosmetic ingredient, and cosmetics do not need FDA approval before they go on sale [2]. The line between cosmetic and drug depends on the claims made. A product sold to improve appearance is a cosmetic, but one claimed to regenerate cells or change the structure or function of the body is legally a drug, which would require approval [2]. That is why EGF serums tend to promise smoother-looking skin rather than repair.

Recombinant EGF has been tested as a medicine, mainly for slow-healing wounds such as diabetic foot ulcers, in randomized trials [7]. Those are drug uses with drug-level evidence, and they say little about what a cosmetic serum does on intact facial skin.

For wounds, the evidence is fairly solid. A 2020 meta-analysis of nine randomized trials with 720 participants found that recombinant EGF nearly tripled the odds of complete healing of diabetic foot ulcers compared with placebo (odds ratio 2.79) and shortened healing by about 14 days, with no difference in side effects [7].
For skin aging, the studies are small and mostly uncontrolled.

EGF serum under the eyes, 12 weeks
Under-eye hollowness scores fell from 2.06 to 1.63 on average [6]
EGF for thin, easily bruised skin, 6 weeks
Skin thickened on ultrasound; bruise spots fell from about 15 to 2 [8]

Recombinant EGF rated better for texture and firmness; wrinkle scores barely moved in either group [4]

blocks.text: None of these compared EGF with a plain serum, so they cannot separate EGF from moisturizer, sunscreen, and the expectation of improvement. A 2021 systematic review of 49 articles concluded that most aesthetic studies point toward benefit but are not rigorous enough to establish that it works [3]. The 2026 pilot's own authors called its results exploratory and limited by its small, all-female sample [4].

In the published studies, topical EGF was well tolerated, and the adverse effects reported were transient [3][5]. The bigger question is theoretical. The EGF receptor belongs to a family of growth signals linked to cancer biology: one cancer-causing viral gene codes for a protein that closely resembles the receptor [1]. No study has linked cosmetic EGF to skin cancer, but the trials above ran for weeks to a few months, far too short to judge long-term risk [3][4].

name: Orforglipron
evidenceNote: Orforglipron was approved by the FDA in April 2026 on the strength of two 72-week phase 3 trials involving more than 4,700 adults, with further phase 3 work in type 2 diabetes published.
summary: Orforglipron (Foundayo) is a once-daily GLP-1 pill for weight management, FDA-approved in April 2026, that can be taken with or without food.
keyTakeaway: Orforglipron is a once-daily tablet that activates the GLP-1 receptor, the same target as semaglutide, but it is a small chemical molecule rather than a peptide. In the 72-week ATTAIN-1 trial, adults with obesity on the top dose lost an average of 11.2% of body weight, against 2.1% on placebo. The FDA approved it as Foundayo on April 1, 2026 for chronic weight management, 50 days after filing. Unlike oral semaglutide, it carries no fasting or water rules. It is not yet approved for type 2 diabetes, and online research versions are not the approved product.

blocks.text: Orforglipron is a weight management drug developed by Eli Lilly under the code LY3502970 and sold as Foundayo. It belongs to the GLP-1 receptor agonist family that includes semaglutide and liraglutide, but it differs from them in one basic way: it is not a peptide. It is a small synthetic molecule with a calcium salt, built to survive digestion and be absorbed as a tablet [2][3].

That design matters for how it is taken. Peptide GLP-1 drugs are mostly injected, and the one existing peptide tablet, oral semaglutide, has to be swallowed on an empty stomach with a small sip of water and a wait before eating. Foundayo's label lets it be taken once a day at any time, with or without food [2]. It sits in this library as an exception to the peptide rule because it reaches the same receptor as the GLP-1 peptides.

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) is a hormone the gut releases after a meal. It signals fullness to the brain, prompts insulin release when blood sugar is high, and slows stomach emptying. Orforglipron binds and activates the human GLP-1 receptor, and in animal studies it reached neurons in brain areas that govern appetite and food intake [2].

People taking it eat less, and the label reports that more of the weight lost is fat than lean tissue. The slowing of stomach emptying is strongest after the first dose and fades over time [2]. One quirk: orforglipron does not activate the rat or mouse GLP-1 receptor, so the thyroid tumor findings seen with other GLP-1 drugs in rodents could not be tested the usual way. The label still carries the class boxed warning for that reason [2].

Yes. The FDA approved Foundayo on April 1, 2026, for long-term weight reduction alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity in adults with obesity, or adults with overweight and at least one weight-related condition [1]. It was the first new molecular entity cleared under the Commissioner's National Priority Voucher program, which aims for decisions within about two months.

items.text: Phase 2 results in 272 adults with obesity show weight loss of 9.4% to 14.7% at 36 weeks across doses [5].
Phase 3 results published for early type 2 diabetes (ACHIEVE-1) and for obesity without diabetes (ATTAIN-1) [3][4].
FDA approves Foundayo for chronic weight management 50 days after filing, 294 days ahead of its original review goal date [1].
Lilly reports filings for weight management or type 2 diabetes in more than 40 countries [6].

blocks.text: Type 2 diabetes is not an approved use in the United States as of the August 2026 label, though orforglipron is still being studied for it [2][6]. Powders and capsules sold online as research orforglipron are not Foundayo, and the FDA has not checked them for identity, purity, or dose.

Foundayo is prescribed for weight management in adults with a body mass index of 30 or more, or 27 or more with a condition such as high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, or sleep apnea. The dose is raised step by step over several months to limit stomach side effects, and the label advises against combining it with any other GLP-1 drug [2].

rows: 3,127 adults with obesity or overweight, no diabetes
Weight down 7.5%, 8.4%, and 11.2% at the three trial doses, against 2.1% on placebo [3]
1,613 adults with type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 27 or more

blocks.text: In ATTAIN-1, 54.6% of people on the highest trial dose lost at least a tenth of their weight and 18.4% lost at least a fifth, compared with 12.9% and 2.8% on placebo [3]. The trial doses (6, 12, and 36 mg) were given in an investigational formulation; the label expresses them as equivalent strengths of the marketed tablet [2].

The side effect pattern matches the GLP-1 class, with the digestive tract taking most of it. In the pooled 72-week weight trials, 60% to 69% of people on Foundayo reported a gastrointestinal effect, compared with 37% on placebo, and up to 6% stopped for that reason [2].

items: Nausea in 26 to 35% of people, depending on dose, against 10% on placebo [2].
Constipation in 20 to 27%, diarrhea in 21 to 25%, and vomiting in 13 to 24% [2].
Indigestion, stomach pain, bloating, burping, headache, tiredness, and hair loss [2].

Serious but less common: pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, kidney injury from fluid loss, allergic reactions, worsening diabetic eye disease, and low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas [1][2].

blocks.text: Because the liver enzyme CYP3A4 clears orforglipron, strong inhibitors of that enzyme raise blood levels, and the label caps the dose when they are used together [2]. The drug is not used in people who have had medullary thyroid cancer, whose relatives have had it, or who have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 [1].

name: Oxytocin
evidenceNote: Synthetic oxytocin injection (Pitocin and generics) is FDA-approved for inducing or strengthening labor and for controlling bleeding after birth. Uses outside the delivery room, such as nasal sprays for social or mood effects, are not approved, and the largest trial in autism found no benefit.
summary: Oxytocin is a nine-amino-acid hormone given by hospital IV to start or strengthen labor and to limit bleeding after birth. Nasal sprays are unapproved.
keyTakeaway: Oxytocin is the pituitary hormone that drives uterine contractions and milk let-down. Its synthetic form, Pitocin and generic versions, is an FDA-approved injection used in hospitals to bring on or speed up labor and to limit blood loss once the baby is born. The label carries a boxed warning against elective induction and requires continuous monitoring, because overstimulation can harm mother and baby. A 290-child trial of nasal oxytocin for autism found no improvement over placebo. Nasal sprays marketed for bonding, mood, or sex are not approved products.

blocks.text: Oxytocin is a nonapeptide, a chain of nine amino acids closed into a ring by a bond between two sulfur atoms. The hypothalamus makes it and the posterior pituitary gland releases it into the blood. Its best known jobs are tightening the muscle of the uterus during labor and pushing milk out during breastfeeding [2].

As a medicine, oxytocin is made synthetically, which keeps it free of vasopressin and other pituitary proteins that contaminated older animal extracts. The brand Pitocin contains 10 units per milliliter and is given only by injection [1]. Generic oxytocin injections are also sold in the United States.

Oxytocin holds a place in chemistry history. Vincent du Vigneaud worked out the structure of the posterior pituitary hormones and then built oxytocin from its amino acids, closing the sulfur ring by hand. That work won him the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which cited the first synthesis of a polypeptide hormone [2].

Synthetic oxytocin replaced the variable gland extracts that had been used in obstetrics. The current Pitocin application in the FDA's database dates to November 1980, and its labeling was most recently revised in 2021 [3].

Uterine muscle contracts when calcium rises inside its cells and switches on the enzyme that lets contractile proteins pull together. Oxytocin binds receptors on that muscle and raises intracellular calcium. The number of receptors climbs steeply through pregnancy and peaks in early labor at term, which is why the same dose can produce very different responses from one person to the next [1].

The hormone clears quickly. Its half-life in plasma is roughly 1 to 6 minutes, so an IV infusion takes effect almost at once and fades within about an hour of stopping; an intramuscular shot acts within 3 to 5 minutes and lasts 2 to 3 hours [1]. That short action is what lets clinicians adjust an infusion minute by minute.

Oxytocin differs from vasopressin, the antidiuretic hormone, at only two of its amino acids. At large doses it can therefore raise blood pressure and make the kidneys hold water, which underlies some of its most serious risks [1].

Yes. Pitocin is approved under NDA 018261 and remains on the market as a prescription injection [3]. Its labeling opens with a boxed notice: because the data are not adequate to weigh benefits against risks, it is not indicated for elective induction, meaning induction without a medical reason [1].

The label also limits where it is used. For induction or augmentation, oxytocin is to be given only by IV and only in a hospital with adequate medical supervision, with the patient under continuous observation by trained staff [1].
For compounding, oxytocin is listed by the FDA in 503B Category 1 and marked as a component of an approved drug [4]. That listing does not make any compounded nasal spray an approved product.
The approved uses fall before and after delivery. Before delivery, oxytocin can start or build up contractions when a medical problem makes a vaginal birth the goal [1].

items: Induction of labor for a medical reason, such as Rh problems, maternal diabetes, preeclampsia near term, or ruptured membranes when delivery is needed [1].
Stimulating or reinforcing labor that has stalled, in selected cases of weak contractions [1].
Supporting treatment of an incomplete or inevitable miscarriage, alongside other procedures [1].
Producing contractions in the third stage of labor and controlling bleeding after birth [1].

blocks.text: How fast to raise the infusion has been studied directly. A Cochrane review of nine trials and 2,391 women compared high-dose with low-dose oxytocin regimens for induction at term. High doses did not raise the rate of vaginal birth within 24 hours or change the cesarean rate, but they increased uterine hyperstimulation (contractions that come too often or last too long) by about 86% [5]. Most trials carried a moderate to high risk of bias.

Most of the serious risks follow from oxytocin doing its job too well. Too much drug, or a uterus that is unusually sensitive, can cause contractions that are too strong or too frequent, spasm, or uterine rupture [1].

items: In the mother: nausea, vomiting, irregular heartbeat, high blood pressure episodes, allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, bleeding after birth, and a clotting disorder called afibrinogenemia [1].
Water intoxication: severe fluid retention with seizures and coma has occurred with slow infusions over 24 hours, and deaths have been reported [1].
In the baby: slow heart rate, arrhythmias, low Apgar scores, jaundice, retinal bleeding, seizures, brain injury, and fetal death have been reported [1].

blocks.text: The label advises against oxytocin, except in unusual circumstances, in situations such as fetal distress, partial placenta previa, prematurity, or a uterus prone to rupture after major surgery such as a prior cesarean [1]. Electronic fetal monitoring is the main way to catch overdosing early.

Oxytocin earned a reputation as a bonding or trust hormone, and nasal sprays are promoted online and by some clinics for social anxiety, relationships, and sexual function. None of these products is FDA-approved, and the approved label covers injection only [1].

The most rigorous test of the idea came in autism. A 24-week trial randomized 290 children and adolescents to nasal oxytocin or placebo. Social withdrawal scores improved by almost the same amount in both groups (3.7 versus 3.5 points), and secondary measures of social function and IQ did not differ [6]. Side effects were similar between groups, but the trial gives no support to claims that nasal oxytocin reliably changes social behavior.

name: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12
evidenceNote: The published work is cell studies, lab tests on donated skin, and safety patch tests. No independent placebo-controlled trial of this peptide on its own in people has been published.
summary: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a fatty-acid-linked elastin fragment used in anti-aging skincare. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an FDA-approved drug.
keyTakeaway: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is the six-amino-acid sequence VGVAPG, a repeating unit of the skin protein elastin, with a palmitic acid tail added so it sinks into the outer skin. It appears in anti-aging creams and serums at very low concentrations, reported up to 20 parts per million. Lab work shows the bare fragment draws skin fibroblasts toward it, and a 2025 study on donated human skin found the peptide forms a gel that stiffened a damaged skin barrier. Proof that it smooths wrinkles in people is thin. It is regulated as a cosmetic, which needs no FDA approval, and a US industry safety panel judged it safe as used.

blocks.text: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a skincare ingredient made of six amino acids, valine, glycine, valine, alanine, proline and glycine (written VGVAPG), joined to palmitic acid, a common fatty acid [2]. The VGVAPG sequence repeats many times in elastin, the stretchy protein that lets skin spring back after it is pinched [4].

The fatty tail is there to help a water-loving peptide get into the oily outer layer of skin. In lab measurements, adding the palmitoyl tail to an elastin-like peptide made it stick to skin proteins about ten times more than the same peptide without it, possibly because the molecules clump into self-assembled aggregates [3]. A related ingredient, myristoyl hexapeptide-12, uses a different fatty acid on the same sequence [2].

In ingredient lists it is named on its own or appears inside blends, sometimes listed as palmitoyl oligopeptide. Cosmetic chemists group it with matrikines, short peptides copied from pieces of the skin's support structure that are thought to signal repair [2].

The original idea comes from a 1984 study showing that VGVAPG on its own attracts fibroblasts, the cells that build collagen and elastin, and monocytes, a type of immune cell. The effect was strongest at very low concentrations and could be blocked by an antibody against elastin, suggesting the cells recognize it as a piece of elastin [4]. The theory behind the cosmetic use is that a fragment like this tells skin cells that elastin has been broken down and needs rebuilding.

A second possible action is physical. A 2025 study applied a 1 percent solution of the peptide to full-thickness human skin donated after surgery and tracked it with mass spectrometry imaging. The peptide passed through the outer stratum corneum into the epidermis, where it picked up calcium and other ions already in the skin and set into a gel. After the skin's own fats were stripped away, treated samples recovered stiffness and barrier properties in mechanical testing [1].

A 2026 safety framework ran the sequence through six bioinformatic tools. They matched it to the chemotactic region of human elastin and flagged no toxin or allergen signals [2]. These are lab and computer findings; none measure wrinkles on a living face.

No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetics and their ingredients, apart from color additives, do not require FDA approval before sale. Whether a product counts as a cosmetic or a drug depends on its intended use, so a cream that claims to change the structure or function of the skin, rather than its appearance, can be treated as a drug [5].

In the US, ingredient safety is reviewed by an expert body called the Cosmetic Ingredient Review (CIR). Its 2018 assessment of hexapeptide-12 and its fatty acid versions found palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 safe in cosmetics at the uses and concentrations then reported [2]. The data it relied on included a human repeat insult patch test in 53 adults that found no irritation or allergy, and leave-on products reported concentrations up to 20 ppm [2].

The strongest published evidence concerns how the peptide behaves, not whether it changes how skin looks. The donated-skin study shows it penetrates the upper layers and forms a gel, and the 1984 cell study shows the bare fragment draws fibroblasts in a dish [1][4]. Reviews cite topical testing in which the peptide improved elasticity and tone, but those results have not been confirmed in an independent, placebo-controlled trial of palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 used alone [1].

rows: Unmodified VGVAPG attracted both cell types [4]
Purified skin proteins, lab binding assay
Palmitoyl tail raised binding about tenfold [3]
Entered epidermis, formed a gel, restored barrier stiffness [1]

blocks.text: Most commercial skincare combines several peptides with moisturizers, retinoids or sunscreen, which makes it hard to credit any single ingredient with a visible result. There is also an open scientific question worth knowing about. Researchers studying aging have proposed that elastin fragments released naturally from arteries, lungs and skin enter the bloodstream and feed low-grade inflammation [6]. That work concerns fragments the body makes itself; the CIR data indicate very little cosmetic peptide passes through the skin [2].

name: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4
evidenceNote: One double-blind, placebo-controlled split-face trial in 93 women supports a modest effect on fine lines, with a few smaller trials behind it. All are short, and none measured collagen in living human skin.
summary: A collagen-signal peptide sold as Matrixyl in anti-aging creams. One 93-person randomized trial showed modest fine-line gains; it is a cosmetic, not a drug.
keyTakeaway: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 is a five amino acid fragment of collagen joined to a fatty acid so it can enter the skin, sold to brands as Matrixyl. In cell studies the bare peptide prompted fibroblasts to make more collagen. In the best human test, a 12-week, double-blind split-face trial in 93 women, a moisturizer with the peptide reduced wrinkles and fine lines more than the same moisturizer without it. The effect is modest and measured on appearance. It is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient, which the FDA does not approve.

blocks.text: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 is a short chain of five amino acids, lysine, threonine, threonine, lysine, and serine (KTTKS), with palmitic acid attached to one end [1]. The fatty acid is there to help a water-loving peptide pass through the oily outer layer of the skin. In ingredient catalogs and reviews it appears under the trade name Matrixyl [4].

It was designed for one job: to be applied to the face as an anti-wrinkle ingredient that encourages collagen production [1]. Today it turns up in many moisturizers, serums, and eye creams, frequently next to other peptides, niacinamide, or retinoid-type ingredients. It is not a medicine and is not injected.

Collagen is made in a longer starting form, and pieces are trimmed off as it matures. In 1993, researchers found that a five amino acid stretch from one of those trimmed pieces of type I collagen was the smallest part able to strongly boost production of collagen types I and III, along with fibronectin, in cultured fibroblasts, the cells that build the skin's support layer [2]. The idea behind the ingredient is that the fragment acts as a feedback signal telling those cells that collagen is being broken down and needs replacing [2][4].

Getting the peptide where it can act is the hard part. In skin taken from hairless mice, both the plain and palmitoylated forms broke down quickly, but the palmitoyl version lasted longer and could be found in the outer layer, the epidermis, and in small amounts in the dermis, while the plain peptide was not found in any layer [3]. Neither form passed all the way through the skin in that test [3].

No. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, and US law does not require cosmetics or their ingredients, apart from color additives, to be approved before sale [7]. The company marketing a product is responsible for making sure it is safe, and the FDA can take action against products that are harmful or mislabeled [7].

The line between cosmetic and drug turns on intended use. A product that promises to change how skin looks is a cosmetic; one that promises to affect the body's structure or function, such as regenerating cells, is legally a drug that needs approval [8]. That is why labels for these products tend to speak of the appearance of fine lines rather than rebuilding collagen.

The central trial enrolled 93 white women aged 35 to 55 and ran for 12 weeks. Each woman used a plain moisturizer on one side of her face and the same moisturizer with 3 ppm of the peptide on the other, without knowing which was which, and the side was chosen at random [1]. The peptide side showed significantly fewer wrinkles and fine lines by both image analysis and expert grading, and participants noticed the difference themselves [1].

rows: Fewer wrinkles and fine lines than the plain moisturizer; well tolerated [1]
Crow's feet improved more with the peptide cream than with acetyl hexapeptide-3 or placebo [5]
Multi-ingredient products containing pal-KTTKS smoothed eye-area skin [6]

blocks.text: Smaller studies point the same way but add little certainty. An eight-week trial in 21 Indonesian women compared the peptide with acetyl hexapeptide-3 and a placebo cream for crow's feet, and the authors called it a first look that needs a larger sample [5]. Two split-face studies of eye-area products found smoother skin after four weeks, but those products also held niacinamide, carnosine, and another peptide, so the effect cannot be traced to this ingredient alone [6].

What is missing is direct evidence that the cream raises collagen in living human skin. The collagen effect was shown in cultured cells [2], while the human trials measured wrinkle appearance over weeks [1][5].

Side effects appear to be uncommon. In the 93-woman trial the peptide was well tolerated on facial skin over 12 weeks [1]. As with any skin care product, irritation or an allergic reaction to another ingredient in the formula is possible, so a reaction to a Matrixyl product is not always a reaction to the peptide itself.

name: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7
evidenceNote: Published support for the peptide by itself is laboratory work on skin cells and skin samples. The few human studies tested finished creams that mix it with several other actives, without a placebo group, so they cannot show what this one ingredient contributes.
summary: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is a skincare peptide found in Matrixyl 3000. Lab data are promising; no human study has tested it alone.
keyTakeaway: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is a four-amino-acid peptide (glycine, glutamine, proline, arginine) attached to a fatty acid so it can sink into the skin's outer layer. It is sold mainly as part of Matrixyl 3000, paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1, in anti-wrinkle creams and eye products. In lab tests on skin cells it raised type III collagen after UV exposure. Human studies so far tested multi-ingredient products without placebo groups. As a cosmetic it needs no FDA approval, and it is not a drug.

blocks.text: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is a cosmetic ingredient built from a chain of glycine, glutamine, proline and arginine (GQPR in one-letter code), linked to palmitic acid, a common fatty acid. The fatty tail is added to help a water-loving peptide move into skin, since most peptides of this kind struggle to get past the skin's outer barrier [3].

It is best known as one half of Matrixyl 3000, a branded blend that pairs it with palmitoyl tripeptide-1 (Pal-GHK) [1]. That blend appears in anti-aging serums, creams and eye products. The ingredient belongs to a group often called signal peptides, short chains intended to nudge skin cells toward repair activity [4].

Topical anti-aging peptides are usually sorted into four groups: signal peptides, enzyme-inhibitor peptides, neurotransmitter-inhibitor peptides and carrier peptides [4]. Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is marketed as a signal peptide, meant to prompt fibroblasts, the cells in the dermis that make collagen and elastin, to produce more of the proteins that keep skin firm.

Some laboratory support exists. In a 2026 screening study, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 raised levels of type III collagen in human skin fibroblasts exposed to UV light, without harming the cells. A blend of four peptides, including this one, did more than any single peptide, and in donated skin tissue it raised collagen types I, III and IV [2].

Whether the peptide reaches those cells in living skin is a separate question. A 2026 imaging study of three women who applied a Matrixyl 3000 serum found both peptides throughout the stratum corneum, the dead outer layer of skin, but only on the surfaces between cells, with signal falling quickly with depth [1]. A review of anti-wrinkle peptides concluded that most do not cross the skin well enough to reach their targets without delivery aids [3].
No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. In the US, cosmetic products and their ingredients, apart from color additives, do not require FDA approval before they are sold [6].

What makes a product a cosmetic or a drug is its intended use, shown by its label claims and marketing. FDA notes that some claims can turn a product into a drug, even one sold as a cosmetic, such as a promise to regenerate cells [6]. Peptide creams are therefore typically marketed for the look of fine lines rather than as treatments that change skin structure.
No published clinical trial has tested palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 on its own against a placebo cream. The human studies that exist evaluate finished products in which it is one of several actives.

In one example, 37 women aged 20 to 55 used an eye cream containing yeast and rice ferment, N-acetylneuraminic acid, palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 for 12 weeks. Instrument readings showed hydration up 28%, elasticity up 19% and ultrasound collagen density up 55%, and dermatologists reported fewer fine lines by week 8. The authors noted the study was small and lacked a placebo group [5].

More type III collagen after UV; blend stronger than any one peptide [2]
Peptide found in the outer skin layer, between cells only [1]

blocks.text: Taken together, the evidence shows the peptide can act on skin cells in a dish and sits in the outermost skin layer after use. It does not yet show, in a controlled human test, that this ingredient by itself reduces wrinkles.

Reported problems are rare. In the 12-week eye cream study, dermatologists saw no redness, bumps, scabbing or peeling in any participant [5], and the screening study found no toxicity to skin cells at the levels tested [2].

Those findings describe particular products used for a few months. As with any skincare ingredient, irritation or an allergic reaction to some other component of the formula is possible, and a patch test on a small area is a common way to check before regular use.

name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1
evidenceNote: Its activity is described in cell studies, supplier data, and patents. The only published human study found tests a serum mixing it with other peptides, so no result can be credited to this ingredient alone.
summary: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a fatty-acid-linked GHK peptide used in anti-wrinkle creams such as the Matrixyl 3000 blend. Human evidence for it alone is lacking.
keyTakeaway: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is the three-amino-acid peptide GHK (glycine, histidine, lysine) with a palmitic acid tail attached to help it enter skin. It is a cosmetic ingredient made by Sederma, sold alone and as half of the Matrixyl 3000 blend with palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7. Cell studies suggest it prompts skin fibroblasts to make collagen and other support proteins. Human evidence is thin: one 32-person, 28-day study of a multi-peptide eye serum reported fewer wrinkles, but had no placebo and could not isolate this ingredient. As a cosmetic it needs no FDA approval, provided labels stick to appearance claims.

blocks.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a lab-made cosmetic ingredient. Its core is GHK, a three-amino-acid sequence (glycine, histidine, lysine) found in collagen, joined to palmitic acid, a common fatty acid [2]. The fat tail makes the peptide more oily, which is meant to help it cross the outer layer of skin. In ingredient lists it is sometimes written as pal-GHK.

For about two decades it was sold under the name palmitoyl oligopeptide, a label that confusingly covered two different molecules. In 2013 the name was retired and the two were given distinct names, one of which is palmitoyl tripeptide-1 [2]. The supplier, Sederma (part of Croda), sells it on its own as Biopeptide CL and combined with palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 as Matrixyl 3000, a common anti-aging peptide blend [3].

It is classed as a signal peptide, meaning it is meant to send a message to skin cells rather than fill or plump the skin directly. In cell culture, it is reported to act through the TGF-beta pathway and push dermal fibroblasts, the cells that build skin's support layer, to make more extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen [3]. The idea is that short collagen fragments are a natural cue that matrix has been broken down and needs rebuilding.

Whether enough of it reaches those cells in real skin is an open question. A review of anti-wrinkle peptides concluded that most have poor skin permeability, because peptides tend to be large, water-loving, and easily broken down by skin enzymes, and that many may not reach their targets at useful concentrations without delivery aids [5]. The palmitic acid tail is one such aid, but how well it works for this peptide in finished products has not been measured independently.

No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetics and their ingredients (apart from color additives) can be sold without FDA approval [1]. What decides whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug is its intended use, judged largely by the claims made for it. A cream that promises to improve the look of fine lines stays a cosmetic. A product claiming to regenerate cells or treat a disease is making drug claims and would need drug approval [1].
That is why products containing palmitoyl tripeptide-1 talk about firmer-looking skin and smoother appearance rather than rebuilding collagen inside the body.

Very little of the evidence is independent. A 2021 review of cosmetic peptides found that most information about palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and its relatives appears in patents and supplier brochures rather than peer-reviewed journals, and that randomized clinical studies are few [2]. One review repeats a report that Biopeptide CL performs comparably to retinoids without their irritation, but no published head-to-head trial backs that up [3].

Not peer-reviewed in many cases; dishes are not skin [2]
