blocks.text: The eye serum study is the closest thing to human data. It was a single-group study with instrument measurements and questionnaires, co-authored with a biotechnology company, and the serum contained palmitoyl tripeptide-1 together with palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 and other peptides [3][4]. With no comparison group and several actives, it cannot show what this ingredient contributes. Settling the question would take a randomized, vehicle-controlled trial of palmitoyl tripeptide-1 on its own, measured over months rather than weeks, and no such trial has been published.

Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is used in leave-on creams and serums, and none of the studies cited here reported safety problems with it. In the eye serum study, no product-related adverse reactions were seen [4]. A review of peptides in sensitive-skin products notes that their safety data come mainly from manufacturers and from the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel [2]. As with any skin product, irritation or allergy remains possible in individuals.

name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38
evidenceNote: The collagen-boosting claims rest on the supplier's lab and skin-sample tests. The only peer-reviewed human study is an industry-funded, open-label trial of 35 women using a serum that also contained vitamins C and E, so the peptide's own effect cannot be separated out.
summary: A three-amino-acid peptide with a fatty tail, used in anti-wrinkle creams at a few parts per million. Lab data are promising; human evidence is thin.
keyTakeaway: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a short peptide of lysine, oxidized methionine, and lysine, linked to a fatty acid so it can enter the outer skin. Developed by the French ingredient maker Sederma, it is added to anti-aging serums and creams. Lab and skin-explant studies report that it signals skin cells to make more collagen and other support proteins. In people, the only published study tested it inside a vitamin C and E serum without a control group. As a cosmetic ingredient it needs no FDA approval.

blocks.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is the ingredient-list name for palmitoyl-lysyl-dioxymethionyl-lysine, a chain of three amino acids attached to palmitic acid, a common fatty acid [1]. The middle amino acid is methionine in an oxidized form, which is why the code is sometimes written as KMO2K [1][2].

It comes from a family of lysine-based peptides patented by the French cosmetic ingredient company Sederma, with a priority date in 2009 [2]. The patent describes it as active at very low levels, on the order of a few parts per million in a finished product [2]. The published human study used it at 5 ppm, or five milligrams per kilogram of serum [1].

The fatty acid tail has a practical purpose. Attaching a palmitoyl group is a common way to help cosmetic peptides pass through the outer layer of skin and hold up against the skin's protein-cutting enzymes [3].

Cosmetic chemists group skin peptides into three types: signal peptides, carrier peptides, and peptides that interfere with nerve signals to muscle [3]. Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a signal peptide. The idea is that when the skin's supporting matrix breaks down, small protein fragments called matrikines tell nearby cells to repair it, and a synthetic mimic can send the same message [1][3].

In cell culture and in samples of donated human skin kept alive in the lab, the peptide has been reported to increase production of six matrix components: collagen types I, III, and IV, hyaluronic acid, fibronectin, and laminin [1][2]. Collagen gives skin much of its strength and hyaluronic acid helps it hold water. The patent also describes increased aquaporins, channels that move water through cells [2].

These results come from the supplier's own testing, filed as a patent rather than published in a peer-reviewed journal [1][2]. They show what the molecule can do to cells in a dish or a tissue sample. They do not show how much of a cream's peptide reaches the living cells of the dermis in real use.

No, and it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetics and their ingredients, apart from color additives, can be sold without FDA approval [4]. Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, so no regulator has reviewed evidence that it reduces wrinkles.

Whether a product counts as a cosmetic or a drug depends on what it claims. A product meant to change the structure or function of the body meets the legal definition of a drug, and the FDA judges intended use from labels, advertising, and websites [4]. That is why anti-aging products usually promise to improve the look of wrinkles rather than to rebuild collagen, even when the ingredient was chosen for its effect on collagen in the lab.

The only peer-reviewed human study found tested a serum that combined 15% vitamin C, vitamin E, and 5 ppm palmitoyl tripeptide-38 [1]. Thirty-five women with an average age of 64 and visible sun damage applied it to the face once a day for eight weeks, and researchers measured skin texture with 3D imaging and tone with photographs [1].

rows: Improved, in line with the instrument readings [1]

blocks.text: Several limits apply. There was no placebo or untreated comparison group, which the authors acknowledged [1]. The serum held three active ingredients, and vitamin C on its own is known to affect skin tone, so the study cannot say what the peptide contributed [1]. The trial was funded by the company that makes the serum, and the lead author works for a cosmetic science consultancy [1].

The study's authors also cite a vehicle-controlled trial of the peptide alone that reported smoother forehead and crow's feet lines at 5 ppm, but that trial appeared in a trade magazine rather than a peer-reviewed journal [1]. Until a controlled, independently run trial is published, the effect of the peptide by itself on wrinkles in people remains unproven.

sections.heading: Is it safe on the skin?

blocks.text: In the eight-week study, participants kept a daily log of side effects, and no adverse effects were attributed to the serum [1]. Thirty-five people over two months is far too few to detect uncommon reactions such as contact allergy.

The amounts used are tiny, a few parts per million, which limits exposure [1][2]. As with any cosmetic, irritation is more likely to come from the rest of the formula, such as high-strength vitamin C or fragrance, than from a trace peptide. There are no data on use during pregnancy or on broken skin.

name: Palopegteriparatide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in August 2024 on the phase 3 PaTHway trial, a 26-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in 82 adults with hypoparathyroidism, with open-label follow-up now running past three and a half years.
summary: A once-daily injection that slowly releases parathyroid hormone, approved in 2024 to replace the missing hormone in adults with hypoparathyroidism.
keyTakeaway: Palopegteriparatide is teriparatide, the active part of parathyroid hormone, tethered to a carrier that releases it slowly so blood levels stay steady through the day. Sold as Yorvipath, it was approved by the FDA in August 2024 for adults with hypoparathyroidism, a condition where the body makes too little of the hormone. In its phase 3 trial, 95% of patients on the drug no longer needed active vitamin D at 26 weeks, against 24% on placebo. Calcium must be monitored, and it is not recommended for people at higher risk of bone cancer.

blocks.text: Palopegteriparatide is a prodrug, an inactive form the body converts into the working drug. The working part is PTH(1-34), the first 34 amino acids of the 84-amino-acid human parathyroid hormone, which is the region that does the hormone's job [1]. It is attached through a linker to an inert, branched polyethylene glycol (PEG) carrier, from which it is released over time [1].

It is made by Ascendis Pharma and sold as Yorvipath, a prefilled pen injected under the skin once a day [1][3]. It treats hypoparathyroidism, in which the parathyroid glands in the neck make too little hormone and blood calcium runs low [1][2].

Standard care for hypoparathyroidism has been calcium pills plus active vitamin D, which raise blood calcium but do not restore normal hormone signalling [2]. Ascendis built palopegteriparatide on its TransCon linker technology to give steady hormone exposure through the day, and tested it under the name TransCon PTH [1][2].

items.text: PaTHway phase 3 trial reports 26-week results in 84 adults [2]
FDA approves Yorvipath for adults with hypoparathyroidism [3]
3.5-year PaTHway results published; label revised the same month [1][4]

blocks.text: Once injected, the linker breaks apart on its own under normal body conditions and frees PTH(1-34), giving continuous exposure rather than a short spike [1]. The released hormone has an apparent half-life of about 60 hours [1].

PTH(1-34) acts on the parathyroid hormone 1 receptor, found on bone cells and kidney tubule cells, in the same way as the body's own hormone [1]. It raises blood calcium and lowers phosphate by three routes: releasing calcium from bone, helping the kidneys hold on to calcium while flushing out phosphate, and boosting production of active vitamin D, which increases calcium absorption from food [1]. That is why patients can step down from calcium pills and vitamin D once the right dose is found.
Yes. The FDA approved Yorvipath on August 9, 2024 [3]. It is indicated for hypoparathyroidism in adults [1].

The label sets limits. It has not been studied for the temporary hypoparathyroidism that can follow surgery, and its starting scheme was tested only in adults whose blood calcium had first been brought to at least 7.8 mg/dL with calcium and vitamin D [1]. The dose is adjusted to blood calcium, up to a maximum of 30 mcg a day, and must be given as one injection rather than two, since splitting it makes the delivered dose less predictable [1].

It is prescribed as hormone replacement for adults with chronic hypoparathyroidism [1]. In the PaTHway trial, participants were randomized three to one to palopegteriparatide, starting at 18 mcg a day, or placebo, while their calcium and vitamin D were reduced according to a set algorithm [2].

rows: Met the FDA's full response definition

blocks.text: The trial's own primary endpoint, normal calcium plus independence from standard therapy, was met by 79% on the drug against 5% on placebo, and the drug group also scored better on hypoparathyroidism symptom scales [2]. The FDA's stricter definition gave 68.9% [1]. In the open-label extension, 73 people reached week 182, and of those, 96% were off therapeutic calcium doses, all were off active vitamin D, and 89% had normal calcium [4]. Kidney function measures improved and urine calcium normalized on average [2][4].

In the 26-week blinded period, the most common side effects were injection site reactions in 39% against 5% on placebo, vasodilatory symptoms such as dizziness or a drop in blood pressure on standing in 28% against none, and headache in 21% against 10% [1].

items: Diarrhea: 10% vs 5% on placebo [1]
Back pain: 8% vs 0% [1]
High blood calcium: 8% vs 0% [1]
Throat pain: 7% vs 0% [1]

blocks.text: Calcium can swing too high or too low, so it is measured regularly [1]. Severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with parathyroid hormone drugs including this one [1]. Rats given PTH drugs developed osteosarcoma, a bone cancer; an increased risk has not been seen in human observational studies, but the drug is not recommended for people already at raised risk [1]. High calcium can also make digoxin, a heart drug, more toxic [1].

name: Parathyroid hormone
evidenceNote: Recombinant PTH(1-84) was FDA-approved in 2015 on the strength of the 134-patient phase 3 REPLACE trial, though the product has since been discontinued worldwide for manufacturing reasons.
summary: Parathyroid hormone (Natpara) is a recombinant copy of the body's calcium hormone, FDA-approved in 2015 for hypoparathyroidism and since discontinued.
keyTakeaway: Natpara is a lab-made copy of the full 84-amino-acid parathyroid hormone, the body's main regulator of blood calcium. In the 24-week REPLACE trial, 53% of people with hypoparathyroidism on daily injections halved their calcium and active vitamin D pills while keeping calcium stable, against 2% on placebo. The FDA approved it in January 2015 as an add-on to calcium and vitamin D. Takeda stopped making it worldwide at the end of 2024 because of unresolved manufacturing problems, and the EU authorization was withdrawn in July 2026. It is a different drug from teriparatide.

blocks.text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is made by four small glands in the neck, next to the thyroid. It keeps blood calcium in a narrow range, which nerves, muscles, and the heart depend on. The natural hormone is a chain of 84 amino acids, written PTH(1-84) [1].

As a drug, the full-length hormone was sold as Natpara by NPS Pharmaceuticals, later part of Takeda. It is produced in bacteria using recombinant DNA and carries the same 84-amino-acid sequence as the human hormone [1]. It is often confused with teriparatide, which contains only the first 34 amino acids, is used for osteoporosis, and has its own entry in this library. Natpara was meant for the opposite problem: people who make too little parathyroid hormone.

PTH raises blood calcium in three ways. It tells the kidneys to hold on to calcium instead of passing it into urine. It switches on the kidney enzyme that turns stored vitamin D into its active form, which increases calcium absorption from food. And it speeds bone turnover, releasing calcium from the skeleton into the blood [1].

In hypoparathyroidism, most often caused by damage to the glands during neck surgery, that signal is missing. Standard care replaces its downstream effects with large doses of calcium and active vitamin D (calcitriol), which can leave calcium swinging between too low and too high and push extra calcium into the urine. Replacing the hormone itself was meant to restore the natural control. After an injection, blood calcium peaks about 10 to 12 hours later and stays above baseline for more than a day [1].

Yes, but the approved product is no longer made. The FDA approved Natpara on January 23, 2015, as an add-on to calcium and vitamin D to control low calcium in hypoparathyroidism, limited to patients who cannot be well controlled on those alone [1]. It was available only through a restricted program because of a bone cancer signal in rats.

blocks.text: Because changing or stopping PTH can drop calcium quickly, the discontinuation notice stressed close monitoring of blood calcium and careful adjustment of calcium and vitamin D during any switch [3]. A different, long-acting PTH-based drug, palopegteriparatide, has its own entry in this library.

sections.heading: What was parathyroid hormone prescribed for?

blocks.text: Natpara was prescribed for adults with long-standing hypoparathyroidism whose calcium could not be kept steady with supplements and active vitamin D. It was not studied in the form caused by calcium-sensing receptor mutations or in the temporary low calcium that can follow surgery [1]. Doses were adjusted to keep blood calcium in the lower half of normal, with checks every few days after any change [1].

rows: Halved calcium and active vitamin D while calcium stayed stable

blocks.text: REPLACE enrolled people aged 18 to 85 at 33 sites in eight countries, most of whom had lost gland function after surgery [1][2]. On average they had lived with the condition for 15 years and were taking about 2,000 mg of calcium a day [1]. The trial showed the hormone could replace much of the pill burden. It was not designed to show fewer kidney stones, fractures, or hospital visits, and it ran for only 24 weeks.

The most common problems were calcium running too low or too high, which is why monitoring was built into the label. Low calcium shows up as tingling, numbness, and muscle cramps; high calcium as nausea, vomiting, and fatigue [1].

items: Tingling and numbness, headache, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, joint pain, and limb pain [1].
High urine calcium, which over time can strain the kidneys [1].
Severe low calcium if the drug is stopped or interrupted suddenly [1].
Possible bone cancer (osteosarcoma): rats given parathyroid hormone developed it in a dose- and time-dependent way, and a human risk could not be excluded, which led to a boxed warning [1].

blocks.text: Because of that bone cancer signal, the label advised against use in people with a raised baseline risk, such as those with Paget's disease of bone, unexplained high alkaline phosphatase, open growth plates, inherited conditions linked to osteosarcoma, or past radiation to the skeleton [1]. Digoxin users needed extra care, since swings in calcium change how that heart drug acts.

name: Pasireotide
evidenceNote: FDA-approved since 2012 for Cushing's disease and since 2014 in a monthly form for acromegaly, based on randomized phase 3 trials of 162 and 358 patients.
summary: Pasireotide (Signifor) is a somatostatin-mimicking peptide that lowers cortisol in Cushing's disease and growth hormone in acromegaly. FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Pasireotide is a ring-shaped synthetic peptide that copies somatostatin, the body's hormone brake. Unlike older drugs in its class, it binds strongly to the receptor subtype most common on the pituitary tumors behind Cushing's disease. The FDA approved twice-daily Signifor in 2012 for Cushing's disease when surgery fails or is not possible, and monthly Signifor LAR for acromegaly and Cushing's disease. In the pivotal trial, 26% on the higher dose normalized urine cortisol by six months. High blood sugar is its defining side effect, affecting most patients.

blocks.text: Pasireotide is a cyclohexapeptide, a synthetic ring of six amino acids, designed to mimic somatostatin, a natural hormone that switches off the release of many other hormones [1]. Recordati Rare Diseases sells it in two forms: Signifor, a solution injected under the skin twice a day, and Signifor LAR, a long-acting form given once a month [1][2].

It treats two rare pituitary conditions. In Cushing's disease, a benign pituitary tumor releases too much ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone), which drives the adrenal glands to overproduce cortisol. In acromegaly, a different pituitary tumor releases excess growth hormone, and treatment is judged by bringing growth hormone and IGF-1 back to normal [2].

There are five somatostatin receptor subtypes, SSTR1 through SSTR5, spread across different tissues. Pasireotide binds four of them. Its tightest grip is on SSTR5, where its binding is in fact slightly stronger than natural somatostatin's, and it also binds SSTR2, SSTR3, and SSTR1 [1].

That profile is the point. The corticotroph tumor cells behind Cushing's disease frequently carry large amounts of SSTR5 while expressing other subtypes weakly. When pasireotide activates those receptors, ACTH secretion falls, and cortisol output falls with it [1]. The trial investigators described this broad binding profile, with high affinity for SSTR5, as unique [3].
Because somatostatin also restrains other hormones, pasireotide's effects reach beyond the pituitary. Its most important side effects, rising blood sugar and gallstones, are covered below [1].
Yes. The FDA approved Signifor (NDA 200677) as a new molecular entity on December 14, 2012, and approved Signifor LAR (NDA 203255), a new formulation, on December 15, 2014 [4][5].

blocks.text: The Cushing's approval rests on a double-blind phase 3 trial of 162 adults with urine cortisol at least 1.5 times the upper limit of normal. They were randomized to 0.6 mg or 0.9 mg twice daily. The main goal, normal urine cortisol at six months without a dose increase, was met by 12 of 82 patients (15%) on the lower dose and 21 of 80 (26%) on the higher dose. Median urine cortisol fell by about half within two months, and normalization was more likely when starting levels were less than five times the upper limit [3].

Beyond the lab numbers, blood and saliva cortisol and ACTH levels also fell, and the physical signs of Cushing's disease eased during the year of treatment. Patients who did not respond by month three had their dose raised, but the label notes that dose increases appeared to add little to urine cortisol response [1][3].

For acromegaly, a randomized, double-blind trial enrolled 358 patients who had never taken an acromegaly drug and compared monthly Signifor LAR with another somatostatin analog. At 12 months, 31.3% on pasireotide reached both a growth hormone below 2.5 mcg/L and a normal IGF-1, against 19.2% on the comparator [2]. In that trial, monthly pasireotide started at 40 mg and could be raised to 60 mg after three or six months if hormone levels stayed high [2].

rows: Normal urine cortisol at 6 months: 15% (0.6 mg) and 26% (0.9 mg) [3]
Full biochemical control at 12 months: 31.3% vs 19.2% [2]

blocks.text: Side effects are common. In the Cushing's trial, 98% of patients reported at least one adverse reaction, 25% had a serious adverse event, and 17% stopped because of side effects. There were no deaths [1].

Blood sugar is the defining issue. Nearly every patient in the trial had worsening glucose within the first two weeks, including those who started with normal levels, and hyperglycemia-related events affected 118 of 162 patients. Seventy-four needed a new glucose-lowering medicine [1][3]. The label calls for intensive glucose monitoring when starting and after dose changes [1].

Other warnings include cortisol dropping too low (hypocortisolism), slow heart rate and QT prolongation on the ECG, liver test elevations, gallstones and their complications, deficiencies of other pituitary hormones, and fatty stools from poor fat absorption [1].

name: Pegcetacoplan
evidenceNote: Pegcetacoplan holds three FDA approvals, each backed by phase 3 trials: a head-to-head trial against eculizumab in PNH, a placebo-controlled trial in two rare kidney diseases, and two sham-controlled eye trials.
summary: Pegcetacoplan is an FDA-approved C3 complement blocker used for PNH, two rare kidney diseases (Empaveli) and geographic atrophy in the eye (Syfovre).
keyTakeaway: Pegcetacoplan is a pair of short synthetic peptides joined by a long PEG chain that blocks C3, the central protein of the complement system. Under the name Empaveli it has been FDA-approved since 2021 for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), and since 2025 for C3 glomerulopathy and primary IC-MPGN in people aged 12 and older. In the PNH trial it raised hemoglobin 3.84 g/dL more than eculizumab. As Syfovre it is injected into the eye for geographic atrophy. Its boxed warning covers serious infections from encapsulated bacteria, so vaccination is required first.

blocks.text: Pegcetacoplan is a synthetic drug made of two identical 15 amino acid peptides attached to either end of a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) chain. The whole molecule weighs about 43.5 kDa [1]. The PEG chain keeps it in the body far longer than a bare peptide would last.

It targets the complement system, a set of blood proteins that tags and destroys microbes and damaged cells. When complement is overactive or poorly controlled, it attacks the body's own tissue. Pegcetacoplan is marketed under three names: Empaveli for blood and kidney diseases in the US, Aspaveli in Europe, and Syfovre for an eye disease [1][4].

Complement works as a cascade. C3 sits near the top, and when it is split, one fragment (C3b) coats cells to mark them for removal while the chain reaction goes on to build the membrane attack complex, which punches holes in cell membranes. Pegcetacoplan binds C3 and C3b and stops C3 from being split, so both branches are held back [1].

That upstream position is what set it apart in PNH. In PNH, red blood cells lack surface proteins that normally shield them from complement. Older drugs such as eculizumab block C5, further down the cascade, which stops red cells bursting inside blood vessels. But C3b still coats the cells, and the spleen and liver then clear them, a process called extravascular hemolysis. Blocking C3 addresses both routes [1][2]. In C3 glomerulopathy, the same logic applies to the kidney, where C3 fragments build up in the filtering units and drive damage [1][3].
Yes, under two brand names with different routes and uses [1][4].

items.text: Empaveli approved for adults with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, based on the PEGASUS trial [1][2].
Syfovre approved as an injection into the eye for geographic atrophy, the late dry form of age-related macular degeneration [4][5].
Empaveli label expanded to people aged 12 and up who have C3 glomerulopathy or primary immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN), based on the VALIANT trial [1][3].

blocks.text: Empaveli is available only through a restricted program (REMS) because of its infection risk, and prescribers must confirm vaccination status before treatment starts [1].

PNH is a rare acquired blood disorder in which red cells are destroyed by complement, causing anemia, fatigue and dark urine. The PEGASUS trial enrolled 80 adults whose hemoglobin stayed below 10.5 g/dL despite eculizumab. After a 4-week period on both drugs, people were randomly assigned to pegcetacoplan alone, injected under the skin, or to continue eculizumab by IV [2].

rows: Episodes of renewed red cell destruction

blocks.text: The trial was open label, so patients and doctors knew which drug was given, which matters most for the fatigue scores. The hemoglobin and transfusion results are objective measures [2]. C3 glomerulopathy and IC-MPGN are rare kidney diseases that cause protein to leak into urine and often progress to kidney failure. In VALIANT, 124 adolescents and adults were randomized to pegcetacoplan or placebo for 26 weeks. Protein in urine fell by 68% relative to placebo, and 60% of treated patients halved their protein levels compared with 5% on placebo. A biopsy-based score of disease activity did not differ significantly between the groups, so the effect on kidney tissue itself is less settled than the effect on protein loss [3].

Geographic atrophy is an advanced form of dry macular degeneration in which patches of retina waste away. Syfovre is given by a doctor as an injection into the eye every 25 to 60 days. Its approval rests on two phase 3 studies, OAKS and DERBY, that together treated 839 patients [4].

Empaveli carries a boxed warning: by blocking complement, it raises the risk of serious and sometimes fatal infections from encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type B. Vaccines against these bacteria must be completed or updated at least 2 weeks before the first dose unless delaying treatment is riskier [1].

In PNH, the most common side effects were injection site reactions, infections, diarrhea, abdominal pain, respiratory infections, limb pain, low potassium, fatigue, dizziness, headache and rash [1]. In PEGASUS, injection site reactions hit 37% of people on pegcetacoplan versus 3% on eculizumab, and diarrhea 22% versus 3%, with no cases of meningitis in either group [2]. In the kidney trial, the common complaints were infusion site reactions, fever, colds, flu, cough and nausea [1]. VALIANT reported no serious infections from encapsulated bacteria and no more adverse events than placebo [3].

Syfovre has eye-specific risks: infection inside the eye, retinal detachment, inflammation, raised eye pressure, conversion to wet macular degeneration, and retinal vasculitis or blood vessel blockage. The most common complaints were eye discomfort, new wet AMD, vitreous floaters and small conjunctival bleeds [4].

name: Pegvisomant
evidenceNote: Approved in 2003 after a 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 112 people with acromegaly, backed by long-term open-label follow-up and a registry of more than 2,000 patients.
summary: Pegvisomant (Somavert) blocks the growth hormone receptor. It is FDA-approved for acromegaly when surgery or radiation have not worked or are not suitable.
keyTakeaway: Pegvisomant is an engineered copy of growth hormone that binds the growth hormone receptor without switching it on, so the body's own hormone can no longer act. Sold by Pfizer as Somavert, it received FDA approval in 2003 as a treatment for acromegaly. In its pivotal trial, IGF-1 returned to normal in 89% of people on the highest dose, against 10% on placebo; in long-term registry use the figure is closer to 53% to 73%. Liver enzymes need monitoring, and the pituitary tumor itself is not shrunk.

blocks.text: Pegvisomant is a modified form of human growth hormone made by recombinant DNA technology. It has 191 amino acids, like growth hormone, but with changes that turn it from an activator into a blocker, and it carries several chains of polyethylene glycol (PEG) that slow its removal from the body [1].

It is used for acromegaly, a condition in which a usually benign pituitary tumor makes too much growth hormone. In adults that excess enlarges the hands, feet and facial features and is linked to diabetes, heart disease and joint damage. Pfizer markets pegvisomant as Somavert [5]. Surgery to remove the tumor is usually tried first, and pegvisomant is one of the medical options when that does not fully control the disease [1].

Growth hormone works mostly by binding a receptor on liver and other cells, which then produce insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), the hormone that drives most of acromegaly's effects. Pegvisomant binds the same receptor selectively and stops the natural hormone from signalling through it [1]. IGF-1 falls, along with related proteins such as IGFBP-3, and in lab tests the drug did not bind 19 other cytokine receptors, including the prolactin receptor [1].

Because pegvisomant blocks the hormone's effect rather than its production, growth hormone levels in the blood actually rise on treatment, as the body loses the IGF-1 feedback that normally restrains it [1][2]. That is why doctors track IGF-1, not growth hormone, and why the drug does not target the tumor itself. Pegvisomant also looks enough like growth hormone to confuse standard growth hormone lab tests [1].

Yes. Somavert was approved on March 25, 2003, under a biologics license now held by Pfizer, and remains a prescription product [5]. The label approves it for acromegaly in people who have had an inadequate response to surgery or radiation, or for whom those treatments are not appropriate, with the stated goal of bringing IGF-1 back to normal [1].

Treatment starts with a 40 mg loading dose given under medical supervision, then a daily injection under the skin. The dose is adjusted in 5 mg steps according to IGF-1 results taken every four to six weeks, not according to symptoms or growth hormone levels [1].

Its only approved use is acromegaly. In the pivotal 12-week trial, 112 adults were randomized to placebo or 10, 15 or 20 mg a day. IGF-1 fell by 27%, 50% and 63% across the three doses, and people on 15 or 20 mg had smaller ring sizes, less soft-tissue swelling, less sweating and less fatigue than those on placebo [2].

rows: 97% of those treated 12 months or more [3]
2,090 patients in routine care, up to 12 years
53% at year 1, rising to 73% at year 10 [4]

blocks.text: The gap between trial and registry results matters. Trials enrolled selected patients under close follow-up, while the registry reflects routine care, where average daily doses climbed from 12.8 mg in year 1 to 18.9 mg by year 10 as doctors adjusted treatment [4]. Most registry patients had already had surgery, radiation or other drugs before starting [4]. In the long-term trial, fasting insulin and glucose also fell, and when people stopped the drug their growth hormone levels returned to baseline within 30 days, showing the blockade simply lifts once treatment ends [3].

The most commonly reported effects in trials were infections such as colds, pain, nausea, diarrhea, abnormal liver tests, flu-like symptoms and injection site reactions [1]. In the 12-week trial these were each reported by a minority, and the overall rate of side effects was similar across doses and placebo [1][2].

items: Liver: transaminases rose up to 15 times the upper limit in under 2% of people in open-label trials, and postmarketing reports include rises above 20 times with raised bilirubin. Liver tests are checked before starting and during treatment [1].
Low blood sugar in people with diabetes, because lowering growth hormone improves insulin sensitivity; diabetes drugs may need reducing [1].
Lipohypertrophy, a lump of fatty tissue at injection sites [1].
Antibodies to growth hormone in about 17% of people, without an apparent effect on response [1].

Tumor growth: two of 160 people in long-term trials had their pituitary tumor enlarge, and the registry recorded an increase on 6.8% of scans, so the label calls for the tumor to be watched with MRI [1][3][4].

blocks.text: People taking opioids often needed higher doses to normalize IGF-1, for reasons that are not understood [1]. Because restoring normal hormone levels can improve fertility, the label also advises discussing pregnancy risk with women who could conceive [1].

name: Pemvidutide
class: GLP-1 and glucagon dual receptor agonist
evidenceNote: Two randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trials (one in fatty liver disease with biopsy endpoints, one in obesity) support it. No phase 3 result exists yet, so it sits below the deep tier.
summary: Altimmune's weekly GLP-1 and glucagon injection for fatty liver disease. Phase 2 cleared liver inflammation in about half of patients; phase 3 began in 2026.
keyTakeaway: Pemvidutide is an experimental weekly injection from Altimmune that activates both the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, aimed mainly at MASH, the inflamed form of fatty liver disease. In the 212-patient IMPACT trial, liver inflammation resolved without worsening scarring in 58% of patients on 1.2 mg after 24 weeks, versus 20% on placebo, but the scarring endpoint itself was not met. It is not FDA-approved. In January 2026 the FDA gave it a designation that speeds review for drugs showing early promise in serious disease, and a phase 3 trial started that August.

blocks.text: Pemvidutide is an investigational peptide drug developed by Altimmune, a biotech company in Maryland. It is injected once a week under the skin and is being tested chiefly for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, or MASH: fatty liver disease that has progressed to inflammation and liver cell damage and can lead to scarring and cirrhosis [1].

The drug belongs to the same broad family as semaglutide, but with a twist. Instead of acting on one gut hormone receptor, it acts on two, GLP-1 and glucagon, in roughly equal measure [2]. Altimmune is also testing it in alcohol use disorder and alcohol-associated liver disease, and an earlier phase 2 trial studied it for obesity [3][2].

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide 1) is a gut hormone that reduces appetite through the brain and slows digestion, which leads to weight loss. Glucagon, a pancreatic hormone, works more directly on the liver. Activating its receptor pushes liver cells to break down fatty acids for energy and to make less new fat [4].

The idea behind the dual design is that fat can be cleared from the liver faster than weight loss alone would achieve. The trial results fit that reasoning: liver fat fell by around three quarters on the higher doses within 24 weeks, while average body weight fell by about 6% [4]. Because the drug is balanced between the two receptors rather than led by GLP-1, it is not expected to match the weight loss of semaglutide or tirzepatide, and its developer has positioned it around the liver instead.
No. Pemvidutide is not approved for any condition. It has collected several FDA designations that speed up review, which signal regulatory interest but are not approvals [2].

items.text: Altimmune reports 48-week results from MOMENTUM, its phase 2 obesity trial [3].
24-week results of the IMPACT phase 2b trial in MASH are published in The Lancet [1].
End-of-phase 2 meeting with the FDA agrees the outline of a registrational trial [2].

FDA grants BTD, its expedited designation for drugs that may improve substantially on existing treatment of a serious condition, for MASH, adding to Fast Track status for MASH and alcohol use disorder [2].
The PERFORMA phase 3 trial begins enrolling about 1,790 patients with MASH [5].

blocks.text: PERFORMA is designed to support accelerated approval from liver biopsy results at 52 weeks, expected in 2029, with full approval resting on liver-related events such as cirrhosis complications tracked over about five years [5].

The main evidence is IMPACT, a randomized, double-blind phase 2b trial in 212 adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and moderate or advanced scarring (fibrosis stage F2 or F3). Participants received 1.2 mg or 1.8 mg of pemvidutide weekly, without a gradual dose increase, or placebo. A repeat liver biopsy at 24 weeks measured two goals: clearing the inflammation and reducing scarring [1].

The trial therefore met one of its two main goals. The inflammation finding was clear, but the improvement in scarring was too small to separate from placebo at 24 weeks, which is short for fibrosis to change. The authors noted that longer trials were planned [1]. Altimmune reported in December 2025 that 48-week data showed further gains on blood and imaging tests of liver scarring, but those figures came in a company statement rather than a published paper [2].

An earlier, smaller trial in 64 people with fatty liver disease found relative drops in liver fat of 56% to 76% over 24 weeks across three doses, compared with 14% on placebo, measured by MRI [4]. In MOMENTUM, a 48-week obesity trial in 391 adults without diabetes, weight fell 15.6% on the 2.4 mg dose against 2.2% on placebo [3].

On the 1.8 mg dose in that liver fat study, 85% of participants cut their liver fat at least in half, and 54% reached a level considered normal (5% or less). The study was an extension of an earlier 12-week trial, so it followed only those who completed the first phase [4].

Side effects in that obesity trial were mostly digestive and rose with dose. Nausea affected about half or more of those on the two higher doses versus 11% on placebo, vomiting about 27% versus 3%, and close to one in five on those doses stopped because of side effects [3]. Those higher-dose obesity numbers are less favorable than the liver trial, where doses were lower and discontinuation was rare [1].

name: Pentapeptide-18
evidenceNote: Support comes from lab and computer modeling studies and small cosmetic tests, some run by formulators, in which the peptide was mixed with other actives such as retinol. No independent, placebo-controlled trial has isolated its effect on wrinkles.
summary: Pentapeptide-18 (Leuphasyl) is a five-amino-acid cosmetic peptide marketed to soften expression lines. Independent evidence is thin.
keyTakeaway: Pentapeptide-18, sold to formulators as Leuphasyl, is a short synthetic peptide added to anti-wrinkle creams. It is designed to act like enkephalins, natural nerve-calming peptides, and so turn down the signal that makes facial muscles contract, an effect sometimes described as Botox-like. The support is mostly lab work, computer modeling, and small cosmetic tests in which it was combined with other ingredients. As a cosmetic ingredient it needs no FDA approval, and a cream that claimed to change muscle function would be regulated as a drug.

blocks.text: Pentapeptide-18 is a synthetic peptide made of five amino acids. It is sold to cosmetic makers under the trade name Leuphasyl and appears on ingredient lists as pentapeptide-18. It belongs to a group sometimes called Botox-like peptides, alongside acetyl hexapeptide-3, better known as Argireline [1].

Dermatology researchers sort anti-aging peptides into four broad types: signal peptides, enzyme-inhibitor peptides, carrier peptides, and neurotransmitter-inhibitor peptides [2]. Pentapeptide-18 sits in the last group, which aims to reduce expression lines, the creases made by repeated movement such as frowning, rather than to rebuild collagen [2][1].

The idea is that pentapeptide-18 imitates enkephalins, small peptides the nervous system uses to quiet signaling. According to this account, it attaches to enkephalin receptors on nerve cells and reduces how much acetylcholine, the chemical that tells muscles to contract, is released at the junction between nerve and muscle. Less acetylcholine would mean a more relaxed muscle and shallower lines [1].

This mechanism is proposed rather than proven in human skin. A key open question for any cream is whether enough peptide passes through the outer skin barrier to reach nerve endings and muscle beneath it, and published work on pentapeptide-18 does not measure that. Recent studies have instead used spectroscopy and computer docking to describe its structure and to predict that it could bind enzymes that break down collagen, such as MMP-13 [3][4].

Researchers have also modified the molecule. Adding a D-tyrosine to one end gave pentapeptide-18 the ability to reduce melanin production in pigment cells and in a 3D human skin model, a lab result that points to possible dual-purpose versions [7].

No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetics are products for cleansing, beautifying, or altering the appearance, and apart from color additives they reach the market without FDA approval [8].

The line is drawn by claims. A product intended to affect the structure or function of the body is legally a drug, and the FDA judges intended use from labels, advertising, and online marketing [8]. A cream that says it makes lines look smoother is a cosmetic; one that claims to block nerve signals or relax muscles the way botulinum toxin does would be making a drug claim.

It is used in serums, eye creams, and face creams marketed for expression lines on the forehead, between the brows, and around the eyes. One study tested emulsions with 0.5%, 1%, and 2% of the peptide applied over the muscles that create those lines, the corrugator between the eyebrows and the orbicularis around the eyes, rather than directly on the wrinkles [1].

Formulators also pair it with other actives. Polish researchers loaded pentapeptide-18 and retinol into solid lipid nanoparticles, tiny fat-based carriers, and confirmed the dispersion stayed stable for four weeks at room temperature [6].

There is very little independent clinical evidence. The 2014 cosmetics study set out to find the best concentration and to measure wrinkle regression with an imaging device, but its summary reports no participant numbers or results, and it is not indexed in PubMed [1]. Two 2026 papers from an Istanbul group are entirely spectroscopic, computational, or cell-based [3][4].

The most recent volunteer data come from a 2024 study of creams combining retinol with peptide-loaded nanoparticles. The products reduced sebum and the number of facial wrinkles, and the nanoparticles appeared to lessen retinol irritation [5]. Two of the authors worked for the cosmetics company involved, and because the creams contained retinol, an established anti-aging ingredient in its own right, the result cannot be credited to pentapeptide-18 alone [5].

In short, the case for pentapeptide-18 rests on a plausible mechanism and supplier-friendly testing. No randomized, placebo-controlled trial run independently has tested it on its own against an inactive cream.

The published studies do not describe a pattern of side effects. In a 2026 lab test, pentapeptide-18 was not toxic to HaCaT cells, a standard human skin cell line, at concentrations up to 1 mg/mL [4]. That is a cell result, not a measure of irritation or allergy in people.

No published study reports patch testing or long-term safety data for the peptide on its own. In the 2024 volunteer study, the lipid carriers lessened the irritation typical of retinol, which speaks to the vehicle rather than the peptide [5].

name: Petrelintide
evidenceNote: One published randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial of 485 treated people, randomized phase 1 studies, and a second phase 2 trial reported only as topline results. Three phase 3 trials began in late 2026.
summary: Petrelintide is a weekly amylin-based injection for weight loss from Zealand and Roche. Phase 2 showed about 8 to 10% loss at 28 weeks; phase 3 began in 2026.
keyTakeaway: Petrelintide is a once-weekly injection that copies amylin, a hormone that signals fullness after meals, rather than GLP-1. In the ZUPREME 1 trial of 485 adults with obesity, weight fell 7.9% to 9.8% at 28 weeks depending on dose, against 1.7% on placebo, and up to 10.7% by week 42. Nausea affected 20% of treated people, but vomiting and diarrhea were no more common than on placebo. Zealand Pharma and Roche started phase 3 trials in late 2026. It is not approved anywhere and is banned in sport as an unapproved substance.

blocks.text: Petrelintide is an investigational peptide modeled on human amylin, a hormone released after eating that acts as a satiety signal. Zealand Pharma reworked the amylin sequence to make it chemically stable and long-acting while keeping its potency, and made it soluble at close to neutral pH, a property chosen so it could later be mixed with other weight-loss peptides in one injection [3].

In March 2025, Roche agreed to co-develop and co-market petrelintide with Zealand in a deal worth up to USD 5.3 billion. The partners plan to test it on its own and in a fixed-dose combination with Roche's GLP-1 and GIP receptor drug, then called CT-388 [4]. A dose-finding study of that pairing, under the drug's newer name enicepatide, is listed as not yet recruiting [10].

Petrelintide activates the receptors that respond to amylin, reproducing the hormone's fullness signal so that people eat less. This is a different pathway from GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, which is why the trial authors describe its mechanism as distinct from incretin-based treatments [1]. The hope behind the program is that weight loss through amylin might come with fewer digestive side effects, and that the two pathways could add together in combination products [3][4].

In phase 1 testing, petrelintide was absorbed slowly after injection under the skin and had a half-life of about 10 days, long enough for once-weekly dosing. Blood levels rose in proportion to dose at steady state [2].

No. Petrelintide is not approved by FDA or any other regulator and can be obtained legally only inside clinical trials. Roche now sponsors three phase 3 trials, named ZUPREME-3, ZUPREME-4, and ZUPREME-5, that began recruiting in September and October 2026. They cover adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes (about 3,900 participants), those with type 2 diabetes (about 600), and those with established cardiovascular disease (about 2,500) [5][6][7].
For athletes, the 2026 WADA Prohibited List bans at all times any drug still under clinical development and not approved by any health regulator, under class S0 [9].

The main evidence is ZUPREME 1, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial at 32 sites in Poland, Romania, and the US. Adults without type 2 diabetes who had obesity, or a BMI of 27 or more with high blood pressure or abnormal blood fats, were assigned five to one to one of five weekly maintenance doses or placebo for 42 weeks. Participants averaged 107 kg and a BMI of 36.7 at the start [1].

Weight kept falling after the primary readout, reaching up to 10.7% by week 42, and the three highest doses gave similar results to one another. Nausea was the most frequent side effect, in 20% of people on petrelintide against 6% on placebo, and was mostly mild and concentrated during dose increases. Vomiting (3% vs 6%), diarrhea (7% vs 7%), and constipation (7% vs 4%) were close to placebo levels, and no deaths occurred [1].

A second phase 2 trial, ZUPREME-2, tested petrelintide in 220 adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes. Zealand's October 2026 topline report gave up to 9.2% weight loss at 28 weeks against about 2% on placebo, with HbA1c lowered by 0.61 to 0.88 points more than placebo and similar dropout from digestive side effects in both groups (1.9% vs 1.7%). These figures had not yet been peer reviewed when reported [8].

For context, the weight loss so far is smaller than the 14.9% average seen with weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg over 68 weeks in the STEP 1 trial, though the trials differ in length and design and no study has compared the two drugs directly [11]. The phase 3 program, with about 7,000 participants in total and a cardiovascular trial among them, will be the first long, large test of benefit and safety [5][6][7].

name: Pinealon
evidenceNote: Nearly all published work on pinealon comes from cell cultures, rats and mice, and almost all of it from the research group that created it. The human reports mentioned in its reviews are small, in Russian, and not controlled trials of pinealon.
summary: Pinealon is an unapproved three amino acid peptide from a St. Petersburg lab, studied in cells and rodents for brain protection. No controlled human trials.
keyTakeaway: Pinealon is a synthetic tripeptide, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and arginine (EDR), from Vladimir Khavinson's peptide bioregulator group in St. Petersburg. In cell cultures it limited oxidative damage, and in rats and mice it protected nerve cells and preserved the connections between them. Its developers propose that it enters the cell nucleus and regulates genes directly, an idea not confirmed by independent labs. No randomized human trial has been published. Pinealon is not FDA-approved and is sold online only as a research chemical.

blocks.text: Pinealon is a tiny synthetic peptide made of just three amino acids: glutamic acid, aspartic acid and arginine, written Glu-Asp-Arg or EDR [1][2]. It was developed by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, who describe it as one of a set of short regulatory peptides, or bioregulators [1][2].

Its name points to the pineal gland, but the research on it focuses on the brain more broadly, especially on protecting nerve cells under stress and in models of aging and Alzheimer's disease [1][4]. Outside that research, it is sold online as a research compound, and nothing in the published record supports using it as a supplement or treatment.

Most peptide hormones work by binding a receptor on the outside of a cell. The Khavinson group proposes something unusual for pinealon: that it is small enough to enter cells and even the nucleus, where it binds histone proteins or DNA itself and changes which genes are switched on [1]. In computer modeling, the group found possible binding sites for EDR in the control regions of genes such as CASP3, SOD2, APOE, PPARA and PPARG, which are involved in cell death, antioxidant defense and Alzheimer's disease [4].

In cell experiments, pinealon reduced the build-up of reactive oxygen species (unstable molecules that damage cells) in rat brain cells, immune cells and a nerve-like cell line, and reduced cell death under oxidative stress. It also delayed activation of ERK 1/2, a growth signaling pathway, and changed the cell cycle at higher doses, which the authors read as a sign it acts on the genome directly [2].

This gene-regulating model is the central claim of the bioregulator field, and it is not established outside it. Docking simulations show where a molecule could fit, not that it does so in a living brain, and the experiments supporting the model come from the same research network that proposed it [1][4].

No. Pinealon has never been approved by the FDA, and no application for approval has been reported. It is not one of the peptides named on the FDA's list of compounding substances with significant safety risks, but that list covers only substances nominated for review, and pinealon's absence says nothing about its safety [6].

Products sold online as pinealon are research chemicals. Nobody checks that the vial holds the stated peptide, at the stated amount, free of contamination. Because pinealon has never gone through a formal human safety program, there is no established profile of side effects, interactions or risks in pregnancy.

blocks.text: The animal results are consistent in direction: pinealon appears to protect nerve cells from oxidative stress and to preserve their connections in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease [2][3][4]. But these are small studies, mostly from one network of institutes. The 2015 aged-rat study came from a university in Rostov-on-Don, though one co-author was based in St. Petersburg, and in that study pinealon was the weaker of the two peptide preparations on oxidative markers [8]. Independent replication outside this circle is missing from the published record we reviewed.

The human side is very thin. The group's 2020 review says EDR improved memory in elderly patients, but it does not present a controlled trial [1]. Earlier reports on short peptides in older people appeared in Russian in the journal Advances in Gerontology, as reviews comparing peptide preparations rather than randomized trials of pinealon alone [5]. A search of ClinicalTrials.gov finds no registered trial of pinealon [7], and no placebo-controlled human trial has been published in an international journal.

sections.heading: Why is the evidence rated low?

blocks.text: Our scale rates compounds by human data. Pinealon has cell work, several rodent studies and a gene-binding hypothesis, but no human trial with a control group, a defined dose and a measured outcome. Animal protection under artificial stress, such as induced oxygen loss or a genetic Alzheimer's model, often fails to carry over to people [3][4][8]. Until a registered, placebo-controlled trial is run and published, claims about memory, sleep or longevity in humans are untested.

name: Plecanatide
evidenceNote: Approved for two adult constipation conditions on the basis of four 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trials enrolling more than 3,000 people in total.
summary: Plecanatide (Trulance) is a once-daily peptide tablet that draws fluid into the gut, FDA-approved for adults with chronic constipation or IBS-C.
keyTakeaway: Plecanatide is a 16-amino-acid copy of uroguanylin, a natural gut peptide, taken as a daily tablet. It acts on the lining of the intestine, which pulls water into the bowel and speeds transit, and almost none of it reaches the blood. The FDA approved it as Trulance in 2017 for chronic idiopathic constipation and in 2018 for IBS-C (the constipation-predominant form of irritable bowel syndrome). In the trials, about 21% of people on the approved dose met a strict durable response target, against 10% to 13% on placebo. Diarrhea is the main side effect. It carries a boxed warning against use in children.

blocks.text: Plecanatide is a synthetic peptide of 16 amino acids held in shape by two internal disulfide bridges [1]. It is a structural analog of human uroguanylin, a natural gut peptide, and like uroguanylin it switches on a receptor called guanylate cyclase-C [1]. In the published phase 3 report it was described as the first uroguanylin analog approved for chronic idiopathic constipation [2]. It is sold as Trulance by Salix Pharmaceuticals [1].

Unlike most peptide drugs, plecanatide is swallowed as a tablet. It does not need to be absorbed to work, because its target sits on the inner surface of the intestine. After a standard dose, levels in the blood were too low to measure in most samples [1].

It treats two common, long-lasting bowel conditions. Chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC) means persistent hard or infrequent stools without an identifiable cause. Irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C) combines constipation with recurring abdominal pain [1].

Plecanatide and its active breakdown product bind to guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C), a receptor on the cells lining the intestine. Activating GC-C raises levels of cyclic GMP (cGMP), a signaling molecule, both inside and outside those cells [1].

Inside the cells, cGMP opens the CFTR channel, which releases chloride and bicarbonate into the gut. Water follows, softening stool and speeding its passage. Outside the cells, higher cGMP has been linked in animal models to lower activity of pain-sensing nerves in the gut, which may explain the pain relief seen in IBS-C [1].

Because the drug works from inside the gut, it does not need to reach the bloodstream, and the label reports negligible systemic availability after a standard dose [1]. Linaclotide, another approved constipation drug, acts on the same receptor and has its own entry in this library.

Yes. The FDA approved Trulance for adults with chronic idiopathic constipation on January 19, 2017, and added irritable bowel syndrome with constipation on January 24, 2018 [4]. It is a prescription medicine taken as a 3 mg tablet once a day, and the tablet can be crushed for people who have trouble swallowing [1].

blocks.text: Plecanatide is prescribed for adults with CIC or IBS-C [1]. Each condition was tested in two 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials. The main outcome was strict: a responder had to show sustained improvement for most of the 12 weeks, not just a better average [1].

For CIC, a responder needed at least three complete spontaneous bowel movements in a week, plus at least one more than at baseline, for at least 9 of the 12 weeks and at least 3 of the last 4 [1]. In the published CIC trial, plecanatide 3 mg also raised the number of complete spontaneous bowel movements by about 2.5 a week, compared with 1.2 on placebo [2]. For IBS-C, a responder had to report both a 30% drop in worst abdominal pain and at least one extra complete bowel movement a week in the same week, for at least 6 of the 12 weeks [3].

These response rates mean most people in the trials did not meet the strict target on either plecanatide or placebo, and the gain from the drug was roughly 7 to 12 percentage points [1]. Improvement in bowel movement frequency was seen as early as the first week [1].

Diarrhea is the main side effect. In the CIC trials it affected 5% of people on plecanatide and 1% on placebo, and in the IBS-C trials 4.3% versus 1% [1]. Most cases began in the first four weeks. Severe diarrhea occurred in 0.6% to 1% of people taking the drug, sometimes within the first day [1]. About 2% of people in the CIC trials stopped because of diarrhea [1].

items: Boxed warning: plecanatide is not used in children under 6, because a single oral dose killed young mice through dehydration, and it is avoided in patients 6 to 17 years old; safety and effectiveness in anyone under 18 have not been established [1]
Not used in people with known or suspected mechanical bowel obstruction [1]
Less common effects included sinusitis, upper respiratory infection, bloating, gas, abdominal tenderness, and raised liver enzymes in a few patients [1]

blocks.text: If severe diarrhea occurs, the label says to suspend dosing and rehydrate the patient, since fluid loss is the main risk [1]. In the CIC trials, 4% of people on plecanatide stopped because of any side effect, compared with 2% on placebo [1].

summary: PN-943 is an experimental oral peptide for ulcerative colitis that blocks gut-homing immune cells. Its phase 2 trial was mixed and development has stalled.
keyTakeaway: PN-943 is an experimental peptide pill from Protagonist Therapeutics designed to do what the injected antibody vedolizumab does: block α4β7 integrin, the molecule that lets certain immune cells home into the gut wall. It was tested in ulcerative colitis. In the 12-week phase 2 IDEAL trial, the higher 450 mg twice-daily dose missed the main goal; the 150 mg dose reached remission in 27.5% against 14.5% on placebo, a gap that was not statistically significant overall. Protagonist has said it will not put further internal resources into the program. PN-943 is not FDA-approved and is not available outside trials.

blocks.text: PN-943 is an investigational peptide taken by mouth, developed by Protagonist Therapeutics for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the group of conditions that includes ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. The company describes it as a gut-restricted antagonist of α4β7 integrin, meaning it is built to act in the intestine rather than throughout the body [4].

Its clinical testing centered on moderate to severe ulcerative colitis [2], a long-term disease in which the lining of the colon becomes inflamed and ulcerated. It has never been sold, and it is not available outside clinical trials.

A subset of memory T cells, a kind of white blood cell, carry a surface protein called α4β7 integrin. It works like a key that fits a docking molecule, MAdCAM-1, found mainly on the inner walls of blood vessels in the gut. When the two connect, the T cells slip out of the bloodstream into the intestinal tissue, where in IBD they help sustain inflammation [5].

Vedolizumab (Entyvio), an approved antibody given by infusion or injection, blocks this same connection and is used for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease [5]. PN-943 aims for the same effect with a pill. Because peptides are usually broken down in the gut, Protagonist engineers structurally constrained peptides meant to survive oral delivery [4].

An earlier oral α4β7 peptide from the same company, PTG-100, offered a hint about how this could work. In mice it reached high levels in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, and in a phase 2a trial its apparent benefit came at doses that did not fully occupy the receptor in blood, suggesting that local action in the gut was what mattered [1]. That study initially missed its own primary endpoint and showed efficacy only after a blinded re-reading of the endoscopy videos [1].

No. PN-943 has completed only phase 2 testing. When the IDEAL results came out in April 2022, Protagonist said it planned a phase 3 study of the 150 mg dose [3]. That trial did not happen. The company's annual reports say it finished the phase 2 trial in early 2023, deprioritized further work that year, and does not intend to dedicate further internal resources to clinical development or manufacturing for PN-943 [4].

blocks.text: IDEAL was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial comparing PN-943 at 450 mg or 150 mg twice daily with placebo, with clinical remission at week 12 as the primary measure [2]. Topline data covered 159 patients with moderate to severe disease [3].

The higher 450 mg dose did not meet the primary endpoint. Results were better at the lower dose, an unusual pattern for a drug: 27.5% of patients on 150 mg reached clinical remission, against 14.5% on placebo. That 13-point difference had a p-value of 0.08, short of the usual threshold for statistical significance. In the subgroup who had never taken a biologic drug, the gap was 16 points and reached significance. The company reported significant improvements on histology (tissue under the microscope) and endoscopy at 150 mg, and side effects at that dose similar to placebo [3].

blocks.text: The predecessor compound gives the only peer-reviewed human data on this approach from the same developer. In its phase 2a trial, people with moderate to severe ulcerative colitis took PTG-100 at 150, 300 or 900 mg once daily, or placebo, for 12 weeks. It was safe and well tolerated in both the healthy-volunteer and patient studies, but its efficacy signal depended on a re-read of endoscopy findings rather than the original analysis [1].

These are topline figures released by the company and reported by the medical press. A full peer-reviewed report of the trial has not been located, so details such as the exact remission definition, dropout rates and adverse event counts cannot be checked [2][3]. With one mixed phase 2 trial and no further development, PN-943's effect in ulcerative colitis remains uncertain.

name: Polymyxin B / Colistin
alsoCalled: Colistin (polymyxin E), colistimethate sodium, Coly-Mycin M
evidenceNote: Both drugs have been in use since the 1950s, before modern trial standards, and their labels rest on that older evidence. Recent randomized trials and a 2019 international consensus guideline now shape how they are used against resistant bacteria.
summary: Polymyxin B and colistin are old peptide antibiotics that break open bacterial membranes, now a last resort for resistant infections. Hard on the kidneys.
keyTakeaway: Polymyxin B and colistin (polymyxin E) are closely related ring-shaped peptide antibiotics made by soil bacteria. They became available in the 1950s, faded because of kidney and nerve toxicity, and returned as a last-line option for gram-negative infections resistant to almost everything else. Both are FDA-approved by injection, and polymyxin B is also a common ingredient in first-aid ointments. Evidence on how best to use them is still thin: a 2018 randomized trial in 406 patients found that adding meropenem to colistin did not improve outcomes. Resistance that spreads between bacteria on plasmids was first reported in 2015.

sections.heading: What is polymyxin B, and what is colistin?

blocks.text: The polymyxins are a small family of peptide antibiotics made by soil bacteria. Polymyxin B is a mix of two closely related forms, B1 and B2, produced by the bacterium Bacillus polymyxa [1]. Colistin, also called polymyxin E, is a sister compound from the same family [3]. Both act as surface-active agents, meaning they behave somewhat like a detergent on bacterial membranes [2].

Colistin is usually given as colistimethate sodium, an inactive precursor (prodrug) that the body converts to colistin, sold in the United States as Coly-Mycin M [2]. Polymyxin B is given directly in its active form [1]. Both became available in the 1950s, before modern drug development rules, which is why their dosing information was long confusing and outdated [3].

Gram-negative bacteria wrap themselves in an extra outer membrane anchored by a fatty molecule called lipid A. Polymyxins penetrate and disrupt the bacterial membrane, making it leaky until the cell dies [1][2]. They kill almost all gram-negative rods, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella, and E. coli, but have no effect on gram-positive bacteria, fungi, or Proteus [1].

Until 2015, every known form of polymyxin resistance came from mutations in the bacterium's own chromosome, which could not easily pass to other strains [5]. In 2015, researchers in China found mcr-1, a gene carried on a plasmid (a mobile loop of DNA that passes between bacteria), which adds a chemical group to lipid A and made colistin useless in a mouse infection model [5]. It turned up in 15% of raw meat samples, 21% of animals, and 1% of hospital patients tested, raising concern that the last line of defense could spread its own failure [5].

sections.heading: Are polymyxin B and colistin FDA-approved?

blocks.text: Yes. Polymyxin B for injection is FDA-approved, labeled as a drug of choice for urinary tract, meningeal, and bloodstream infections caused by susceptible Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and for some other serious infections when less toxic drugs cannot be used [1]. Colistimethate injection is approved for acute or chronic infections due to susceptible gram-negative bacilli, particularly Pseudomonas [2]. Both are prescription drugs given in hospital.
Polymyxin B is also sold over the counter in triple-antibiotic first-aid ointments, alongside bacitracin and neomycin, to help prevent infection in minor cuts, scrapes, and burns [6].

In practice, injectable polymyxins are reserved for infections caused by gram-negative bacteria resistant to safer drugs, such as carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. A 2019 consensus guideline, endorsed by infectious disease and pharmacy societies in the United States and Europe, describes them as salvage therapy for otherwise untreatable infections and gives the first agreed rules for choosing between them, dosing, and preventing kidney failure [3].
Colistin and carbapenem antibiotics reinforce each other in lab tests, so doctors often give them together [4]. The AIDA trial tested whether that helps patients.

rows: 406 adults with serious carbapenem-resistant gram-negative infections, mostly A. baumannii, in Israel, Greece, and Italy
Clinical failure at 14 days: 79% on colistin alone versus 73% on colistin plus meropenem, not a significant difference [4]

blocks.text: Adding meropenem did not improve outcomes for Acinetobacter infections and raised the rate of diarrhea (27% versus 16%), although mild kidney injury was somewhat less common [4]. The trial was too small to settle the question for other bacteria [4]. Polymyxin B can also be injected into the spinal fluid for meningitis, because it does not cross into the brain from the blood, and applied to the eye for Pseudomonas eye infections [1].

Kidney and nerve toxicity are the reasons these drugs fell out of use for decades. The polymyxin B label carries a boxed caution that kidney function must be measured carefully and doses reduced when it is impaired, and that falling urine output or rising blood urea are signals to stop [1]. Kidney injury from colistimethate appears to be dose-dependent and reversible after the drug is stopped [2].

items: Kidney damage, with protein and casts in the urine and rising waste levels in the blood [1]
Nerve effects: numbness or tingling around the mouth and in the limbs, dizziness, slurred speech, blurred vision, and drowsiness [1][2]
Muscle weakness from blocked nerve signals, which can stop breathing, especially soon after anesthesia or muscle relaxants [1]
A kidney tubule disorder causing low potassium and metabolic alkalosis, reported with intravenous polymyxins [1][2]
Fever, hives, itching, and rarely anaphylaxis; pain at injection sites [1][2]

blocks.text: The labels warn against combining polymyxins with other drugs that harm the kidneys or nerves, such as aminoglycoside antibiotics, and against giving polymyxin B and colistin together [1]. People on colistimethate are told not to drive or operate machinery while nerve symptoms persist [2].

name: Pramlintide
evidenceNote: FDA-approved in 2005 after randomized, placebo-controlled trials in more than 4,000 insulin-treated people with diabetes of either type.
summary: Pramlintide (Symlin) is an FDA-approved copy of the hormone amylin, injected at meals alongside insulin in both types of diabetes.
keyTakeaway: Pramlintide is a lab-made version of amylin, a hormone the pancreas normally releases with insulin at meals. The FDA approved it in 2005 as Symlin for adults with either type of diabetes who already inject mealtime insulin yet remain above their glucose goals. Injected before meals, it slows stomach emptying, lowers glucagon and increases fullness; in year-long trials HbA1c fell by roughly 0.6 to 0.7 points from baseline and weight dipped slightly. It carries a boxed warning for severe low blood sugar. FDA records now list Symlin vials as discontinued and the pens with a marketing end date of January 2027.

blocks.text: Pramlintide is a 37-amino-acid synthetic peptide modeled on human amylin, a hormone made by the same beta cells in the pancreas that make insulin. It differs from human amylin at three positions, numbers 25, 28 and 29, where the amino acid proline has been swapped in [1].
Its brand name is Symlin, supplied in the US as the SymlinPen by AstraZeneca, and the FDA classed it as a new molecular entity when it was approved [1][2].

In a healthy person, amylin and insulin are released together when food arrives, and both rise and fall on the same schedule. People with type 1 diabetes make almost none of either, and people with type 2 diabetes make less of both in response to meals [1]. Insulin injections replace one hormone but not the other.

Amylin works on several fronts to keep glucose from spiking after a meal. It slows gastric emptying (the pace at which the stomach passes food on to the intestine) without reducing how much is ultimately absorbed. It suppresses glucagon, a hormone that would otherwise tell the liver to release more glucose. It also signals appetite centers in the brain, so people feel satisfied sooner and tend to eat less [1]. Pramlintide reproduces these effects in human studies [1].
It is short-lived. In healthy people its half-life is about 48 minutes, which is why it is injected before each major meal rather than once a day [1].
Yes. The FDA approved Symlin on March 16, 2005, as a new molecular entity [2]. The most recent labeling supplement on file dates from December 2019 [2].

FDA's own databases show the product leaving the US market. Drugs@FDA lists all three Symlin products under the original application as discontinued [2], and the two SymlinPen listings in FDA's National Drug Code directory carry a marketing end date of January 31, 2027 [3]. The approval itself has not been withdrawn for safety reasons in any record we found.

blocks.text: Pramlintide is meant to be used together with mealtime insulin, in either type of diabetes, when well-managed insulin therapy has still not brought glucose to target [1]. It is not a replacement for insulin, and it is not mixed in the same syringe, because combining them alters how both are absorbed [1]. The label limits it to people who can follow careful glucose monitoring and insulin adjustment under a clinician experienced with insulin, supported by diabetes educators [1].

Across its controlled trials, 2,333 people with type 1 diabetes and 1,852 with type 2 diabetes received it [1]. In a 52-week type 1 trial of 480 patients, pramlintide lowered HbA1c (average blood glucose over about three months) by 0.67 points from baseline by week 13, without weight gain or an overall rise in severe hypoglycemia [4]. In a 52-week type 2 trial of 656 insulin-treated patients, the highest regimen tested cut HbA1c by 0.68 points at 26 weeks and 0.62 at 52 weeks, more than placebo, and also improved weight [5].

blocks.text: The most serious risk is severe hypoglycemia, low blood sugar that needs another person's help to treat, which is the subject of the drug's boxed warning. The risk is highest in type 1 diabetes, and when it happens it appears within three hours of an injection [1]. The label ties safe use to choosing patients carefully, teaching them well and lowering mealtime insulin when pramlintide is started [1].

Nausea is the most common side effect. In pooled type 1 trials it affected 48 percent of people on pramlintide against 17 percent on placebo, and loss of appetite affected 17 percent against 2 percent [1]. Vomiting and headache were also more common than on placebo. Because it slows stomach emptying, it can delay the absorption of pills taken at the same time [1].

name: PT-141
evidenceNote: The molecule has two large phase 3 trials, but only in premenopausal women with low sexual desire using the approved injection. For men and every other use, the human data are small trials, and products sold as PT-141 have never been studied at all.
summary: PT-141 is the lab code for bremelanotide. The molecule is FDA-approved as Vyleesi for one group of women; vials sold online as PT-141 are not.
keyTakeaway: PT-141 is the development name for bremelanotide, a peptide that switches on melanocortin receptors in the brain. Made to drug standards it is Vyleesi, approved by the FDA in 2019 for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized low sexual desire. In the two phase 3 trials the gain over placebo was modest, and about 40% of women had nausea. Products sold online as PT-141 are not that approved drug, have not been checked for identity or purity, and the approved label does not cover men at all.
