blocks.text: PT-141 is the code name Palatin Technologies gave to bremelanotide while the drug was in development. It is a small ring-shaped peptide modelled on alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), one of the body's own melanocortin signals, and it binds the receptors that hormone uses [1].

Today the name lives on mainly in the online peptide market, where vials and sprays labelled PT-141 are sold as research chemicals. The identical molecule, manufactured and tested as a medicine, is the prescription injection Vyleesi [1]. This entry covers the unapproved PT-141 products; the approved drug has its own page under bremelanotide.

Palatin first described PT-141 as a treatment for sexual dysfunction in both sexes. Its early reports came from rats, monkeys and small groups of men, before the program narrowed to women with low desire and moved to an injection under the skin [2][1].

items.text: Palatin reports that PT-141 produces erections in rats and monkeys and a quick, dose-related rise in erectile activity in healthy men and men with erectile dysfunction [2].
A crossover study gives one nasal dose to 18 premenopausal women with arousal disorder and finds more reports of moderate or high desire than with placebo [8].
A trial in 342 men whose erectile dysfunction had not responded to sildenafil reports a benefit from a nasal spray. The journal later placed an expression of concern on the paper [7].
The two RECONNECT phase 3 trials run in premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder [4].
The FDA approves bremelanotide as Vyleesi, with AMAG Pharmaceuticals holding North American rights [1][3].

blocks.text: Bremelanotide is an agonist (a molecule that switches a receptor on) at several melanocortin receptors. The label ranks its potency as MC1R first, then MC4R, MC3R, MC5R and MC2R, and says the MC1R and MC4R actions matter most at the doses used [3]. MC4R is found on nerve cells across the brain, which is why the drug is thought to act on desire centrally rather than on blood flow, the route sildenafil takes [3][1].

The label is plain that the exact way it improves low desire in women is unknown [3]. One early study fits a brain-based effect: a single dose raised the desire women reported but did not change measured genital blood flow during erotic video [8]. MC1R sits on pigment cells, which helps explain the patches of darkened skin seen with repeated dosing.

Not under that name. The only approved form of the molecule is Vyleesi, a 1.75 mg autoinjector used under the skin as needed, at least 45 minutes before sexual activity [3]. It is approved for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD): low desire that started after a period of normal desire, happens in every situation, causes distress, and is not explained by another illness, a relationship problem or a medicine [3].

The label states it is not indicated for postmenopausal women, for men, or to enhance sexual performance. It also caps use at one dose in 24 hours and advises against more than eight doses a month, partly because of its effect on blood pressure [3]. Vials sold online as PT-141 carry none of that oversight: they are labelled for research, are not made under drug manufacturing rules, and nobody outside the seller has verified what they contain.

The strongest data come from RECONNECT, two identical 24-week phase 3 trials that randomized 1,267 premenopausal women with HSDD to bremelanotide 1.75 mg or placebo [4]. Women on the drug improved more on a desire score and reported less distress about low desire, with pooled differences of 0.35 and 0.33 points against placebo. Nausea, flushing and headache each affected at least 10% of the drug group in both trials [4].

rows: Desire score up 0.35 and distress score down 0.33 versus placebo [4]
18 premenopausal women with arousal disorder, one nasal dose
More women reported moderate or high desire; no change in genital blood flow [8]
342 men with erectile dysfunction not helped by sildenafil
33.5% versus 8.5% had a positive response; paper now under an expression of concern [7]

blocks.text: How much those score changes mean in daily life is disputed. An independent reanalysis argued that the desire and distress scales used had little validation in women with HSDD, that eight of the eleven outcomes registered for the trials had gone unpublished, and that on those outcomes the effects ranged from nothing to small [6].

For men, the evidence is thin. The early work was small and run by the developer, and the one larger trial in men now carries a formal expression of concern from its journal [2][7]. No regulator has approved the molecule for erectile dysfunction or for male desire.

Safety data come from about 3,500 people across 43 studies. In the pooled phase 3 trials, nausea affected 40.0% on bremelanotide against 1.3% on placebo, flushing 20.3% against 1.3%, and headache 11.3% against 1.9% [5]. Darkened skin patches were rare at labelled use but appeared in more than a third of people given up to 16 daily doses in a row [5]. Blood pressure rose by up to 6 mmHg systolic after each dose, peaking two to four hours later, and the drug is contraindicated in uncontrolled high blood pressure or known heart disease [3].

Online PT-141 is usually sold as freeze-dried powder for injection or as a nasal spray. The nasal route was used in the early trials but is not how the approved product is given, so the trial results on the injection do not transfer to a spray of unknown strength [8][3]. Repeated daily use, which no label permits, is the pattern that produced skin darkening in more than a third of participants in one study [5].

The practical gap is quality, not chemistry. The trials tested a sterile drug of known dose. A research vial may be under or over strength, contaminated, or a different peptide, and any benefit has only been shown in premenopausal women with HSDD [3][4].

name: Retatrutide
class: GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptor triple agonist
evidenceNote: Three large phase 3 randomized trials (TRIUMPH-1, TRIUMPH-2 and TRIUMPH-3) plus a phase 2 trial all compared retatrutide against placebo. It is rated on that human data; it is still unapproved, and long-term heart outcomes are not settled.
summary: Lilly's once-weekly triple-hormone injection for obesity. Phase 3 trials showed up to 25% weight loss at 80 weeks; it is not FDA-approved yet.
keyTakeaway: Retatrutide is an experimental weekly injection from Eli Lilly that acts on three hormone receptors at once: GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon. In the TRIUMPH-1 phase 3 trial, adults with obesity on the highest dose lost an average of 25.0% of body weight over 80 weeks, against 3.9% on placebo. It is not FDA-approved; Lilly plans to file in early 2027. The FDA has said compounded versions do not qualify under compounding law, so retatrutide sold online is an unapproved product of unknown content.

blocks.text: Retatrutide is an investigational peptide drug made by Eli Lilly, tested under the code LY3437943. It is given once a week as a subcutaneous injection (under the skin) and is being developed mainly for obesity, with further studies in type 2 diabetes, knee osteoarthritis, sleep apnea and fatty liver disease [1].

What sets it apart from semaglutide and tirzepatide is its reach. Semaglutide acts on one gut hormone receptor and tirzepatide on two; retatrutide adds a third, the receptor for glucagon. For that reason it is often described as a triple agonist (a drug that switches on three receptors) [1].

The molecule is built to mimic three hormones the body already makes. GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide 1) and GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) are released from the gut after a meal; they help the pancreas release insulin, slow the stomach, and signal fullness to the brain. Glucagon, made in the pancreas, is better known for raising blood sugar, but it also increases energy expenditure and pushes the liver to burn stored fat [1].

Combining all three in one injection is meant to pair the appetite effect of the gut hormones with the fat-burning effect of glucagon, while the insulin-releasing action of GLP-1 and GIP offsets glucagon's tendency to raise blood sugar. The liver results fit this picture: in a phase 2 substudy, liver fat fell sharply, and the drop tracked weight loss and better insulin sensitivity [2].

No. Retatrutide is not approved for any use in the United States or elsewhere. In July 2026, after two more phase 3 trials met their goals, Lilly said it was finishing the manufacturing section of its application and planned to submit a Biologics License Application to the FDA in the first quarter of 2027 [3]. A decision would follow the FDA review, so a prescription product is not expected before then.

Pharmacies cannot legally fill the gap. In September 2025 the FDA warned companies selling compounded retatrutide that the drug is not on either bulk substance list that compounders may draw from, is not part of any approved drug, and has no official monograph, so it fails the conditions of both section 503A and section 503B of federal law [4].

The first large test was a 48-week phase 2 trial in 338 adults with obesity or overweight. On the 12 mg dose, weight fell 24.2% on average by week 48, compared with 2.1% on placebo, and 83% of that group lost at least 15% of their starting weight [1]. A substudy of 98 participants with fatty liver disease found that liver fat dropped by about 82% at 24 weeks on the two highest doses, and 86% of the 12 mg group reached a normal liver fat level, against none on placebo [2].
The phase 3 program, called TRIUMPH, then tested 4 mg, 9 mg and 12 mg doses over 80 weeks. Results published in 2026 confirmed the phase 2 findings in much larger groups [5][6][3].

blocks.text: Side effects followed the familiar pattern of this drug family. In TRIUMPH-2, diarrhea affected about a third of people on the two higher doses versus 13% on placebo, and nausea reached 28% on 12 mg versus 8%. Low blood pressure and dysesthesia (unusual skin sensations such as tingling) were also more common on retatrutide, and stopping treatment because of side effects was more frequent on the 9 mg dose (12%) than on placebo (5%) [6]. In phase 2, heart rate rose with dose and peaked around week 24 before easing [1].

One question remains open. TRIUMPH-3 enrolled people with established heart disease, but too few heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths occurred to show a difference either way; the hazard ratio was 1.12 with a confidence interval running from 0.64 to 1.96 [3]. Lilly reported that 13.5% of the 12 mg group in that trial stopped because of side effects, compared with 4.8% on placebo [3].

Vials labeled retatrutide are widely marketed online as research chemicals or through telehealth sites. None of these products comes from Lilly, and none has been reviewed for purity, strength or sterility. The FDA has said there are no approved applications for such products and treats them as unapproved and misbranded drugs [4].

The trial results above were obtained with Lilly's own drug, gradual dose increases, and medical monitoring. They say nothing about what a grey-market vial contains, which is the central safety problem with these products.

name: Rusfertide
evidenceNote: Rusfertide was FDA-approved in August 2026 on the strength of VERIFY, a 293-person randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, backed by the earlier randomized REVIVE trial.
summary: A weekly injected peptide that copies the iron hormone hepcidin to curb red blood cell overproduction in polycythemia vera. FDA-approved as Mimrylo in 2026.
keyTakeaway: Rusfertide is a lab-made peptide that copies hepcidin, the hormone that controls how much iron reaches the blood. By rationing iron to the bone marrow, it slows the excess red blood cell production of polycythemia vera, a blood cancer that thickens the blood. The FDA approved it as Mimrylo on August 28, 2026, the first hepcidin mimic for the disease. In the phase 3 VERIFY trial, 77% of people on rusfertide needed no blood removal in the final 12 weeks, against 33% on placebo. Injection site reactions, anemia, and a rise in platelets are the main risks.

blocks.text: Rusfertide is an injectable peptide that copies the action of hepcidin, the body's main iron-regulating hormone [3]. It was developed by Protagonist Therapeutics under the code PTG-300 [3][6], and Takeda holds the approval for the brand Mimrylo [2]. It is used for polycythemia vera (PV), a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm (a blood cancer that starts in the bone marrow) in which the marrow makes too many red blood cells [2][3].

Excess red cells thicken the blood and raise the risk of clots, stroke, and heart attack, so a central goal of PV care is keeping hematocrit, the share of blood made up of red cells, below 45% [2]. That usually means phlebotomy, the regular removal of blood, often alongside drugs that suppress the marrow [2]. Rusfertide gives doctors a way to hold hematocrit down with far fewer of those sessions.

Red blood cells need iron, which is moved out of gut and storage cells into the blood by a transporter protein called ferroportin. Hepcidin is the hormone that shuts this transporter down [3]. Rusfertide acts like extra hepcidin: it blocks ferroportin, so less iron reaches the marrow, and the marrow makes fewer red cells, lowering hematocrit [1][5].

This approach does not target the faulty marrow cells that drive PV; it starves their output of a raw material [5]. In healthy volunteers, single injections caused dose-dependent drops in blood iron and in transferrin saturation, a measure of how much iron is circulating [6]. In an open-label study of 20 patients, rusfertide also improved markers of iron deficiency, such as ferritin, while keeping hematocrit under 45%, and none needed phlebotomy during treatment [5].

Yes. The FDA approved Mimrylo on August 28, 2026, for adults with polycythemia vera, after a priority review [2]. The agency called it the first approved PV treatment that mimics hepcidin [2]. The labeled indication is the treatment of erythrocytosis (too many red blood cells) in adults with PV [1].

items.text: Phase 2 trial in hereditary hemochromatosis shows rusfertide can prevent iron buildup without phlebotomy [7].
REVIVE phase 2 results in PV are published in the New England Journal of Medicine [3].
VERIFY phase 3 results published: 77% vs 33% response with rusfertide vs placebo [4].
FDA approves Mimrylo for erythrocytosis in adults with PV [2].

blocks.text: Rusfertide is prescribed to control red blood cell counts in adults with PV [1]. It is injected under the skin once a week, starting at 19 mg and adjusted to keep hematocrit below 45%, and patients may inject at home after training from a healthcare provider [1][2]. It can be used with or without the marrow-suppressing drugs many PV patients already take [4].

The approval rests on VERIFY, which enrolled 293 adults who needed frequent phlebotomies despite standard care and randomly assigned them to rusfertide or placebo for 32 weeks [4]. The main measure was whether a patient stayed free of phlebotomy eligibility from week 20 to week 32 [4].

rows: Response, no phlebotomy eligibility weeks 20 to 32

blocks.text: People on rusfertide also reported less fatigue and fewer PV symptoms on standard questionnaires [4]. The earlier REVIVE trial pointed the same way: during a 12-week randomized withdrawal phase, 60% of patients kept on rusfertide responded, against 17% switched to placebo, and phlebotomies fell from about 8.7 a year before treatment to 0.6 [3].

Injection site reactions are the most common problem, affecting roughly half of people on rusfertide in VERIFY compared with about a third on placebo injections [1]. They are usually managed with ice, steroid creams, antihistamines, or pain relievers [1]. Anemia was reported in 16% of treated patients against about 4% on placebo, which reflects how the drug works [1].

The label carries three warnings. Platelet counts can rise, so blood counts are checked every two to four weeks [1]. Injection site reactions are common [1]. And because animal studies showed malformations and fetal loss, the drug may harm a developing baby; people who can become pregnant are advised to use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 30 days after the last dose [1]. There are no listed contraindications [1]. No deaths were reported in VERIFY [4].

name: Secretin
evidenceNote: Synthetic human secretin has held FDA approval since 2004 for three diagnostic jobs: measuring pancreatic output, checking for gastrinoma, and guiding endoscopy. It is used once, during a test, rather than as an ongoing treatment.
summary: Secretin is the gut hormone that triggers bicarbonate release from the pancreas. Its synthetic form (ChiRhoStim) is FDA-approved for diagnostic tests.
keyTakeaway: Secretin is a 27-amino-acid hormone released by the small intestine when stomach acid arrives, signaling the pancreas to pour out bicarbonate-rich fluid. Its 1902 discovery gave medicine the idea of a hormone. A synthetic copy, ChiRhoStim, has been FDA-approved since 2004 to test pancreatic function, help diagnose gastrinoma, and help locate pancreatic duct openings during endoscopy. Side effects are rare: 9 of 531 trial patients had nausea. In the late 1990s it was promoted for autism, but 16 randomized trials found no benefit.

blocks.text: Secretin is a peptide hormone made in the lining of the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. When acid, fat or protein from the stomach reaches the duodenum, secretin is released into the blood and travels to the pancreas, telling it to send out fluid rich in bicarbonate, the same chemical as baking soda, which neutralizes stomach acid [1].

The drug version, ChiRhoStim, is synthetic human secretin with an amino acid sequence identical to the natural 27-amino-acid hormone [1]. It is not used to treat disease. Doctors give it during specialized tests to see how well the pancreas works, to look for a hormone-producing tumor called a gastrinoma, and to help find the pancreatic duct openings during endoscopy [1].

Secretin holds a special place in medical history. Writing in 1902, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling published their work on how the pancreas is told to secrete [3]. They showed the signal from the intestine travels as a chemical in the blood rather than along nerves, and named the substance secretin [2][3].

Within three years that finding had grown into the general concept of the hormone, and secretin is regarded as the first substance identified as one [9]. Over the following century it was purified, its structure worked out, chemically synthesized, and its receptor identified and cloned [2].

items.text: Bayliss and Starling describe a blood-borne signal from the intestine that drives pancreatic secretion [3].
A randomized trial in 60 children finds a single dose of synthetic secretin does not help autism [5].
FDA approves ChiRhoStim, synthetic human secretin, as a new molecular entity under priority review [7].
A Cochrane review of 16 trials concludes secretin is not an effective autism treatment [6].

blocks.text: Secretin binds secretin receptors on the cells that line the pancreatic ducts. That opens CFTR channels, the same chloride channels that are faulty in cystic fibrosis, and the cells release large volumes of bicarbonate-rich fluid. Nerve pathways through the vagus nerve also seem to take part, since blocking them blunts the response [1].

This predictable response is what makes it useful in testing. When secretin is injected and the fluid draining from the pancreas is collected, low volume or low bicarbonate points to a pancreas that is not working well. In people with a gastrinoma, secretin paradoxically makes the tumor release more gastrin, a hormone that drives acid production, which helps confirm the diagnosis [1]. Synthetic human secretin has an elimination half-life of about 45 minutes [1].

Yes. FDA approved ChiRhoStim on April 9, 2004, as a new molecular entity under priority review, and it remains a prescription product in two vial strengths [7]. It is given only by intravenous injection in a clinical setting [1].

Earlier products were made from pig secretin, including a synthetic porcine version called SecreFlo that FDA approved in 2002 and that is now listed as discontinued [8]. The approved uses of synthetic human secretin are diagnostic only. Promotion of secretin as a treatment for autism in the late 1990s never led to an approval, and later trials found no benefit [5][6].
ChiRhoStim is approved to stimulate secretions for three diagnostic purposes [1]:

items: Testing exocrine pancreatic function, the pancreas's output of digestive fluid and bicarbonate, in conditions such as chronic pancreatitis [1]
Helping diagnose gastrinoma, by measuring how much gastrin rises after injection [1]

Making the ampulla of Vater and the accessory papilla, where the pancreatic ducts drain, easier to find during endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), a procedure that examines the bile and pancreatic ducts [1]

blocks.text: Secretin has also been studied as an aid to MRI. In a phase 3 trial of 258 people with pancreatitis, adding synthetic human secretin to magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), an MRI scan of the ducts, let radiologists detect duct abnormalities with significantly higher sensitivity than standard MRCP, using ERCP as the reference [4]. That imaging use is not part of the ChiRhoStim label [1].

Side effects are uncommon. In an open-label trial of 531 patients aged 1 to 91, most given a single dose, the most frequent reactions were nausea in 9 people, vomiting in 3, and flushing and upset stomach in 2 each. The label lists no contraindications [1].

The main cautions concern test accuracy rather than safety. People with alcoholic or other liver disease can over-respond, which may hide pancreatic disease. A weak response can follow vagotomy (surgery cutting the vagus nerve), inflammatory bowel disease or anticholinergic medicines. Acid-reducing drugs, including proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers, can raise gastrin and falsely suggest a gastrinoma, so they are usually stopped before testing [1].

No, according to the trials. In 1998, publicity about a child with autism who seemed to improve after a single secretin dose led thousands of families to seek it [5][6]. A 1999 double-blind trial in 60 children found no significant improvement on any measure after a single dose compared with saline [5].

A Cochrane systematic review later pooled 16 randomized trials involving more than 900 children. It found consistent results showing no improvement in the core features of autism with single or multiple doses, and concluded secretin should not be given as an autism treatment [6].

name: Selank
evidenceNote: A few small clinical studies in Russia compared selank with benzodiazepines in people with anxiety, without placebo groups and from one research network. No trial meeting FDA or EMA standards has been reported.
summary: Selank is a seven-amino-acid peptide studied in Russia for anxiety. Human trials are small and unblinded, and it is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Selank is a seven-amino-acid peptide built by Russian scientists from tuftsin, a fragment of an immune protein, with a stabilizing tail added. Small Russian studies in 60 to 70 patients reported that it eased anxiety about as well as older tranquilizers, but none was placebo-controlled or done outside one research network. Lab work points to effects on enkephalin breakdown and GABA signaling. It is not FDA-approved, it is not covered by the 2026 HHS compounding policy, and products sold online are unverified.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Not approved; no recognized compounding pathway

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Proposed: slows enkephalin breakdown and modulates GABA receptors

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Animal studies and small, unblinded Russian anxiety trials

atGlance.label: Sold online
atGlance.value: As injectable powder and nasal sprays, outside any quality control

atGlance.value: Limited research

blocks.text: Selank is a synthetic heptapeptide, a chain of seven amino acids with the sequence Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro. It was developed at the Institute of Molecular Genetics of the Russian Academy of Sciences as a drug for anxiety that would avoid the dependence and memory problems of standard tranquilizers [2].

Its first four amino acids match tuftsin, a natural four-amino-acid peptide known for its effects on the immune system [13]. The extra Pro-Gly-Pro tail is there to make the molecule last longer. Russian researchers describe selank as a tuftsin analog, and it has been tested in rats for anxiety, alcohol and morphine withdrawal, and memory [12].

Two mechanisms have been proposed, both from lab and animal work. The first involves enkephalins, the body's own opioid-like peptides. A 2001 study found that people with generalized anxiety broke down enkephalins unusually fast, and that selank blocked the blood enzymes responsible in a dose-dependent way [1].

The second involves GABA, the brain's main calming signal and the target of benzodiazepines such as diazepam. In binding experiments on rat brain membranes, selank acted as a positive allosteric modulator of GABA receptors, meaning it changed how strongly GABA itself attached [2]. In rats, a single dose changed the activity of 45 of 84 nerve-signaling genes measured within an hour, in a pattern that tracked the changes caused by GABA itself [3].
None of these findings has been confirmed in a controlled human study that measured brain effects directly, so the mechanism remains a hypothesis.

No. Selank has never been submitted to the FDA, and no trial of it has been registered to US or European standards. A 2021 review of sedative drugs described selank as poorly studied and noted that it is sold to US consumers anyway, sometimes as a dietary supplement [8].

The FDA once placed selank acetate in Category 2 of its compounding list, the group of substances raising significant safety concerns. The agency cited a possible risk of immune reactions from clumped peptide and impurities, and said it lacked important safety information for selank given to people [9]. The nomination was later withdrawn, which means no pharmacy request is pending, not that the concerns were resolved [9].
Selank was not among the six peptides that HHS said in October 2026 it would allow licensed pharmacies to compound under conditions, a list that does include its sister peptide semax [15][11].

The clinical evidence consists of a handful of Russian studies that compared selank with a benzodiazepine rather than with a placebo. The published summaries do not describe blinding, and the same group of investigators appears across them.

rows: 62 people with generalized anxiety or neurasthenia; selank (30) vs medazepam (32)
Similar anxiety relief; selank also eased fatigue [4]
60 people with phobic, anxiety, and somatoform disorders; selank vs phenazepam
Clear anxiety relief and mild cognitive effects, lasting a week after the last dose [5]
70 people; phenazepam alone (30) vs phenazepam plus selank (40)
Faster response and fewer benzodiazepine side effects such as sedation and memory problems [6]

blocks.text: These results are encouraging but weak. The groups were small, and without a placebo arm the studies cannot separate the drug's effect from expectation or natural improvement over time. Most papers are published in Russian, which has limited outside scrutiny. No large, randomized, placebo-controlled trial has been reported.

Quality is a separate concern. Belgian regulators who analyzed seized products in 2017 and 2018 identified selank and semax in two unknown, suspicious preparations, and an online search showed both freely sold as powder for injection or as nasal sprays [7].

sections.heading: What is the difference between selank and semax?

blocks.text: The two peptides come from the same Moscow institute and share the same Pro-Gly-Pro stabilizing tail, but their active fronts differ. Selank is built on tuftsin and is studied for anxiety [2]. Semax is built on a fragment of ACTH, the pituitary stress hormone, and Russian clinicians have used it in acute stroke; in rats it increased production of nerve growth factors such as BDNF and NGF after a blocked brain artery [10].

Their US status has also split. In July 2026 an FDA advisory committee voted 8 to 5 to recommend semax for compounding for migraine and related uses [14], and HHS then included intranasal semax in its October 2026 enforcement discretion policy [15][11]. Selank was not among the peptides voted on and has no comparable pathway.

name: Selepressin
evidenceNote: Selepressin was tested in two randomized, placebo-controlled trials, a 53-patient phase 2a study and the 868-patient SEPSIS-ACT trial. The larger trial was stopped for futility, showing no benefit on its primary or key secondary outcomes.
summary: Selepressin is an experimental IV drug designed to raise blood pressure in septic shock. Its large phase 2b/3 trial was stopped for futility.
keyTakeaway: Ferring Pharmaceuticals developed selepressin, an experimental blood-pressure drug, to treat septic shock. It is a modified form of vasopressin built to act only on the V1a receptor, which tightens blood vessels, and to skip the V2 receptor that controls water retention. A small early trial showed it could stand in for norepinephrine. But the 868-patient SEPSIS-ACT trial was stopped for futility: ventilator- and vasopressor-free days were 15.0 versus 14.5 on placebo, and 90-day mortality was nearly identical. It is not FDA-approved, and no further trials are registered.

atGlance.value: Not approved; development stopped, no trials active

atGlance.label: How it works

blocks.text: Selepressin is a synthetic peptide related to vasopressin, the body's own hormone for holding on to water and tightening blood vessels. It was developed by Ferring Pharmaceuticals as a treatment for septic shock, the stage of severe infection in which blood vessels relax so much that blood pressure collapses despite fluids [2][4].

In septic shock, intensive care teams use vasopressors to push blood pressure back up. The standard first choice is norepinephrine, a catecholamine (an adrenaline-like drug). It does not always work, and at high doses it can cause heart rhythm problems and other effects [1]. Selepressin was designed as a non-catecholamine alternative. It has only ever been given in clinical trials.

Natural vasopressin acts on several receptors. The V1a receptor sits on the smooth muscle of blood vessels and makes them contract, raising pressure. The V2 receptor in the kidney makes the body retain water. Selepressin was built to switch on V1a selectively [1].

The developers hoped that focusing on V1a would raise blood pressure while limiting fluid buildup and leaky blood vessels, a major problem in sepsis, and while sparing patients high catecholamine doses [1][3]. Experimental work had suggested selective V1a drugs might outperform vasopressin itself [3]. That reasoning was strong enough to justify a large trial, which is where the idea was tested on outcomes that matter to patients.

No. Selepressin has not been approved by the FDA or any other major regulator. Its pivotal trial was terminated for futility, and the ClinicalTrials.gov registry lists no newer studies of the drug [4].

items.text: Phase 2a trial in early septic shock registered [3].
SEPSIS-ACT, an adaptive phase 2b/3 trial, begins at 63 hospitals in five countries [1][4].
SEPSIS-ACT stopped for futility at the end of its first part; phase 2a results published the same month [1][3].
SEPSIS-ACT results published, showing no benefit over placebo [1].

blocks.text: The first randomized trial was small and encouraging. Among 53 patients in early septic shock, those given the middle dose of selepressin could keep a safe blood pressure without norepinephrine more often than those on placebo, needed far less norepinephrine over 7 days, and ended with a lower fluid balance [3]. A higher dose was dropped after one of two patients had the infusion stopped for possible safety reasons [3].

SEPSIS-ACT was designed to settle the question. It used an adaptive design, in which a statistical algorithm shifted patients toward the best-performing of three dose levels before a planned head-to-head with placebo [2]. The trial enrolled 868 adults needing norepinephrine at 63 hospitals in Belgium, Denmark, France, the Netherlands, and the United States, and was stopped for futility before the second part began [1].

None of these differences was statistically significant. Rates of heart rhythm problems (27.9% vs 25.2%), cardiac ischemia (6.6% vs 5.6%), and reduced blood flow to the gut or limbs were similar in both groups [1]. The early promise on blood pressure and norepinephrine use did not translate into patients coming off the ventilator or out of the ICU sooner, or into better survival.

The adaptive design was itself a response to history. Septic shock has a long record of treatments that looked promising in small studies and then failed in large ones, and the trial's planners built SEPSIS-ACT to test doses and efficacy in one program so that a weak drug could be stopped early [2]. In that sense the design did its job: it stopped a drug that was not helping at the end of part one, before the planned comparison with placebo.

sections.heading: How is selepressin different from vasopressin?

blocks.text: Vasopressin itself is an FDA-approved drug used in septic shock when catecholamines are not enough, and it acts on both V1 and V2 receptors. Selepressin was an attempt to keep the blood-vessel effect and drop the kidney water effect [1]. The SEPSIS-ACT result means that targeting V1a alone has not been shown to help patients, so vasopressin remains the version of this hormone used in intensive care.

name: Semaglutide
evidenceNote: Approved by FDA for type 2 diabetes, weight management, heart risk reduction, kidney protection in diabetes, and a form of fatty liver disease, each on the strength of large randomized trials.
summary: Semaglutide is an FDA-approved GLP-1 drug, given weekly by injection or daily by tablet, for type 2 diabetes, weight loss, heart, kidney, and liver disease.
keyTakeaway: Semaglutide is a long-acting copy of GLP-1, a gut hormone that raises insulin after meals and dampens appetite. Novo Nordisk sells it as Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for weight management. In the 1,961-person STEP 1 trial, weekly injections cut body weight by 14.9% over 68 weeks versus 2.4% on placebo, and in SELECT they lowered heart attacks, strokes, and heart deaths by 20%. Its labels carry a boxed warning about thyroid tumors seen in rodents. Compounded copies lost their shortage exemption in 2025.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Approved since 2017; sold as Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Activates GLP-1 receptors to raise insulin when glucose is high, slow the stomach, and curb appetite

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Type 2 diabetes, chronic weight management, heart risk reduction, diabetic kidney disease, and MASH with fibrosis

atGlance.label: How it's taken
atGlance.value: Weekly injection under the skin, or a daily tablet on an empty stomach

atGlance.label: Evidence strength
atGlance.value: FDA approved

blocks.text: Semaglutide is a lab-made peptide that matches human glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) at 94% of its sequence. Natural GLP-1 lasts only minutes in the blood. Semaglutide is changed in two ways that stretch that to about a week: it resists the enzyme DPP-4 that normally destroys GLP-1, and it binds tightly to albumin, the main carrier protein in blood, which slows its clearance by the kidneys [1].

One molecule now sits behind several branded products. Ozempic began as the once-a-week diabetes pen, and since early 2026 the name also covers a once-daily tablet that sits alongside Rybelsus, the original oral version [1][3]. Wegovy is the weight-management brand, sold as a weekly injection, a higher-dose Wegovy HD injection, and a daily 25 mg tablet [2][9]. The doses and indications differ by product, so the brands are not interchangeable.
Semaglutide entered the US market for diabetes and then expanded, one outcome trial at a time, into weight, heart, kidney, and liver indications.

items.text: First US approval, as the weekly Ozempic injection for type 2 diabetes [1].
The STEP 1 trial reports 14.9% average weight loss with the 2.4 mg weekly dose [4].
SELECT shows fewer heart attacks, strokes, and cardiovascular deaths in people with obesity and heart disease but no diabetes [5].
FLOW shows slower kidney decline in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease [6].
FDA declares the semaglutide shortage resolved, ending the main legal basis for mass compounding [10].
Wegovy injection gains accelerated approval for MASH with moderate to advanced liver scarring [2].
Wegovy tablets are approved for weight management and heart risk reduction [2].
FDA approves Wegovy HD, a 7.2 mg weekly dose, after a 54-day review [9].

blocks.text: Semaglutide switches on the GLP-1 receptor, the same target as the body's own hormone. In the pancreas, this boosts insulin release and lowers glucagon release, but only when blood glucose is elevated, so on its own it rarely drives sugar too low [1]. It also slows the rate at which food leaves the stomach, which is why the labels warn that it can change how other oral medicines are absorbed [2].

The weight effect comes mainly from reduced hunger and calorie intake. GLP-1 receptors sit in several brain areas that regulate appetite, and in animal studies semaglutide reached and activated neurons in those regions [2]. Because the elimination half-life is about one week, the drug stays in circulation for roughly five weeks after the last dose [1]. That long tail is why the Wegovy label advises stopping at least two months before a planned pregnancy [2]. How it lowers cardiovascular risk has not been established [2].

Yes. Semaglutide has been FDA-approved since 2017 and now holds approvals across three product lines: Ozempic injection [1], Rybelsus and Ozempic tablets [3], and Wegovy injection and tablets [2]. The MASH indication is an accelerated approval, which means it rests on liver biopsy improvements and can be withdrawn if a confirmatory trial fails to show clinical benefit [2].

Compounded semaglutide is not FDA-approved. Pharmacies were allowed to make copies while the drug was officially in shortage. FDA ruled the shortage resolved on February 21, 2025, the grace period for state-licensed pharmacies has since ended, and as of April 2026 semaglutide is on neither the shortage list nor the 503B bulks list [10].

items: Blood sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes, as Ozempic injection or Rybelsus and Ozempic tablets [1][3].
Fewer major cardiovascular events (heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death) in type 2 diabetes with established heart disease or high cardiovascular risk [1][3].
Slower loss of kidney function, and fewer cases of kidney failure and cardiovascular death, when type 2 diabetes comes with chronic kidney disease [1].
Long-term weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and in children 12 and older with obesity (injection only) [2].
Fewer major cardiovascular events in adults with established heart disease who also have obesity or overweight [2].
Noncirrhotic MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, an inflammatory fatty liver disease) with stage F2 to F3 fibrosis, injection only [2].

rows: 1,961 adults with obesity or overweight, no diabetes, 68 weeks
17,604 adults with heart disease and BMI 27 or higher, no diabetes
Major cardiovascular events 6.5% vs 8.0% (20% lower risk)
3,533 adults with type 2 diabetes and kidney disease

blocks.text: Digestive effects lead the list. On Ozempic, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and constipation each affected at least 5% of patients [1]. In STEP 1 these were mostly mild to moderate and faded over time, but 4.5% of people on semaglutide stopped because of them, against 0.8% on placebo [4]. The Wegovy label adds headache, fatigue, dizziness, reflux, and hair loss to the common list, and notes that altered skin sensation was more frequent at the higher HD dose [2][9].

Every semaglutide label carries a boxed warning because the drug caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents; whether this happens in humans is unknown, and the drug is contraindicated when medullary thyroid cancer runs in the patient or their family, or with MEN 2 syndrome [1][2]. Other listed risks include pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, kidney injury from dehydration, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, worsening diabetic eye disease, a faster heart rate, serious allergic reactions, and food being inhaled into the lungs during anesthesia [2].

name: Semax
evidenceNote: Human data come from small Russian stroke and cerebrovascular studies, mostly open-label or compared against non-randomized control groups. No large blinded trial has been run, and none has been registered outside Russia.
summary: Semax is a seven-amino-acid ACTH fragment used in Russia for stroke. Evidence in people is small and unblinded, and it is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: Semax is a synthetic heptapeptide built from a piece of ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) joined to a Pro-Gly-Pro tail. It is given as nasal drops in Russia, where it is used for stroke and other brain disorders. Rat studies show it raises BDNF and other nerve growth factors after brain injury. Human evidence is limited to small Russian studies, such as one comparing 30 treated stroke patients with 80 controls. It is not FDA-approved. Since October 2026, an HHS interim policy tolerates pharmacy compounding of intranasal semax on prescription while rulemaking continues; that is not an approval.

atGlance.value: Not approved; intranasal compounding tolerated under an interim HHS policy since October 2026

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Raises brain levels of BDNF and NGF, growth factors that help nerve cells survive, in rat studies

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Rat studies plus small, mostly unblinded Russian studies in stroke patients

blocks.text: Semax is a synthetic peptide of seven amino acids, Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro. Its first four residues copy positions 4 to 7 of ACTH, the pituitary hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol. The last three, proline-glycine-proline (PGP), form a short tail that has some activity of its own in rat studies [4]. Because it reproduces the general shape of the ACTH(4-10) region, it is usually described as an ACTH(4-10) analog [1].

Semax was developed by Russian researchers as a nootropic (a drug intended to support thinking) and a neuroprotective agent (one intended to limit damage to nerve cells), and the same research group still publishes much of the work on it [1]. It is approved for clinical use in Russia, where it has been given for ischemic stroke, the kind caused by a blocked artery [2][4].

Outside Russia, semax circulates as a research chemical. Chemists at Sciensano, the Belgian public health institute, who analyzed seized products in 2017 and 2018 found semax and selank and noted that both were freely sold online as nasal sprays and as powders for injection [3].

Most of what is known comes from rats. In rats with an artery to the brain tied off to mimic stroke, semax increased the transcription (gene activity) of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF), and their receptors in the damaged cortex. These growth factors help neurons survive and form new connections. The effect was specific to the injured tissue, while the Pro-Gly-Pro tail on its own produced broader, less targeted changes [4].

In other rat work, semax reduced anxiety-like behavior and normalized brain levels of serotonin and other monoamines (signaling chemicals) in animals exposed early in life to an antidepressant [1]. A 2018 Russian study in stroke patients reported that semax raised blood BDNF levels during rehabilitation, which fits the animal findings but does not by itself show better recovery [8].

In Russian practice semax is given through the nose, and the 2026 US compounding policy is limited to that route [6]. How much intact peptide reaches the human brain after nasal use has not been well measured.

No. Semax has never been approved by the FDA, and no company has run a trial of it for US approval. In its compounding safety review, the FDA said it had no, or limited, safety information for the proposed routes and flagged a possible risk of immune reactions from peptide clumping and impurities [9].

The picture shifted in 2026. On July 24, the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 5, with one abstention, to recommend adding semax to the 503A bulks list for migraine, cerebral ischemia, and trigeminal neuralgia [10]. FDA staff had opposed it, saying their review found insufficient evidence for those conditions [14], while supporters pointed to its use in Russia [2].

On October 30, HHS published an interim policy saying it would not act against pharmacies or physicians that compound semax and five other peptides while formal rulemaking continues [5][6]. For semax, the policy covers the free base form for intranasal use only [6]. The policy states that compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and can be revisited if a safety or quality problem appears [5].

The human studies were published in Russian journals and are small. Most were open-label, meaning patients and doctors knew who received semax, and several compared treated patients with separate control groups rather than randomizing them.

rows: 30 patients with acute ischemic stroke, compared with 80 conventionally treated controls
Some speeding of neurological recovery, especially of motor deficits, when semax was added to standard care
110 patients in early or late stroke rehabilitation, with or without semax
Higher blood BDNF levels that stayed raised through the study

blocks.text: These results help explain why semax is used in Russia, but they fall short of the evidence regulators usually require. Without randomization and blinding, improvements can reflect who was chosen for treatment or what investigators expected. The Belgian analysts went further, writing that to their knowledge neither semax nor selank had completed any clinical trials [3].

A larger Russian study of 187 patients with chronic cerebrovascular insufficiency (reduced blood flow to the brain) described semax as well tolerated with few side effects [13]. Studies of this size cannot detect uncommon harms, and the long-term effects of repeated use, especially of unregulated products sold online, are unknown.

sections.heading: What is the difference between semax and selank?

blocks.text: The two are often sold together because both are short synthetic peptides developed in Russia, both are offered online as nasal sprays, and both are marketed for the brain [3]. They come from different parent molecules and are promoted for different effects.

name: Sermorelin
evidenceNote: Sermorelin was once FDA-approved for children with growth hormone deficiency, but the uses it is sold for now, such as aging, body composition and sleep, rest on small, short studies of a few dozen adults or fewer.
summary: Sermorelin is a short copy of the hormone that tells the pituitary to release growth hormone. Once approved for children, its US approvals were withdrawn in 2009.
keyTakeaway: Sermorelin is the first 29 amino acids of GHRH, the brain hormone that prompts the pituitary to release growth hormone. The FDA approved it as Geref for testing pituitary function in 1990 and for children with growth hormone deficiency in 1997. The maker discontinued both in 2008, and the FDA later confirmed this was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. No sermorelin product is FDA-approved today, though compounding pharmacies and clinics still supply it, mostly for aging. In a 16-week study of 19 older adults, a close analog raised growth hormone and IGF-1 but increased lean mass only in men. It is prohibited in sport.

blocks.text: Sermorelin is a synthetic peptide matching the first 29 amino acids of human growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), the signal the hypothalamus sends to the pituitary gland to release growth hormone [2].

EMD Serono sold it in the United States as Geref [1]. Today sermorelin is sold through compounding pharmacies with a prescription, through anti-aging and wellness clinics, and through unregulated online sellers, whose products may be contaminated or mislabeled [5].

Sermorelin had two FDA approvals. The first, in December 1990, was a small ampule used as a diagnostic test of whether the pituitary could release growth hormone. The second, in September 1997, was a larger vial for treating idiopathic growth hormone deficiency in children with growth failure [1].

In 2008 EMD Serono told the FDA it was discontinuing both products and asked for the approvals to be withdrawn, which took effect in June 2009. After a 2012 citizen petition, the FDA reviewed its records and concluded in 2013 that Geref had not been withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness. That finding means a generic version could in principle be approved [1]. No other sermorelin product appears in the FDA's approved drug records.

blocks.text: Sermorelin binds GHRH receptors on growth hormone-producing cells in the pituitary and prompts them to release their stores, so growth hormone rises within minutes [2]. Growth hormone then drives the liver to make IGF-1, which carries out many of growth hormone's effects on tissue [3].

Sermorelin is often promoted for sleep, based on the observation that the biggest nightly growth hormone pulse coincides with deep, slow-wave sleep. A 2004 study tested the link in healthy young men by blocking their own GHRH overnight. Growth hormone release was suppressed by 93%, but the share of slow-wave sleep did not change, leading the authors to conclude GHRH is needed for the nighttime growth hormone surge but probably does not generate deep sleep [6].

Not at present. Both Geref approvals were withdrawn in 2009 at the maker's request, and no replacement product has been approved [1]. Sermorelin that is prescribed today comes from compounding pharmacies or from clinics and websites, outside any current FDA approval [5].

The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency lists sermorelin as prohibited in sport because it can boost muscle growth, endurance and recovery, and calls a therapeutic use exemption highly unlikely because better-established treatments for growth hormone deficiency exist [5].

The strongest human data come from its original use in children. A 1999 review found that a single intravenous dose of 1 microgram per kilogram worked as a fairly specific test for growth hormone deficiency, with fewer false positives than other stimulation tests. For treatment, limited data showed nightly injections under the skin raised growth speed in some prepubertal children over 12 months, though the increase was smaller than with injected growth hormone, and the effect on final adult height was never established [2].

Adult data are thin. In a 1997 study, 19 healthy adults aged 55 to 71 injected a close analog of sermorelin, [Nle27]GHRH(1-29), nightly for 16 weeks after a month of placebo. Growth hormone and IGF-1 rose in both sexes and skin got thicker. Lean body mass, insulin sensitivity, well-being and libido improved in men but not in women, and sleep quality did not change in either group [3]. A companion analysis of the same volunteers reported increases in several immune cell types [4].

blocks.text: These adult studies were small, single-blind, short and without a separate placebo group running in parallel. None measured outcomes such as fractures, strength, disability or survival, and none ran long enough to judge long-term risks of raising IGF-1. Side effects in the pediatric data were mostly facial flushing and injection-site pain [2], while the 1997 adult study reported a temporary rise in blood lipids [3].

name: Setmelanotide
evidenceNote: FDA approved for a handful of rare obesity disorders. The newest indication, acquired hypothalamic obesity, rests on a 52-week randomized placebo-controlled trial of 142 patients; the genetic indications rest on small open-label trials, which is normal for diseases this rare.
summary: A daily injection approved for rare forms of obesity caused by a broken brain appetite pathway, including hypothalamic obesity since March 2026.
keyTakeaway: Setmelanotide is a synthetic peptide that switches on the MC4 receptor, a brain switch that controls hunger and energy use. The FDA first approved it in 2020, sold as Imcivree, for obesity caused by rare genetic defects upstream of that receptor, then added Bardet-Biedl syndrome and, in March 2026, acquired hypothalamic obesity. In the hypothalamic obesity trial, BMI fell about 18% more than with placebo over a year. It does not treat common obesity, and darker skin and nausea are frequent side effects.

blocks.text: Setmelanotide is a lab-made peptide that mimics part of the body's own appetite control system. It is sold by Rhythm Pharmaceuticals as Imcivree, a daily injection for a small set of obesity disorders in which the brain's hunger signal is broken [1].

These are not ordinary weight problems. People with them often feel intense, constant hunger (called hyperphagia) from early childhood, and diet and exercise rarely hold their weight down. The label is explicit that the drug is not expected to work for common, polygenic obesity, which has many small genetic and lifestyle causes [1].

Deep in the brain, the hypothalamus reads leptin, a hormone made by fat tissue, and turns that signal into a message carried along a short chain of genes. POMC makes a precursor protein, PCSK1 cuts it into the active hormone, and that hormone lands on the MC4 receptor, which tells the body it has eaten enough and can burn energy [2]. A defect anywhere along that chain, including in the leptin receptor (LEPR) itself, leaves the MC4 receptor under-stimulated and hunger switched on [2].

Setmelanotide skips the broken links and activates the MC4 receptor directly [1]. It is about 20 times less active at two related receptors, MC3 and MC1 [1]. The MC1 receptor sits on pigment cells in the skin, and its activation explains why the drug darkens skin and moles regardless of sun exposure [1].

In acquired hypothalamic obesity, the chain is damaged by an injury to the hypothalamus or a loss of its function rather than by an inherited gene. The drug acts at the same receptor, downstream of the damage [1].

Yes. Setmelanotide was first approved in the United States in 2020 [1]. The label has since grown to cover Bardet-Biedl syndrome, a rare inherited condition, and children as young as 2 [1]. On March 19, 2026, the FDA added acquired hypothalamic obesity for patients aged 4 and older, the first approved treatment for that condition, and the European Commission authorized the same use [3].

blocks.text: It is prescribed to reduce excess weight and keep it off in three groups: people with a genetic test showing a harmful or uncertain variant in POMC, PCSK1, or LEPR; people with Bardet-Biedl syndrome; and people with obesity after damage to the hypothalamus [1]. Variants classed as benign do not qualify [1].

How a patient qualifies differs by group. Bardet-Biedl syndrome and hypothalamic obesity are diagnosed clinically, from symptoms and medical history, while the three gene-based uses require a genetic test that confirms a qualifying variant [1]. Dosing starts low and is raised over the first weeks, with separate schedules for young children and for severe kidney disease, and the label advises against use in end-stage kidney failure [1].

rows: BMI fell 15.8% on the drug and rose 2.6% on placebo, an 18.4-point difference [1]
POMC or PCSK1 deficiency, open-label, 1 year
8 of 10 lost at least 10% of body weight [1][2]
5 of 11 lost at least 10% of body weight [1][2]

blocks.text: Hunger dropped as well. In the POMC and LEPR trials the worst daily hunger score fell by about 27% and 44% [2], and in the hypothalamic obesity trial it fell by almost one point more than placebo on a 0 to 10 scale [1]. The effect depends on staying on the drug: when it was paused for four weeks in the genetic trials, patients regained about 5 kg on average, then lost weight again once it restarted [1].

Darker skin is the most distinctive effect. In the hypothalamic obesity trial, 58% of treated patients had skin, nail, or freckle darkening against 10% on placebo, and 15% had new or darker moles against 6% [1]. The label calls for a full skin check before starting and at intervals during treatment [1].

items: Nausea: 55% versus 25% on placebo in the hypothalamic obesity trial [1]
Vomiting: 38% versus 19% [1]
Injection site reactions: up to 96% of patients in the small genetic deficiency trials [1]
Spontaneous erections: about a quarter of male patients with Bardet-Biedl syndrome [1]

blocks.text: The label also warns about depression and suicidal thoughts, serious allergic reactions, and unwanted sexual arousal in both sexes; an erection lasting more than four hours needs emergency care [1]. Patients with hypothalamic damage can have fragile adrenal and fluid balance, and in that trial 5% had a serious episode of adrenal insufficiency, with sodium swings in those who also had diabetes insipidus [1].

name: Sincalide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 1976 as a diagnostic agent and still marketed, with a second version approved in 2022. It is a test drug given once during an imaging study, not a treatment.
summary: A synthetic eight-amino-acid piece of the gut hormone CCK, given by IV during scans to make the gallbladder contract and test how well it empties.
keyTakeaway: Sincalide is a synthetic copy of the last eight amino acids of cholecystokinin, the gut hormone that makes the gallbladder squeeze. Sold as Kinevac since 1976, it is a diagnostic drug: given by IV during imaging, it makes the gallbladder contract so doctors can measure how much bile it empties, and it is also used to collect pancreatic juice and speed barium through the bowel. A 60-minute infusion gives the most consistent readings, and a gallbladder ejection fraction under 38% is considered abnormal. Nausea and abdominal discomfort are common.

blocks.text: Sincalide is a laboratory-made octapeptide, a chain of eight amino acids, matching the C-terminal end of cholecystokinin (CCK) [1]. CCK is a natural digestive hormone, and because sincalide is its final eight amino acids it is often called CCK-8 [1].

It is a diagnostic drug rather than a treatment. Given by vein during an imaging test, it makes the gallbladder contract and empty, so doctors can see whether the organ is working normally [1]. It is sold as Kinevac by Bracco, and MAIA Pharmaceuticals sells an equivalent version [2][3].

Kinevac was approved in the United States in 1976 as a new molecular entity [2]. MAIA filed its own version, which the FDA rates as therapeutically equivalent to Kinevac, and received approval in November 2022 [3].

items.text: FDA approves Kinevac [2]
Multicentre study sets the standard 60-minute infusion and normal ejection fraction values [4]
FDA approves MAIA's sincalide for injection [3]
Kinevac label adds stronger warnings on anaphylaxis and a sulfite allergy contraindication [1]

blocks.text: Sincalide acts like the body's own CCK. Injected into a vein, it makes the gallbladder contract and shrink, emptying bile in much the same way as the body's own CCK does [1]. After a single 0.02 mcg/kg injection, the strongest contraction came within 5 to 15 minutes, and a drop in gallbladder size of at least 40% is generally treated as a satisfactory squeeze [1].

It has other effects on the digestive tract. It stimulates the pancreas to secrete, increases movement of the intestine, tightens the pylorus (the valve at the stomach outlet), and slows stomach emptying [1]. Given together with secretin, another gut hormone, it boosts the volume of pancreatic fluid and its output of bicarbonate and enzymes, which lets doctors analyse a sample to judge how the pancreas is working [1].

Yes. Kinevac was approved on July 21, 1976 and remains a prescription product [2]. MAIA's sincalide for injection was approved on November 22, 2022 [3]. Both are 5 mcg vials of powder mixed and given by vein [1][3].

All approved uses are diagnostic and limited to adults; safety and effectiveness in children have not been established [1]. Sincalide is not approved to treat gallbladder disease, digestive symptoms, or appetite, and it is not taken at home.
The label lists three uses in adults [1]:

items: Making the gallbladder contract during imaging, or to collect a concentrated bile sample from the duodenum for analysis of cholesterol, bile salts, and crystals [1]
Stimulating pancreatic secretion together with secretin before taking a duodenal sample to test enzyme activity and look at cells [1]
Speeding a barium meal through the small bowel, which shortens X-ray and fluoroscopy time and the radiation that comes with it [1]

blocks.text: One use is cholescintigraphy, often called a HIDA scan, a nuclear medicine test that tracks a radioactive tracer through the liver and gallbladder. A 2010 study in 60 healthy volunteers at four centres compared 15, 30, and 60-minute infusions of the same dose on separate days [4]. The 60-minute infusion gave the least variable results, and the lowest normal gallbladder ejection fraction (the share of bile the gallbladder pushes out) was set at 38% [4]. The authors recommended that method as the standard [4].

The label also describes infusing sincalide over 50 minutes for gallbladder studies or 30 minutes for barium studies, as an alternative to a rapid injection, to lower the chance of stomach side effects [1].

The most frequent side effects, seen in 20% or more of people, are abdominal discomfort or pain and nausea [1]. A fast injection can also bring on brief vomiting, cramping, dizziness, or flushing, which is why slower infusions are an option [1]. Vasovagal reactions, a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure that can cause fainting, have also been reported [1].

Each vial contains sodium metabisulfite, and serious allergic reactions including anaphylactic shock have occurred during or soon after a dose, so people with a known sulfite or sincalide allergy should not receive it [1]. It is also not used when the bowel is blocked [1]. In people with small gallstones, the contraction can push a stone into a bile duct [1]. Because it acts on smooth muscle, it may carry a risk of preterm labour or miscarriage in pregnancy [1].

summary: SLU-PP-332 is a lab compound that switches on ERR receptors and mimics parts of endurance exercise in mice. It has never been tested in humans.
keyTakeaway: SLU-PP-332 is a small synthetic molecule, not a peptide, designed at Saint Louis University to activate the estrogen-related receptors (ERRs) that drive muscle's response to aerobic exercise. In mice it raised endurance, energy expenditure, and fat burning, reduced fat mass in obese animals, and protected the heart in a heart failure model. No study in humans has been published or registered. It is not FDA-approved for any use, and athletes are covered by WADA's ban on unapproved substances. Products sold online as a "peptide" are unregulated research chemicals.

blocks.text: SLU-PP-332 is an experimental compound made by chemists and pharmacologists at Saint Louis University, which gives it the SLU in its name. It is a small molecule built around a naphthalene ring system, not a chain of amino acids, even though it is often sold alongside peptides [1][5]. The team first described it in 2023 as a pan-agonist of the estrogen-related receptors, meaning it switches on all three members of that receptor family [1].

It drew attention as a possible "exercise mimetic", a drug that would trigger some of the body's responses to training without the training. Several of its inventors hold shares in Myonid Therapeutics, a company developing medicines aimed at these receptors [1]. The group has since reported a second, chemically different compound, SLU-PP-915, which can be absorbed when swallowed [4].

Estrogen-related receptors (ERRα, ERRβ, and ERRγ) are proteins inside the cell nucleus that turn on genes. Despite the name, they do not respond to estrogen. They control genes for building mitochondria, burning fatty acids, and running the chemical cycles that produce energy, and muscle needs them to adapt to aerobic exercise [4]. Making drugs that activate ERRα had proved difficult, and SLU-PP-332 was reported as the first useful tool that reaches all three, with its strongest effect on ERRα [1].

In muscle cells it increased mitochondrial activity and oxygen use. In mice it shifted muscle toward type IIa fibers, which rely more on oxygen and resist fatigue, and switched on a set of genes normally seen after a bout of aerobic exercise [1]. The authors reported that activation of ERRα in particular was needed for the endurance gain [1]. The compound is not absorbed well by mouth, so in the later comparison study it was given by injection into the abdomen [4].

No. SLU-PP-332 is not approved by the FDA or by any other regulator for any use. A search of ClinicalTrials.gov finds no registered study of it in people [8]. A 2026 systematic review of the ERR agonists reached the same point: all the evidence is from animals and cells, and clinical trials are needed before anything can be said about humans [6].

For athletes, the World Anti-Doping Agency bans at all times any drug with no approval from a health regulator for human use, under its S0 class [7]. Its separate list of banned metabolic modulators already includes related exercise mimetics such as AICAR and GW1516 [7]. Anti-doping scientists have begun mapping how human liver enzymes break SLU-PP-332 down, so that tests can detect its use [5].
The published work is small in volume and comes almost entirely from one research network. All of it is preclinical.

Diet-induced obese mice and ob/ob mice
Higher energy use and fat burning, less fat gain, better insulin sensitivity [2]
Mice with heart failure from pressure overload

blocks.text: The obesity study used mice fed a high-fat diet and a genetic strain that overeats. In both, the compound behaved like training: it raised whole-body energy use and fatty acid oxidation and reduced the build-up of fat [2]. In the heart failure study, it activated a broad set of fat-burning and mitochondrial genes in heart muscle and largely normalized the heart's chemical profile, without changing how thick the heart wall grew [3].

What has not been studied matters as much. There are no human data on dose, blood levels, half-life, or side effects. ERRs act in many tissues. The 2026 review found no evident toxicity in the animal work, but those experiments were built to test benefit, not to serve as formal safety testing [6]. Mouse endurance and weight results often fail to carry over to people, which is why the authors themselves describe the compound as a chemical tool rather than a medicine [4].

Vials and capsules labeled SLU-PP-332 are sold online as "research use only" and marketed with the nickname "exercise in a pill." These are unregulated chemicals with no FDA review of what they contain, how pure they are, or whether injectable versions are sterile. Because the compound was shown to work poorly by mouth in mice, capsule products raise a further question about whether they would do anything at all [4]. No human study supports any dose that sellers suggest [6][8].

name: SLU-PP-915
class: Oral pan-ERR agonist (small molecule, not a peptide)

summary: SLU-PP-915 is an experimental exercise-mimicking drug that raised running endurance in mice. It has never been tested in people and is not FDA-approved.
keyTakeaway: SLU-PP-915 is a lab-made small molecule, not a peptide, that switches on estrogen-related receptors (ERRs), proteins that control how muscle and heart cells burn fuel. It was designed as an oral follow-on to SLU-PP-332, which mice do not absorb well by mouth. In mice it lengthened treadmill runs when given by mouth and improved heart pumping in a heart failure model. No human study exists, so its safety and effects in people are unknown. It is not FDA-approved, and anti-doping laboratories have already built tests to detect it.

blocks.text: SLU-PP-915 is an experimental drug candidate from a series of compounds built to switch on estrogen-related receptors, or ERRs. Despite the name, ERRs do not respond to estrogen. They are a family of three proteins (ERR alpha, beta and gamma) inside cells that turn on genes for mitochondria, the parts of a cell that convert fat and sugar into usable energy [4].

Chemists first described SLU-PP-915 in 2023, when it was labelled compound 10s in a new series of molecules built on a thiophene ring. Its most distinctive feature is a boronic acid group, which in lab tests made the molecule more resistant to breakdown by liver enzymes [1]. It is a small synthetic chemical, not a peptide, even though it is often sold alongside peptides online.
The compound is usually discussed as an exercise mimetic, a drug meant to reproduce some of the changes that endurance training causes in muscle, without the training itself.

When muscle is trained for endurance, ERRs help rebuild it to burn more fat and hold more mitochondria. SLU-PP-915 binds the ERRs directly and activates all three with roughly equal strength, which researchers call a pan-agonist profile [1]. In cell and mouse tissue, it raised the activity of known ERR target genes, including PGC-1 alpha, a master switch for building mitochondria, and DDIT4, a gene that rises after a bout of aerobic exercise [1].

In mouse muscle, those gene changes after a dose matched or exceeded the changes caused by treadmill running, depending on which muscle was examined, and the drug added to the effect of training when both were combined [2]. In the heart, the same research network found that ERR gamma was the main receptor responsible for the protective effects they observed [3].

ERRs are active in many organs, including the heart, liver and muscle [4]. A drug that turns them on throughout the body could have effects well beyond muscle, and none of those effects have been measured in people.

No. SLU-PP-915 is a preclinical research compound. No human trial has been registered or published, and the FDA has not reviewed it for any purpose. Its own developers describe it as a chemical tool for exploring what long-term ERR activation might do [2].

It is not a compounding ingredient either, so no licensed pharmacy can lawfully make it into a medicine. Products labelled SLU-PP-915 that are sold online as research chemicals have no verified identity, purity or dose.

Sport bodies have taken notice. In 2026 the German Sport University's anti-doping laboratory in Cologne mapped how human liver enzymes break SLU-PP-915 down, identifying seven metabolites so that testing labs can catch its use as a performance enhancer [5].
The research record is short and comes from one connected group of investigators. The key studies are summarized below.

rows: Activated all three ERRs and raised exercise-linked genes [1]
Mice with pressure overload heart failure
Better ejection fraction, less scarring, longer survival [3]
Longer running distance and time, by mouth or by injection [2]

blocks.text: The exercise study is the one most often quoted. Mice given SLU-PP-915 ran farther and for longer, by a similar margin to SLU-PP-332 when both were injected into the abdomen, and the effect held when SLU-PP-915 was given by mouth after adjusting for the amount that reached the blood [2]. The heart study tested both compounds in mice whose hearts were strained by narrowing the main artery. Both raised ejection fraction (the share of blood pumped out with each beat), reduced scar tissue and improved survival over six weeks, without changing heart muscle thickness [3].

These are short animal experiments. They do not show how the drug behaves in a human body, what amount would matter, or whether long-term activation of ERRs in the liver, heart or other organs is safe. Claims that SLU-PP-915 burns fat or builds endurance in people have no human data behind them.

sections.heading: How is SLU-PP-915 different from SLU-PP-332?

blocks.text: The two share a target but not a chemical structure. SLU-PP-332 came first and improved running in mice, but it is poorly absorbed when swallowed, so animal studies gave it by injection. SLU-PP-915 belongs to a separate chemical series and was developed partly to fix that problem [2]. In a liver enzyme study, SLU-PP-332 produced nine breakdown products and SLU-PP-915 seven, with only SLU-PP-332 forming the conjugated, ready-to-excrete type [5]. Neither has been tested in a human trial.

name: Somapacitan
evidenceNote: Somapacitan is FDA-approved for adults and children, backed by randomized phase 3 trials in adult growth hormone deficiency (REAL 1), children with deficiency (REAL 4), and three other childhood growth conditions (REAL 8).
summary: Somapacitan (Sogroya) is a once-weekly growth hormone injection, approved for children and adults lacking growth hormone and for three other childhood growth disorders.
keyTakeaway: Somapacitan is human growth hormone with one amino acid swapped and an albumin-binding chain attached, which lets a single injection last a week instead of a day. In children with growth hormone deficiency, weekly doses produced growth of 11.2 cm a year, close to the 11.7 cm seen with daily injections. The FDA approved it as Sogroya for adults in 2020, for children with deficiency in 2023, and for three more childhood growth conditions in February 2026. Like all growth hormone, it is prohibited in sport at all times.

blocks.text: Somapacitan is a long-acting form of human growth hormone made by Novo Nordisk and sold as Sogroya. The protein part is the same 191 amino acids as natural growth hormone except for one position, number 101, where leucine is replaced with cysteine. A small fatty side chain is attached at that spot. The drug is produced in bacteria using recombinant DNA [1].

Standard growth hormone (somatropin) has to be injected daily, which is a real burden for children who may need treatment for years and for adults on lifelong replacement. Somapacitan was designed so that one subcutaneous (under the skin) injection a week could do the same job [1][2]. It is one of several weekly growth hormone products, alongside lonapegsomatropin and somatrogon, which reach the same goal with different chemistry [6]. Somapacitan's approach keeps the hormone almost unchanged and borrows the body's own albumin as a carrier.

Once in the body, somapacitan binds the growth hormone receptor on target cells, the same receptor natural growth hormone uses. Some effects come directly from that signal, while others come from IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1), which the liver makes in response and which drives much of growth in children [1]. Doctors use blood IGF-1 levels to judge whether the dose is right.

The weekly schedule comes from the side chain. It binds reversibly to albumin, the most common protein in blood, which slows the drug's removal and extends its half-life. The bound drug acts as a circulating reserve that releases active hormone over days [1]. The body breaks the whole molecule down before excretion, and no intact drug leaves in urine or stool.
Yes. Sogroya is an FDA-approved biologic, and its approved uses have widened in three steps [1][4].

items.text: First approval, for adults whose pituitary no longer makes enough growth hormone [4].
Extended to children 2.5 years and older whose growth fails because they make too little growth hormone [4].
Three more pediatric uses added: children born small for gestational age who have not caught up by age 2, growth failure with Noonan syndrome, and idiopathic short stature [1][5].

blocks.text: Novo Nordisk has also asked the FDA to add Turner syndrome, with a decision expected in 2026 [4]. For athletes, the World Anti-Doping Agency names somapacitan as an example of a prohibited growth hormone analogue, banned both in and out of competition [6].

In children, it is prescribed to improve height in four groups: those with growth hormone deficiency, those born small for gestational age who have not caught up by age 2, those with Noonan syndrome (a genetic condition that often causes short stature), and those with idiopathic short stature, meaning no cause can be found. In adults, it replaces growth hormone the pituitary no longer makes [1]. Treatment is supervised by a specialist and the dose is adjusted to growth response or IGF-1 levels.

Truncal fat fell 1.06 points on somapacitan and rose 0.47 on placebo; visceral fat and lean mass also improved [1][2]
Growth of 11.2 cm a year on weekly somapacitan, against 11.7 cm on daily somatropin [1][3]
10.4 cm a year on somapacitan, against 9.2 cm on daily somatropin [1][4]

blocks.text: The pediatric trials compared the weekly drug with daily growth hormone rather than with placebo, because withholding treatment from children who need it would not be ethical. They were designed to show somapacitan was not meaningfully worse, and they met that bar [3][4]. In some REAL 8 groups the daily comparator was given below its highest US-approved dose, which the label points out when reading the comparisons [1]. In adults, the REAL 1 benefits held through 86 weeks of treatment [2].

Side effects resemble those of daily growth hormone. In children with growth hormone deficiency, the most frequent were colds and other nose and throat infections (about 16% in both groups), fever, headache, and bronchitis [1]. Across the newer pediatric groups, respiratory infections, ear infections, and diarrhea were each reported in at least 10% [4]. In adults in REAL 1, the overall pattern of adverse events, injection site reactions included, was similar to that of daily growth hormone [2].

items: Adults: back pain in 10% against 3.3% on placebo, joint pain in 6.7%, indigestion, dizziness, swelling of the legs, and raised blood pressure [1].
Raised blood phosphate and creatine kinase levels in some adults, which were intermittent and did not progress [1].

Class warnings for all growth hormone: higher blood sugar, raised pressure inside the skull, fluid retention, low adrenal or thyroid function coming to light, hip growth-plate slippage and worsening scoliosis in children, and pancreatitis [1].
Injection site changes such as fat loss or buildup when sites are not rotated [1].

blocks.text: Somapacitan is not used during active cancer, acute critical illness, severe diabetic eye disease, or in children whose growth plates have closed [1]. The label notes a higher risk of new tumors in childhood cancer survivors treated with growth hormone, and sudden deaths have been reported with growth hormone in children with Prader-Willi syndrome who are severely obese or have breathing problems [1].
