name: Somatropin (rhGH)
evidenceNote: Recombinant growth hormone has held FDA approval since 1985, covering hormone deficiency at any age plus several childhood growth disorders. Its label rests on decades of clinical studies across those conditions.
summary: Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone. FDA approves it to replace missing hormone and to treat several childhood growth disorders.
keyTakeaway: Somatropin is human growth hormone made by bacteria using recombinant DNA, identical in sequence to the hormone the pituitary gland makes. It replaced growth hormone taken from cadaver pituitaries, which was withdrawn in the US in 1985 after it was linked to a fatal brain disease. It is FDA-approved for children with growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome and other growth disorders, and for adults with proven deficiency. Its label states it is not indicated for adults without deficiency. WADA bans it in sport at all times.

blocks.text: Somatropin is the drug name for human growth hormone made by recombinant DNA technology, meaning the human gene is placed into bacteria that then produce the hormone. The result is a protein of 191 amino acids, about 22,000 daltons in size, with a sequence identical to growth hormone from the human pituitary gland [1].

Growth hormone is made by the pituitary, a pea-sized gland at the base of the brain. In children it drives growth in height. In adults it keeps acting on muscle, fat, bone and blood sugar. Somatropin is used to replace the hormone when the body does not make enough, and to boost growth in several genetic and developmental conditions that cause short stature [1].

Several companies sell somatropin under different brand names, including Norditropin [1]. It is distinct from the newer long-acting growth hormone analogues such as somapacitan, lonapegsomatropin and somatrogon, which are modified versions designed for weekly rather than daily injection [5].

Before recombinant hormone existed, growth hormone was extracted from pituitary glands collected from cadavers. In the US, a federally funded program distributed this pituitary hormone from 1963 to 1985, treating about 7,700 people, many of them children who were not growing [2].

In 1985, health officials learned that three young men treated with pituitary hormone had died of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a rare and fatal brain disease spread by infectious proteins. Distribution stopped immediately. Thirty-six cases of CJD have since been identified among US recipients. Growth hormone made by recombinant methods carries no risk of CJD infection [2].

items.text: US program begins distributing growth hormone extracted from cadaver pituitaries [2].
Pituitary hormone is withdrawn after CJD deaths [2]. On October 18, FDA approves Genentech's Protropin, the first recombinant growth hormone [3].
Initial US approval of Norditropin (somatropin) [1].
Protropin production ends as demand shifts to its successor, Nutropin [3].
Genentech discontinues Nutropin AQ in the US for business reasons, citing no safety or quality issue [4].

blocks.text: Somatropin binds growth hormone receptors on the surface of cells. That signal switches on genes for several proteins, most importantly insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which carries out much of growth hormone's work. Some effects come directly from growth hormone and others through IGF-1 [1].

In children, the key target is the growth plates, the zones of cartilage near the ends of long bones where lengthening happens. Somatropin stimulates the cartilage cells there to multiply, which speeds height growth. Throughout the body it also increases protein building, releases stored fat for energy, and pushes the liver to put out more glucose, which is why it can raise blood sugar [1].

Yes. Recombinant growth hormone has been FDA-approved since 1985, and somatropin products such as Norditropin have been on the US market since 1987 [1][3]. Products differ in their approved conditions and devices, so the uses listed for one brand do not automatically apply to another.

The label is explicit that somatropin is not indicated for adults who are not growth hormone deficient [1]. Use for anti-aging, body composition or athletic performance falls outside every approved use. In sport, growth hormone, its analogues and fragments are banned in and out of competition by the World Anti-Doping Agency [5].
Approved uses vary by brand. Norditropin, as one example, is approved for the following [1]:

items: Children whose growth is slowed because the pituitary makes too little growth hormone [1]
Short stature in Noonan syndrome and Turner syndrome, two genetic conditions [1]
Children born small for gestational age who have not caught up in growth by age 2 to 4 [1]
Idiopathic short stature, meaning very short height with no identified cause [1]
Growth failure in Prader-Willi syndrome, a genetic disorder affecting appetite and growth [1]
Adults with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency, as replacement [1]

blocks.text: Treatment is supervised by a specialist, usually a pediatric or adult endocrinologist. The label calls for an eye examination before starting, to look for swelling at the back of the eye, and doses are adjusted based on growth response and blood IGF-1 levels [1].

Common side effects in clinical studies included upper respiratory infections, fever, sore throat, headache, ear infections, swelling, joint and muscle pain, tingling, and impaired glucose tolerance [1].

The label lists several serious risks. Somatropin can raise blood sugar and unmask or worsen diabetes. It can cause raised pressure inside the skull, with headache and vision changes. In children, it can be linked to a slipped growth plate at the hip, worsening of existing scoliosis, and pancreatitis. Thyroid levels and adrenal function can shift once treatment starts [1].

Somatropin is not used in people with active cancer, because it can speed the progression of an existing tumor. Childhood cancer survivors who had head or brain radiation face a higher risk of a second tumor, especially meningiomas, if later treated for growth hormone deficiency [1].

Two warnings involve deaths. In two placebo-controlled trials of critically ill adults without growth hormone deficiency, mortality was 42% with high-dose somatropin versus 19% with placebo, so the drug is contraindicated after major surgery, trauma or in acute respiratory failure. Sudden deaths have also been reported in children with Prader-Willi syndrome who were severely obese or had breathing problems during sleep [1].

name: Survodutide
class: Glucagon and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist
evidenceNote: Multiple randomized phase 3 trials have been published in 2026, including SYNCHRONIZE-1 (725 adults) and SYNCHRONIZE-2 (752 adults with type 2 diabetes), alongside a phase 2 biopsy trial in liver disease. It is not approved anywhere.
summary: Survodutide is a weekly injected peptide that activates both glucagon and GLP-1 receptors. Phase 3 trials show weight loss and liver fat reduction; not approved.
keyTakeaway: Survodutide is Boehringer Ingelheim's weekly injection that activates two receptors at once: GLP-1, which curbs appetite, and glucagon, which is thought to raise energy use and clear liver fat. In the 76-week SYNCHRONIZE-1 trial, adults with obesity lost 12.2% to 13.0% of body weight against 5.4% on placebo. In a phase 2 biopsy trial, it resolved liver inflammation far more often than placebo. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are very common. It remains investigational and is not FDA-approved; vials sold online are not the studied drug.

blocks.text: Survodutide, first known by its lab code BI 456906, is an experimental peptide from the German drugmaker Boehringer Ingelheim. It is a dual agonist: one molecule that switches on both the glucagon receptor and the GLP-1 receptor. It is given as a once-weekly injection under the skin [2].

Boehringer is testing it on two fronts. The SYNCHRONIZE program studies weight loss in obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes [2][3]. The LIVERAGE program studies metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), the inflammatory, scarring form of fatty liver disease, including a phase 3 trial of an estimated 1,800 people with moderate or advanced liver fibrosis [5].

GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide reduce appetite and have transformed obesity treatment, but researchers have looked for ways to add to them [2]. Glucagon is the logical partner for the liver. It is the hormone that tells the liver to release stored fuel, and adding glucagon receptor activity is thought to help burn liver fat and raise energy expenditure.

The phase 2 liver trial was built on the idea that hitting both receptors might work better for MASH than GLP-1 activity alone [1]. A 2026 Nature Medicine report on its liver trial describes it simply as a glucagon receptor and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist under investigation for obesity and related diseases [4].

Because glucagon on its own pushes blood sugar up, a fair question is whether a glucagon-activating drug worsens diabetes. In the diabetes trial it did not: glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c, a three-month blood sugar average) still fell by 0.8 to 0.9 percentage points on survodutide, against 0.2 on placebo [3].

No. Survodutide has not been approved by the FDA or any other regulator. The phase 3 obesity trials published in 2026 describe it as an investigational drug [2][3], and the phase 3 MASH trials are still enrolling, with the main fibrosis trial not expected to complete its primary analysis until 2031 [5].

blocks.text: SYNCHRONIZE-1 randomized 725 adults without diabetes who had a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with a weight-related condition, to survodutide up to 3.6 mg, up to 6.0 mg, or placebo for 76 weeks, with lifestyle counseling for all. Counting everyone regardless of whether they stopped treatment, weight fell 12.2% and 13.0% on the two doses versus 5.4% on placebo [2].

SYNCHRONIZE-2 ran the same design in 752 adults with type 2 diabetes. Weight fell 8.2% and 9.8% on the two doses versus 3.9% on placebo at 76 weeks, and more than half of treated participants lost at least 5% of their weight [3].

blocks.text: The liver results stand out. In the phase 2 biopsy trial, MASH improved without worsening of scarring in 47%, 62%, and 43% of people on the 2.4, 4.8, and 6.0 mg doses, against 14% on placebo. Fibrosis improved by at least one stage in about a third of treated patients versus 22% on placebo [1]. SYNCHRONIZE-MASLD later confirmed large reductions in liver fat measured by MRI over 48 weeks, though its authors noted the short duration and that it recruited only in the United States and Spain [4].

Digestive side effects are the main drawback. They affected 80.9% and 89.7% of people on the two doses in SYNCHRONIZE-1, against 47.9% on placebo, and were usually mild to moderate [2]. In the phase 2 liver trial, nausea (66% vs 23%), diarrhea (49% vs 23%), and vomiting (41% vs 4%) were all much more common than on placebo, while serious adverse events were similar (8% vs 7%) [1]. No deaths were reported in SYNCHRONIZE-1 [2].

Because survodutide is still in trials, the only legitimate supply goes to enrolled study participants. Products sold online under the name are unregulated research chemicals with unknown content. The trials escalated doses gradually over many weeks under medical supervision, partly because digestive side effects cluster during dose escalation [4].

name: TB-500
evidenceNote: No human trial of the TB-500 fragment has been published, and the FDA says it has found no human exposure data. The healing claims borrow from animal work and a few small trials of the full-length protein, a different molecule.
summary: TB-500 is a synthetic piece of thymosin beta-4 sold for injury recovery. It is unapproved, untested in people, and banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: TB-500 is a short synthetic peptide, usually the seven-amino-acid piece of thymosin beta-4 that binds actin, sold for muscle, tendon, and wound recovery. No human trial of the fragment exists; the claims are borrowed from animal studies and small trials of the much larger full-length protein. It is not FDA-approved. In July 2026 an FDA advisory committee voted 8 to 6 to back compounding it, against the advice of FDA scientists, and since October 28, 2026 federal policy lets licensed pharmacies compound it while rulemaking is pending. WADA bans it at all times.

blocks.text: TB-500 is a product name, not a drug name. It refers to synthetic peptides sold for recovery from muscle, tendon, and ligament injuries, and anti-doping labs have long suspected its use in sport. When a Belgian anti-doping lab analyzed a TB-500 product, the active ingredient was a seven-amino-acid sequence (Ac-LKKTETQ), the acetylated 17 to 23 stretch of the natural protein thymosin beta-4 [2]. The FDA's own listing describes TB-500 the same way [3].

Thymosin beta-4 itself is a much larger natural protein that platelets, macrophages, and many other cell types release after an injury [1]. The fragment is a small part of it. Because labeling in this market is loose, a vial sold as TB-500 may contain the short fragment, the full protein, or something else entirely.

The proposed mechanism comes from the parent protein. Thymosin beta-4 binds actin, the protein that forms each cell's internal skeleton, and that binding helps cells move. In animal and lab studies, the full protein drew stem and progenitor cells into damaged tissue, encouraged new blood vessels, calmed inflammation, and reduced scarring in skin, eye, heart, and brain injury models [1].

The fragment in TB-500 contains the actin-binding motif, so sellers assume it carries the same benefits. That assumption has not been tested in people. The fragment is far shorter than the protein, may be broken down differently, and has been studied much less. Mechanism data on the full protein are a reason to study the fragment, not evidence that it works.

No. TB-500 is not approved for any use, and no company has filed it as a new drug. What changed in 2026 is its position with compounding pharmacies, which make drugs for individual patients from bulk ingredients.

The FDA's safety page lists the fragment among nominations that were withdrawn in April 2026 and notes that the agency has found no human exposure data and lacks key safety information [3]. On July 23, 2026, the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 6, with one abstention, to recommend adding TB-500 to the 503A bulks list for wound healing. FDA scientists had recommended against it, citing safety, efficacy, and characterization concerns [4][10]. On October 28, 2026, HHS announced it would not take action against licensed pharmacies and physicians compounding six peptides, TB-500 among them, while formal rulemaking proceeds [9]. The policy requires the ingredient to come from an FDA-registered facility with a certificate of analysis and asks compounders to report serious adverse events [5].

Enforcement discretion is not approval. It does not mean the FDA found TB-500 safe or effective, and it has no stated end date. In sport, the WADA list bans thymosin beta-4 and its derivatives, naming TB-500 as an example, in and out of competition [8].

blocks.text: For the TB-500 fragment, there is no published human trial of benefit or safety. Everything sold under the name rests on research into the full-length protein, and even that human evidence is thin.

blocks.text: The two human studies shown both used the whole protein, applied to skin or eyes rather than injected, and both were small. The eye-drop trial was designed and funded by the company developing the product [7]. They are early signals about the full protein in specific wounds, not evidence about a seven-amino-acid fragment injected for sports injuries.
So the recovery claims attached to TB-500 have not been shown in people. Questions about dose, purity, how long the fragment lasts in the body, and long-term effects remain unanswered.

sections.heading: How is TB-500 different from thymosin beta-4?

blocks.text: Thymosin beta-4 is the full-length natural protein, and it is the version that has reached small clinical trials for corneal and skin wounds [6][7]. TB-500 is a seven-amino-acid synthetic piece of it [2]. Regulators treat them separately: the 2026 compounding votes and the HHS policy name TB-500, the fragment, not the full protein [4][5]. Anti-doping rules, by contrast, ban both [8].

name: Teduglutide
evidenceNote: Teduglutide is approved by the FDA for short bowel syndrome on the strength of a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, supported by a two-year extension study.
summary: Teduglutide (Gattex) is an FDA-approved GLP-2 analog that helps people with short bowel syndrome absorb more and rely less on IV nutrition.
keyTakeaway: Teduglutide is a lab-made version of GLP-2, a gut hormone that helps the lining of the small intestine grow and absorb. Sold as Gattex, it has been FDA-approved since 2012 for adults, and now children aged 1 and older, with short bowel syndrome who depend on intravenous nutrition. In the pivotal trial, 63% of people on teduglutide cut their weekly IV volume by at least 20%, against 30% on placebo. Because it makes intestinal tissue grow, the label requires colon screening before and during treatment, and it is not a weight or gut health product for anyone else.

blocks.text: Teduglutide is a 33 amino acid analog of glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2), a hormone released by L-cells in the lower part of the small intestine. It is made in bacteria using recombinant DNA [1]. It is sold in the United States as Gattex and in Europe as Revestive. It is not related to the GLP-1 drugs used for diabetes and weight loss, even though the names look similar.

The drug exists for one group of people: those with short bowel syndrome (SBS), a condition where so much small intestine has been removed or lost that the remainder cannot absorb enough fluid and nutrients. Many people with SBS live on parenteral support, meaning nutrition and fluids infused straight into a vein for several nights a week. Teduglutide aims to make the remaining bowel work harder so that some of that IV support can be cut back [1].

Teduglutide is given as one injection under the skin each day. It is cleared fairly quickly, with a half-life of about 2 hours in healthy adults and about 1.3 hours in people with SBS, so its effect on the bowel builds through steady daily dosing rather than from long-lasting blood levels [1].

The drug binds GLP-2 receptors on several cell types in the gut wall, including hormone-secreting cells, the supporting cells under the lining, and gut nerve cells. Switching on those receptors releases local growth signals such as IGF-1, nitric oxide and keratinocyte growth factor [1]. GLP-2 also increases blood flow to the intestine and slows stomach acid secretion. In the pivotal trial, teduglutide raised blood levels of citrulline, a marker of how much working intestinal lining a person has [2].

The same growth effect is the main safety concern. A drug that makes intestinal tissue grow could, in theory, speed the growth of polyps or existing tumors, which is why the label builds screening into treatment [1].

Yes. The FDA first approved Gattex in 2012 for adults with SBS who depend on parenteral support, and the current label extends that to children aged 1 year and older [1]. It is a prescription drug supplied as a powder that is mixed with sterile water and injected under the skin once a day, with the amount set by body weight.

items.text: FDA approves Gattex for adults with short bowel syndrome who need parenteral support, with a risk program (REMS) attached [1][5].
Approval extended to children aged 1 year and older [1].
FDA approves a supplement ending the Gattex REMS, finding that prescribers, mostly gastroenterology specialists, already understand the risks and monitoring [5].

blocks.text: Ending the REMS did not change the safety warnings themselves. The FDA said in its 2026 letter that the risk information in the prescribing label and in clinical practice guidance remains available to doctors [5].

The only approved use is short bowel syndrome in people who rely on parenteral support [1]. The pivotal phase 3 study, known as STEPS, enrolled 86 adults who had depended on IV nutrition for at least a year. After 24 weeks, the researchers counted how many people had reduced their weekly IV volume by more than 20% [2].

rows: Responders (20% or greater cut in weekly IV volume)
Average drop in weekly IV volume
At least one fewer IV day per week

blocks.text: Those figures come from the trial report and the FDA label [1][2]. A two-year open-label extension, STEPS-2, followed 88 people. Among those who stayed on teduglutide for the full 30 months, 93% met the response definition and their weekly IV volume fell by an average of 7.6 liters, about two thirds of their starting amount. Thirteen people in the extension stopped needing parenteral support altogether [3]. Because STEPS-2 had no placebo group, its numbers show durability rather than proving the effect on their own.

In the placebo-controlled adult studies, the most common side effects were abdominal pain (30% vs 22% on placebo), nausea (23% vs 20%), upper respiratory infections (21% vs 12%), abdominal swelling (20% vs 2%), injection site reactions, vomiting, fluid overload and allergic-type skin reactions [1]. People with a stoma (an opening on the abdomen where the bowel empties into a bag) often noticed changes to the stoma, which can swell as the bowel lining grows [1].

items: Faster growth of tumors: the label says to stop the drug if an intestinal cancer appears, and to weigh benefits and risks for other cancers [1].
Polyps: adults need a colonoscopy and upper endoscopy before starting, again after 1 year, and at least every 5 years after that. Children have stool blood tests and scheduled bowel exams [1].
Intestinal obstruction, and problems with the gallbladder, bile ducts and pancreas, which the label asks doctors to monitor with lab tests [1].
Fluid overload, because better absorption means more fluid stays in the body. This matters most for people with heart disease [1].

blocks.text: In STEPS-2, abdominal pain, catheter infections and weight loss were the most frequent problems reported over two years, while average weight and blood albumin stayed stable as IV support was reduced [3].

Doctors judge teduglutide by how much IV support a person can drop, not by symptoms alone. STEPS set the standard: a responder was anyone whose weekly parenteral volume fell by more than 20% at both week 20 and week 24, with IV volumes adjusted only when urine output showed the body was absorbing more [2][4]. In practice that means treatment is tracked with fluid balance checks and lab work over months. The FDA label adds that in an earlier placebo-controlled study, 75% of responders who continued into an extension study kept their response after a year [1].

name: Teriparatide
evidenceNote: Approved in 2002 on a randomized, placebo-controlled fracture trial in 1,637 postmenopausal women, with further controlled trials in men and in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.
summary: Teriparatide is the active front section of parathyroid hormone, given as a daily injection. It is FDA-approved to build bone in high-risk osteoporosis.
keyTakeaway: Teriparatide is a recombinant fragment of parathyroid hormone: the opening 34-amino-acid stretch that carries nearly all of the hormone's activity. Injected once a day, it stimulates bone-building cells more than bone-removing ones, so it adds new bone rather than only slowing loss. Approved by the FDA in 2002 as Forteo, it cut new spine fractures from 14.3% to 5.0% in its pivotal trial. Generic versions are now approved too. Rats given high doses developed bone cancer, so use beyond two years is reserved for people still at high fracture risk.

blocks.text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is an 84-amino-acid hormone made by four small glands in the neck, and it is the body's main regulator of calcium and phosphate in bone and kidney [1]. Teriparatide reproduces only its first 34 amino acids, the section that does the biological work. It binds PTH receptors as strongly as the full hormone and has the same effects on bone and kidney [1].

The version sold by Eli Lilly as Forteo is made by recombinant DNA technology in E. coli bacteria [1]. It belongs to a small group of anabolic, or bone-building, osteoporosis drugs, in contrast to the more common antiresorptive drugs such as bisphosphonates, which work by slowing bone breakdown.

Bone is constantly remodelled: osteoclasts remove old bone and osteoblasts lay down new bone. A single daily dose of teriparatide stimulates osteoblasts more than osteoclasts, so new bone forms on both the spongy inner bone and the dense outer layer [1]. In people this shows up as more skeletal mass, higher markers of bone turnover, and stronger bone [1].

Timing is the key. The same hormone at a constant high level, as in hyperparathyroidism (an overactive parathyroid gland), harms the skeleton because breakdown then outpaces building [1]. Daily injections create a short pulse instead. Calcium in the blood rises for a few hours, peaking about four to six hours after a dose, and is back to baseline by 16 hours [1].

Yes. Forteo was approved on November 26, 2002, and is still marketed by Lilly [3]. The label lists the first US approval of teriparatide as 1987, which predates Forteo; that earlier injectable, Parathar, is now listed as discontinued [1][6]. Several other teriparatide products have since been approved, including Bonsity in 2019 and generic versions from 2023 onward [4][5].

items.text: The pivotal fracture trial in 1,637 postmenopausal women is published [2].
FDA approves Forteo [3].

The first generic teriparatide injections are approved, including one from Apotex [5].

blocks.text: The label covers three groups at high risk of fracture, or who have failed or cannot tolerate other osteoporosis treatment: postmenopausal women with osteoporosis; men with primary or hypogonadal (low testosterone) osteoporosis; and men and women with osteoporosis caused by long-term glucocorticoid (steroid) use at 5 mg a day of prednisone or more [1].

The pivotal trial randomized 1,637 postmenopausal women who already had spine fractures to daily injections of 20 or 40 mcg or placebo, all with calcium and vitamin D, for a median of 21 months of observation [2]. On 20 mcg, new spine fractures fell from 14% to 5% and new non-spine fragility fractures from 6% to 3%, and spine bone density rose 9 percentage points more than on placebo [2].

rows: Rose in 94% of men over a median 10 months [1]

blocks.text: In men and in glucocorticoid users, the trials measured bone density rather than fractures, which is why the men's indication is worded as increasing bone mass [1]. The label adds that use for more than two years in a lifetime should only be considered for people who remain, or again become, at high risk of fracture [1].

In the main trials, the most common side effects were joint pain, general pain and nausea; joint pain affected 10.1% on teriparatide against 8.4% on placebo, and leg cramps 2.6% against 1.3% [1]. At least one short-lived episode of raised blood calcium a few hours after a dose occurred in 11% of women and 6% of men on the drug [1]. A brief drop in blood pressure on standing, which can cause lightheadedness, was seen in 5% of volunteers in short-term studies, mostly with the first doses [1].

The main concern comes from rats. In two-year rat studies, osteosarcoma, a malignant bone tumor, appeared at every dose tested and reached 40% to 50% of animals in the highest-dose groups [1]. In people, rare cases have been reported after approval, but two large US insurance claims studies found 3 cases among 379,283 users and none among 153,316, a rate similar to comparison groups [1]. The label still advises avoiding it in people at higher baseline risk: children and young adults with growing bones, Paget's disease of bone, prior skeletal cancer or bone metastases, and past radiation therapy involving the skeleton [1].

name: Terlipressin
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2022 on the strength of CONFIRM, a 300-patient randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, and backed by years of use in other countries.
summary: A hospital IV drug that tightens blood vessels to restore kidney function in hepatorenal syndrome. FDA-approved in 2022 with a boxed warning for respiratory failure.
keyTakeaway: Terlipressin, sold in the US as Terlivaz, is a lab-made relative of the hormone vasopressin. It is given intravenously in hospital to adults with advanced liver disease whose kidneys are failing quickly, a condition called hepatorenal syndrome. In the CONFIRM trial, kidney function recovered in 32% of patients on terlipressin versus 17% on placebo. The FDA approved it in September 2022, the first drug approved for this condition in the US. It carries a boxed warning: serious or fatal respiratory failure occurred in 14% of treated patients.

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Narrows blood vessels in the gut, which lowers pressure in the liver's veins and sends more blood to the kidneys.

blocks.text: Terlipressin is a synthetic peptide of 12 amino acids, built on the structure of lysine-vasopressin, a natural hormone that controls blood vessel tone and water balance [1]. In the US it is sold as Terlivaz and is given only by intravenous injection (into a vein) in a hospital setting.

It treats one specific and dangerous complication of liver disease. Hepatorenal syndrome, or HRS, is kidney failure that develops in people with advanced cirrhosis (severe liver scarring), usually alongside ascites, a buildup of fluid in the abdomen. The kidneys themselves are not damaged at first; they fail because blood flow to them collapses. Without a liver transplant, the outlook is very poor [2].

In advanced cirrhosis, blood vessels in the gut widen and pressure builds up in the portal vein, the large vessel that carries blood into the liver. The rest of the circulation then behaves as if it were low on fluid, and the kidneys respond by clamping down their own blood supply. That is the chain of events behind HRS.

Terlipressin works on vasopressin V1 receptors on blood vessel walls, with about twice as much preference for V1 as for the V2 receptors found in the kidney's water-handling tubules. It acts on its own and is also gradually converted in the body into lysine-vasopressin. By narrowing the dilated vessels, it lowers portal pressure, raises overall blood pressure, and restores the effective blood volume that the kidneys sense, so kidney blood flow can recover [1]. Blood pressure rises and heart rate slows within about five minutes of a dose [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Terlivaz in September 2022 for adults with hepatorenal syndrome whose kidneys are deteriorating quickly, with the goal of restoring their function. The agency described it as the first approved medicine for this condition in the US. The application went through priority review and had fast track and orphan drug designations [2].

Terlipressin was not new to medicine at the time. It had already been used for HRS in many countries and was part of European treatment guidelines; CONFIRM was run to confirm its benefit and safety for a US approval [3]. The label notes that patients whose serum creatinine (a blood marker of kidney function) is above 5 mg/dL are unlikely to benefit [1].

Its only US approval is hepatorenal syndrome with rapidly worsening kidney function in adults [1]. It is a short hospital course: the label limits treatment to a maximum of 14 days, adjusts it according to creatinine on day 4, and stops it if kidney function has not improved [1]. Albumin, a protein given by IV to expand blood volume, was strongly encouraged alongside it in the pivotal trial [3].
CONFIRM randomized 300 adults with type 1 HRS in a 2 to 1 ratio to terlipressin or placebo for up to 14 days [3].

rows: Any creatinine at or below 1.5 mg/dL in 14 days [3]
Reversal in patients with body-wide inflammation (SIRS) [3]
Death from breathing problems by day 90 [3]

blocks.text: The trial showed that terlipressin brings kidney function back for a meaningful minority of patients, but it did not show that more of them survived to day 90. Liver transplant, the definitive treatment, was performed in about a quarter of patients in each group [3].

The label carries a boxed warning, the FDA's strongest, for serious or fatal respiratory failure. In the main trial this happened in 14% of patients on terlipressin and 5% on placebo. People with fluid overload or the most severe grade of acute-on-chronic liver failure face the highest risk, and treatment is not started in anyone whose blood oxygen is below 90% [1].

Because the drug constricts blood vessels, it can reduce blood flow to the heart, brain, limbs or gut, and it is not used in people with ongoing ischemia (blocked blood supply) in those areas. These complications can also make a patient on a transplant waiting list ineligible for a new liver [1]. Terlipressin can cause uterine contractions and may harm a fetus [1].
In the trial, 12% of patients on terlipressin stopped early because of side effects, compared with 5% on placebo [1]. The most common reactions were:

items: Abdominal pain (about 20% vs 6% on placebo) [1]
Nausea (16% vs 10%) and diarrhea (13% vs 7%) [1]
Respiratory failure (16% vs 7%) and shortness of breath (13% vs 5%) [1]
Fluid overload, fluid around the lungs, sepsis and a slow heart rate, each in 5% to 9% [1]
After approval elsewhere: headache, low blood sodium, and rare skin necrosis or gangrene [1]

name: Tesamorelin
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 2010 after two randomized, placebo-controlled trials in more than 800 adults with HIV, each lasting 26 weeks with a 26-week extension. The approval covers one narrow use: reducing excess belly fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy.
summary: A daily injection that prompts the pituitary to release growth hormone, approved to shrink excess belly fat in adults with HIV-related lipodystrophy.
keyTakeaway: Tesamorelin is a lab-made copy of the brain hormone that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. The FDA approved it in 2010, sold as Egrifta, to reduce deep belly fat in adults with HIV who have lipodystrophy. In the pivotal trials, fat around the organs fell by about 15 to 20% against placebo over six months, while body weight barely changed. The fat returned when treatment stopped. The label does not cover weight loss or general anti-aging use, and the drug is banned in sport.

blocks.text: Tesamorelin is a synthetic version of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), a 44-amino-acid peptide made by the hypothalamus, the small region at the base of the brain that controls the pituitary gland [2]. It is the active ingredient in Egrifta, a prescription medicine made by Theratechnologies [1].

Its one approved job is narrow: reducing the deep abdominal fat that builds up in some people with HIV who take antiretroviral therapy, a condition called lipodystrophy (an abnormal redistribution of body fat) [1]. The label is explicit that it is not a weight loss drug, since its effect on body weight is neutral [1].

In the 2000s, older HIV drug regimens left many patients with a thick waist and fat packed around the organs, even when the rest of the body grew thinner. Growth hormone itself was known to shrink this fat but carried side effects, so researchers tested a GHRH analog that would raise the body's own growth hormone in its natural pulses instead [2].

items.text: A 12-month randomized trial in 404 adults with HIV confirms reductions in visceral fat [2]
FDA grants first approval of tesamorelin as Egrifta [1]
A randomized trial reports lower liver fat in people with HIV and fatty liver disease [3]
FDA approves Egrifta WR, an 11.6 mg vial mixed once a week instead of daily [1]

blocks.text: Tesamorelin binds the GHRH receptor on cells in the pituitary called somatotrophs, and in lab tests it does so about as strongly as the body's own hormone [1]. Those cells respond by making and releasing growth hormone in pulses. Growth hormone breaks down stored fat and builds tissue, and many of its effects run through IGF-1, a growth factor produced mainly by the liver [1].

This is an indirect route. Rather than supplying growth hormone from outside, tesamorelin turns up the body's own production, so the normal feedback loops that limit growth hormone stay in place. In the trials, IGF-1 rose by about two thirds over six months, a gain of roughly 105 to 120 ng/mL more than with placebo [1].

The fat loss falls mostly on visceral adipose tissue, the fat stored deep in the abdomen around the organs, rather than on the fat just under the skin [1][2]. Trunk fat fell by about 1 kg and lean mass rose by about 1.2 to 1.3 kg, while total weight hardly moved [1].

Yes. Tesamorelin was first approved in the United States in 2010 [1]. The most recent version, Egrifta WR, was approved in March 2025 and replaces Egrifta SV; the two use different vial strengths and mixing steps and cannot be swapped for each other [1].

The approval is limited to adults with HIV and lipodystrophy who carry excess abdominal fat [1]. Use for general weight loss, body building, or anti-aging falls outside the label, and the long-term effect on heart health has not been established [1]. Clinics that prescribe compounded tesamorelin for other purposes are working outside the approval.

Tesamorelin is prescribed to reduce excess visceral fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy [1]. The two pivotal trials enrolled 816 adults aged 18 to 65 on stable antiretroviral therapy, randomized two to one to a daily injection or placebo for 26 weeks, with fat measured by CT scan at the lower spine [1].

The benefit depends on staying on treatment. When people who responded were switched to placebo for the next 26 weeks, their visceral fat climbed back by 16 to 22% in that time, while those who stayed on the drug kept their reduction [1]. The second trial's authors also reported less distress about body image [2].

Outside the label, a randomized trial in 61 people with HIV and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease found that a year of tesamorelin cut liver fat by about a third relative to baseline, and 35% reached normal liver fat compared with 4% on placebo [3]. That finding has not led to a new approved use.

Most side effects trace back to higher growth hormone levels, which cause the body to hold more fluid. Joint pain, limb pain, swelling of the legs, muscle aches, and tingling or numbness all occurred more often with tesamorelin than with placebo [1].

items: Injection site reactions such as redness and itching: 25% versus 14% on placebo [1]
Joint pain: 13% versus 11% [1]
Muscle pain and leg swelling: 6% each versus 2% [1]
Allergic reactions such as rash and hives: 4% [1]

blocks.text: Blood sugar can rise. In the trials, 5% of tesamorelin users reached an HbA1c (a three-month average of blood sugar) of 6.5% or higher, against 1% on placebo, so glucose is checked before and during treatment [1]. The label also calls for monitoring IGF-1, since the long-term effect of persistently high levels is unknown [1].

The drug is not used during pregnancy, in people with active cancer, or in people whose hypothalamic-pituitary system has been damaged by surgery, radiation, or disease [1]. About half of trial patients developed antibodies to tesamorelin within six months, though those with and without antibodies saw similar fat reductions [1].
For athletes, tesamorelin is named on the World Anti-Doping Agency list as a GHRH analog and is prohibited in and out of competition [4].

name: Thymosin alpha-1
evidenceNote: Several randomized human trials exist, in hepatitis B and in sepsis, but most were open-label or single-blind, and the largest and best-designed one, a 1,106-patient phase 3 sepsis trial, found no effect on survival.
summary: A 28-amino-acid thymus peptide used abroad for hepatitis B and as an immune booster. Not FDA-approved; its largest trial found no survival benefit.
keyTakeaway: Thymosin alpha-1 is a 28-amino-acid peptide first isolated from calf thymus in 1977, and a synthetic version is approved in more than 35 countries, mainly for hepatitis B and C. Randomized trials in hepatitis B reported higher rates of viral clearance than no treatment. In sepsis, a small trial hinted at fewer deaths, but a 2025 phase 3 trial in 1,106 adults found 28-day mortality of 23.4% against 24.1% on placebo. It is not FDA-approved, and an FDA advisory panel voted against allowing pharmacies to compound it.

blocks.text: Thymosin alpha-1 is a short protein chain of 28 amino acids that occurs naturally in the thymus, the gland behind the breastbone where T cells (a type of white blood cell) mature [2]. The drug version is made synthetically and is known by the generic name thymalfasin [3].

It is described as an immunomodulator, a substance that adjusts how the immune system responds rather than attacking a germ directly [1]. Outside the United States it is approved in more than 35 countries to treat hepatitis B and C and as an immune stimulant or vaccine adjuvant (an add-on that strengthens the response to a vaccine) [1]. In the US it is not an approved medicine.

Allan Goldstein and colleagues studied thymosin fraction 5, a mixture of peptides extracted from calf thymus. In 1977 they isolated one of its components, worked out its full amino acid sequence, and named it thymosin alpha-1 [2]. A synthetic version followed, and by the late 1990s it was being tested in randomized trials for chronic hepatitis B [3].

items.text: Thymosin alpha-1 isolated from calf thymus and sequenced [2]
Randomized trial in 98 people with chronic hepatitis B reports more viral clearance [3]
ETASS sepsis trial in 361 patients reports a borderline drop in deaths [5]
FDA advisory committee votes 17 to 4 against adding it to the 503A bulks list [8]

blocks.text: The original work placed thymosin alpha-1 among the thymus peptides that may guide how T cells develop and function [2]. Later laboratory studies pointed to a second route. In laboratory and mouse experiments, it made dendritic cells, the immune cells that present pieces of a germ to T cells, mature and release interleukin-12, a signal that steers the immune system toward fighting infections [4].

That effect ran through toll-like receptors, sensors that detect microbes, and the MyD88 signaling pathway [4]. In mice given bone marrow transplants, the peptide sped the recovery of white blood cells and protected the animals from a lung infection with the mould Aspergillus [4]. How closely these lab findings explain what happens in patients is not settled.

No. Thymosin alpha-1 has never been approved by the FDA for any use. The 2009 review that counts approvals in more than 35 countries also noted late-stage US testing for hepatitis C and melanoma at that time, but none of it led to a US approval [1].

Compounding has been contested. The FDA once placed it in its category of compounding substances that may carry significant safety risks, citing possible immune reactions and too little safety information; the nomination was later withdrawn [9]. At a December 4, 2024 meeting, the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 17 to 4 against adding both forms of the peptide to the 503A bulks list, with several members saying they saw no convincing evidence of effectiveness for the uses under review [8].

In late October 2026, HHS announced it would not act against pharmacies compounding six peptides, BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500, while formal rulemaking continues [12][10]. Thymosin alpha-1 was not one of them.

The strongest support comes from chronic hepatitis B. In a 1998 Taiwanese trial, 98 patients were randomized to 26 weeks of injections, 52 weeks of injections, or no treatment [3]. Eighteen months after starting, the virus and its e antigen (a marker of active replication) had cleared in 40.6% of the 26-week group against 9.4% of untreated patients, and biopsies showed less liver inflammation [3]. A Japanese trial of 316 patients compared two dose levels without a placebo arm and found similar response rates for both [7].

rows: Complete viral response 40.6% (26 weeks) vs 9.4% untreated
ALT normal in 36.4% at 72 weeks; no placebo group

blocks.text: Sepsis, a dangerous whole-body reaction to infection, was the next test. The 2013 ETASS trial in six Chinese hospitals reported fewer deaths at 28 days with thymosin alpha-1, but the difference was borderline and the trial was not double-blind [5]. The TESTS trial then randomized 1,106 adults at 22 centres to injections every 12 hours for seven days or a placebo [6]. Death rates were nearly identical, and no secondary or safety outcome differed between groups [6].

A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 sepsis trials found lower mortality when all were pooled, but the benefit vanished when only high-quality or multicentre trials were counted, and the authors judged the total sample too small for a firm answer [11]. Across these trials side effects were mild, mostly fluctuations in liver enzymes in the hepatitis studies [7]. Wellness uses such as general immune support, long COVID, or anti-aging have not been tested in randomized trials.

name: Thymosin beta-4
evidenceNote: Several randomized human trials exist, but almost all tested eye drops or wound gels, and the two largest (dry eye, 601 and 700 people) missed their primary endpoints. Injected thymosin beta-4 for muscle or injury recovery, the way it is sold online, has no controlled human trial.
summary: Thymosin beta-4 is a natural repair peptide sold online for recovery. Its eye-drop and wound trials were mostly small or negative, and it is banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: Thymosin beta-4 is a 43-amino-acid peptide found in most human cells that binds actin, part of the cell's internal scaffold, and helps cells move into injured tissue. Animal studies of wound, eye, and heart repair are extensive. Human trials have mostly tested eye drops: two large dry-eye phase 3 trials of 601 and 700 people showed no clear advantage over placebo on their main measures, while an 18-person trial in a corneal nerve disease showed a trend toward healing. No trial has tested injections for muscle or tendon recovery. It is not FDA-approved and WADA bans it.

blocks.text: Thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) is a naturally occurring peptide of 43 amino acids [2]. It is present in many cell types and is released by platelets, macrophages, and other cells after an injury, where it appears to protect tissue and limit inflammation [1]. Its best-known partner inside cells is actin, the protein that forms the cell's internal scaffolding and lets cells change shape and crawl [1].

Drug developers have tested synthetic Tβ4 as eye drops (code RGN-259) and as a topical gel for skin wounds. Separately, it is sold online as a "research peptide" for injection, marketed for muscle, tendon, and injury recovery. Many of those products are actually TB-500, a short synthetic fragment rather than the full peptide (see below).

Because it binds actin, Tβ4 influences how cells move. In laboratory and animal models, this translates into faster migration of skin cells and blood vessel cells into wounds, mobilization of stem and progenitor cells, new blood vessel growth, lower inflammation, and fewer of the myofibroblasts that lay down scar tissue [1].

These effects have been studied in models of skin wounds, corneal injury, heart attack, and brain injury, and they are the basis for the clinical programs below [1]. The review most often cited for these mechanisms shares authors with the eye-drop trials, so it presents the case for Tβ4 rather than a neutral appraisal [1][6]. None of this shows that an injection of Tβ4 speeds recovery of a strained muscle or tendon in people.

No. No Tβ4 product is approved by FDA for any use. The eye-drop program has run several phase 3 trials, the most recent of which, in neurotrophic keratopathy, completed in July 2026 without posted results [7]. For compounding, FDA lists the thymosin beta-4 fragment LKKTETQ, known as TB-500, among nominations that were withdrawn, and says it found no human exposure data and lacks basic safety information on it [8].

In sport, the 2026 WADA Prohibited List names thymosin-β4 and its derivatives, including TB-500, under growth factors and growth factor modulators (class S2.3), which are banned in and out of competition [9].
Tβ4 has more human trial data than most peptides sold for recovery, but nearly all of it concerns the eye or chronic wounds, and the large trials did not deliver clear wins.

blocks.text: The neurotrophic keratopathy trial (a disease in which damaged corneal nerves leave sores on the eye that will not heal) was stopped early for a business reason after 18 patients, so its trend toward faster healing is suggestive at best [6][10]. A follow-up phase 3 trial of 70 patients finished in 2026 and had not reported results [7].

Outside the eye, a Chinese company has completed a 90-patient phase 2b trial of injected recombinant Tβ4 after heart attack, with results not posted [11]. No randomized human trial has tested Tβ4 or TB-500 for muscle growth, tendon healing, or sports recovery. Those uses rest on animal studies and anecdote, and products sold online are not checked for identity, purity, or sterility.

sections.heading: Is TB-500 the same as thymosin beta-4?

blocks.text: Not exactly. FDA describes TB-500 as a thymosin beta-4 fragment with the seven-amino-acid sequence LKKTETQ, a small piece of the full 43-amino-acid molecule [8][2]. Vendors often market it as "synthetic thymosin beta-4," but the clinical trials above used the full-length peptide, and FDA notes it has found no human exposure data for the fragment [8]. Anti-doping rules treat the two the same way: both are banned [9].

name: Thymulin
evidenceNote: Human data are almost entirely measurements of natural thymulin levels in blood, which fall with age and zinc deficiency. Giving thymulin as a treatment has been tested mainly in animals, with only an old uncontrolled report in people.
summary: Thymulin is a zinc-bound thymus hormone that helps T cells mature. It falls with age, but has not been tested as a treatment in controlled human trials.
keyTakeaway: Thymulin is a nine-amino-acid hormone made only by the thymus, the gland where T cells mature. It works only when bound to a zinc ion, and blood levels fall with age and with zinc deficiency. In animals, giving thymulin has reduced inflammation and, in a 2026 mouse study, improved the response of tumors to immunotherapy in older mice. Human evidence for using it as a treatment is close to nil: no controlled trial has been published. It is not FDA-approved, and products sold online are unregulated research chemicals.

blocks.text: Thymulin is a hormone produced exclusively by epithelial cells of the thymus, a small organ behind the breastbone where T cells, a type of white blood cell, learn to work properly [1]. Its peptide part has nine amino acids, pGlu-Ala-Lys-Ser-Gln-Gly-Gly-Ser-Asn, and it was first named facteur thymique sérique (serum thymic factor) [7].

The peptide alone does nothing. Thymulin becomes biologically active only when it binds a single zinc ion, which is why it is also written FTS-Zn [1]. Its activity in blood drops early when the body runs short of zinc, so it has served researchers as a sensitive sign of zinc deficiency [2][3].
Thymulin levels decline with age [4]. That decline is the basis for its current marketing as an anti-aging or immune-support peptide, a use that has not been tested in people.

Thymulin was discovered in the early 1970s. Through the following decades it was characterized as a thymic hormone involved in T-cell development, both inside the thymus and in the rest of the body [1]. Later work showed traffic in both directions with the hormonal system: pituitary and other hormones influence how much thymulin the thymus releases, and thymulin in turn appears to act on the pituitary [1].

Published attempts to give thymulin to patients are scarce. An open trial in rheumatoid arthritis, without a placebo group, appeared as a short letter in 1987 [5]. Since then, therapeutic research has moved mostly into animals, including gene therapy experiments in rats [1].

Zinc-bound thymulin helps immature T cells develop and supports the balance of T-helper cells, particularly the Th1 type that drives defense against viruses and tumors. When zinc runs low, thymulin loses activity, Th1 signaling such as interleukin-2 drops, and natural killer and cytotoxic T-cell activity falls [2].

In a controlled experiment where volunteers ate a mildly zinc-deficient diet, thymulin activity dropped within 8 to 12 weeks, before blood and cell zinc levels had clearly fallen [3]. In a small randomized study of 27 people with Crohn's disease and low thymulin, high-dose zinc supplements for three months restored thymulin activity, while a lower dose and placebo did not [6]. These studies show that thymulin depends on zinc in people, but they did not give thymulin itself.

Thymulin also seems to calm inflammation. In animals it had anti-inflammatory and pain-relieving effects in the brain [1]. A 2026 mouse study found that thymulin suppressed the production of inflammatory cytokines by myeloid cells (a family of immune cells) by blocking NF-κB, a central inflammation switch [4].

No. Thymulin has never been approved by the FDA, and no trial giving it as a treatment is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov. It does not appear on the FDA's list of peptides reviewed for compounding safety risks [8], and it was not among the six peptides covered by the federal enforcement discretion policy of October 2026 [10][9].

That leaves thymulin with no legal route to patients as a prescription drug in the United States. It is sold online as a research chemical, which means no regulator checks the identity, purity, sterility, or zinc content of the product. Since the peptide is inactive without bound zinc [1], an unverified product may not even contain the active form.

blocks.text: The most striking recent result is the 2026 mouse study. Researchers found that pro-inflammatory myeloid cells become more common with age in both mice and humans, and that a circulating factor in young animals kept them in check. They identified thymulin as that factor. Treating older mice with thymulin improved T-cell attack on tumors, lengthened survival, and made tumors more responsive to anti-PD-L1, an immunotherapy drug, in an age-dependent way [4].

These findings point to a hypothesis worth testing in people, especially in older patients receiving cancer immunotherapy. They do not show that thymulin is safe or useful for anyone today. How much to give, how long it lasts in the blood, and what side effects it causes in humans have not been established in modern studies.

name: Tirzepatide
class: Dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist
evidenceNote: Tirzepatide is an FDA-approved prescription drug backed by large phase 3 programs in type 2 diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea, and a 13,000-person cardiovascular outcomes trial.
summary: Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection that activates GIP and GLP-1 receptors, approved as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound for weight and sleep apnea.
keyTakeaway: Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injectable peptide that activates the GIP and GLP-1 receptors at once, two targets normally hit by gut hormones. In the 72-week SURMOUNT-1 trial, adults with obesity on the top dose lost an average of 20.9% of body weight, against 3.1% on placebo. The FDA has approved it as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes (including heart risk reduction since August 2026) and as Zepbound for chronic weight management and obstructive sleep apnea. The shortage that allowed mass compounding ended in 2024, so pharmacy copies and online research vials are not the approved product.

atGlance.value: Approved: Mounjaro (2022), Zepbound (2023)

atGlance.value: Activates GIP and GLP-1 receptors to cut appetite and improve insulin release

blocks.text: Tirzepatide is a synthetic peptide made by Eli Lilly that acts on the receptors for two incretins, the hormones the gut releases after a meal. It is sold under two brand names that contain the same molecule: Mounjaro, labeled for type 2 diabetes, and Zepbound, labeled for weight management and sleep apnea [1][2].

The drug is given as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection once a week. A C20 fatty acid chain is attached to the peptide so it binds to albumin, the main protein in blood, which slows its clearance and stretches its action across seven days [2]. It was the first medicine approved that activates both the GIP and the GLP-1 receptor in a single molecule.

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) and GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) are released by the intestine when food arrives. Both prompt the pancreas to release insulin, but only when blood sugar is elevated, which is why the drug lowers glucose without causing low blood sugar on its own. Tirzepatide also suppresses glucagon, the hormone that raises blood sugar between meals [2].

The weight effect comes mainly through appetite. Receptors for both hormones sit in brain regions that control hunger, and in animal studies tirzepatide reaches and activates neurons there. People taking it eat fewer calories, and the label notes that more of the weight lost is fat than lean tissue [2]. GLP-1 activity also slows how quickly the stomach empties, which adds to fullness and explains much of the nausea early in treatment.

Yes. The FDA has approved tirzepatide under two brand names and for four uses. Mounjaro carries the diabetes and cardiovascular indications, and Zepbound carries the weight and sleep apnea indications [1][2].

items.text: Mounjaro approved to improve blood sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes [1].
Zepbound approved for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition [4].

Zepbound cleared for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea when obesity is present, making it the first drug for that condition [5]. The same month, the FDA confirmed the tirzepatide shortage was over [7].
Mounjaro label extended to children 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes [1].
Mounjaro approved to lower the risk of heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death for people with type 2 diabetes whose cardiovascular risk is high [1].

blocks.text: While the drug was in shortage, compounding pharmacies were allowed to make copies. After the FDA declared the shortage resolved, its enforcement grace periods ended in March 2025, and an April 2026 update notes that tirzepatide sits on neither the shortage list nor the bulk list outsourcing facilities can draw from [7]. Products sold online as research tirzepatide are not reviewed by the FDA for purity or dose.

As Zepbound, it is prescribed alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity for adults with a body mass index of 30 or more, or 27 or more with a condition such as high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes. It is also prescribed for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity [2]. As Mounjaro, it is prescribed to improve blood sugar in type 2 diabetes and to reduce major cardiovascular events in high-risk adults with that disease [1].

blocks.text: In SURMOUNT-1, about half of participants on the 10 mg dose and 57% on the 15 mg dose lost at least a fifth of their starting weight, compared with 3% on placebo [3]. The FDA has said the sleep apnea benefit most likely follows from the weight loss rather than a separate effect on the airway [5]. The cardiovascular trial compared tirzepatide with dulaglutide, an older GLP-1 drug already shown to protect the heart, rather than with placebo [6].

Most side effects involve the digestive tract and are most frequent while the dose is being stepped up. In the pooled weight trials, about 56% of people on tirzepatide reported a gastrointestinal effect, compared with 30% on placebo, and up to 4% stopped treatment because of one [2].

items: Nausea in 25 to 29% of people, depending on dose, compared with 8% on placebo [2].
Diarrhea in 19 to 23%, constipation in 11 to 17%, and vomiting in 8 to 13% [2].
Injection site reactions, tiredness, burping, heartburn, and hair loss in roughly 4 to 8% [2].
Less common but serious: pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, kidney injury from dehydration, serious allergic reactions, and low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas [1][2].

blocks.text: Both labels carry a boxed warning because tirzepatide caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rats. Whether this happens in people is unknown, and the drug is not used in anyone who has had medullary thyroid cancer, or whose relatives have had it, or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 [1][2]. The labels also warn about stomach contents entering the lungs during anesthesia, since slower stomach emptying can leave food behind before a procedure.

sections.heading: What is the difference between Mounjaro and Zepbound?

blocks.text: There is no chemical difference. Both contain tirzepatide in the same strengths, from 2.5 mg to 15 mg per weekly dose [1][2]. The labels differ in who they are approved for, which shapes insurance coverage: Mounjaro for people with type 2 diabetes, Zepbound for weight management and sleep apnea whether or not diabetes is present. Each label advises against combining tirzepatide with any other GLP-1 drug [2].

name: Tripeptide-10 citrulline
evidenceNote: The case for it rests on the maker's lab tests of collagen fibers and one small randomized skin study of 24 volunteers, six per group, measuring wrinkle depth with an imaging device. There are no larger or independent controlled trials.
summary: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a skincare peptide built to mimic decorin, a protein that keeps collagen fibers orderly. Evidence is lab work and one small study.
keyTakeaway: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a short synthetic peptide used in anti-aging creams and serums, sold to formulators as Decorinyl. Despite the name, it is four amino acids long. It was designed to copy the part of decorin, a skin protein, that binds collagen and keeps its fibers even. In the developer's lab tests it made collagen fibers thinner and more uniform. One randomized study of 24 volunteers reported smoother skin surface measurements after 20 to 60 days. As a cosmetic ingredient it needs no FDA approval, and whether enough of it passes the skin barrier to reach collagen in the dermis has not been shown.

blocks.text: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a synthetic peptide made for skincare. Its name is an INCI name, the standardized label used on cosmetic ingredient lists, and it is a little misleading: the molecule is actually a tetrapeptide, a chain of four amino acids, one of which is citrulline [1]. It was first described in a 2008 paper by its developers [1] and is supplied to brands under the trade name Decorinyl [3].

Reviews of cosmetic peptides group it with the signal peptides, ingredients meant to send messages to skin cells or tissue rather than simply moisturize [3]. A 2026 safety paper places it among the matrikines, peptides that mimic fragments of the skin's own structural proteins [5].

Collagen gives the dermis (the thick layer under the skin's surface) its strength, but how well collagen works depends partly on how its fibers are arranged. Decorin, a protein that coats collagen fibrils, helps control their assembly and prevents them from clumping into irregular bundles. As skin ages, functional decorin declines, and collagen fibers become disorganized, which reduces the skin's tensile strength [1].

The developers identified two short sequences in decorin that bind collagen, engineered variants with stronger binding, and screened a library of candidates in a test of collagen fiber formation. Tripeptide-10 citrulline performed best. In those lab experiments it behaved like decorin, regulating fiber formation and making the fibers thinner and more uniform in diameter [1]. The aim, in the authors' framing, was collagen quality rather than quantity [1].

No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetic products other than color additives can be sold without FDA approval [4]. A product's claims matter, though: if a label says it changes the structure or function of the body, the FDA can treat it as a drug, even if it is marketed as a cosmetic [4].

Independent safety review is also limited. A 2026 overview of cosmetic peptide safety listed the peptides assessed by the Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel, the main US body that evaluates cosmetic ingredients, and tripeptide-10 citrulline was not among them [5].

sections.heading: What is tripeptide-10 citrulline used for?

blocks.text: It appears in anti-aging skincare marketed for firmness, suppleness and fine lines. The original paper pitched it as a way to improve skin suppleness through better cohesion of collagen fibers [1]. It is often formulated alongside other peptides, such as acetyl hexapeptide-3, and one of the few human studies tested exactly that pairing [2].

The foundation is the 2008 paper from its developers, which reported only lab results on collagen fiber formation, without any testing on human skin [1]. Lab effects on isolated collagen do not show that a cream reaches the dermis, where collagen lives.

The only controlled human study found was published in 2017. Twenty-four healthy volunteers were randomized to four groups of six: tripeptide-10 citrulline alone, acetyl hexapeptide-3 alone, the two combined, or neither, for 60 days. Skin surface roughness was measured with an imaging device, and water loss through the skin with a second instrument. The groups using tripeptide-10 citrulline showed some significant differences in roughness measures at 20 and 60 days, and the authors described this as clinical evidence of anti-wrinkle activity, while noting that the combination's mechanism was unclear [2].

rows: Lab tests of collagen fiber formation
24 volunteers randomized to 4 groups for 60 days
Some improvements in skin roughness measures [2]

blocks.text: Six people per group is too few to draw firm conclusions, and the study measured skin surface texture rather than wrinkles as graded by experts or by users. A broader problem applies to all cosmetic peptides: their size and water-loving chemistry make it hard to cross the skin's outer barrier. Reviews put the ideal size for skin penetration under about 500 daltons, while this peptide weighs roughly 531 [3].

No specific adverse effects have been reported in the published studies of tripeptide-10 citrulline, but those studies were small and short [1][2]. As with any skincare ingredient, irritation or allergic reactions are possible, often from other components of the formula. Because it has not been through a Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessment, there is no independent panel finding on safe concentrations [5].

Most of the cosmetic peptides that panel has reviewed were judged safe as currently used. The 2026 framework argues for adding computer-based screening to the standard checks on irritation, skin sensitization and whole-body toxicity when new peptides are assessed [5].

name: Triptorelin
evidenceNote: Triptorelin was approved in 2000 for advanced prostate cancer on a randomized trial against leuprolide, and in 2017 for central precocious puberty on a single-arm trial measuring hormone suppression. Both uses rest on hormone endpoints that track the disease closely.
summary: Triptorelin is a lab-made GnRH hormone that, given continuously, shuts down testosterone and estrogen. Approved for advanced prostate cancer and early puberty.
keyTakeaway: Triptorelin is a 10-amino-acid copy of the brain hormone GnRH, built to be far more potent than the natural version. Given as a slow-release injection, it first triggers a brief hormone surge, then switches off the pituitary signals that drive the testes and ovaries. The FDA approved it as Trelstar for advanced prostate cancer in 2000 and as Triptodur for central precocious puberty in children 2 and older in 2017. In its pivotal prostate trial, 96.2% of men stayed at castrate testosterone levels through nine months. Hot flashes are the most common effect. WADA bans it in male athletes.

blocks.text: Triptorelin is a synthetic decapeptide, a chain of ten amino acids, modeled on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) [1]. GnRH is released by the hypothalamus in the brain and tells the pituitary gland to make luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which in turn drive the testes and ovaries to make testosterone and estrogen.

Its sixth position holds D-tryptophan, a mirror-image form of an ordinary amino acid [1]. In lab tests, triptorelin was 100 times more active than natural GnRH at releasing LH from pituitary cells and 20 times better at occupying the receptor [1]. It is formulated as a pamoate salt in tiny microgranules that release the drug slowly from a muscle injection [1]. Verity Pharmaceuticals markets it as Trelstar for adults, and Azurity markets a pediatric product, Triptodur [3][4].

The body normally releases GnRH in short pulses. Triptorelin, released steadily from its depot, occupies the receptor without a break. At first that acts like a very strong pulse: LH, FSH, testosterone, and estradiol all surge [1]. In men with prostate cancer, testosterone rises above baseline in the first week and falls back by the end of the second [1].

With continuous exposure the pituitary stops responding. Usually within two to four weeks, LH and FSH output drops and the testes nearly stop making steroid hormones, bringing testosterone down to the level seen after surgical removal of the testes [1]. The effect is a reversible, drug-induced castration. Prostate cancer depends on testosterone to grow, which is why lowering it slows the disease. In children with early puberty, the same shutdown pauses sexual development and the rapid bone maturation that comes with it [2].

Yes. The FDA approved Trelstar on June 15, 2000, and Triptodur, an extended-release version for children, on June 29, 2017 [3][4]. Both are prescription drugs given by a healthcare provider [1][2]. In sport, the World Anti-Doping Agency lists triptorelin among the testosterone-stimulating peptides banned in male athletes, because its initial surge can raise testosterone [5].

Trelstar treats advanced prostate cancer [1]. It comes in three strengths, given as one injection into the buttock every 4, 12, or 24 weeks [1]. Triptodur treats central precocious puberty, puberty that starts too early because the brain's hormone signals switch on ahead of schedule, in children aged 2 and older; it is given once every 24 weeks and stopped at the age when puberty would normally begin [2].

blocks.text: The prostate trial found triptorelin brought testosterone down more slowly than leuprolide in the first month, but held it down just as well after that [6]. Nine-month survival was higher on triptorelin (97.0% versus 90.5%), a secondary finding the trial was not designed to prove [6]. The pediatric trial had no comparison group and judged success by hormone levels and growth markers rather than adult height [2].
Most side effects come from the hormone changes themselves. In the monthly-dose prostate trial, the most frequent treatment-related reactions were [1]:

items: Hot flashes: 58.6% [1]
Bone and skeletal pain: 12.1% [1]
Erectile dysfunction: 7.1% [1]
Headache: 5.0% [1]
Injection site pain and high blood pressure: 3.6% each [1]

blocks.text: The early testosterone surge can briefly worsen prostate cancer symptoms, including bone pain, urinary blockage, and, rarely, spinal cord compression with leg weakness, so men with spinal metastases are watched closely in the first weeks [1]. Long-term suppression can raise blood sugar and cholesterol, and GnRH agonists have been linked to a small increase in heart attack, stroke, and sudden cardiac death in men [1]. Convulsions, serious skin reactions, and allergic reactions have also been reported [1].

In children, the most common reactions in the Triptodur trial were colds and sore throats, headache (13.6%), and injection site reactions [2]. Vaginal bleeding was reported in 7.7% of girls, and the label notes that sex hormones rise briefly at the start of treatment before falling [2]. The label also warns of mood changes such as irritability and aggression, seizures, and pseudotumor cerebri, a rise in pressure around the brain that causes headache and vision problems [2].

class: Synthetic analog of the IGF-1 tripeptide GPE
evidenceNote: Rated on the earlier programs only. Each had a randomized placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, but the Fragile X study ran just 28 days and the brain injury results were never posted or published, and neither use advanced.
summary: Before trofinetide was approved for Rett syndrome, it was tested for Fragile X syndrome and brain injury. Those uses never went past phase 2.
keyTakeaway: Trofinetide, coded NNZ-2566 during development, is a small oral and intravenous peptide based on GPE, a three-amino-acid fragment of the growth factor IGF-1. It is FDA-approved as Daybue for Rett syndrome, but this entry covers its earlier programs. A 28-day randomized trial in 72 males with Fragile X syndrome reported a signal at the higher dose that was never confirmed in a larger trial. Phase 2 studies in moderate to severe brain injury and in concussion ended without posted results, and one was terminated early. Trofinetide is not approved for either condition, and no new trial in them is registered.

sections.heading: What is the trofinetide predecessor research?

blocks.text: Trofinetide is a synthetic tripeptide developed by Neuren Pharmaceuticals and first disclosed in 2000. It is a version of glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE), a natural three-amino-acid fragment cut from insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), with one added methyl group [7]. During development it carried the code NNZ-2566 [3].

Trofinetide is now an approved medicine for Rett syndrome, sold as Daybue by Acadia Pharmaceuticals [1]. Alongside its early Rett studies, Neuren also tested it in two other areas: traumatic brain injury, including concussion, and Fragile X syndrome, an inherited condition that causes intellectual disability and behavioral symptoms [3][4]. This entry covers those other programs. The approved Rett syndrome use has its own entry.

No one has pinned down exactly how it works. Even the approved Daybue label states that the way trofinetide helps people with Rett syndrome is unknown [1]. The working theory is that it improves the shape of nerve cells and how synapses, the junctions between neurons, function [7].

That broad idea is why one compound was tried in such different settings: two genetic conditions that disturb how the brain's wiring develops, and the injured adult brain. A shared theory is not shared evidence, though, and each condition needed its own trials.
For Rett syndrome, yes. The FDA approved Daybue on March 10, 2023, for adults and children aged 2 and older with Rett syndrome, after a 187-patient phase 3 trial called LAVENDER [8][1][6].

For Fragile X syndrome and traumatic brain injury, no. Neither use appears in the approved label, which covers Rett syndrome only [1]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no trofinetide study in either condition that started after 2014, so neither program is active today [9].

The Fragile X trial is the only one of the earlier programs with published results. It randomly assigned 72 adolescent and adult males to trofinetide at 35 or 70 mg/kg twice daily, or to a strawberry-flavored placebo, for 28 days [2][3]. Its main purpose was safety, and both doses were well tolerated. The higher dose met prespecified success criteria on a combined model across several symptom areas, and three Fragile X specific measures improved from baseline, which the authors described as a preliminary sign of efficacy [2].

That result came with real limits. Four weeks is short for a lifelong developmental condition, the trial used a new analysis model, and the authors themselves put the chance of a false positive at about 4.5 percent [2]. No confirmatory trial followed.

The brain injury work started earlier. INTREPID2566 was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation phase 2 trial in which 261 patients with traumatic brain injury received the drug as an intravenous infusion; its primary outcome was safety, measured as adverse events through three months [4]. A second phase 2 trial in adolescents and adults with concussion, using an oral solution, was terminated after enrolling 32 people [5]. Neither registry entry has posted results, and no later trials in brain injury are registered [9].
In short, the predecessor programs showed that trofinetide was tolerable and gave one faint efficacy signal in Fragile X, but never produced the confirmatory evidence an approval requires.

sections.heading: How do these programs differ from the approved Rett syndrome use?

blocks.text: The gap is the size and design of the evidence. In Rett syndrome, the LAVENDER phase 3 trial randomly assigned 187 girls and young women to trofinetide or placebo for 12 weeks and met both of its main goals, a caregiver behavior questionnaire and a clinician's overall rating of improvement [6]. That trial, plus earlier phase 2 work, is what the 2023 approval rests on [8].

Nothing comparable exists for Fragile X syndrome or brain injury. The same side effects would be expected in any use: in LAVENDER, diarrhea affected 80.6 percent of people on trofinetide against 19.1 percent on placebo, and the label also warns about vomiting and weight loss [6][1]. Results in one disorder do not carry over to another, so the approval says nothing about whether trofinetide helps people with Fragile X syndrome or recovering from a brain injury.

summary: The first approved drug for Rett syndrome, an oral analog of a tiny piece of IGF-1. FDA-approved since 2023; diarrhea is very common.
keyTakeaway: Trofinetide is a synthetic version of glycine-proline-glutamate, a three amino acid fragment of the growth factor IGF-1, taken by mouth twice a day. In March 2023 the FDA approved it as Daybue, the first treatment for Rett syndrome, for patients aged 2 and up. In the 12-week LAVENDER trial it improved caregiver and clinician ratings of Rett symptoms more than placebo, though the effects were small to moderate. Diarrhea affected about 82% of treated patients. The EU authorised it, as Daybu, in August 2026 for ages 5 and older.
