blocks.text: Trofinetide is a drug for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic disorder of brain development [1] that affects communication, walking, hand use, attention, breathing, and seizure control [5]. Chemically it is a lab-made copy, slightly altered, of GPE (glycine, proline, glutamate), the three amino acids that open the chain of the growth factor IGF-1 [1].

It is sold in the United States by Acadia Pharmaceuticals as Daybue, an oral solution, and as Daybue STIX, a powder mixed into liquid [2][3]. It is swallowed or given through a gastrostomy (stomach) tube twice a day, with the dose set by body weight [2]. In the European Union the same drug is authorised under the name Daybu [8].

The honest answer is that no one knows exactly. The FDA label states plainly that the way trofinetide produces its effects in Rett syndrome is unknown [2]. It was chosen because it is derived from IGF-1 [1], but how that origin turns into changes in symptoms has not been worked out.

It is given by mouth or feeding tube, not by injection [2]. Its effect showed a dose relationship in early testing: in the pediatric phase 2 trial, only the highest dose clearly beat placebo, and improvement tracked with how much drug reached the blood [4].

That phase 2 study enrolled 82 girls aged 5 to 15, who received placebo or one of three doses for six weeks [4]. All three doses were well tolerated, and the top dose of 200 mg/kg twice a day improved the caregiver questionnaire, a clinician rating of key concerns, and the global impression score compared with placebo [4]. Those results set up the larger LAVENDER trial [5].

Yes. The FDA approved Daybue on March 10, 2023, as a new molecular entity with priority review and orphan drug status [3]. It is labeled for Rett syndrome in adults and children aged 2 years and older [2]. Label updates followed in 2024, 2025, and 2026, including a change backed by new clinical data in March 2026 [3].

blocks.text: Trofinetide has one labeled use: Rett syndrome [2]. The trials measured changes in core symptoms such as behavior, communication, and overall clinical picture [1]. The EU authorisation is narrower in age, covering the neurobehavioural symptoms of Rett syndrome in patients aged 5 and older [8].

Approval rested on LAVENDER, a 12-week trial in 187 girls and women aged 5 to 20 who were randomly assigned to trofinetide or placebo [1][5]. Both main measures favored the drug. On the Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire, a caregiver-rated scale, scores fell by 4.9 points against 1.7 on placebo, and clinicians' global ratings were modestly better too [1]. The effect sizes were small to moderate (0.37 to 0.47) [1]. On a key secondary measure of communication and social skills, scores held steady with trofinetide (down 0.1) while they slipped by 1.1 on placebo [1].

rows: Change in Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire (lower is better)
Clinical Global Impression, Improvement (lower is better)
Change in communication score (higher is better)

blocks.text: Longer follow-up is uncontrolled. In LILAC, 154 participants continued for 40 weeks, and caregiver scores kept improving [6]. In LILAC-2, 77 participants stayed on for up to 32 more months; scores improved by 11.8 points from the original baseline at week 104, and most caregivers interviewed were satisfied [7]. Without a placebo group, these extensions cannot separate drug effect from expectation or natural change.

Diarrhea is by far the most common side effect, affecting 82% of patients on the drug against 20% on placebo in the label's trial data, and vomiting affected 29% against 12% [2]. The label tells families to stop laxatives before starting and to pause, lower, or stop the drug if diarrhea becomes severe or dehydration is suspected [2]. In the 40-week extension, diarrhea was the leading reason people stopped, in 21.4% of participants [6].

The other two warnings are weight loss, which calls for regular weight checks, and vomiting, which has led to aspiration and aspiration pneumonia in some patients [2]. Less common effects included fever, seizures, anxiety, reduced appetite, and fatigue [2]. People with moderate kidney impairment receive lower doses, and the drug is not recommended in severe kidney impairment [2].

name: Vancomycin
evidenceNote: Vancomycin has been FDA-approved since 1958 and is a long-standing standard treatment for serious infections caused by resistant gram-positive bacteria. Its labels are backed by nearly seven decades of clinical use and trials.
summary: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic, FDA-approved since 1958, given by vein for serious MRSA-type infections and by mouth for C. difficile diarrhea.
keyTakeaway: Vancomycin is an antibiotic made by a soil bacterium found in a sample sent from Borneo in 1952, approved by FDA in 1958. It kills gram-positive bacteria, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), by blocking how they build their cell walls. Given by vein it treats bloodstream, heart valve, bone, skin and lung infections; taken by mouth it stays in the gut and treats C. difficile diarrhea. Kidney injury and hearing damage are the main risks, so blood levels are monitored. Resistant enterococci appeared in the 1980s.

blocks.text: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic, a large molecule built from a ring of amino acids decorated with sugars. It is produced by the soil bacterium Amycolatopsis orientalis [1]. It works against gram-positive bacteria, the group that includes staphylococci, streptococci, enterococci and clostridia, and it has no activity against gram-negative bacteria, mycobacteria or fungi [1].

It comes in two very different forms. Given into a vein, it treats infections throughout the body. Swallowed, it is barely absorbed from the gut, so it acts only inside the intestine; that is useful for gut infections and useless for anything else [2][3].

In the early 1950s, Eli Lilly was hunting for antibiotics that could kill penicillin-resistant staphylococci. In 1952 a missionary in Borneo mailed a soil sample to a Lilly chemist, and a microbe in it produced a compound that killed most gram-positive bacteria and resisted attempts to breed resistance in the lab. Early preparations were brown with impurities, earning the nickname Mississippi mud, and the purified drug was named vancomycin, from the word vanquish [3].

With no good alternative for resistant staph, FDA approved it in 1958. Use then faded as methicillin and early cephalosporins arrived, and vancomycin was held back for people with serious penicillin allergy or resistant infections [3]. It returned in force from the 1980s, driven by the spread of MRSA and by its role in treating colitis caused by C. difficile; use rose more than a thousandfold over two decades [3].

blocks.text: Bacteria wrap themselves in a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, a mesh of sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides. Vancomycin latches onto the D-alanyl-D-alanine tip of the growing peptide chains, which blocks the enzymes that would link them into the wall [3]. Without a sound wall, the bacterium breaks apart; the label describes its killing action as mainly inhibition of cell wall building, with added effects on membrane permeability and RNA synthesis [1].

Resistance comes from changing that target. Resistant enterococci swap the D-alanyl-D-alanine ending for D-alanyl-D-lactate or D-alanyl-D-serine, which vancomycin binds poorly [3]. Because its antibacterial effect tracks drug exposure over time, and because the kidneys clear about 75% of a dose in the first 24 hours, dosing is adjusted to kidney function and checked with blood levels [1].

Yes. Vancomycin was first approved in the US in 1958 and is now made by many manufacturers as injections, premixed bags and oral products [1][3]. The injectable form carries indications for serious infections, and oral capsules sold as Vancocin carry separate gut indications [1][2].

Both labels include FDA's standard antibiotic stewardship language: vancomycin should be used only for infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria, to slow the spread of resistance [1][2].
The intravenous form is approved in adults and children for the following infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria [1]:

items: Septicemia, a bloodstream infection [1]
Infective endocarditis, infection of the heart valves [1]
Skin and skin structure infections [1]
Bone infections [1]
Lower respiratory tract infections, such as pneumonia [1]

blocks.text: Oral vancomycin is approved for diarrhea caused by Clostridioides difficile and for staphylococcal enterocolitis, an intestinal infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant strains. The label notes that injecting it does not treat these gut infections, and swallowing it does not treat infections elsewhere [2].

For MRSA bloodstream infections, vancomycin has long served as the comparator that newer drugs are measured against. In a 2006 trial of 246 patients with S. aureus bacteremia, daptomycin was tested against standard therapy of vancomycin or an anti-staph penicillin, each with low-dose gentamicin, and success rates were similar at 44% and 42% [4].

The most common adverse reactions to the injection are infusion reactions, acute kidney injury, hearing loss and low white blood cell counts, along with rare anaphylaxis [1]. Infusing it too fast can cause vancomycin infusion reaction, formerly called red man syndrome: itching and flushing of the face, neck and upper body, and sometimes low blood pressure. It is therefore given over 60 minutes or longer [1].

Kidney injury is the risk most closely watched. It is more likely at high blood levels, with longer courses, in critically ill people, and alongside other drugs that strain the kidneys; the label specifically notes more acute kidney injury when it is combined with piperacillin-tazobactam [1]. Ototoxicity (ear damage) can show up as ringing, hearing loss or dizziness and may be permanent [1].

Rare but severe skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and DRESS, require stopping the drug. Like other antibiotics, intravenous vancomycin can itself trigger C. difficile diarrhea [1]. Oral vancomycin is better tolerated; in two phase 3 trials, the most common effects were nausea (17%), abdominal pain (15%) and low potassium (13%) [2].

name: Vasopressin
class: V1 and V2 vasopressin receptor agonist
evidenceNote: Vasostrict was FDA-approved in 2014 for vasodilatory shock, and its use has been tested in large randomized trials such as VASST (778 patients) and VANISH (409 patients), which shaped how it is used alongside norepinephrine.
summary: Vasopressin is the body's water-saving hormone, given by IV drip in intensive care when shock drags blood pressure down. FDA-approved as Vasostrict since 2014.
keyTakeaway: Vasopressin is a small peptide hormone that tells the kidneys to save water and, in larger amounts, narrows blood vessels. Its synthetic form, Vasostrict, gained FDA approval in 2014 for adults in vasodilatory shock (septic shock is the common example) whose pressure stays low after fluids and catecholamine drugs. It works through a different receptor than norepinephrine, so it can add pressure when that drug is not enough. In the VASST trial, adding it to norepinephrine did not lower 28-day mortality (35.4% vs 39.3%). Its main risks are reduced blood flow to the heart, gut, and fingers, and low sodium.

blocks.text: Vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone, is a small peptide hormone released by the pituitary gland. Its everyday job is to tell the kidneys to keep water when the body is running low. At higher concentrations, it also squeezes blood vessels and raises blood pressure. The drug form is synthetic 8-L-arginine vasopressin, identical to the human hormone [1].

As a medicine, it is an intensive care drug. Doctors give it as a continuous drip to people in shock whose blood pressure stays dangerously low after fluids and first-line drugs. It is sold as Vasostrict, made by Par, along with vasopressin injections from other manufacturers [1][2]. Related drugs built on the same hormone include desmopressin and terlipressin, and the experimental selepressin.

Vasopressin acts on two main receptor types. On the smooth muscle of blood vessels, it binds V1 receptors and sets off a calcium signal that makes the vessel wall contract, which raises blood pressure. In the kidney, it binds V2 receptors and makes the body reabsorb water [1].

rows: Water is kept rather than excreted (antidiuresis) [1]

blocks.text: In vasodilatory shock, most often caused by sepsis, blood vessels lose their tone and the usual catecholamine drugs such as norepinephrine become less effective. Vasopressin raises pressure through a separate pathway, so it can work alongside those drugs. Its action is brief: the half-life at shock doses is 10 minutes or less, it reaches a steady level about 30 minutes into an infusion, and only about 6% leaves the body unchanged in urine [1]. Pregnancy changes this: the placenta releases an enzyme that breaks vasopressin down, so by the third trimester the body clears it about four times faster than usual, returning to normal within two weeks of delivery [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Vasostrict in April 2014 [2]. Its label limits it to adults with vasodilatory shock whose blood pressure is still too low after fluid resuscitation and catecholamines [1]. The label's own clinical studies section is brief, citing rises in blood pressure across seven studies in septic shock and eight in shock after heart surgery [1].

items.text: VASST trial reports no mortality reduction from adding vasopressin to norepinephrine in septic shock [3].
FDA approves Vasostrict (NDA 204485) for vasodilatory shock [2].
VANISH trial finds early vasopressin does not improve kidney failure-free days compared with norepinephrine [4].

blocks.text: Vasopressin is given to adults whose shock comes from widened blood vessels, for example from sepsis or after heart surgery, when blood pressure stays low despite fluids and catecholamine vasopressors [1]. It is usually added to norepinephrine rather than given first, and the trials explain why.

rows: 28-day mortality 35.4% with vasopressin vs 39.3% with more norepinephrine, not significant [3]
Septic shock, vasopressin started within 6 hours
No difference in kidney failure-free days or mortality; fewer patients needed dialysis (25.4% vs 35.3%) [4]

blocks.text: In VASST, people with less severe shock did better on vasopressin (26.5% vs 35.7% mortality), but the trial was not designed to prove a subgroup effect, and the test for a difference between strata was not significant [3]. VANISH tested whether vasopressin could replace norepinephrine as the first drug and found it did not improve the main kidney outcome, though the confidence interval left room for a benefit [4]. The practical result is that vasopressin is mostly used to support blood pressure and lower catecholamine doses, not as a drug proven to improve survival.
Because vasopressin narrows blood vessels, its main risks come from too little blood reaching organs. The label lists these as the most common adverse reactions [1]:

items: Reduced cardiac output and slow heart rate (bradycardia) [1]
Fast or irregular heart rhythms, including atrial fibrillation [1]
Ischemia (loss of blood flow) in the heart, gut, skin, fingers, and toes [1]
Low blood sodium (hyponatremia) [1]

blocks.text: The label also warns that it can worsen heart function, and that after the drip stops some patients develop temporary diabetes insipidus, passing large amounts of dilute urine with rising sodium, so fluids and electrolytes are monitored [1]. It is contraindicated in people allergic to vasopressin, and the multiple-dose vial also in those allergic to its preservative chlorobutanol [1]. In VASST, rates of serious adverse events were about 10% in both groups [3].

name: Vosoritide
evidenceNote: Granted accelerated FDA approval in 2021 after a 52-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in 121 children showed faster growth. Whether that faster growth adds up to a taller adult height is still being confirmed, and the FDA is reviewing that long-term data.
summary: A daily injection that speeds bone growth in children with achondroplasia, the most common form of dwarfism, under accelerated approval since 2021.
keyTakeaway: Vosoritide is a modified version of C-type natriuretic peptide, a natural signal that tells growth plates to keep building bone. The FDA gave it accelerated approval in 2021, sold as Voxzogo, to increase height growth in children with achondroplasia whose growth plates are still open. In the pivotal trial, children grew about 1.6 cm a year faster than on placebo. Its effect on final adult height is not yet established; a filing for full approval is under FDA review, with a decision due by February 2027.

atGlance.value: Accelerated approval in 2021 as Voxzogo; full approval under review

atGlance.value: Activates the NPR-B receptor in growth plate cartilage, offsetting the overactive FGFR3 signal that stunts bone growth

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Children with achondroplasia whose growth plates are still open

blocks.text: Vosoritide is a lab-made version of C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP), one of the small signaling molecules the body uses to control how fast the long bones grow [1]. It is sold by BioMarin as Voxzogo, a daily injection for children with achondroplasia [1].

Achondroplasia is an inherited condition that causes short stature with shortened limbs. It results from a gain-of-function change in the FGFR3 gene that slows the growth plates, the cartilage zones near the ends of bones where lengthening happens [1]. When the pivotal trial began, no treatment had been shown to work for the condition [2].

In achondroplasia, the FGFR3 receptor is stuck in a more active state. Inside cartilage cells it pushes down on a growth pathway called MAPK, so the cells that should multiply and mature into new bone do so too slowly [1].

Vosoritide binds a different receptor on the same cells, natriuretic peptide receptor B (NPR-B). That signal cuts into the MAPK pathway at a step called RAF-1 and blocks the brake that FGFR3 applies, so the cartilage cells resume dividing and maturing [1]. In mouse models of the condition, it widened the growth plates and partly or fully corrected the short-limbed shape [1].

Natural CNP is broken down almost as soon as it is released. Vosoritide is a 39-amino-acid version of the human peptide with two extra amino acids added at one end, which make it resistant to neutral endopeptidase, the enzyme that degrades CNP [1]. Even so, its half-life is only about 21 to 28 minutes, so the effect relies on a daily dose [1]. It only helps while growth plates are open, and the label calls for stopping once there is no further growth potential [1].

Yes, under accelerated approval. The FDA first approved it in 2021 for children with achondroplasia and open growth plates, based on faster yearly growth [1]. Accelerated approval means the agency accepted a measure that is reasonably likely to predict benefit, here growth speed, while confirmatory evidence is gathered [1]. The label covers children of any age whose growth plates are open, and includes safety data from infants as young as four months [1].

In July 2026 the FDA accepted BioMarin's application to convert this to full approval, based on long-term follow-up studies that include adult height outcomes, and set a decision date of February 28, 2027 [3]. Separately, a phase 3 trial in 80 children with hypochondroplasia, a milder condition also caused by FGFR3 changes, met its main goal in May 2026, and the company planned to file for that use [4]. Neither use beyond achondroplasia is approved.

items.text: Phase 3 trial enrolls 121 children aged 5 to 14 [2]
FDA grants accelerated approval for achondroplasia [1]
Positive phase 3 results reported in hypochondroplasia [4]
FDA accepts filing for full approval; decision due February 28, 2027 [3]

blocks.text: Doctors prescribe vosoritide so that children with achondroplasia gain more height while their growth plates remain open [1]. Caregivers usually give the injection at home each day, with the amount set by the child's weight [1].

The pivotal trial randomized 121 children aged 5 to 14 with genetically confirmed achondroplasia to vosoritide or placebo for 52 weeks. Each child's growth rate had been measured for at least six months beforehand, so the trial could compare speed before and after [1][2].

The faster growth held up over two years of open-label follow-up [1]. The trial authors noted that it was not yet known whether final adult height would increase or what long-term treatment might cost in harms [2]. Body proportions did not change over the first year, so the drug adds length without, so far, altering the limb-to-trunk pattern of the condition [1].

Reactions at the injection site are nearly universal and very frequent. In the main trial, 85% of children on vosoritide had them, at a rate of about 120 events per child per year compared with 29 on placebo injections [1]. Two children stopped because of pain and anxiety around the injections [1].

items: Injection site swelling: 62% versus 36% on placebo [1]
Vomiting: 27% versus 20% [1]
Joint pain: 15% versus 7% [1]
Low blood pressure episodes: 13% versus 5% [1]
Dizziness: 10% versus 3% [1]

blocks.text: Vosoritide can briefly lower blood pressure, usually about half an hour after a dose and lasting about half an hour [1]. The label asks that children be well fed and hydrated before each injection, and children with significant heart or vessel disease were not studied [1]. Excess hair growth has been reported since approval [1].

name: Ziconotide
class: N-type calcium channel blocker (cone snail conotoxin)
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in December 2004 on three double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in 457 patients with severe chronic pain. The benefit in the slow-dosing trial that set today's schedule was modest.
summary: A synthetic cone snail venom peptide infused into the spinal fluid for severe chronic pain when other treatments fail. Approved in 2004 as Prialt.
keyTakeaway: Ziconotide is a synthetic copy of a 25-amino-acid toxin from the fish-hunting cone snail Conus magus. It blocks N-type calcium channels on pain nerves in the spinal cord, and it is not an opioid. Approved as Prialt in 2004, it is pumped directly into the spinal fluid for severe chronic pain in people who cannot use or no longer respond to other options. In the slow-titration trial, pain fell 12% against 5% on placebo after three weeks. Its label's boxed warning covers serious mental and neurological effects.

blocks.text: Ziconotide is a synthetic version of a conopeptide, a small toxin found in the venom of Conus magus, a marine cone snail that hunts fish [1]. It is a chain of 25 amino acids held in shape by three internal bridges [1]. It is the active ingredient in Prialt, now marketed by Esteve [4].

It is a painkiller, but neither an opioid nor an anti-inflammatory drug [1]. It cannot be swallowed or given into a vein for this use. Instead it is delivered intrathecally, meaning into the fluid around the spinal cord, by a programmable pump implanted under the skin or worn outside the body [1].

Under the early code name SNX-111, ziconotide was tested in people whose pain had not responded to high doses of opioids [2]. A trial run from 1996 to 1998 at 32 centres in the United States, Australia, and the Netherlands treated patients with cancer or AIDS and found large reductions in pain, but the fast dose increases it used caused frequent side effects [1][2]. A later trial used a much slower schedule and lower doses and was better tolerated [3].

items.text: Randomized trial in 111 people with cancer or AIDS pain [2]
FDA approves Prialt [4]
Slow-titration trial in 220 adults with severe chronic pain published [3]
Latest revision of the US prescribing information [4]

blocks.text: Pain signals from the body travel along sensory nerve fibres called A-delta and C fibres into the back of the spinal cord, where they hand the message to the next nerve. Ziconotide binds N-type calcium channels on the endings of these pain fibres, in the outer layers of the spinal cord's dorsal horn [1]. Animal studies suggest that blocking those channels stops the release of the chemical messengers that pass the signal along [1].

Because it works on a different target from opioids, it does not cause the breathing suppression seen with opioid overdose; in overdoses the main effects were dizziness, confusion, sedation, and low blood pressure [1]. For the same reason it cannot ease opioid withdrawal, so opioids are tapered gradually rather than stopped when someone switches [1]. In the spinal fluid it has a half-life of about 4.6 hours [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Prialt on December 28, 2004, and it remains available by prescription [4]. The label limits it to severe, long-term pain where delivery into the spinal fluid is justified and where other treatments, such as painkillers by mouth, add-on drugs, or morphine into the spine, have failed or caused intolerable effects [1].

It must be given by, or under the direction of, a physician experienced in intrathecal delivery [1]. The label carries a boxed warning that severe psychiatric symptoms and neurological impairment can occur, and it is not used in anyone with a history of psychosis [1].

It is prescribed for severe, long-lasting pain that has not responded to other approaches, usually in people already on high doses of opioids [1][2]. The approval rests on three placebo-controlled trials in 457 patients that tested a fast and a slow dosing schedule; the fast schedule caused substantially more side effects [1].

rows: 111 adults with cancer or AIDS pain
Pain score improved 53.1% vs 18.1% on placebo; 50% vs 17.5% responded
Pain score improved 12% vs 5% on placebo at week 3 (label analysis)

blocks.text: The slow-titration trial is the one that matches the current label schedule. Patients started at 2.4 mcg a day with small increases two or three times a week, and ended on an average of 6.9 mcg a day after three weeks [1]. Starting pain averaged 81 on a 100 mm scale [1]. The share of people whose pain improved by at least 30% was 16% on ziconotide and 12% on placebo, and use of opioids outside the spine fell by 24% and 17% [1]. The published report of the same trial gave improvements of 14.7% and 7.2% [3].

Side effects are common and mostly involve the brain. Across the trials, the most frequent were dizziness, nausea, confusion, and nystagmus (involuntary eye movements), each in at least a quarter of patients [1]. In the slow-titration trial, dizziness affected 46% against 13% on placebo, nausea 40% against 29%, and confusion 15% against 5% [1].

items: Hallucinations in 12% and paranoid reactions in 3% of treated patients [1]
Confusion in 33%, memory problems in 22%, and speech difficulty in 14% [1]
More suicidal thoughts and attempts than with placebo in controlled trials [1]
Meningitis in 3%, mostly in patients using external pumps and catheters [1]
Raised creatine kinase, a muscle enzyme, in 40% [1]
Episodes of reduced consciousness or unresponsiveness in 2% [1]

blocks.text: Confusion was more common in people aged 65 and older, 42% against 29% in younger patients [1]. Because of the effects on alertness, the label cautions against driving or operating machinery during treatment [1]. The cognitive effects generally reverse within two weeks of stopping the drug, and the drug can be stopped abruptly without withdrawal effects [1].

name: Zilucoplan
evidenceNote: Zilucoplan has been FDA-approved since October 2023, based on the 174-patient phase 3 RAISE trial and supporting phase 2 and long-term extension data.
summary: Zilucoplan (Zilbrysq) is a daily self-injected peptide that blocks complement protein C5, approved in 2023 for antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis.
keyTakeaway: Zilucoplan is a ring-shaped synthetic peptide that blocks C5, a protein in the complement part of the immune system that damages the nerve-muscle junction in myasthenia gravis. In the 12-week RAISE trial, daily injections improved a daily-living symptom score by 4.39 points, against 2.30 on placebo. The FDA approved it as Zilbrysq in October 2023 for adults with generalized myasthenia gravis who test positive for acetylcholine receptor antibodies. It is the first self-injected C5 inhibitor, and like every drug in its class it carries a boxed warning for meningococcal infection and requires vaccination first.

atGlance.value: Binds complement protein C5 and stops it forming the membrane attack complex

blocks.text: Zilucoplan is a prescription drug for myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition where the immune system targets the junction at which nerves signal muscles, causing weakness that worsens with use. It is made by UCB and sold as Zilbrysq [1].

Chemically, zilucoplan is a macrocyclic peptide: a chain of 15 amino acids, including several unnatural ones, closed into a ring and fitted with a fatty acid and a long polyethylene glycol tail [1]. The ring helps it grip its target tightly, and the tail lets it bind albumin and linger in the blood long enough for a once-daily shot. Most other drugs that block the same target are large antibodies given by intravenous infusion, so a small self-injected peptide is a different way of delivering the same idea.

In most people with generalized myasthenia gravis, antibodies bind to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle side of the junction. Those antibodies switch on complement, a cascade of blood proteins that normally helps kill bacteria. The end of that cascade builds the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), which punches holes in the muscle membrane and destroys receptors.

Zilucoplan binds C5, the protein that must be split to start building that complex, and blocks its cleavage into C5a and C5b [1]. In the phase 3 trial, complement activity was about 97.5% inhibited by the end of the first week. The label notes that the exact way this improves myasthenia gravis is not fully known, but it is presumed to come from less C5b-9 being deposited at the nerve-muscle junction [1].

Yes. The FDA approved Zilbrysq on October 17, 2023, for generalized myasthenia gravis in adults whose blood tests positive for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies [3]. The European Commission authorized it on December 1, 2023, as an add-on to standard therapy for the same group [4].

Because blocking C5 weakens defense against Neisseria meningitidis, the bacterium behind meningococcal meningitis, the drug is available in the United States only through a restricted program called the Zilbrysq REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy). Prescribers must enroll, and patients must be vaccinated against meningococcal disease at least two weeks before the first dose unless delaying treatment is the greater risk [1]. The European authorization adds a similar written vaccination declaration and a patient alert card [4].

Zilucoplan is prescribed for adults with generalized myasthenia gravis who carry acetylcholine receptor antibodies, the most common form of the disease. It has not been approved for people whose disease is driven by other antibodies or who have no detectable antibodies. The daily amount is set by body weight, in three fixed strengths [1].

RAISE enrolled people aged 18 to 74 at 75 sites in Europe, Japan, and North America, with moderate to severe disease [2]. Most were already on standard treatment: about 85% took cholinesterase inhibitors, 63% took steroids, and 51% took other immune-suppressing drugs, and these were kept stable during the trial [1]. The improvement on zilucoplan was therefore on top of existing therapy. Long-term safety and benefit are being followed in an open-label extension study [2].

In RAISE, adverse events of any kind were reported by 77% of people on zilucoplan and 70% on placebo, and serious events and serious infections were similar between groups [2]. The label lists the reactions that were more common on the drug [1].

items: Injection site reactions such as bruising or pain in 29%, against 16% on placebo [1].
Upper respiratory infections in 14%, against 7% [1].
Diarrhea in 11%, against 2% [1].
Raised pancreatic enzymes: lipase in 7% and amylase in 5%; pancreatitis and pancreatic cysts were later seen in about 3% of people in the extension studies [1].
Morphea, a patch of hardened skin, in 10 of 213 people in the extension studies, usually more than a year into treatment [1].

blocks.text: The most serious risk is meningococcal infection, which can become fatal quickly and can occur even in vaccinated people. That risk is the subject of the boxed warning, and the drug is not used in anyone with an unresolved meningococcal infection [1]. Baseline lipase and amylase tests are taken before starting. Animal data suggest it may harm a developing fetus [1].
